customer: A platform/SRE team at a mid-size SaaS company running 60-200 microservices on Kubernetes, with Datadog or Grafana (Loki/Prometheus/Tempo) plus PagerDuty/incident.io. They pay an "AI SRE" vendor (Resolve.ai, Traversal, Cleric, Neubird, Parity, Datadog Bits AI, incident.io AI SRE) either per-seat or per-investigation, on the order of $2k-$15k/month. What they are buying is a bot that, within ~3 minutes of a page firing, posts into the incident Slack channel: a ranked root-cause hypothesis, the specific evidence (log pattern, trace, metric break, suspect deploy), and a suggested mitigation. Concretely they pay to compress the "which of my 15 services is actually broken" phase of MTTR — the 10-40 minutes an on-call spends fanning out across dashboards. They also pay for the postmortem draft afterward. Note the secondary bill: the investigation itself burns metered observability queries (Datadog indexed-log search, Splunk SVC-hours), which is a real cost line the LLM tokens sit alongside.
why_repeated:
Four distinct repeat modes, and they have wildly different reuse surfaces — collapsing them is the main way this domain gets misanalysed.

R1 — Re-run inside the same live incident (~20% of production runs). The agent is re-triggered when a second alert joins the incident, when the on-call replies "no, check the write path not the cache", or when someone clicks re-investigate. 3-6 invocations per incident spread over 20-90 minutes. Each is a fresh webhook-triggered process, so it re-does the same evidence gathering over a window that has only extended by minutes.

R2 — Postmortem / review run, 1-5 days later (~5%). Identical incident window, now-immutable telemetry, different question ("write the timeline and the contributing factors"). Provider prefix cache is long dead by then.

R3 — A new firing of a recurring alert on the same service (~70%). This is the dominant mode and the honest one: same alert rule, same service, same runbook, same topology, but a different time window, so every byte of telemetry is new.

R4 — Vendor-side eval replay (huge volume, but it is the vendor's CI, not the customer's runs). A frozen corpus of 200-500 past incidents replayed nightly and on every prompt/model change. Artifacts are 100% identical; the thing that changed is the system prompt or the model id — i.e. the change is at the graph ROOT, which transitively invalidates every model operation and leaves only the tool operations reusable. This is the mode where a reuse store degenerates into exactly the VCR/fixture cache that eval harnesses already hand-roll.
run_cadence: Customer production: event-driven, not scheduled. A team with 100 services and reasonable alert hygiene pages 3-15 times/day; with the noise that actually exists in the field (~74% of alerts are reported as non-actionable noise), the agent is often wired to auto-triage every routed alert, giving 20-80 runs/day. Consecutive runs on the SAME alert rule + service pair are the meaningful repeat unit: for a chronically noisy alert that is minutes-to-hours apart; for a typical alert, days-to-weeks apart. R1 re-runs are minutes apart. R2 is days apart. Vendor eval replay (R4) is nightly plus per-PR, 200-500 runs per batch.

graph.description:
Shape is a wide-fan-out DAG bolted onto the front of a genuinely sequential tail. Depth 1-6 is: intake -> parallel stable-context fetch -> one planning model call -> a ~170-op embarrassingly parallel telemetry sweep -> per-suspect model analysis (fan-in ~14) -> cross-service correlation. Depth 7-14 is the adaptive verification loop: 4 rounds of (3-6 targeted queries chosen BY the model, then a reasoning call), which is a true chain — each round's tool arguments are a function of the previous round's model output, so nothing in it is predictable ahead of time and nothing in it is reusable unless the entire upstream is bit-identical. Depth 15 is the write-up.

Token convention below: for tool ops, typical_input_tokens is the serialized call arguments and typical_output_tokens is the serialized result that lands in context; for model ops, input is the full assembled context (system + tool defs + accumulated evidence) and output is generated tokens.

The critical structural fact: the ~170 telemetry ops sit at depth 4, upstream of every expensive model op. The artifacts that are stable across runs (runbooks, service catalog, dashboards) are read at depth 2 and are cheap; the artifacts that always change (logs, metrics, traces) are read at depth 4 and everything costly is downstream of them. So the stable/unstable split is exactly backwards from what a reuse layer wants.

Sizing reality-check: ~750k input tokens and ~30k output tokens of model work per investigation, i.e. roughly $2-4 uncached at Sonnet-class rates, which is consistent with vendors pricing investigations at single-digit dollars. Telemetry scale anchor: Microsoft's OpenRCA ships 335 failure cases with >68GB of logs/metrics/traces across 3 enterprise systems, i.e. hundreds of MB of raw telemetry per incident window — which is why every log op in this graph is an AGGREGATION query (pattern/count-by) rather than a raw dump. No competent implementation puts raw log lines in context; it puts a pattern table in context and then pulls 20-50 exemplar lines per interesting pattern.

layers.name: intake
layers.consumes: nothing (graph root)
layers.reads_artifacts: the alert payload + incident record from PagerDuty/incident.io: monitor id, service, threshold, firing timestamps, linked runbook URL, current responders

layers.name: stable_context
layers.consumes: intake (1 op, each of the 8 reads the service name out of it)
layers.reads_artifacts: one each: (1) service catalog + dependency edges for the alerting service and its 1-hop neighbours (Backstage/service map API), (2) the alert's runbook markdown, (3) dashboard JSON + SLO definitions, (4) deploy history for the last 24h across the blast radius (Argo/Spinnaker/GitHub Deployments), (5) feature-flag + config audit log (LaunchDarkly/Consul) for the window, (6) kubectl get/describe for the owning Deployment/StatefulSet, (7) ownership + on-call, (8) top-5 semantically similar past postmortems

layers.name: plan
layers.consumes: intake (1) + stable_context (8) = 9 upstream ops
layers.reads_artifacts: none directly

layers.name: metric_queries
layers.consumes: plan (1 op); the plan emits the suspect list and the queries are templated per (service, signal)
layers.reads_artifacts: 24 metric-series bundles: ~15 suspect services x 6-8 golden signals (rate, error rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, saturation: cpu, mem, conn-pool, queue depth) over window ±30min at 15s resolution, returned downsampled to ~60-120 points

layers.name: log_queries
layers.consumes: plan (1 op)
layers.reads_artifacts: 30 service-hour log buckets. Per suspect service: 1 pattern/cluster query (Datadog Log Patterns or Loki `| pattern` + count by error_class) returning a ~40-row table, then 2-3 exemplar-fetch queries pulling 20-50 raw lines for the top patterns, plus a correlation-id follow query. A busy service emits 10k-2M lines/hour in this window; the pattern query is what makes that tractable.

layers.name: trace_queries
layers.consumes: plan (1 op)
layers.reads_artifacts: 6 trace bundles: 1-2 trace-search calls returning ~200 trace summaries for error/slow requests, then 8-10 full-trace fetches (40-200 spans each, pruned to the error path and the top-3 slowest spans)

layers.name: change_diffs
layers.consumes: stable_context#4 (deploy history) — 1 op
layers.reads_artifacts: 6 code artifacts: the diff + PR body for each deploy that landed in the blast radius within 24h before the alert (DORA elite teams deploy multiple times per business day, so 2-8 candidate deploys is realistic)

layers.name: suspect_analysis
layers.consumes: ~14 upstream ops each: its own service's ~7 metric_queries + ~4 log_queries + ~1 trace_query, plus plan and the shared stable_context block
layers.reads_artifacts: none directly

layers.name: correlate_rank
layers.consumes: all 12 suspect_analysis ops + change_diffs (6) + plan
layers.reads_artifacts: none directly

layers.name: verify_query
layers.consumes: the verify_reason op of the previous round (or correlate_rank for round 1) — 1 op; arguments are model-authored, not templated
layers.reads_artifacts: re-reads narrow slices of the same log/metric/trace artifacts with new filters (specific pod, specific error_class, specific trace_id, tighter window), plus occasionally a new artifact: a DB slow-query log, a load-balancer access log, an upstream provider status page

layers.name: verify_reason
layers.consumes: its round's 3-4 verify_query ops + the previous verify_reason (chain)
layers.reads_artifacts: none directly

layers.name: writeup
layers.consumes: correlate_rank (2) + all 8 verify_reason ops
layers.reads_artifacts: none directly

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 0% (postmortem re-run or eval replay of a frozen window) to ~92% (next firing of the same alert, days later); ~13% for a re-run minutes later inside the same live incident
change_rate.basis:
Composite ESTIMATE built from partly-sourced components. Sourced pieces: (a) telemetry for a CLOSED window is effectively immutable — streaming-ingestion literature puts late-arriving events at roughly 1% beyond 2-5 minutes and negligible beyond ~15 minutes, so re-reading yesterday's hour bucket returns the same facts; (b) code/config artifacts churn at deploy cadence, and DORA 2025 has elite teams deploying multiple times per business day with change-failure rate 0-15%, so a service's code differs between two alert firings a week apart but its runbook and catalog entry almost never do; (c) OpenRCA (Microsoft, ICLR'25) confirms the per-incident telemetry scale (335 failures / >68GB) that makes the telemetry layer dominate artifact count. NOT sourced: the run-mode mix (70/20/5/5 for R3/R1/R2/R4) and the 65% weighted figure — those are my estimates from how these products are wired, and I would not defend them past ±15 points. Per-mode arithmetic: R3 changes 70 of 78 artifacts (~90%); R1 changes ~10 of 78 (~13%, the live hour bucket plus new metric points); R2 ~2%; R4 0%. Weighted: 0.70(90) + 0.20(13) + 0.05(2) + 0.05(0) ≈ 66%.

Two hazards that inflate the effective change rate above the true one, and both are engineering problems rather than facts about the world: (i) the time window is a LITERAL ARGUMENT — two runs 40 minutes apart on the same recurring alert pass different from/to values, so every telemetry op key differs even where the underlying data overlaps 95%, unless you snap windows to fixed buckets; (ii) observability APIs are not byte-deterministic — result ordering, float rollups, tier migration (indexed -> archive -> rehydrated), and recording-rule downsampling all change the serialized response for identical facts. Without aggressive canonicalisation (snap to hour buckets, sort, round, strip request ids and query latency fields) the measured hit rate on R2/R4 is 0% for reasons that have nothing to do with the data changing.
change_rate.where_changes_land: At the graph ROOT and at depth 4, which is the worst possible placement. The alert payload (depth 1) differs on literally every R3 run — different firing timestamp, different threshold breach value, different incident id — which alone changes the plan op's key and therefore transitively every one of the 24 model ops. The telemetry artifacts (depth 4, ~60 of 78 artifacts) also all differ on R3. The genuinely stable artifacts — runbook, service catalog, dashboard JSON, ownership, past postmortems, roughly 8-13 of 78 — are read only by the 8 cheap stable_context tool ops at depth 2, and their stability buys nothing downstream because every downstream op ALSO depends on changed telemetry. So in the dominant mode, reuse survives on ~8/225 ops (3.5%) and 0/24 model ops, unless you normalise the alert payload (drop incident id and exact firing timestamp from the plan op's inputs), which is a hand-tuned key-shaping decision, not something transitive hashing gives you. In the R2/R4 modes the entire telemetry sweep (168 ops) is reusable and free, but in R4 the root prompt is exactly what changed, so all 24 model ops miss by construction and you get a tool-fixture cache.

session_structure:
A competent engineer gets a lot here, and the reuse layer has to beat this, not a naive loop.

1. One conversation per investigation, append-only. The agent loop appends tool results to a single growing message list, so model call N+1's prefix is model call N's entire context. With a rolling cache breakpoint at the end of the prefix, every call after the first hits cache on ~95%+ of its input. Across 24 model calls averaging ~34k input, that is roughly 780k input tokens of which ~700k are cached reads at 10%, plus a 25% write premium on the deltas.

2. Deliberate context ordering, static-to-dynamic, with Anthropic's 4 breakpoints spent as: (bp1) system prompt + tool schemas + output JSON schema — identical across every investigation this customer ever runs; (bp2) org-static context: service catalog, dependency graph, runbook corpus digest, alert-rule definitions — changes weekly at most, ~15k tokens, and is shared across ALL of that customer's investigations, so it stays warm all day under the 1h tier if any alert fires hourly; (bp3) incident-static: alert payload, deploy list, k8s state — fixed for the life of this incident, so all R1 re-runs within the hour hit it; (bp4) rolling, at the tail of the conversation.

3. Never put anything time-varying above a breakpoint. No "current time", no query latency, no request ids, no responder list in the prefix. Sort tool results deterministically before appending.

4. Fan-out discipline at the suspect_analysis layer. The 12 suspect calls share bp1-bp3 plus the shared evidence block; only the per-service evidence tail differs, so shared evidence goes BEFORE service evidence with a breakpoint between. Critically, issuing all 12 concurrently means none of them sees another's cache write, so all 12 pay the write premium on the shared block. The tuned baseline serialises one call first to warm the prefix, then fans out the remaining 11 — a real, measured effect that a naive parallel implementation gets wrong.

5. Choose the 1h TTL tier for bp1-bp3. Alert traffic of 20-80 runs/day means the org-static block is re-hit within an hour most of the working day, so the write premium amortises across many investigations.

6. Prompt-side cost control that has nothing to do with caching but is part of a tuned baseline: aggregate before ingest (log patterns, not log lines), downsample series server-side, prune traces to error paths. This is what keeps 68GB-scale telemetry down to ~750k tokens.

What this baseline provably cannot do, and where the reuse layer's only honest opening is: prefix caching makes it cheaper to RE-SEND a tool result, never cheaper to RE-EXECUTE the Datadog query. For R2 and R4 the provider cache is dead or bypassed, and the 168-op telemetry sweep costs real vendor query quota and 30-120s of wall clock every single time.
grader:
Deterministic, no LLM, exact and free ground truth, via a seeded incident generator — the fault is known by construction, not by annotation.

GENERATOR. `gen(seed) -> (telemetry corpus, manifest)`. It simulates a 15-service topology (fixed DAG, service names from a fixed catalog) over a 3-hour window at 1s granularity. It picks, from `seed`: one root-cause service `C` from the catalog, one fault type `F` from a closed enum {cpu_saturation, memory_leak_oom, network_latency_injection, packet_loss, disk_io_stall, db_conn_pool_exhaustion, bad_deploy_regression, config_flag_flip, upstream_dependency_5xx, cert_expiry, thread_pool_deadlock, cache_stampede}, a fault start `T0` (second resolution), and a duration. It then emits, from templates: (a) Loki-format JSONL logs per service per hour with a realistic 10k-500k lines/hour baseline plus fault-induced error patterns that propagate to downstream services with per-hop delay, (b) Prometheus-format series per service per golden signal with the fault's signature injected, (c) OTLP traces where the fault service's spans show the characteristic latency/error shape, (d) a git history + deploy log where exactly one deploy `D` (a real commit sha in the fixture repo) is causally upstream when F == bad_deploy_regression, (e) runbooks, service catalog, dashboards. The manifest records C, F, T0, D, and the exact `error_class` string the fault emits. Decoy signal is mandatory: 2-4 unrelated services also degrade in-window from benign causes, and 1-3 unrelated deploys land in-window, so exact-match is not guessable.

SERVING. Telemetry is served by a local read-only Loki/Prometheus/Tempo (or a flat-file shim exposing the same query API) so tool calls are hermetic, free, deterministic, and network-independent. Same API surface as production, so the agent code is unmodified.

SCORING. The agent must emit one JSON object validating against a fixed JSON Schema: {root_cause_service, fault_type, fault_start_utc, suspect_deploy_sha|null, primary_error_class}. Schema-invalid output scores 0, no repair, no retry.
  primary_score = 1.0 iff ALL of: root_cause_service == C (exact string), fault_type == F (exact enum member), |fault_start_utc - T0| <= 60s, and (suspect_deploy_sha == D if F == bad_deploy_regression else suspect_deploy_sha is null).
  Sub-scores recorded separately for analysis: service_hit, type_hit, timing_hit, deploy_hit, error_class_hit (exact string equality).
Everything is string/integer comparison against the manifest. No judge, no embedding similarity, no human.

WHY THIS SHAPE. It gives the property this specific benchmark needs and that a fixed corpus cannot: CONTROLLED CHANGE RATE. `gen(seed)` and `gen(seed, perturb=k%)` produce corpora that differ in a precisely known fraction of artifacts, and the perturbation can be aimed — flip only the live hour bucket (R1), flip all telemetry but hold catalog/runbooks (R3), flip nothing but change the system prompt (R4). That lets you sweep the reuse curve as a function of change rate and change LOCATION rather than asserting a single number.

REALISM ANCHOR. Validate that the synthetic task is not degenerate by running the same agent against Microsoft's OpenRCA (335 real failures, >68GB telemetry from 3 enterprise systems), whose own grader is the same exact-match shape — predicted datetime + component + reason against record.csv. If accuracy on the generator tracks accuracy on OpenRCA, the generator is a valid stand-in; if the generator is much easier, raise decoy density until it isn't.
reuse_story:
Three mechanisms, in descending order of honesty.

1. The strongest one is not about tokens at all. The 168-op telemetry sweep costs metered observability queries (Datadog indexed-log search, Splunk SVC-hours) and 30-120s of wall clock, and provider prefix caching does nothing for it — it makes re-sending a result cheap, never re-executing the query. For R2 (postmortem, days later) and R4 (nightly eval replay of 300 frozen incidents) the underlying window is immutable, so a content-addressed tool-result store serves the entire sweep for free. In R4 that turns a 500-incident nightly eval from hours of API-throttled wall clock into minutes, and it is the difference between running the eval per-PR and running it weekly. This is real value, but note what it is: a plain memoiser on tool calls. It does not need transitive keying through model outputs, and eval harnesses already hand-roll it as VCR/fixture caching.

2. Time-bucket snapping converts a near-total miss into a partial hit for recurring alerts. If telemetry ops key on hour-snapped windows rather than raw from/to, two firings of the same noisy alert 40 minutes apart share every completed hour bucket in their trailing context, and only the live bucket differs. On a rolling-24h context this is 23/24 of the log/metric reads. This is genuine and it is the main lever worth benchmarking.

3. Cross-customer, cross-run reuse of the stable_context layer: catalog, runbooks, dashboards, past-postmortem retrieval. Real hit rate near 100%, real value near zero — 8 cheap tool ops out of 225, and the provider's 1h tier already keeps that block warm all working day at 10% of input rate.
reuse_threats:
Ordered by how badly each one hurts.

1. WRONG-END STABILITY. In the dominant mode (R3, ~70% of production runs) the stable artifacts sit at depth 2 and cost almost nothing, while the changing artifacts sit at depth 4 upstream of every one of the 24 model calls. Transitive keying therefore invalidates 100% of the expensive work. The graph's structure guarantees this — it is not a tuning failure.

2. ROOT-LEVEL CHANGE IN THE ONE MODE WITH PERFECT ARTIFACT STABILITY. R4 eval replay has 0% artifact churn, which looks like the ideal case, but the thing being iterated on IS the system prompt or the model id. Both are inputs to every model op's key. So the mode with 100% reusable artifacts yields 0% reusable model calls, by construction, forever.

3. THE PROVIDER ALREADY OWNS R1. Re-runs inside a live incident are minutes to <1h apart — exactly the 1h cache tier's window. A competently structured agent (one conversation, breakpoints at bp1-bp3) already gets that block at 10% of input rate for free. The reuse layer's marginal win in R1 is the difference between 10% and 0% on the shared prefix, minus its own overhead, on the run mode where the total spend is smallest.

4. NON-DETERMINISTIC TOOL RESPONSES. Observability APIs return unstable orderings, float rollups, tier-migrated payloads, and embedded query-latency/request-id fields. Hash the raw response and R2/R4 hit rates are 0% for reasons unrelated to the data. Canonicalising requires per-backend, hand-written normalisers — real, ongoing engineering that the "just hash everything" framing hides.

5. THE VERIFICATION TAIL IS A CHAIN BY DESIGN. Depth 7-14 is 32 ops whose arguments are model-authored. Any nonzero temperature, any model version bump, any reordering upstream, and the whole tail diverges. Even in a bit-identical replay it only reuses if sampling is fully deterministic, which providers do not guarantee.

6. STALENESS IS A CORRECTNESS RISK HERE, NOT A PERFORMANCE ONE. Serving a cached telemetry result for a window that is still open — or that was rehydrated, or whose retention tier dropped lines — means the agent reasons about a system state that no longer exists during a live incident. The safe rule (never serve the live bucket, only buckets closed >15 min, per the ~1% late-arrival tail) removes exactly the data the live incident cares about most.

7. VALUE CONCENTRATION. Even at its best, this saves dollars on a workload whose per-run cost is $2-4 in tokens plus some query quota, against an outage costing the customer far more per minute. The buyer's willingness to pay is anchored to MTTR, not to inference spend, so a 40% cost reduction is not a purchase reason on its own.
confidence:
Medium. Well grounded: the telemetry scale and the exact-match grading shape (OpenRCA, 335 failures / >68GB / three systems, graded on datetime + component + reason); the agent toolset (log/trace/metric query + kubectl + code read, per SREGym); deploy cadence and change-failure rate (DORA 2025); late-arrival behaviour (~1% beyond 2-5 min) that makes closed windows immutable; alert-noise levels (~74% non-actionable) driving run volume. Estimated, and I would not defend past ±30-40%: the operation counts per layer (225 ops / 24 model ops), the per-op token sizes, and the R3/R1/R2/R4 run-mode mix that produces the 65% headline change rate. No vendor publishes per-investigation op counts or token profiles, so those are reconstructed from how the tool loops must work given the data volumes.

What would raise it to high: (1) an actual agent trace from one of these products — even 20 real investigations' worth of tool-call logs would pin the op counts, the fan-out width, and the verification-loop depth exactly; (2) a customer's alert history showing the true distribution of (alert rule, service) repeat intervals, which is the single number that decides whether hour-bucket snapping is worth building; (3) a measured determinism audit of Datadog/Loki/Tempo query responses replayed over a closed window — if the raw responses are not byte-stable, threat #4 dominates everything else and the honest answer becomes "build normalisers first, then re-ask the question".

customer: The payer is a compliance-automation (GRC) vendor of the Vanta/Drata/Hyperproof class, not the end enterprise. They sell a per-tenant subscription (~$25k-$120k/yr for mid-market and enterprise tenants) whose headline promise is "continuous compliance": the control set is not just monitored by deterministic API checks, it is *re-attested* against unstructured evidence and re-narrated for each framework. The deterministic half (Okta MFA is on, S3 buckets are private) is cheap and is not this workload. This workload is the expensive half the tool cannot do with rules: read the policy PDFs, the pen-test report, the vendor SOC 2s, the access-review spreadsheets, the change tickets, and decide per control whether the collected evidence actually satisfies the stated requirement, with citations, then word the conclusion three different ways for SOC 2, ISO 27001:2022 and FedRAMP Moderate. Concretely modelled tenant: 450-employee B2B SaaS, ~$80M ARR, 6 AWS accounts, three frameworks live. At list model rates one full nightly run for that one tenant is ~$100 of tokens (computed below); a vendor with 400 such tenants is spending on the order of $1M/month on this single pipeline. That is why they would buy a reuse layer.
why_repeated: Four independent forcing functions, all real: (1) SOC 2 Type II opinions cover an observation period, so the evidence population and its sufficiency must be re-evaluated continuously across 6-12 months, not once; (2) the evidence itself is live — identity exports, vulnerability scans and change tickets are regenerated every day, so yesterday's conclusion is not defensible against today's population; (3) the product promise is a dashboard that is green or red *this morning*, which requires a run last night; (4) during audit fieldwork the compliance team pulls the same report daily for 2-6 weeks while remediating, and each remediation is supposed to flip a control from GAP to SATISFIED within a day. Crucially, the *control side* of the graph is near-frozen while the *evidence side* churns — the run is repeated because of the evidence, not the controls.
run_cadence: Nightly per tenant (Drata publicly runs its automated tests daily, Vanta hourly; the LLM attestation layer is the expensive one and is nightly in every implementation I would expect). Bursts to daily-plus-on-demand for 2-6 weeks during audit fieldwork and during a remediation sprint. A full unconditional recompute (ignoring all incremental state) happens on framework version bumps (ISO 27001:2013→2022, FedRAMP Rev4→Rev5, PCI 3.2.1→4.0 — roughly one per framework every 3-8 years), on model upgrades, and on rubric edits, which in practice happen far more often than framework bumps.

graph.description: A wide layered DAG with two independent roots that meet at a fan-out layer. Root A is the tenant's evidence corpus (372 artifacts pulled by 24 connectors, normalised into 744 evidence cards). Root B is the control catalogue (312 unified internal controls crosswalked from 478 framework requirements: SOC 2 Security+Availability+Confidentiality = 38 criteria, ISO 27001:2022 = 93 Annex A controls + 24 clause requirements, FedRAMP Moderate Rev 5 = 323 controls). Root B contains ZERO tenant data and is byte-identical across every tenant and every night. The two roots meet at retrieval (top-k=8 evidence cards per control) and then at the 2,496-op sufficiency-judgment fan-out, which is 63% of total token spend. Above the fan-out the graph narrows fast: 312 per-control rollups, 478 per-framework-requirement attestations (the same control conclusion re-worded for SOC 2 vs ISO vs FedRAMP), 3 framework gap consolidations, 1 executive delta, then deterministic rendering of the SoA spreadsheet, the OSCAL SSP, the exception register and Jira tickets for new gaps. Depth 11, mean fan-in 2.64 — this is emphatically NOT a chain, and it is not 500 independent ops either: it is one massive independent layer (2,496 pairwise judgments) suspended between a frozen root and a churning root, with two narrow reduction layers on top. The single most consequential structural detail is that layer 4 (index_build) is a global reduction over all 744 evidence cards, so under naive transitive keying ANY changed artifact changes the index hash, which changes every retrieval key, which changes every judge key — 100% invalidation from a 0.3% change. Whether this benchmark shows 83% reuse or 0% reuse turns entirely on whether the judge op is keyed on (control_assertions_hash, evidence_card_hash) pairwise or on the retrieval op's output hash. Both are defensible readings of the stated keying rule; only one works.

layers.name: connector_fetch
layers.consumes: nothing — these are graph roots
layers.reads_artifacts: Each call reads 1-180 external artifacts from a live API: AWS Config/Security Hub (6 accounts), Okta (users, groups, MFA, app assignments, admin roles), GitHub org settings + branch protection + PR metadata, Jira change tickets, HRIS roster, MDM device posture, LMS training completions, 4 vulnerability scanners, SIEM config, Confluence/Drive policy repo, vendor-management portal, background-check vendor. Together they cover all 372 artifacts. Artifact class sizes: 40 governance docs (policies, boundary/SSP narrative, board minutes, contracts) at 3k-15k tokens each; 180 automated posture-result JSON blobs at 400-3,000 tokens; 12 identity/HR/device/training exports, the largest of which (asset inventory 240k tok, Okta users 180k tok) dominate; 29 change-management artifacts (4 rolling exports + 25 sampled change records); 6 vulnerability artifacts; 68 vendor records and vendor SOC 2/ISO PDFs; 23 incident/BCDR/access-review artifacts; 14 logging/monitoring/org artifacts.

layers.name: evidence_card_extract
layers.consumes: 1 connector_fetch op each. 34 bulk exports are deterministically sharded into 12 chunks each (408 units); the remaining 338 artifacts are single-unit. 408+338=746, rounded to 744.
layers.reads_artifacts: One artifact or one shard of one artifact.

layers.name: card_embed
layers.consumes: 1 evidence_card_extract each
layers.reads_artifacts: none — embeds the structured card only

layers.name: index_build
layers.consumes: all 744 card_embed ops plus the 744 cards for the BM25 side — fan-in 744
layers.reads_artifacts: none

layers.name: control_decompose
layers.consumes: nothing — graph root, and the important one: it reads NO tenant data
layers.reads_artifacts: Static reference data only: the unified control text plus the 1-3 framework requirement texts crosswalked onto it, plus a fixed decomposition rubric. Output is the list of testable assertions ('evidence must cover the full observation period', 'must be approved by a role senior to the requester', 'sample of 25 required'), the required evidence types, and the sampling rule.

layers.name: retrieve_candidates
layers.consumes: index_build (1) + control_decompose (1) — fan-in 2. Hybrid BM25 + dense, top-k=8.
layers.reads_artifacts: none

layers.name: sufficiency_judge
layers.consumes: control_decompose (1) + retrieve_candidates (1) + the specific evidence_card_extract (1) — fan-in 3. 312 controls x 8 candidates.
layers.reads_artifacts: A ~2,200-token verbatim excerpt from the source artifact, re-read so the judgment cites real spans rather than the lossy card.

layers.name: control_rollup
layers.consumes: control_decompose (1) + its 8 sufficiency_judge ops — fan-in 9
layers.reads_artifacts: none

layers.name: requirement_attest
layers.consumes: the 1-3 control_rollup ops mapped to this framework requirement — mean fan-in 1.5
layers.reads_artifacts: the framework's own style/wording guide (SOC 2 description language vs ISO Statement of Applicability vs FedRAMP SSP implementation statement)

layers.name: framework_gap_consolidate
layers.consumes: ~159 requirement_attest ops each (one per framework)
layers.reads_artifacts: none

layers.name: exec_summary_delta
layers.consumes: 3 framework_gap_consolidate ops + the prior run's summary artifact
layers.reads_artifacts: prior run summary (1 artifact)

layers.name: render_and_ticket
layers.consumes: ~2 upstream ops each: 5 deterministic renders (SoA XLSX, OSCAL SSP JSON, exception register CSV, SOC 2 description Markdown, evidence index) + 9 Jira ticket creations for newly-opened gaps
layers.reads_artifacts: none

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 8-35% night-over-night at artifact granularity; ~2-4% at row granularity; 100% on a framework version bump or a rubric/model edit
change_rate.basis: Built bottom-up from sourced component rates, then summed — the composite 14.8% figure is my estimate, not a published number. No public dataset on GRC evidence-artifact churn exists; I searched for one and there isn't one, so I refuse to dress this up as sourced. Component rates and their provenance: (a) Governance docs, 40 artifacts — ISO 27001 A.5.1 mandates review at least annually plus on significant change, and practitioners revise an active policy 2-4x/yr, giving ~0.8%/day for this class (annual-review requirement is SOURCED; the 2-4 revisions is estimated). (b) Automated posture results, 180 artifacts — DORA 2024 puts 19% of orgs at elite and 22% at high deployment frequency (SOURCED), so a company of this profile deploys many times daily, but the *check result payloads* (pass/fail plus failing-resource list) are far stickier than raw configs; I estimate 18% of these differ night-over-night. (c) Identity/HR/device/training exports, 12 artifacts — Mercer's 2025 US Turnover Survey of 2,617 orgs puts voluntary turnover at 13%, SHRM's 2025 benchmark at 9% median/13% mean, tech-sector projections at 20-25% total (SOURCED); at 450 headcount that is ~90-110 joiner/leaver events/yr, ~0.4/workday. But group membership, app assignment, device posture and training completions move constantly, so I put this class at ~100% of artifacts changed nightly while only ~1-3% of ROWS change. (d) Change-management, 29 artifacts — the 4 rolling exports are append-only and change 100% nightly; the 25 sampled change records rotate at ~5%/day if the sampler is deterministically seeded over a rolling window and 100%/day if it is not. (e) Vulnerability, 6 artifacts — scanners run daily and NVD publishes on the order of 80-100 CVEs/day, so the 4 scan exports change ~100% nightly; the pen-test report is annual. (f) Vendor records, 68 — vendor SOC 2s are annual documents, a mid-market company adds 1-2 SaaS vendors/month, ~1%/day. (g) Incident/BCDR/access-review, 23 — episodic, ~1.5%/day. Weighted sum = 55 of 372 = 14.8%. Confidence on the composite: medium-low. The number I would most want to falsify with real telemetry is (b), which contributes 32 of the 55 changed artifacts and is a pure estimate.
change_rate.where_changes_land: Overwhelmingly at the LEAVES of the evidence root (layer 2, evidence_card_extract), and heavily concentrated within it. The control root (layer 5, control_decompose, 312 ops) changes essentially NEVER — zero tenant data touches it, so between two consecutive nightly runs it changes 0% of the time, and across two different tenants it also changes 0%. It flips to 100% only on a framework version bump. That asymmetry is the whole reuse story. On the evidence side changes are NOT uniform: they concentrate in identity, vulnerability and change-management artifacts, which map to the access-control, change-management and vulnerability-management control families — roughly 35% of the 312 controls. So although a uniform-change model predicts 1-(0.85)^8 = 73% of controls would have at least one changed candidate in their top-8, the real clustering puts it nearer 45-55%. Consequences by layer for a typical repeat run, assuming pairwise judge keying: control_decompose ~100% reusable, evidence_card_extract ~85%, card_embed ~85%, sufficiency_judge ~83% (this is the money — it is 63% of run cost), control_rollup ~50%, requirement_attest ~45%, gap_consolidate and exec_summary 0%. Under naive keying through index_build, every one of those drops to 0% except control_decompose, which is worth ~$2.50 of a ~$102 run.

session_structure: A competent engineer would not treat these as 5,090 independent chat calls; they would shape the sufficiency_judge layer specifically, because it is 2,496 of the calls and $64 of the $102. Concretely, and this is the baseline to beat, not a straw man: (1) Fatten the system block deliberately. Instead of an 800-token judge rubric they write a ~3,500-token system block — rubric, the SATISFIED/PARTIAL/GAP decision tree, 6 worked few-shot exemplars, the citation-format spec, the stale-evidence and wrong-scope traps — and mark it with a cache_control breakpoint. This block is byte-identical across all 2,496 calls, all three frameworks, all nights, and all 400 tenants. Making the prefix *bigger* is the correct move once it is cached at 10%, because it buys accuracy at a tenth of the price. (2) Order the calls by control, not by evidence, and put the 620-token control_decompose output as a second cache breakpoint after the system block. It is shared by the 8 calls for that control and sits above the 1,024-token minimum cacheable prefix because the 3,500-token system block precedes it. (3) Put the variable material — the 500-token evidence card and the 2,200-token raw excerpt — strictly last, in that order, never interleaved with anything stable. (4) Fire one warm-up call per new prefix and only then fan out the remaining 7, because under concurrent fan-out every concurrent caller pays the cache *write* at 1.25x rather than the read at 0.1x; naively firing all 8 at once turns a saving into a 25% penalty. (5) Run the whole judge layer inside one window with bounded concurrency (~30) so the system prefix never ages out of the 5-minute TTL; a 2,496-call layer at ~1.5s each and concurrency 30 finishes in ~2 minutes, so the 5-minute tier suffices and the 1-hour tier is not needed for this layer. Buy the 1-hour tier only for the cross-layer system blocks that span the whole ~25-minute run. (6) Apply the same two-breakpoint shape to evidence_card_extract (1,200-token fixed extraction schema, ~23% of input cached), control_rollup (1,320-token rubric+assertions, ~29% cached) and requirement_attest (900-token framework style guide, ~35% cached). Arithmetic on the judge layer under this baseline: 6,800 tokens in, of which 3,500 system is cached ~100% after warm-up and 620 control is cached 7/8 = 542, so 4,042 tokens or 59% of input bills at 10%. Effective input cost = (2,758 + 404)/6,800 = 46.5% of uncached. Across the whole run the tuned baseline removes roughly 38-44% of input token cost and 0% of output token cost, so about 33-38% of total run cost, taking $102 to roughly $66. That is the number the reuse layer has to beat, and it must beat it while composing with it, since the reuse layer can only skip calls, and the calls that survive still want their prefixes cached.
grader: Deterministic, no LLM, exact and free ground truth via a seeded synthetic-organisation generator. Generator: seed s produces (i) a catalogue of 312 unified controls where each control carries a machine-checkable requirement predicate over structured facts — e.g. control C_117 = requires(evidence_type='access_review', system in {aws,okta,github}, recency_days<=90, approver_role='manager', population_complete=true, min_count=1) — plus the 478 framework-requirement edges onto it; (ii) 372 evidence artifacts rendered as realistic surface text (policy prose, CSV exports, JSON scan output, PDF-style report text) each of which EMBEDS a known set of structured facts. Because the generator authored both sides, it computes the exact ground truth in closed form and for free: per control, the status in {SATISFIED, PARTIAL, GAP}, the exact minimal set of artifact IDs that satisfies it, and the exact set of unmet assertion IDs. The generator deliberately injects four adversarial classes at fixed rates: distractors (right evidence type, wrong system), stale evidence (recency_days just past threshold), unapproved evidence (missing approver field), and cross-system duplicates (so citation sets are not uniquely determined and must be graded as set-F1 against any minimal cover). GRADER, run over the agent's emitted JSON (control_id, status, cited_artifact_ids, unmet_assertion_ids): (1) status exact-match accuracy over 312 controls — string equality; (2) citation set micro-F1 against the ground-truth minimal cover, crediting any valid minimal cover; (3) unmet-assertion set micro-F1, which catches 'right verdict, wrong reason'; (4) hallucination gate — any cited artifact ID absent from the run's artifact manifest scores that control 0 and increments a hard counter; (5) cross-framework consistency — for any two of the 478 framework requirements mapped to the same unified control, the emitted statuses must be equal; pure equality check, needs no ground truth at all. Score = 0.40*status_acc + 0.30*citation_F1 + 0.20*assertion_F1 + 0.10*consistency. Pass gate: status_acc >= 0.92 AND hallucinated_citations == 0. FOR THE REPEAT RUN, which is the point of the benchmark: the generator applies a seeded mutation set at the empirically-derived class rates (identity/vuln/change-mgmt exports mutated ~100%, posture results 18%, policies 0.8%, etc., composite ~15% of artifacts) and recomputes ground truth in closed form for run N+1. This is what makes the benchmark honest about reuse: a reuse layer that serves a stale conclusion is caught as a status mismatch or a citation-F1 drop, so the harness reports cost AND staleness-induced error on the same axis. A reuse layer that achieves 83% hit rate at 0.94 status accuracy is a different product from one that achieves 83% at 0.71, and only the paired measurement distinguishes them. Both metrics are computed by pure Python over JSON; no model is ever in the grading loop; ground truth costs nothing because it was generated, not annotated.
reuse_story: Two mechanisms, of very different quality. The weak one: control_decompose is 312 model ops that read zero tenant data. Its key is (control text, framework version, rubric version, model id), which is identical across every night and every one of the vendor's 400 tenants, so it hits ~100% forever. It is also worth only ~$2.50 of a $102 run, and any competent team already caches it in a Postgres table because it is obviously static — the reuse layer gets no credit here. The strong one: sufficiency_judge is 2,496 ops and $64 of the $102. Each judgment is a pure function of (this control's assertions, this evidence card, this excerpt). With ~15% of artifacts changing nightly and changes clustered in three control families, roughly 83% of those 2,496 pairs are bit-identical to last night's. Skipping them removes 100% of their tokens, not the 90% of the prefix that provider caching removes, and the two compose: reuse skips the call, prefix caching discounts the ~420 that survive. Combined, a $102 run should land near $18-24 versus $66 for the tuned-prefix-cache-only baseline. Secondary reuse: 85% of evidence_card_extract and card_embed, and ~50% of control_rollup. There is also a genuine cross-tenant surface beyond control_decompose that is easy to miss — the 68 vendor SOC 2/ISO report PDFs are the SAME documents across every customer of that vendor (every tenant using Datadog reads Datadog's SOC 2), so their extract and judge ops hit across tenants at content-hash granularity. For a GRC vendor with 400 tenants that is a real, and I think under-appreciated, multiplier.
reuse_threats: Seven, roughly in order of how likely each is to zero out the win. (1) THE INDEX REDUCTION. index_build is a global fan-in over all 744 cards. Under the stated keying rule its output hash changes if any single card changes, so all 312 retrieval keys change, so all 2,496 judge keys change — a 0.3% input change causes 100% invalidation. The fix is to key the judge on (control_assertions_hash, evidence_card_hash) pairwise and treat retrieval as a routing decision outside the key, but that is a deliberate design choice, not something the generic transitive rule gives you, and it silently weakens the correctness guarantee (a new artifact that *should* have displaced a stale one from the top-8 will never be judged). This single issue is the difference between 83% reuse and 3%. (2) NON-DETERMINISTIC EXPORTS. Okta, AWS, Jira and scanner exports embed generated_at timestamps, pagination cursors and unstable row ordering. A substantively identical export has a different sha256 every night, so layers 2 and 7 hit 0% no matter how good the keying is. Fixing this requires a canonicalising normaliser per connector — strip volatile fields, sort rows by a stable key — which is 24 pieces of per-connector engineering, not a generic layer. I think this, not the change rate, is the largest practical blocker in this domain. (3) FIXED-OFFSET CHUNKING. The 34 bulk exports are sharded into 12 chunks each. If chunking is by byte/token offset, inserting one row at the top of a 240k-token asset inventory shifts every boundary and invalidates all 12 chunks plus everything downstream. Content-defined chunking (FastCDC over stable row keys) is required, and interacts badly with the sorting fix in (2). (4) RUBRIC CHURN MAY DOMINATE ARTIFACT CHURN. Every false positive a compliance analyst sees triggers a rubric edit, and rubric text is in the prefix of layers 5, 7 and 8. If rubrics change weekly — which matches how these teams actually operate during the first six months of a deployment — then the effective change rate for the expensive layers is 100%/week regardless of the 15% artifact rate, and the reuse layer's measured value collapses to whatever it earns on the 6 days between edits. I would want this instrumented before believing any headline number. (5) PREFIX-CACHE INTERACTION, AND IT IS NEGATIVE. Skipping 83% of judge calls leaves ~420 survivors scattered across controls — roughly 1.3 per control instead of 8. The second cache breakpoint (the 620-token control assertions block) was earning 7/8 reads per write; at 1.3 calls per control it earns 0.3 reads per 1.25x write and becomes a net loss. The reuse layer must know to drop that breakpoint on incremental runs, or it hands back part of what it saved. The first breakpoint (3,500-token system block) survives fine at 420 calls. (6) AUDITOR ACCEPTANCE. Serving a control conclusion from a hash-keyed store means no model re-read that evidence during this period. For a Type II opinion over an observation window, 'the evidence bytes were identical so we reused the conclusion' is a defensible argument, but the auditor and ultimately the regulator have to accept it, and the vendor's own attestation language may not permit it. This is a non-technical adoption risk that is specific to this domain and that I would not bet against blocking a sale. (7) OUTPUT-SIDE COST. Reuse saves input and output tokens equally, which is a genuine advantage over prefix caching (which saves zero output). But output is only 18% of this run's cost, so the advantage is smaller than it sounds; the reuse win here is fundamentally about call elimination, not about the input/output asymmetry.
confidence: Medium overall, with a wide spread by component. HIGH on the control-side numbers: FedRAMP Moderate Rev 5 = 323 controls, ISO 27001:2022 Annex A = 93, SOC 2 Common Criteria = 33, SCF crosswalks 1,500+ controls across 200+ frameworks — all sourced. HIGH on the structural claim that the control root is frozen and the evidence root churns; that follows from the definition of the work, not from data. HIGH on the tuned-baseline arithmetic and on the claim that a well-shaped prefix-cache baseline already removes ~35% of run cost. MEDIUM on the graph shape and op counts — 312 unified controls, 372 artifacts, top-k=8, 2,496 judge ops are my construction of what a real mid-market three-framework tenant looks like; they are internally consistent and cost out to a believable $102/run, but I have not seen a production GRC vendor's actual op counts. LOW-to-MEDIUM on the 15% change rate: the component rates are sourced (Mercer/SHRM turnover, DORA deployment tiers, ISO annual policy review) but the composite is my weighting, and the largest single contributor — 18% nightly churn in the 180 automated posture-result artifacts, which alone is 32 of the 55 changed artifacts — is a pure estimate with no data behind it. WHAT WOULD RAISE CONFIDENCE, in priority order: (a) one week of connector-level content-hash telemetry from a single real GRC tenant, which would settle both the 15% figure and, more importantly, threat (2) — how many exports are byte-stable at all after canonicalisation; (b) a rubric/prompt version changelog from a live deployment, to test whether threat (4) dominates; (c) the real distribution of controls-per-changed-artifact, to replace my 45-55% clustering estimate with a measured one; (d) confirmation of whether production systems already gate the judge fan-out on an mtime/etag dirty bit, because if they do, the incumbent baseline is not 'no caching' but a coarse hand-rolled version of exactly this reuse system, and the honest headline number is the margin over that, not over a full recompute.

customer: A ~250-person B2B SaaS company (Series C, ~25 infra-touching engineers) running 3 AWS accounts + 1 GCP project, ~5,800 Terraform-managed resources spread over 40 root modules ("workspaces") in one IaC monorepo (~1,150 .tf files, ~190k lines HCL, ~85 internal + registry modules). They already pay for the deterministic half of this: Spacelift/env0 or Terraform Cloud for run orchestration and drift detection, plus Checkov/tfsec and a Rego policy pack in CI. What they pay an LLM layer for on top is the part the scanners cannot do: (a) triaging the ~340 post-baseline static findings per fleet-scan into "act / suppress / already-excepted", because raw scanner output has a pass rate of only 44-69% per repo and the false-positive tax is what kills adoption; (b) classifying each drift record as benign-volatile vs. config-lag vs. security-relevant vs. incident-artifact, using the CloudTrail actor and the owning module as context; (c) cross-resource exposure reasoning (is this SG + subnet + IGW + NACL combination actually internet-reachable?) which single-resource rules structurally cannot express; (d) writing the per-workspace and fleet-level narrative that goes to the platform team and, quarterly, to the SOC 2 auditor. Budget reality: they will pay four figures a year for this, not five, unless the fleet is 10x bigger.
why_repeated: Three independent forcing functions, all of which mean the same graph is re-executed against a near-identical input set. (1) Drift is generated continuously by things outside Terraform: driftctl's authors surveyed ~200 DevOps teams and 96% named "bypassing the IaC tool" as the leading cause, 50% named application/deployment-induced drift. Drift that is not looked for is not found — the canonical war story is four months of console changes during incidents surfacing all at once. (2) The policy corpus moves under a static config: Checkov ships new checks continuously (1,000-1,500+ built-in policies today), so the same unchanged HCL becomes non-compliant without anyone editing it. (3) Compliance evidence: SOC 2 / CIS attestation requires showing that every resource was evaluated on a recurring cadence, not that it was evaluated once. That third reason is important for the reuse story because it is an explicit demand for re-evaluation, which is in tension with serving a cached verdict.
run_cadence: Nightly full-fleet audit at 02:00 UTC (the primary, benchmarked cadence): 365 runs/year over an input set that is ~90% byte-identical night to night. A per-PR variant of the same pipeline runs on the ~3-8 IaC PRs/day but scoped to the 1-3 touched workspaces (roughly 1/15th of the graph). A full unscoped re-run is also triggered on Checkov pack bumps and quarterly before audit evidence collection. Wall clock for the nightly run is ~20-25 minutes, dominated by 40 `terraform plan -refresh-only` calls against live cloud APIs at 8-way parallelism.

graph.description: Wide at the base, narrow at the top: 40 independent per-workspace pipelines (init -> refresh-only plan -> normalize -> scan) that fan out to ~180 leaf-level model triage ops, then funnel through 40 per-workspace summaries into a single fleet rollup. Depth 10 but the deep path is thin — most operations sit at depth 4-7 with fan-in 1-3. Two structural facts dominate any reuse analysis. First, the layer that costs the most wall clock (tf_plan_refresh, 40 ops, 2-9 min each) is IMPURE by construction: its output depends on live cloud API state that is not a hashable artifact you can inspect before executing, so its reuse key cannot be computed without running it. You can only reuse-key from plan_normalize downstream. Second, four artifacts sit at the root of essentially every model op — the system/policy preamble, the Checkov pack version, the .terraform.lock.hcl provider pin, and the org exception register — so a change to any one of them invalidates 100% of the 223 model ops at once. The graph is therefore not one long chain (good) but it has four single points of total invalidation (bad). Token sizes below: tool-op 'tokens' are the text size of arguments and of the emitted output; the plan JSON is enormous (median 4.2 MB per workspace) and is never fed to a model whole — the normalizer is what makes the workload tractable, and it is also the thing that determines whether cross-run reuse works at all.

layers.name: workspace_discover
layers.consumes: nothing — graph root; parameterised by the monorepo commit SHA
layers.reads_artifacts: full repo tree at HEAD: 2,400 files, of which 1,150 are .tf (~190k lines HCL, mean ~52 lines/.tf file, consistent with the 549-repo / 41,550-script / 2.16M-LOC Terraform corpus), plus 40 backend.hcl and 40 .tfvars

layers.name: tf_init
layers.consumes: workspace_discover (1 upstream op, 1:40 fan-out)
layers.reads_artifacts: that workspace's .tf files (median 29 files), its .terraform.lock.hcl, and the source of median 6 referenced modules (registry tarballs or git refs)

layers.name: tf_plan_refresh
layers.consumes: tf_init 1:1
layers.reads_artifacts: workspace .tf + .tfvars + remote state object (median 1.9 MB, ~100-750 resources per workspace per HashiCorp sizing guidance; this fleet's median is 145) + LIVE cloud API reads, one per managed resource. This is the impure boundary of the graph.

layers.name: plan_normalize
layers.consumes: tf_plan_refresh 1:1
layers.reads_artifacts: the volatile-attribute denylist (~380 entries: aws_autoscaling_group.desired_capacity, aws_ecs_service.task_definition/desired_count, aws_lambda_function.last_modified/source_code_hash/version, aws_db_instance.latest_restorable_time, IAM policy JSON key ordering, SG rule ordering, helm_release metadata, route53 weights, etc.) plus the previous run's normalized snapshot for that workspace

layers.name: checkov_scan
layers.consumes: tf_init 1:1
layers.reads_artifacts: workspace .tf + resolved module sources + the Checkov policy pack (1,000-1,500 built-in checks; ~121 are AWS-relevant per the 812-project study) + .checkov.baseline

layers.name: tflint_scan
layers.consumes: tf_init 1:1
layers.reads_artifacts: workspace .tf + .tflint.hcl + the aws/google provider rulesets

layers.name: opa_conftest
layers.consumes: plan_normalize 1:1
layers.reads_artifacts: ~140 org-authored Rego files (tagging standard, allowed instance families, mandatory encryption, prod-account guardrails) evaluated against the normalized plan

layers.name: cloudtrail_lookup
layers.consumes: plan_normalize (mean 1.9 drift records per workspace op)
layers.reads_artifacts: CloudTrail / Cloud Audit Logs LookupEvents for (resource ARN, 36h window) — who made the out-of-band change, from which principal and console session

layers.name: drift_triage
layers.consumes: plan_normalize (1) + cloudtrail_lookup (mean 1.6); the 75 surviving drift records are grouped by (workspace, resource_type) into 48 calls
layers.reads_artifacts: provider schema fragment for that resource type (~1,200 tok), the org drift-handling policy doc, the source of the owning module

layers.name: finding_triage
layers.consumes: checkov_scan / tflint_scan / opa_conftest (mean 1.4 upstream ops); ~900 raw findings -> ~340 after baseline suppression -> grouped by (rule_id, workspace) into 120 calls
layers.reads_artifacts: the rule catalog entry + remediation guidance for that rule, the 3 .tf files surrounding each flagged resource, the module's default values, and the org exception register (~1,800 tok, the record of every previously-accepted risk)

layers.name: exposure_reasoning
layers.consumes: plan_normalize (1) + finding_triage (~4) + drift_triage (~2); fires only for workspaces whose network or IAM surface changed
layers.reads_artifacts: the normalized resource graph for that workspace (nodes + edges: SG/NACL/route table/IGW/NAT/ALB/IAM trust relationships), ~11,000 tok

layers.name: workspace_summary
layers.consumes: drift_triage (~1.2) + finding_triage (~3.0) + exposure_reasoning (~0.35) = mean 4.6
layers.reads_artifacts: CODEOWNERS / workspace ownership map, and the previous run's summary for that workspace (for a delta narrative)

layers.name: fleet_rollup
layers.consumes: all 40 workspace_summary ops
layers.reads_artifacts: CIS AWS Foundations / SOC 2 control mapping document

layers.name: sinks
layers.consumes: workspace_summary (18 jira_upsert ops) + fleet_rollup (dashboard_write, slack_post)
layers.reads_artifacts: existing Jira issue index for dedup

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 4% on a quiet weekend night to 35%+ on a night when the Checkov pack, a provider pin, or the prompt/policy preamble moved; ~100% of downstream model-op keys invalidate on those days regardless of how few leaves moved
change_rate.basis:
This is a blend of one sourced component and one estimated component, and I want to be explicit about which is which because they point in opposite directions.

SOURCED (the ~1,800 repo/policy artifacts, ~21% of the input set): the median GitHub pull request modifies 2 files (measured across both human and agentic PRs); commit size is heavy-tailed, so a small number of commits touch hundreds of files. Jiang & Adams (MSR 2015, 'Co-evolution of infrastructure and source code', OpenStack) found IaC specification files are large and churn frequently — comparable to test files — and the 2025 OpenStack IaC code-review study (>300k reviews) found IaC changes carry 1.82x the churn of non-IaC changes. At 3-8 IaC commits/day for this team, that is ~10-25 changed .tf files per night out of 1,150, i.e. 1-2% of the repo artifacts. I am confident in this half.

ESTIMATED (the ~5,800 live cloud resource observations, ~69% of the input set): I found no published measurement of night-over-night attribute churn in Terraform state, and I do not believe one exists. My estimate is ~12% of resource observations differ by raw content hash between consecutive nightly refreshes. The reasoning is mechanical rather than intuitive: the resources touched by application deploys (ECS services and their task-definition revisions, Lambda last_modified/version/source_code_hash, ASG and EKS nodegroup desired capacity, target-group attachments, Route53 weights) are 8-15% of a typical SaaS fleet and change on every deploy; a further 1-2% carry attributes that move on a clock regardless of activity (e.g. aws_db_instance.latest_restorable_time). This is exactly the 'phantom diff' phenomenon that makes lifecycle{ignore_changes} standard practice — the Terraform community's own advice is that ignoring desired_capacity is 'almost always necessary' for ASGs and task_definition equally so for ECS. Note the crucial asymmetry: ignore_changes suppresses these in the plan DIFF, but the refresh still writes the new attribute values into state, so the raw state artifact hash changes anyway. Anything that hashes state naively sees the noise; anything that hashes the plan diff sees less of it.

So there are two honest numbers, not one. Raw content-hash change rate: ~9.5% of 8,400 artifacts (27 repo files + ~700 live observations). Semantic change rate after the volatile-attribute canonicalizer: ~1.6% — about 75 of 5,800 resources show a real diff on any given night, and only ~6 of those are NEW drift not present in the previous night's report (standing unremediated drift dominates the count). The 6x gap between 9.5% and 1.6% is entirely the product of a hand-maintained ~380-entry denylist. That denylist, not the cache, is the load-bearing engineering.
change_rate.where_changes_land:
Bimodal, and the two modes have completely different consequences.

LEAVES (the common case, ~95% of nights): a resource observation changes, invalidating exactly one plan_normalize op, its 1-2 cloudtrail_lookup ops, one drift_triage op, one workspace_summary, and the fleet_rollup. Blast radius per changed leaf is ~5 ops out of 559. Ten changed leaves concentrated in 3 workspaces invalidate maybe 25-40 ops. Reuse survives beautifully here — ~93-95% of model ops would hit a cross-run store.

ROOTS (1-2 nights per week, plus every prompt edit): the Checkov pack version, the .terraform.lock.hcl provider pin, the system/policy preamble, the org exception register, or the model id. Each of these is read by every model op in its layer, so any one of them moving takes the reuse hit rate for that layer to exactly zero. Checkov ships new checks roughly weekly; provider pins move ~monthly; prompt edits happen whenever the team is iterating, which early on is most days. Amortised over a quarter I would expect the realised cross-run hit rate on model ops to be ~70-80%, not the ~95% the leaf-level arithmetic suggests.

The root-vs-leaf split also determines whether reuse is SAFE, not just profitable. A leaf change invalidating a leaf op is correct. A root change is the case where a naive key that omits, say, the exception-register hash would serve a stale 'already excepted' verdict for a risk that was un-excepted this morning. Getting the key composition wrong here does not cost money, it hides a finding.

session_structure:
A competent engineer gets a large win from provider prefix caching on this workload, and the reuse layer has to beat this, not the naive baseline.

WHAT GOES IN THE CACHED PREFIX. Three nested breakpoints (Anthropic allows 4):
- Block A, invariant for the whole run (~19,000 tok): system prompt, the org security-policy document, the drift-classification taxonomy with its decision rules, 8 few-shot examples of correctly-triaged findings, and the CIS/SOC-2 control mapping. Written once at run start, read by all 223 model ops.
- Block B, per-group (~1,800-3,000 tok): for finding_triage this is the rule catalog entry + remediation guidance + the exception-register slice for that rule_id; for drift_triage it is the provider schema fragment for that resource type + the resource-type-specific drift policy.
- Block C, per-call tail (~900-3,000 tok): the actual finding, the normalized before/after, the surrounding .tf context, the CloudTrail actor.

CALL ORDERING. This is where the skill shows. Sort the 120 finding_triage calls by rule_id and the 48 drift_triage calls by resource_type, then execute each group contiguously, so Block B is a live prefix for the 4-12 calls that share it. Do not interleave the two layers. Run one warm-up call per group serially to establish the prefix BEFORE fanning out the rest — under concurrent fan-out every in-flight caller pays the cache-write price rather than the read price, which silently converts a 0.1x line item into a 1.25x one and is the single most common way teams leave the win on the floor.

TTL. The whole nightly run is 20-25 minutes wall clock, so Block A written at t=0 is still live for the last call under the 5-minute TTL only if calls are continuous; use the 1-hour extended TTL and the run comfortably fits inside one window with slack for the terraform plans. This matters: the model ops are gated behind 40 plans that take 2-9 minutes each, so there is a real risk of a >5-minute gap between the first and second model call.

SEPARATE FROM THE CACHE. Batch the per-finding tails: 4-8 findings sharing a rule_id go in ONE call with a structured JSON output array rather than 8 calls. That alone removes ~40% of the call count without touching the cache. Also drop the exposure_reasoning graph payload to a pruned 2-hop neighbourhood rather than the full workspace graph.

WHAT THE TUNED BASELINE ACHIEVES. Of 1.66M input tokens per run, ~72% land as cache reads at 0.1x, ~6% as cache writes at 1.25x, ~22% fresh. Effective input multiplier 0.37x. At Sonnet rates that is ~$1.82 input + ~$1.49 output = ~$3.31 per nightly run, versus ~$6.46 with caching off. Roughly a 2x total-cost improvement, and ~5x on the input line alone.

AND THE GAP THE REUSE LAYER IS AIMED AT: the provider cache TTL is at most an hour. Between two nightly runs 24 hours apart the carryover is exactly zero. The provider mechanism cannot see across runs at all — that, and only that, is the opening.
grader:
Fully synthetic, seeded, no LLM anywhere in the grading path. Ground truth is written before the run, so it is exact and free.

GENERATOR. A Python script `gen_fleet.py --seed S --workspaces 40` emits (a) a Terraform monorepo from 9 parameterised root-module templates (vpc, eks-cluster, rds-postgres, s3-static-site, lambda-api, ecs-service, iam-baseline, cloudfront-cdn, msk) with randomised names/CIDRs/tags, targeting the measured corpus shape (~29 .tf files and ~145 resources per workspace, ~52 lines per file); and (b) a `live_state.json` per workspace, derived from the config-implied state and then perturbed by a seeded mutation script. No cloud account, no network, no cost.

MUTATION CATALOG (each mutation appends one exact record to ground_truth.jsonl):
- DRIFT_ATTR(addr, attr, old, new) — real out-of-band change. ~60 per fleet.
- DRIFT_DELETE(addr) — resource removed outside Terraform. ~4.
- UNMANAGED_ADD(addr, type) — resource exists in cloud, absent from state. ~11.
- POLICY_VIOLATION(rule_id, addr) — config edited to violate a specific Checkov/Rego rule, with the rule id and CIS control recorded. ~35, drawn from the real policy ids so a real scanner can corroborate.
- EXCEPTED_VIOLATION(rule_id, addr, exception_id) — a violation that IS covered by an entry the generator also wrote into the exception register. Correct behaviour is to report it as suppressed, not as actionable. ~9. This is the trap for over-eager triage.
- VOLATILE_NOISE(addr, attr) — a mutation drawn only from the denylist (ASG desired_capacity, Lambda last_modified, ECS task_definition revision, IAM policy JSON key reordering, SG rule reordering). ~700, matching the measured ~12% raw-churn estimate. Correct behaviour is to emit NOTHING.
- EXPOSURE_CHAIN(addrs[]) — a multi-resource combination (public subnet + 0.0.0.0/0 SG + IGW route + public ALB fronting an unauthenticated target) where no single resource violates any single rule. ~5. Only the graph reasoning layer can find these; a per-resource scanner provably cannot.

CONTRACT. The pipeline writes findings.jsonl of {resource_address, finding_type, rule_id, severity, verdict, workspace} plus rollup.json of integer counts.

SCORE (all set/integer arithmetic):
1. micro-F1 of reported (resource_address, finding_type, rule_id) triples against the non-noise ground-truth records. PASS >= 0.95.
2. Noise false-positive rate = |findings on VOLATILE_NOISE addresses| / |VOLATILE_NOISE records|. PASS <= 0.02. This is the metric that actually separates systems.
3. Exception handling: every EXCEPTED_VIOLATION must appear with verdict=="suppressed" and the matching exception_id. Exact match required.
4. Severity fidelity: reported severity must equal the catalog severity for that rule_id. Exact string equality.
5. Rollup consistency: rollup.json counts must equal counts computed directly from findings.jsonl. Integer equality — catches a summarisation layer that invents or drops findings.

REUSE-SPECIFIC GRADE (the part that matters for evaluating the store, and the reason to build this rather than reuse an existing IaC benchmark). Generate run N+1 from seed S with `--evolve` applying a realistic delta: 1.6% of leaves semantically changed, 12% raw-churned, plus three switchable root perturbations (--bump-policy-pack, --bump-provider-pin, --edit-preamble). Then require that findings.jsonl from the incremental run is BYTE-IDENTICAL to findings.jsonl from a cold from-scratch run on the same inputs. Report alongside it: model-op store hit rate, wall clock, and total provider spend. A system that gets a 95% hit rate but fails byte-identity has not saved money, it has silently dropped a finding — and on this workload that is a compliance incident, not a regression.
reuse_story:
Between two nightly runs the config is ~98.5% unchanged and, after the volatile-attribute canonicalizer, ~98.4% of resource observations are semantically identical. The 223 model ops are keyed on (normalized resource record or finding record, rule/schema fragment, exception-register hash, policy-pack version, prompt version, model id). On a typical night ~6 of 75 drift records and ~4 of 340 static findings are genuinely new, so ~93-95% of leaf-level model ops (drift_triage, finding_triage) hit the store. The upper layers do not: workspace_summary regenerates for any workspace with any changed child (~11 of 40 nightly), and fleet_rollup regenerates essentially every night because its fan-in of 40 makes it near-certain that something moved. That is fine — those are 41 of 223 ops.

The mechanism the provider cannot replicate is simply time: prefix caching expires within an hour, and these runs are 24 hours apart, so provider-side carryover across runs is exactly zero no matter how well the engineer tunes it. Everything the reuse layer wins here is win the provider structurally cannot offer.

A secondary and possibly larger win is consistency rather than cost. Today a resource that nobody touched can be classified "benign" on Monday and "security-relevant" on Tuesday purely from sampling variance, which destroys trust in the nightly report and produces phantom Jira churn. Serving the same key from the store makes the report stable by construction, and stability is the property this buyer actually complains about. Cross-user reuse is also plausible for the finding_triage layer specifically: (rule_id, canonicalised resource shape) recurs across customers because everyone's aws_s3_bucket looks broadly alike — though see the threats, because this is where it gets dangerous.
reuse_threats:
1. THE DOLLARS ARE SMALL, AND THIS IS THE main objection. The tuned baseline costs ~$3.31 per nightly run. Even a perfect 100% cross-run hit rate saves under $3.31/night, ~$1,200/year for this customer. Scale to a genuine enterprise fleet (400 workspaces, 60k resources) and it is ~$17k/year. Real, but it is not a line item anyone escalates about, and the reuse layer has to be nearly free to operate to net out positive. Wall clock is no better a story: the run is dominated by 40 live `terraform plan -refresh-only` calls at 2-9 minutes each, which are impure and can never be reuse-keyed. Eliminating 95% of model-op latency cuts total run time by roughly a quarter.

2. FOUR SINGLE POINTS OF TOTAL INVALIDATION. The Checkov pack (moves ~weekly), the provider pin (~monthly), the prompt/policy preamble (whenever anyone iterates), and the model id each sit upstream of every model op in their layer. On those nights the hit rate is 0% and you have paid storage plus key-computation for nothing. Amortised realised hit rate is more like 70-80% than 95%. You can mitigate by keying finding_triage on the specific rule definition rather than the whole pack version — but that is a real engineering project against a tool that does not expose per-rule content hashes, and it is exactly the kind of optimisation that silently goes stale.

3. THE CANONICALIZER IS THE PRODUCT AND IT IS A CORRECTNESS HAZARD. Without the ~380-entry volatile-attribute denylist, the raw leaf change rate is ~12% and the reuse win largely evaporates. With it, the win is real — but the denylist is hand-maintained per provider, per resource type, and drifts behind provider releases. Suppress one field too many and you have built a system that reliably hides a real change. On this workload the failure mode of a bad cache is not a wrong answer, it is a missing answer, which is the one failure mode nobody notices until the audit.

4. COMPLIANCE MAY REJECT CACHED VERDICTS OUTRIGHT. The SOC 2 / CIS use case is an explicit demand that every resource be evaluated on a cadence. "We served last night's verdict from a store because the bytes matched" is defensible engineering and an awkward conversation with an auditor. Expect to need a periodic forced-cold run (weekly at minimum), which caps the achievable savings further.

5. STALE-SAFE-VERDICT RISK. A cached "benign" for an unchanged resource is correct only if the world's judgement of that configuration has not changed. New CVEs, new CIS revisions, and new attack classes change the verdict on byte-identical config. The policy-pack version in the key covers the Checkov-encoded half of that; it does not cover the model's own evolving judgement, which is precisely the part the customer is paying for.

6. CROSS-USER REUSE IS A LEAK SURFACE. Sharing finding_triage results across customers requires the key to include only the canonicalised resource shape — but the inputs to those ops include the customer's exception register, module source, and CloudTrail principals. Any imprecision in what is hashed versus what is sent becomes a cross-tenant data path in a security product. I would not ship cross-user reuse on this workload without the key being computed over a provably-redacted input, and that redaction costs accuracy.

7. THE HONEST COMPARISON. On the per-PR cadence (the other way this pipeline runs), the tuned provider cache already handles the intra-run repetition well, and consecutive PRs touch different workspaces, so cross-run overlap is much lower than the nightly figure. The nightly cadence is where reuse looks good; do not generalise its numbers to the PR path.
confidence:
Medium overall, with a clear split by component.

HIGH confidence: the graph SHAPE (layered-DAG, wide base, narrow apex, impure plan layer at depth 3), the existence and severity of the volatile-attribute problem, the tuned-baseline structure, and the grader design. These follow from how Terraform, Checkov, OPA and provider prefix caching actually work and I would defend them as written.

MEDIUM confidence: operation counts and token sizes. 559 ops / 223 model ops / 8,400 artifacts is a coherent instance for a 40-workspace, 5,800-resource fleet, anchored on published corpus stats (76 .tf files and ~52 lines/file mean across 41,550 scripts; median 56 Checkov checks triggered per AWS repo with 44-69% pass rates; 100-750 resources per state as the HashiCorp-recommended band). But the exact fan-out of findings into model calls is a design choice a real customer would make differently, and a factor of 2 either way is entirely plausible.

LOW confidence: the 12% raw night-over-night live-state churn figure. It is a mechanical estimate from deploy-touched resource classes, not a measurement, and I could not find any published number for it. It is also the single most decision-relevant number in this whole spec, because it sets the ceiling on reuse.

WHAT WOULD RAISE IT: (a) two consecutive nights of `terraform show -json` from one real fleet, diffed at the attribute level with and without a denylist — that one artifact converts the low-confidence number to measured, and it is a half-day of work for any customer willing to share it; (b) a month of Checkov release-tag timestamps to pin the root-invalidation frequency exactly rather than "roughly weekly"; (c) a Spacelift/env0/Firefly drift-event export to replace my estimated 75-standing/6-new drift split. Absent (a), I would not quote the 93-95% leaf hit rate to anyone as anything other than an upper bound.

Sources: [Firefly State of IaC 2025](https://www.firefly.ai/state-of-iac-2025), [Assessing the adoption of security policies by developers in Terraform (812 projects, Empirical Software Engineering)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11868142/), [Exploring Security Practices in Infrastructure as Code (549 repos / 41,550 scripts)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.03952), [Towards understanding code review practices for IaC: OpenStack (>300k reviews, 1.82x churn)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10664-025-10654-w), [On the Use of Agentic Coding: PR size, median 2 files](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.14745v3), [Characterizing Commits in Open-Source Software](https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3571473.3571508), [driftctl / infrastructure drift survey of ~200 teams](https://www.infoq.com/news/2021/01/infrastructure-drift-driftctl/), [Checkov policy count](https://www.checkov.io/7.Scan%20Examples/Terraform%20Plan%20Scanning.html), [Terraform phantom diffs / ignore_changes](https://encore.dev/articles/terraform-phantom-diffs), [Terraform state sizing](https://medium.com/@alexott_en/working-with-huge-terraform-states-2cb493db5352).

customer: A ~250-engineer B2B SaaS company running ~90 microservices on Kubernetes across 3 regions, monitored by Prometheus/Alertmanager plus ~60 Datadog monitors. Roughly 1,200 alerts/day reach the triage path (consistent with the "500-1,200 alerts/day is where engineers tune out" band in the DevOps.com/Catchpoint-derived reporting), producing on the order of 8-15 real incidents/day — an alert:incident ratio of ~80:1 raw, ~10:1 after the vendor's rule-based dedup, which the pingfatigue/Google-SRE table classifies as "painful". Today they pay for: (1) PagerDuty/incident.io seats plus event volume, (2) an "AI on-call / AIOps" add-on — either a vendor (BigPanda, incident.io AI, Datadog Watchdog/Bits) or, increasingly, an in-house triage service built on the Claude or OpenAI API, and (3) the real cost, engineer-hours: ~70% of SREs report on-call stress driving burnout/attrition (Catchpoint SRE Report 2025). The LLM API bill sits with whoever owns the triage service — the vendor if bought, the platform team if built. That API bill, currently in the low-thousands-of-dollars-per-month range for a shop this size, is the only thing a reuse layer can cut. Note that a reuse layer sells to the *builder* of the triage service, not to the SaaS company: the buyer's felt problem is latency and page quality, not tokens.
why_repeated: This is not a workload that is "run again" in the batch-job sense — it is a permanently running control loop, which is a much stronger repeat premise. The triage service wakes on a fixed tick and processes a sliding window of alerts. I am anchoring the window geometry on the only published production parameters I could find for exactly this pipeline: Huawei Cloud X's deployed alert-aggregation system (COLA, ICSE-SEIP 2024, arXiv 2403.06485) uses a 10-minute aggregation window with a 50% slide. So consecutive runs *overlap by construction*: half of the alerts in run N were also in run N-1. On top of that, the alert population itself is heavily repetitive.
