Alertmanager's own dedup key is fingerprint = hash(alertname + sorted labels); a condition that stays true stays FIRING across many evaluation cycles and is re-sent every repeat_interval. And the fingerprint distribution is Pareto: in the mature alarm-management literature the top 10-20 alarms produce 50-80% of all annunciations. So the same ~120 alert fingerprints generate the large majority of the work, every day, on every shift, for years. The stable corpora are enormous relative to the volatile input: Cloud X carries 3,000 SOPs of 3-4 A4 pages each; our customer carries ~180 runbooks and ~1,400 historical postmortems, and those barely move.
run_cadence: Every 5 minutes, continuously — 288 runs/day, 105,000 runs/year, per tenant. Window is 10 minutes wide with a 5-minute slide (50% overlap), matching COLA's deployed configuration. Volume is diurnal (roughly 2.5x day-vs-night) and has a heavy tail: during an alert storm a single window carries 300-800 alerts instead of the typical 24. The storms are ~1% of windows and are where essentially all of the business value of the system lives.

graph.description:
One run = one 10-minute triage window. Shape is a wide fan-out at the per-alert layer, a HARD fan-in to a single correlation op, a modest fan-out to per-candidate-incident evidence gathering and reasoning, then a fan-in to one policy op and three side-effecting actions.

Typical window composition (the generator must reproduce this): 24 alert records, of which ~18 are continuations/re-sends of alerts already firing at the start of the window and ~6 are newly-fired fingerprints. Those 24 alerts resolve to 3 candidate incidents (2 attaching to already-open incidents, 1 genuinely new) plus ~9 alerts classified as noise/suppressible.

Edge structure, exactly: each alert_normalize op consumes ingest_fetch[alert_window] and ingest_fetch[catalog] (2 edges x 24 = 48). correlate_cluster consumes ALL 24 alert_normalize outputs plus ingest_fetch[deploys, open_incidents, dep_graph] (27 edges). Each evidence_gather op consumes correlate_cluster (18 edges). Each incident_triage op consumes correlate_cluster plus its own 6 evidence_gather ops (7 x 3 = 21 edges). policy_decide consumes the 3 incident_triage outputs plus ingest_fetch[open_incidents] (4 edges). Each act_sideeffect consumes policy_decide (3 edges). Total 121 edges over 55 ops.

The single most important structural fact: correlate_cluster fans in over every alert_normalize output in the window. Because ~6 genuinely new fingerprints arrive in a typical window, its transitive key changes on essentially every run, and with it every op at depth 3 and below. The reusable surface is therefore confined to layer 2 (alert_normalize) — 24 small ops — while layers 4-6 (the expensive ones, 57k input tokens of runbook-grounded reasoning) recompute every time. Nominal per-run totals: ~162,600 input tokens, ~7,170 output tokens.

Non-cacheable by construction and must be excluded from any reuse store: act_sideeffect (paging a human, creating an incident, posting to Slack), and the PromQL/log sub-ops of evidence_gather (they are queries over [now-15m], so their key can never repeat, and they sit directly upstream of the most expensive layer).

layers.name: ingest_fetch
layers.consumes: nothing — these are the graph roots
layers.reads_artifacts: (1) Alertmanager /api/v2/alerts for the 10-min window -> 24 alert JSON records; (2) incident tracker open-incident list -> ~6 open incidents with alert-set and timeline; (3) CI/CD deploy feed, trailing 6 hours -> ~40 deploy records; (4) Backstage service catalog -> 90 services with owner/team/tier/oncall-rotation; (5) service-mesh dependency graph -> ~90 services, ~230 edges, recomputed hourly

layers.name: alert_normalize
layers.consumes: ingest_fetch — 2 of the 5 ops per alert (alert_window slice + catalog slice); 1 alert record each
layers.reads_artifacts: one Alertmanager alert JSON (labels, annotations.summary, annotations.description, startsAt/endsAt, generatorURL, fingerprint) plus the matching alert-rule definition (PromQL expr, for-duration, annotation templates) from the ~340-rule catalog

layers.name: correlate_cluster
layers.consumes: ALL 24 alert_normalize outputs (24 x 180 tok) + 3 ingest_fetch ops (dep graph 2,000, open incidents 3,000, deploys 1,600)
layers.reads_artifacts: none directly — operates on upstream outputs only

layers.name: evidence_gather
layers.consumes: correlate_cluster (1 edge each). Composition: 3 runbook searches (1/incident, BM25+vector, returns top-3 runbooks), 3 past-incident searches (returns top-5 summaries), 9 PromQL/Datadog metric queries (3/incident: error rate, latency p99, saturation), 3 log-pattern queries
layers.reads_artifacts: runbook corpus (180 markdown files, ~2,400 tok each — 9 distinct files touched per run); past-incident index (~1,400 postmortem summaries, ~350 tok each — 15 touched); live Prometheus TSDB over [now-15m]; Loki/Datadog log store over the window

layers.name: incident_triage
layers.consumes: correlate_cluster (1) + its own 6 evidence_gather ops. Per op: cluster's normalized alerts ~900, 3 runbooks ~7,200, 5 past-incident summaries ~1,750, 3 metric results ~2,700, log sample ~1,500, deploy window ~1,600, system prompt/severity rubric/output schema ~3,400
layers.reads_artifacts: indirectly the runbooks and postmortems surfaced by evidence_gather; directly, the severity policy document and the team escalation matrix

layers.name: policy_decide
layers.consumes: 3 incident_triage outputs (2,100) + ingest_fetch[open_incidents] (3,000) + on-call schedule and suppression/maintenance-window policy (~3,100 in the prompt)
layers.reads_artifacts: on-call rotation schedule, active maintenance windows, per-team paging policy and quiet hours

layers.name: act_sideeffect
layers.consumes: policy_decide (1 edge each): create_or_update_incident, post_to_incident_channel, page_oncall
layers.reads_artifacts: none — these WRITE. Must never be served from a reuse store; a cache hit here silently stops paging a human, which is a safety incident, not a cost regression

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 16% (with an aggressive volatile-field canonicalizer, quiet window) to 100% (alert storm, or naive byte-hashing of the rolling-window artifacts)
change_rate.basis:
ESTIMATE, derived from documented mechanism rather than measured. I searched for a published measurement of alert-payload byte churn between consecutive monitoring windows and could not find one — it does not appear to exist in the literature. What IS sourced: the 10-minute window with 50% slide (COLA/Huawei Cloud X, arXiv 2403.06485, deployed in production over 500,000 alerts across 60+ services, Jan-Jun 2023); Alertmanager's dedup semantics (fingerprint = hash(alertname + sorted labels), firing alerts persist and re-send every repeat_interval); the Pareto concentration of alert volume (top 10-20 rules = 50-80% of annunciations, alarm-management literature via exida); SOP corpus size and page-count (3,000 SOPs at 3-4 A4 pages, same paper); deploy frequency bands (DORA 2025 — only 16.2% of orgs deploy on-demand; a 90-service shop at ~20 deploys/business day). The 38% is my arithmetic over those mechanisms, per artifact class:

- Alert payloads (24 of 67 artifacts): under naive byte hashing, 24/24 change every run. Every re-send carries a fresh endsAt, a fresh current-value interpolated into annotations.description, a fresh generatorURL timestamp, and often a fresh pod-name suffix. Under a canonicalizer that strips volatile fields and keys on {alertname, sorted labels, severity, annotation template}, ~10/24 change (the ~6 new fingerprints plus state transitions).
- Deploy feed (1): rolling 6-hour window, so entries age OUT every run even when nothing is deployed. Byte-changes 100% of runs; canonical set-of-deploy-IDs changes ~21% of runs (2.5 deploys/hr against a 5-min tick).
- Open incident state (1): changes on ~40% of runs from human acks/comments/resolutions.
- Dependency graph (1): topology weekly; edge weights hourly, i.e. 1 run in 12.
- Alert rule definitions (15 touched of ~340): monitoring-rule PRs land maybe 5/week, so P(change in any given 5-min run) ~= 0.25%.
- Service catalog (1): effectively 0% per run.
- Runbooks (9 touched of 180): ~15 edits/month over 180 files = ~0.001% per run. Effectively frozen.
- Past-incident corpus (15 touched of ~1,400): append-only, +3-8/week; the retrieved top-5 changes only when a similar new incident lands. ~0% per run.

Naive total: (24 + 1 + 0.4 + 0.08 + ~0) / 67 = 38%. Canonicalized: ~10.6/67 = 16%. Separately, the 12 metric/log tool results are 100% novel every run and are not counted in the 67 because they are op outputs, not external artifacts — but they matter more than any of the above, see below.
change_rate.where_changes_land:
At the roots, and specifically in the widest layer — the worst possible placement for a transitively-composed key, and I want to be blunt that this is not a close call.

Every changed alert invalidates its own alert_normalize op, which is fine and expected. The problem is correlate_cluster: it fans in over ALL 24 alert_normalize outputs. A typical window contains ~6 genuinely new fingerprints, so correlate_cluster's key changes on essentially 100% of runs, and everything at depth 3 through 7 — all 18 evidence_gather ops, all 3 incident_triage ops (57,000 input tokens, the expensive layer), policy_decide, and the actions — recomputes unconditionally. Reuse is structurally confined to layer 2, which is also the cheapest layer.

Compounding this, the metric and log sub-ops of evidence_gather are queries over [now-15m] against a live TSDB. Their keys can NEVER repeat, by construction, and they sit directly upstream of incident_triage. So even if you somehow fixed the correlate_cluster fan-in, incident_triage would still miss.

The inverse is also true and is the one genuinely good piece of news: the *large* artifacts are the *stable* ones. Runbooks (180 x 2,400 tok = 432k), the past-incident corpus (~490k), the service catalog, the rule catalog — these are 80%+ of the nominal token mass of the system and they move on a scale of weeks. But that is precisely the mass the provider's own prefix cache already captures for free, which is why it is not available as a differentiator (see the baseline).

The actionable finding: the reuse layer's payoff here is gated on an architectural change to the customer's graph — decomposing correlate_cluster from one all-window fan-in into N incremental pairwise ops (new alert vs each open cluster) — not on anything the store itself does. If a vendor cannot get customers to restructure, layers 3-7 never hit.

session_structure:
This workload is close to the best case for provider-native prefix caching and the tuned baseline is genuinely strong. A competent engineer does the following, and any reuse layer has to beat this, not a naive implementation.

CADENCE IS THE GIFT. Runs happen every 5 minutes, forever, 288/day. A 5-minute-TTL cache races the tick boundary, so use the 1-hour TTL tier (2x write, 0.1x read, anthropic-beta: extended-cache-ttl-2025-04-11). At ~1,200 cache reads/day against a handful of writes, the 2x write premium is noise. Unlike bursty workloads, the prefix here is essentially never cold — TTL expiry is a non-issue. This removes the single biggest structural advantage a cross-run store normally has.

LAYER 2 (alert_normalize, 24 calls/run, ~6,900 calls/day). One static prefix carrying: system prompt + symptom taxonomy + few-shot examples (~2,800), the FULL 90-service catalog (~5,400), and the FULL ~340-rule alert-rule catalog (~85,000, hoisted rather than retrieved per-alert). Mark one cache_control breakpoint at the end of that block: ~93,000 cached tokens. Per-call variable suffix is just the alert JSON, ~600 tokens. These are 24 independent single-turn calls, NOT a conversation — threading them would add nothing and would serialize the fan-out.
  CRITICAL SEQUENCING: do not launch the 24 calls concurrently from cold. Concurrent fan-out makes every one of the N callers pay the cache write, because none of them sees the others' write land. Issue one warm-up call, await it, then fan out the remaining 23. On a continuously-running loop this only matters on the first tick after a deploy or a model change, but that is exactly when a naive implementation eats a 24x write.

LAYER 3 (correlate_cluster, 1 call/run). Order the message most-stable-first so the breakpoint falls as late as possible: clustering rubric + output schema (~1,900) -> dependency graph (~2,000) -> breakpoint -> open incidents (~3,000) -> deploys (~1,600) -> this window's 24 normalized records (~4,320). ~3,900 cached, ~8,900 uncached. Do not try to cache past the dependency graph; it moves hourly and a stale-prefix miss costs more than the read discount saves.

LAYER 5 (incident_triage, 3 calls/run) — this is where the real money is and where the strongest baseline move lives. Rather than retrieving 3 runbooks per incident and paying full input rate on ~7,200 tokens each time, hoist the top ~40 runbooks by historical retrieval frequency into the static cached prefix. Pareto says those 40 cover ~80% of alerts. That is ~96,000 tokens read at 0.1x on every triage call instead of ~7,200 read at 1.0x. Do the same for the top ~200 past-incident summaries (~70,000 tokens). Add triage policy, severity rubric, escalation matrix, output schema (~3,400). Total cached prefix ~170,000 tokens; per-call variable suffix is only the cluster's normalized alerts (~900), the fresh metric results (~2,700), and the log sample (~1,500) — about 5,100 uncached tokens. Fall back to retrieval only for the ~20% tail.

LAYER 6 (policy_decide, 1 call/run). Suppression policy, escalation matrix, on-call schedule in the cached prefix (~3,100); the 3 triage verdicts plus open-incident state as suffix (~2,100).

NET EFFECT OF THE TUNED BASELINE. Nominal input is ~162,600 tok/run before hoisting and roughly 430,000 after (because hoisting deliberately inflates nominal input to convert it into cached input). Of that, ~93,000 (L2) + ~3,900 (L3) + ~170,000 x 3 (L5) + ~3,100 (L6) is served at 0.1x. What remains at full rate: 24 x 600 alert bodies (14,400) + L3's 8,900 suffix + 3 x 5,100 triage suffixes (15,300) + L6's 2,100 = about 40,700 genuinely uncached input tokens per run, plus ~7,170 output tokens which no cache discounts.

So the tuned baseline has already reduced the effective input bill by roughly 75-80% relative to naive, and it did so on exactly the artifacts (runbooks, catalogs, rubrics, postmortems) that a cross-run reuse store would otherwise have claimed as its win. Any reuse layer is competing for the residual ~40,700 uncached input tokens and ~7,170 output tokens per run.

One more baseline move worth naming because it is free and often missed: pin the model id and set temperature 0 for L2 and L3. Not for cost — for prefix stability and for making the graph's output hashes reproducible at all.
grader:
DETERMINISTIC, NO LLM, EXACT AND FREE GROUND TRUTH — achieved by generating the world from a seed, because real alert data has no free exact ground truth (incident membership is a human judgement call and postmortem labels are inconsistent).

FIXTURE UNIVERSE (seeded once, committed as byte-stable files — this also honestly tests the reuse layer's "stable artifacts" assumption): 90 services with a declared dependency DAG (~230 edges), 340 alert rule definitions, 180 runbook markdown files (~2,400 tokens each, each mapped to exactly one fault_type), 1,400 past-incident records, a service->owning-team map, an on-call schedule, and a severity policy.

GROUND-TRUTH GENERATION. Sample a seeded sequence of root faults: (service, fault_type, t0, severity_class). Propagate each through the dependency DAG with deterministic per-edge propagation latency and a declared blast radius (descendants within k hops), emitting alerts stamped with true_incident_id, true_root_service, true_fault_type, true_runbook_id. Independently emit noise alerts with true_incident_id = null at a seeded rate calibrated to a 10:1 alert:incident ratio (the "painful" band in the Google-SRE-derived table). Replay 288 consecutive 5-minute windows = one simulated day = 288 runs, with the 10-minute/50%-overlap geometry so consecutive runs share half their alerts exactly as production does.

MANDATORY GENERATOR PROPERTY — without this the benchmark flatters the reuse layer and is worthless: every alert emission must inject fresh volatile fields into the payload — current metric value interpolated into annotations.description, a fresh k8s pod-name suffix, endsAt, updatedAt, and a timestamped generatorURL — at rates matched to real Alertmanager re-send behaviour. Byte-level reuse must be forced to fail on re-sends, because it fails on re-sends in production. A generator that emits byte-identical repeat alerts is measuring a fiction.

SCORED QUANTITIES, all exact, all pure-Python over the emitted JSON:
1. CLUSTERING. Compare the emitted partition of the window's alerts to the ground-truth partition by Adjusted Rand Index (closed-form, deterministic). Also report raw pair-counts (TP/FP/FN on same-incident pairs).
2. ROOT-CAUSE SERVICE. Exact string equality against the seeded root fault's service. Per-incident 0/1.
3. PAGE vs SUPPRESS. Ground truth = (true_incident_id != null AND true_severity_class in {sev1, sev2}). Exact 0/1, scored as F1.
4. OWNING TEAM. Exact match against the fixture catalog's owner field.
5. RUNBOOK SELECTION. Exact match against the seeded fault_type -> runbook_id map.
6. ATTACH-vs-NEW. Exact 0/1 against whether that root fault was already open at window start.

COMPOSITE: score = 0.35*ARI + 0.25*rootcause_acc + 0.20*page_F1 + 0.10*team_acc + 0.10*runbook_acc.
HARD GATE, not averaged in: false_suppress_rate on sev1 ground truth must be <= 0.01. A missed page is categorically different from a wrong team assignment and must not be tradeable against it.

COST/REUSE MEASUREMENT rides alongside and is only valid if quality holds. Replay all 288 windows twice — cold store and warm store — and compare effective input tokens (cached tokens counted at 0.1x, cache writes at 2x) against the tuned-prefix-cache baseline running the identical replay. A reuse layer's saving only counts if the composite score moves by less than 0.01 ARI and the false_suppress gate still passes. Otherwise it bought savings with quality, which in this domain means it stopped paging someone.
reuse_story:
The honest positive case has three legs, and only the first is strong.

1. LAYER-2 FINGERPRINT REUSE IS REAL AND CROSS-TENANT. alert_normalize is 24 of the 29 model ops. Its input is one alert plus one rule definition, and under a canonicalizer that strips volatile fields the key repeats constantly: alert fingerprints are Pareto-distributed (top 10-20 rules = 50-80% of volume), firing alerts re-send for hours, and the window slides at 50% overlap. Steady-state hit rate of 55-75% on this layer is credible. Crucially, this reuse is shareable ACROSS CUSTOMERS in a way code reuse never is: KubePodCrashLooping / CPUThrottlingHigh / TargetDown on a labelled service normalize identically for every Prometheus shop on earth. A multi-tenant vendor's store gets denser with every tenant added, and the ~120-fingerprint head is shared by all of them. That is a genuine compounding asset.

2. LATENCY, NOT TOKENS, IS THE SELLABLE WIN. A 5-minute triage loop with 24 parallel normalization calls has a real wall-clock budget. Serving 14 of 24 from a store collapses the layer-2 critical path to near zero and leaves the budget for the deep triage calls. The buyer feels this; they do not feel the token line.

3. OUTPUT TOKENS ARE UNDISCOUNTED. Prefix caching gives 0% on output. Layer 2 emits 24 x 180 = 4,320 output tokens/run, ~1.24M/day/tenant, at full rate. A store hit saves 100% of that, whereas the tuned baseline saves 0% of it. This is the one axis where the reuse layer is not merely competing for a residual.

Quantified against the tuned baseline: per layer-2 call the baseline pays ~93,000 x 0.1 + 600 = ~9,900 effective input tokens plus 180 output. A store hit saves all of it. At ~14 hits/run that is ~139,000 effective input + 2,520 output tokens saved per run — which, measured against the tuned baseline's total, lands in the region of 10-18% of effective input and ~35% of output tokens. That is a real number and it is not zero. It is also, notably, entirely from the cheapest layer, and it evaporates in exactly the windows the customer cares about.
reuse_threats:
Eight specific reasons this does not pay off, roughly in order of how much they hurt.

1. THE FAN-IN KILLS EVERYTHING BELOW DEPTH 3. correlate_cluster consumes all 24 alert_normalize outputs. ~6 new fingerprints arrive per window, so its transitive key changes on essentially every run, invalidating all 18 evidence_gather ops, all 3 incident_triage ops (57,000 nominal input tokens — the expensive layer), policy_decide, and the actions. Layer 3+ hit rate is ~0% in practice, not "low". Fixing it requires the CUSTOMER to restructure their clustering into incremental pairwise ops. A store cannot do that for them.

2. TIME-BOUNDED TOOL RESULTS CAN NEVER HIT. The 9 PromQL and 3 log queries are over [now-15m] against a live TSDB. Their keys are novel by construction, forever, and they sit directly upstream of incident_triage. Even a perfect fix to (1) leaves layer 5 missing.

3. THE PROVIDER'S CACHE ALREADY ATE THE STABLE MASS. Runbooks, postmortems, the service catalog, the rule catalog — ~80% of nominal tokens and the only artifacts with a genuinely low change rate — are exactly what a competent engineer hoists into a 1h-TTL cached prefix for free. At a 5-minute run cadence the prefix is never cold and TTL expiry never bites. The reuse layer inherits the residual, not the prize.

4. ROLLING-WINDOW ARTIFACTS ARE SILENT CACHE POISON. "Last 6 hours of deploys" and "last 10 minutes of alerts" byte-change every single run even when nothing happened, purely from entries aging out. Byte-hashing yields 0% reuse on them. Canonicalizing them is the only fix and canonicalization is a correctness liability, not a free win — see (6).

5. STORMS ARE 100% NOVEL. The ~1% of windows that carry 300-800 alerts and justify the system's existence consist almost entirely of never-before-seen fingerprints. Reuse contributes approximately nothing precisely when the customer is watching.

6. STALENESS IS A CORRECTNESS BUG, NOT A COST TRADE-OFF. Serving a triage verdict for a fingerprint seen 3 days ago is actively wrong if the service has since been redeployed, rescaled, or had its dependencies changed. Making the key sound requires folding deploy state, config version, and topology into it — which reintroduces exactly the churn you were trying to eliminate. There is no configuration of this system that is both safe and high-hit-rate; that tension is structural.

7. SIDE-EFFECT OPS MUST BE EXCLUDED, AND THE FAILURE IS SILENT. page_oncall, create_incident, post_to_channel. A cache hit on page_oncall means a human does not get woken up and the system reports success. Every artifact of that failure looks identical to healthy operation. This needs to be an explicit deny-list with a test, not an emergent property of key composition.

8. NON-DETERMINISM THRASHES DOWNSTREAM KEYS. At temperature > 0, alert_normalize emits different JSON for identical input, so its output hash differs, so every descendant key differs even on a layer-2 hit. Requires temperature 0, fixed seed, and a pinned model id — and the pin fights the vendor's need to roll models, since a model bump invalidates the entire store at once.
confidence:
MEDIUM overall, but unevenly distributed, and I want to be explicit about which parts are which.

HIGH confidence: the graph SHAPE and the location of the reuse-killing fan-in. This follows from the documented architecture of every deployed system of this kind, and the window geometry (10 min, 50% slide) is taken directly from Huawei Cloud X's production configuration in arXiv 2403.06485. I am also high-confidence that the tuned prefix-cache baseline described here is achievable and that it captures most of the stable token mass — the caching mechanics are documented and the 5-minute cadence against a 1-hour TTL makes it trivially warm.

MEDIUM confidence: operation counts and token sizes. 24 alerts/window and 3 candidate incidents are my arithmetic from ~1,200 alerts/day over a 10-minute window, which is a defensible mid-size-SaaS figure but is a choice, not a measurement. Runbook size (~2,400 tok) is derived from the paper's "3 to 4 A4 pages". Alert payload size (~600 tok) is estimated from the Alertmanager webhook schema; I searched for published byte-size distributions and found none.

LOW confidence: the 38% change rate. It is derived from mechanism, not measured. No one appears to have published the byte-churn of alert payloads between consecutive monitoring windows. The 16-100% range is wide because the answer depends almost entirely on a canonicalizer that is an implementation choice, and I would not defend the point estimate hard.

WHAT WOULD RAISE IT, in order of value per unit effort:
(a) One week of raw Alertmanager webhook payloads from a real 50-100 service shop. That gives the true fingerprint recurrence curve, the true volatile-field churn, and the true storm distribution in a single dataset, and would move the change rate from LOW to HIGH. This is the single highest-value artifact and it is cheap to obtain from any friendly customer.
(b) A trace of an existing LLM triage service's actual call structure — to confirm whether real implementations do the per-alert LLM normalization at all, or handle 70% of it with rules and only escalate the residue. If it is mostly rules, the reusable layer shrinks and the whole case gets materially weaker.
(c) A measurement of how many DISTINCT alert fingerprints a tenant sees in 30 days versus 24 hours. That directly sizes the cross-tenant sharing asset, which is the strongest leg of the reuse story and currently rests on the Pareto assumption alone.

One caveat on framing: this domain looks unusually favourable at first glance (288 runs/day, 50% structural overlap, frozen runbook corpus) and I want to flag that the favourable-looking properties are mostly captured by the free provider cache, while the properties the reuse layer actually needs — a shallow graph and slow-moving leaves — are the ones this workload lacks.

customer: A mid-to-large online retailer's review-intelligence team (the shape is Wayfair's, from arXiv 2509.26103, "End-to-End Aspect-Guided Review Summarization at Scale" — 11.8M reviews, 92k products, 129 reviews/product, 124 chars/review, Gemini 1.5 Flash, A/B tested on 493,208 products across 2,329 product classes in March 2025). The same shape is sold as a product by VoC/review-analytics vendors (Bazaarvoice, Yotpo, Trustpilot, Yogi, Revuze) to CPG and retail brands. What is actually paid for: (1) an aspect-sentiment summary block rendered on every product detail page, which is a conversion lever and therefore has a directly attributable revenue number; (2) a merchandising/quality dashboard where category managers see aspect-sentiment trends ("odor complaints on the Kirby sectional up 40% since the fabric supplier changed") and open supplier-quality tickets. Nobody pays for "sentiment classification." They pay for the PDP block and the ticket. Contract value for a mid-market brand is $2k-$15k/month; the LLM bill underneath it, as costed below, is a small fraction of that — which is itself a load-bearing fact for how much a reuse layer can be worth here.
why_repeated: Reviews arrive continuously and the derived artifacts are stale the moment they do. Three distinct repetition drivers, with very different reuse consequences: (1) NIGHTLY INCREMENTAL — new reviews land, affected product summaries and category rollups must be regenerated. This is ~99.9% unchanged input and is the "repeat run" in the ordinary sense. (2) TRIGGERED PER-PRODUCT REFRESH — Wayfair's published rule: a new product enters the pipeline at 10 accumulated reviews, and an existing product retriggers when new reviews reach 10% of its existing review count. This is a hand-built, coarse-grained reuse mechanism already in production. (3) FULL-CATALOG REBUILD — every prompt edit, model version bump, aspect-taxonomy revision, new-tenant onboarding, or post-bug backfill re-runs the entire corpus. This happens roughly every 2-4 weeks in an actively developed pipeline and is where the real money is spent. The change-rate distribution is therefore bimodal, and quoting only the mean is misleading.
run_cadence: Nightly batch (typically a 01:00-05:00 local window, sized to land before the morning merchandising standup), plus a near-real-time trickle path for the top ~2% of SKUs by traffic. Full-catalog rebuilds every 2-4 weeks on prompt/model/taxonomy change. Benchmark run unit: one nightly refresh over a single category vertical (5,000 SKUs, 640,480 standing reviews), presented as the complete declarative DAG rather than the hand-incrementalised slice.

graph.description: Two enormous wide-independent leaf layers (one materialize op and one model op per review, fan-in 1, no cross-talk) feeding a sharply narrowing tree: 640,480 reviews -> 5,000 product summaries -> 22 category rollups. Depth 8, mean fan-in 2.06, but the mean hides everything: 97.8% of ops sit in the two fan-in-1 leaf layers, while the four ops above them have fan-in 12 / 128 / 130 / 227. The critical honesty point about n_operations: 1,310,156 is the size of the DAG *as declared*, which is what a content-addressed reuse system must key. A competent production implementation executes about 3,257 of those ops on a normal night (0.25%), because it hand-writes the incrementality with a `review_aspects` table keyed on review_id and Wayfair's 10%-new-reviews retrigger rule. The gap between 1.31M and 3.3k is not the reuse system's opportunity — it is the reuse system's *competition*, already shipped, in SQL. Structural landmine: the 14 fetch ops at depth 1 carry a watermark cursor and therefore change their inputs every single run by construction. Under naive transitive keying, those 14 root ops invalidate all 1.31M descendants every night. The graph only has a reuse surface at all if the fetch output is immediately shattered into per-review content-addressed artifacts (the materialize_review layer) and every downstream op keys on the review's own content hash rather than on the fetch op's output hash. Any benchmark that skips the materialize layer will report a spuriously catastrophic result.

layers.name: fetch_review_batch
layers.consumes: nothing - these are the roots (12 syndication/marketplace feeds incl. Bazaarvoice and Yotpo, the first-party review DB, and a returns-comments feed)
layers.reads_artifacts: one source API endpoint or DB table each, plus a per-source watermark cursor file that advances every run

layers.name: materialize_review
layers.consumes: 1 fetch_review_batch op (one fetch fans out to ~46,000 reviews on a full pass, ~34 on a nightly)
layers.reads_artifacts: 1 review record: body text, star rating, ISO date, verified-purchase flag, variant SKU, source id. Deliberately EXCLUDES helpfulness vote counts and moderation status from the content hash - including them multiplies the change rate by ~20x for zero semantic gain. Normalizes, language-detects, PII-scrubs, and emits a content-addressed per-review artifact.

layers.name: extract_aspects
layers.consumes: 1 materialize_review op
layers.reads_artifacts: extraction prompt template + JSON schema + 12 few-shot examples + the frozen canonical aspect vocabulary (1,050 entries for this vertical). Wayfair's version: up to 5 aspects per review with sentiment in {positive, mixed, negative}, structured JSON out. Mean review body 180 chars (~45 tok) + metadata (~20 tok) = 65 variable tokens against a 4,400-token fixed prefix. P95 review is 900 chars (~225 tok).

layers.name: consolidate_aspect
layers.consumes: ~12 extract_aspects ops (the occurrences of one raw surface form)
layers.reads_artifacts: consolidation prompt + an embedding-retrieved shortlist of 40 candidate canonical aspects. Maps raw aspect strings below the 95th-percentile frequency (Wayfair: 30 occurrences) to canonical form. Wayfair's real numbers: 178,054 raw aspects -> 19,014 canonical across the whole catalog; this vertical's slice is 9,200 raw -> 1,050 canonical. Wayfair explicitly caches this mapping, so ~35 of the 9,200 actually execute on a normal night.

layers.name: select_reviews
layers.consumes: all extract_aspects ops for one product (mean 128, P50 41, P90 310, max ~9,000) plus their consolidate_aspect mappings
layers.reads_artifacts: none beyond upstream outputs. Deterministic random weighted sampling proportional to aspect-sentiment pair frequency, capped at Wayfair's 200-review context limit.

layers.name: summarize_product
layers.consumes: 1 select_reviews op + up to 200 extract_aspects ops + up to 200 materialize_review ops
layers.reads_artifacts: summarization prompt template + 1 product metadata record (title, category path, stable attributes; price and stock DELIBERATELY excluded from the hash). Emits a structured aspect object plus Wayfair's 300-500 character prose block. Input is 9,800 tokens mean, ~4,800 at the median product, ~20,700 at a head product - and only ~670 of it (instructions + metadata) is shared across products.

layers.name: category_rollup
layers.consumes: ~227 summarize_product ops per product class
layers.reads_artifacts: rollup prompt template + the aspect-sentiment count matrix for the class. Feeds the merchandising dashboard and the supplier-quality ticket queue.

layers.name: quality_gate
layers.consumes: 1 summarize_product op + 1 select_reviews op
layers.reads_artifacts: banned-claims list + rule file. Pure deterministic code: every aspect named in the summary must appear in the product's extracted aspect set (hallucination gate), length bounds, no PII, no medical/safety claims, representative_review_id must actually carry the tuple it illustrates.

layers.name: publish_summary
layers.consumes: 1 quality_gate op (the ~0.8% that fail the gate are not published and fall back to the previous summary)
layers.reads_artifacts: none. Writes to the PDP content store and the dashboard warehouse table.

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 0.05%-0.4% on ordinary consecutive nights; 100% of model-op keys on the ~1-in-21 night when a prompt template, aspect taxonomy, or model version changes. The distribution is bimodal and the mean is a lie - quote both modes or neither.
change_rate.basis: MIXED - partly sourced, partly estimated, and I will say which is which. SOURCED: (a) Corpus growth. Amazon Reviews 2018 -> Amazon Reviews 2023 (McAuley Lab) grew from ~233M to 570M reviews (~2.4x) over five years, i.e. ~19.6% compound annual growth of the cumulative corpus, meaning annual arrivals run ~16-20% of the standing corpus and DAILY arrivals run ~0.05% of it. 640,480 x 0.05-0.08% = 320-510 new reviews/night; I use 480, which independently cross-checks against Seller Labs' per-SKU guidance of ~2-3 reviews/month for a steady mid-tail product (5,000 SKUs x 2.9/month = 483/day). (b) Retrigger threshold. Wayfair's published production rule - retrigger a product summary when new reviews reach 10% of the existing count - is a direct measurement of how much change the operator considers worth recomputing for. (c) Deletion/moderation. A 335,520-deleted-review analysis (Localo, 2026) plus Google's disclosure of 221M Business Profile review deletions in 2025 supports 5-15% of reviews being removed over their lifetime; at a ~3-year mean lifetime that is ~0.009%/day, or ~58 deletions/night here. ESTIMATED, NOT SOURCED: (d) Review edit rate. The Localo data reports that edited reviews have a 254-day median lifetime vs 60 for unedited but gives no edit RATE; I estimate <1% of e-commerce reviews are ever edited, i.e. <0.005%/day, ~5/night. (e) Product-metadata churn. I could find no published figure. I estimate 30-60% of SKUs see a price change daily but only ~3% see a change to a SUMMARIZATION-RELEVANT field (title, stable attributes, variant merge) - ~150 records/night. This estimate carries the most weight of any unsourced number here, because it is the only large source of change at a non-leaf position. Arithmetic: (480 new + 58 deleted + 5 edited + 150 metadata) / 645,500 artifacts = 0.107%.
change_rate.where_changes_land: Overwhelmingly at the LEAVES, and they are almost all ADDITIONS of immutable artifacts rather than mutations of existing ones - reviews are append-only in the source of truth, which is the most reuse-friendly change profile any workload can have. 480 of the 693 daily changes are brand-new review records with no prior key. That is the good news, and it is exactly why the reuse system's headline number here will look spectacular and mean almost nothing (see reuse_threats). The changes that actually hurt land at ROOTS, and there are two classes. First, the ~1-in-21 prompt/taxonomy/model change: a single artifact edit that invalidates 654,702 model-op keys - correctly, since the outputs genuinely differ, but it means the reuse store's hit rate collapses to zero on precisely the runs that cost the most money. Second, and worse, the 14 fetch ops carry an advancing watermark cursor, so under naive transitive keying they change every night and invalidate everything downstream; this is a design landmine, not a property of the domain. There is also a quiet amplification effect in the middle of the graph: 480 new reviews land in ~410 distinct products, and those 410 products spread across essentially all 22 product classes, so 100% of the category_rollup layer recomputes off 0.11% input change. Total recompute closure: ~3,257 ops (0.25% of the DAG), ~1,097 of them model ops (0.17%).

session_structure:
A competent engineer builds this so that provider prefix caching is close to maximally exploited, and the result is a genuinely hard baseline. Layer by layer:

EXTRACTION (640,480 ops, the volume layer). The prompt is 4,400 fixed tokens against 65 variable - a 98.5% shared prefix, the single best case prefix caching can be handed. Concretely: (1) Freeze the prefix. Order is tools -> system -> messages; put instructions, JSON schema, sentiment label definitions, 12 few-shot examples, and the full 1,050-entry canonical aspect vocabulary in the system block, serialize tools with sorted keys, and put a single cache_control breakpoint on the last system block. No timestamps, no product ids, no per-request UUIDs above the breakpoint. (2) SIZE THE PREFIX PAST THE MODEL'S MINIMUM - this is the trap that silently costs teams everything. A 640k-call classification layer screams for Haiku 4.5, whose minimum cacheable prefix is 4,096 tokens; a natural 1,500-token extraction prompt would silently never cache, with no error, just cache_creation_input_tokens: 0. The competent engineer either pads to ~4,400 with content that also improves accuracy (the full canonical vocabulary, more edge-case few-shots) or moves to a model with a 512/1,024 minimum. (3) PACK, and understand that packing beats caching. One review per call bills 4,400 cached (0.1x) + 65 fresh = ~505 token-equivalents per review. Packing 25 reviews per call bills 4,400 cached + 1,625 fresh = ~83 per review, a 6x win that prefix caching alone cannot approach. Pack deterministically by sorting on review content hash so re-runs produce byte-identical packs. (4) Submit through the Batch API for the additional 50% discount - a nightly job has no latency requirement. (5) Pre-warm with a max_tokens: 0 request before submitting the batch, because concurrent requests inside a batch cannot read a cache entry that none of them has finished writing, and you cannot control ordering within a batch. (6) Use ttl: "1h" for full-catalog rebuilds (25,600 packed calls over hours; write costs 2x, reads cost 0.1x, break-even at 3 reads, trivially met); default 5m is fine for the ~20-call nightly.

SUMMARIZATION (5,000 ops, the money layer). 9,800 input tokens of which only ~670 (instructions + product metadata) is shared. The engineer puts the instruction block above a breakpoint, gets a 6-7% saving, and correctly stops - this layer is structurally prefix-cache-hostile because the payload IS the variance. Runs on a Sonnet-class model, sorted by product so head products with 200-review contexts are batched together.

ROLLUP (22 ops). Opus-class, negligible volume, no caching worth configuring.

Model tiering per layer is standard practice and matters for the baseline because each model has its own cache namespace and its own minimum-prefix threshold.

WHAT THIS BASELINE COSTS, so the reuse layer has a number to beat. Full 640k-review extraction pass: 25,600 packed batched calls = ~$5.63 cached input + ~$20.80 fresh input + ~$176 output = ~$203. Nightly incremental extraction (480 reviews, ~20 calls) = ~$0.14. Nightly summarization (560 affected products) = ~$8.30. Scaled to a full 120k-SKU catalog the nightly bill is roughly $200 and the rebuild is roughly $5k. A reuse layer competing on the extraction layer is competing for fourteen cents a night.

TWO THINGS THE TUNED BASELINE STRUCTURALLY CANNOT DO, which is where any honest reuse claim has to live. (a) Prefix caching has a TTL of minutes to one hour. This workload's cadence is 24 hours. Every provider cache entry is cold-dead before the next run starts, so 100% of CROSS-RUN saving is unavailable to the baseline by construction, and belongs to the reuse layer by default. (b) Prefix caching saves on the shared PREFIX; it can never save on an operation whose entire input is unchanged, because it still pays full output-token price for regenerating an identical answer. On the summarization layer, where output is cheap but the 9,800-token input is unique per product, the reuse layer skips the whole call while the baseline pays ~93% of it. That is the reuse layer's real and only structural edge here.
grader:
Fully deterministic, no LLM in the loop, ground truth exact and free by construction. Three components.

1. GENERATOR (provides free exact ground truth). `gen_review(seed) -> (text, gold_tuples)` builds reviews compositionally from a fixed grammar rather than annotating real ones. 14 aspect slots (delivery_speed, packaging, assembly_difficulty, fabric_quality, color_accuracy, comfort, sturdiness, odor, price_value, customer_service, instructions_clarity, size_accuracy, noise, durability). Each aspect ships 6 positive, 6 negative and 4 mixed surface realizations, plus 3 negated forms and 2 comparative forms per polarity ("not as sturdy as I'd hoped" -> sturdiness/negative), so the generator exercises the failure modes that actually matter. A review = 1-5 aspect clauses sampled without replacement + 0-2 DISTRACTOR clauses that mention an aspect noun with no evaluative content ("the box says assembly required") which must produce NO tuple + a star rating that in 15% of cases deliberately contradicts the text, testing that the model reads the text rather than the rating. Gold label is the exact multiset of (canonical_aspect, polarity) pairs the generator emitted. Cost: zero. Ambiguity: zero.

2. PER-LAYER SCORES.
- extract_aspects: micro-F1 over set comparison of predicted vs gold (canonical_aspect, polarity) tuples, after mapping predicted raw aspect strings through the frozen canonical vocabulary by EXACT string match - no fuzzy matching, no embeddings, the vocabulary is part of the fixture. Distractor clauses contribute only to precision.
- consolidate_aspect: exact-match accuracy of raw-surface-form -> canonical-parent, which the generator knows because it emitted the surface form from the parent.
- summarize_product: this is where benchmarks normally reach for an LLM judge, so the task is redesigned to remove the need. The summary is a STRUCTURED object - {aspects: [{aspect, polarity, mention_count, representative_review_id}], overall_polarity, n_reviews_covered} - which is what the PDP renderer consumes anyway; the prose is a template fill over it. The gold object is then computed exactly by pure code from the gold review tuples: top-k aspects by mention count, majority polarity per aspect, ties broken by canonical-vocabulary index. Score = exact match on each polarity + Kendall's tau over the top-8 aspect ranking + a hard assertion that representative_review_id names a review that genuinely carries that (aspect, polarity) tuple + n_reviews_covered equals the true count. Ground truth is a groupby().agg().
- quality_gate / publish: assertion-based, pass/fail.

3. THE REUSE-SPECIFIC GRADER, which is the part that actually tests the system under evaluation. Two checks, both exact.
- OUTPUT EQUIVALENCE: run N+1 with the reuse store enabled and disabled on the same seed and the same change script. Every op whose key matched must return byte-identical output to what was RECORDED on run N (not to a fresh recompute - comparing against the stored output keeps the grader fully deterministic even though the model itself samples nondeterministically). Any divergence is a hard failure, not a score deduction.
- INVALIDATION EXACTNESS: mutate one artifact (edit review #N / delete review #M / bump prompt_version / change a product title) and assert that EXACTLY the true dependency closure recomputed. The generator knows that closure exactly because it authored the graph. Under-invalidation (an op served stale from the store when its inputs changed) is a hard failure - it is the silent-wrong-answer mode and the only one that can quietly corrupt a customer's PDP. Over-invalidation is scored as lost savings, reported as a percentage of the true closure.

CHANGE SCRIPT for producing run N+1 from run N, matching the measured rates: append 480 new reviews, delete 58, edit 5, mutate 150 product metadata records, and on 1-in-21 runs bump the prompt version. All exact, all free.

REPORTED METRIC: extraction micro-F1 and summary exact-match must both stay at or above the no-reuse baseline (a reuse system that saves money by returning worse answers fails outright), and the headline number is dollars saved per run against the tuned baseline in session_structure, not cache hit rate.
reuse_story:
Three mechanisms, in decreasing order of how much I believe them.

1. THE TTL GAP IS REAL AND STRUCTURAL. Provider prefix caching lives for 5 minutes to 1 hour. This workload runs every 24 hours. Every provider cache entry is cold before the next run begins, so 100% of cross-run saving is unavailable to even a perfectly tuned baseline. On the summarization layer specifically this is worth real money: a product whose review set is unchanged produces a byte-identical 9,800-token prompt, and prefix caching cannot span the gap while a content-addressed store trivially can. Roughly 4,440 of 5,000 products (89%) have an unchanged review set on a given night. At full-catalog scale that is ~$180 of the ~$200 nightly summarization bill.

2. CROSS-TENANT DEDUPLICATION OF SYNDICATED REVIEWS. This is the mechanism content-addressing does that review_id memoization structurally cannot. Bazaarvoice syndicates 325M+ reviews from 2,500 brand sites to 1,250-1,750 retailer sites; a single review commonly appears on 10 or more retailer sites, each assigning it a different review_id. A per-tenant `review_aspects` table keyed on review_id re-extracts the same text N times across N tenants. A store keyed on the content hash of the review text plus the prompt version extracts it once. For a multi-tenant VoC vendor this collapses the extraction layer by whatever the true syndication overlap is — and it is the one saving that scales with customer count rather than shrinking with it.

3. CORRECT INVALIDATION AS A CORRECTNESS FEATURE, NOT A COST FEATURE. Hand-written incrementality gets prompt-version invalidation wrong constantly: someone edits the extraction prompt, forgets to bump the version column, and the pipeline serves a mix of old-prompt and new-prompt aspect tuples into the same product summary for weeks. Transitive content-hash keying makes this class of bug unrepresentable. The customer would not describe this as savings, but it is the thing that would actually make them adopt.
reuse_threats:
Five, and the first two are close to disqualifying.

1. THE LEAF-LAYER WIN IS ALREADY SHIPPED, IN SQL. The 99.9% hit rate on the 640,480-op extraction layer looks like a triumph and is worth nothing incremental, because every serious production pipeline already has a `review_aspects` table keyed on review_id and simply never re-presents old reviews. Wayfair's paper states this explicitly ("reusing cached aspect mappings, which eliminates the need to run the aspect consolidation step for previously seen aspects"). Any benchmark that reports leaf-layer hit rate as the headline number is measuring the reuse system against a strawman that no customer runs. Worse, Wayfair's 10%-new-reviews retrigger rule is a coarse hand-built mechanism that already captures most of the ROLL-UP layer saving too — the one place the reuse layer has genuine edge — at zero infrastructure cost. The competition is not "no caching." It is thirty lines of SQL plus one threshold, and it is already in production.

2. THE ABSOLUTE DOLLARS ARE SMALL AND CONCENTRATED IN THE ONE PLACE REUSE CANNOT HELP. Costed against the tuned baseline: nightly extraction over this slice is $0.14; nightly summarization is $8.30; a full-catalog rebuild is ~$203 for extraction. The reuse layer's best case on the nightly is roughly $8 of $8.44. But the expensive event is the full rebuild, and a rebuild happens precisely BECAUSE the prompt or taxonomy changed — which invalidates every key by construction. The reuse store's hit rate is highest exactly when there is least to save and zero exactly when there is most. That inverse correlation is the central economic problem with this workload and it is not fixable by better engineering.

3. PACKING DESTROYS THE OPERATION BOUNDARY. The tuned baseline packs 25 reviews per extraction call, a 6x saving that dwarfs anything caching does. But a packed call is one operation with 25 inputs: change one review and the whole call recomputes, and reuse granularity collapses by 25x. The reuse system either accepts packed granularity (losing most of its hit rate) or forces one-review-per-call (giving back a 6x cost multiplier to win back a saving worth less than the multiplier). There is a partial fix — pack deterministically by content-hash sort so unchanged cohorts produce identical packs — but new arrivals reshuffle cohort membership unless packs are content-addressed and append-only, which is a real design constraint the benchmark must specify or it will produce a flattering wrong answer.

4. THE FAN-OUT-FROM-A-CHANGING-ROOT LANDMINE. The 14 fetch ops carry advancing watermark cursors and change every run by construction. Under literal transitive keying they invalidate all 1.31M descendants nightly and the reuse system scores 0%. The graph only works if fetch output is immediately shattered into per-review content-addressed artifacts. This is not a hypothetical: it is the default shape of every ingestion pipeline, and it means the reuse system's value is contingent on the customer restructuring their DAG. A system that requires the customer to refactor for it to work is competing with the refactor.

5. CONTENT-HASH SCOPE IS A LOADED GUN. Review records carry helpfulness vote counts, moderation status, and reviewer badges that change constantly and mean nothing semantically. Include them in the hash and the measured change rate goes from 0.11% to ~2%+ and the hit rate craters. Exclude them and you are making a semantic judgement the reuse system cannot make for the customer. Same problem on the product side: price changes daily on 30-60% of SKUs and must be excluded from the summarization artifact, but a naive "hash the product row" implementation invalidates half the catalog every night. Every one of these is a per-field human decision, and getting one wrong is invisible until the bill arrives.

Secondary: LLM sampling nondeterminism means a reuse-served output and a fresh recompute genuinely differ, so any "is the cache correct?" check must compare against the stored output rather than a recomputation — fine for the grader, but it means the system cannot self-verify in production.
confidence:
MEDIUM-HIGH on graph shape, layer counts, and token sizes. These come from a published production system with exact figures (Wayfair, arXiv 2509.26103: 11.8M reviews / 92k products / 129 reviews per product / 124 chars per review / 178,054 raw aspects -> 19,014 canonical / 200-review context cap / 300-500 char summaries / 10%-retrigger rule / Gemini 1.5 Flash / 493,208 products in the March 2025 A/B test), cross-checked against a second independent published pipeline (4.7M restaurant reviews, 52,286 businesses, 6-aspect taxonomy, arXiv 2602.21082). Review-length figures are sourced (Amazon 212.55 chars, Yelp 471 chars recommended-review mean, Wayfair 124 chars); I used a blended 180.

MEDIUM on the change rate. The arrival rate is triangulated from two independent sources that agree within 6% (Amazon Reviews 2018->2023 corpus growth implying ~0.05%/day, and Seller Labs per-SKU review velocity implying ~483/day for 5,000 SKUs). The deletion rate is sourced from a 335,520-review study plus Google's 221M/2025 disclosure. The EDIT rate and the PRODUCT-METADATA churn rate are estimates with no source found, and the metadata number carries disproportionate weight because it is the only large source of change at a non-leaf position — if 3% is really 15%, the summarization-layer reuse story weakens by 5x.

LOWER on the syndication-overlap figure underpinning reuse mechanism 2. I established that syndication exists at scale (Bazaarvoice: 325M+ reviews, 2,500 brand sites, 1,250-1,750 retailer sites, "a single review may appear on 10 or more retailer sites" per Yogi) but found NO published number for what fraction of a given ingestion stream is a syndicated duplicate. I asked directly and the vendors do not publish it. This is the single weakest link in the pro-reuse case and I have flagged it rather than inventing a number.

WHAT WOULD RAISE CONFIDENCE, in priority order: (1) A day-over-day diff of one real review feed export (Bazaarvoice, Yotpo, or Trustpilot) counting adds / edits / deletes / metadata mutations — this would replace three estimates with one measurement and takes an afternoon for anyone with feed access. (2) One production pipeline's actual `review_aspects` insert count per night versus its standing row count, which measures the real leaf-layer change rate directly. (3) A content-hash dedup pass over a multi-tenant VoC vendor's ingest for one week, which would settle the syndication-overlap number and with it whether reuse mechanism 2 is worth anything. (4) A count of how often prompt/taxonomy versions actually bump in a mature pipeline — I assumed every 2-4 weeks from general practice, and since that event zeroes the hit rate on the most expensive runs, the reuse system's expected value is roughly linear in this number.

customer: A platform / developer-productivity team at a company with a 200k-2M LOC service repo (or a monorepo with one hot internal library). They pay today for (a) coding-agent API tokens burned by an unattended migration bot, and (b) engineer hours spent hand-finishing whatever the bot could not do. The concrete purchase is "finish the deprecation campaign for internal API X across every caller, without a human touching 100+ call sites". Google's published version of exactly this customer: 3 developers, 39 distinct ID-type migrations over 12 months, 595 submitted code changes / 93,574 edits, 74.45% of changes fully LLM-authored, self-reported ~50% migration-time reduction (arXiv 2504.09691).
why_repeated:
Three independent reasons; only the first two are real repeat runs.

1. NIGHTLY CAMPAIGN SWEEP. The production shape is not a one-shot. Google's migration toolkit literally "runs nightly until completion": find candidate references -> categorize them -> change & validate. A campaign takes days-to-weeks because shards land at the pace of human code review across owning teams (595 changes / 39 migrations ~= 15 owner-sharded PRs per migration). Every night the bot re-derives the candidate set over a repo that has moved, re-triages candidates it already judged, and re-attempts files whose shard has not merged yet. The overwhelming majority of candidate files are byte-identical to last night.

2. INTRA-RUN REPAIR LOOP. Within one run the agent edits, typechecks, runs tests, repairs. 2-4 iterations is normal. Between iterations 1-5 files of ~26 changed; the other ~85 candidate files and their triage verdicts are untouched, yet a conversational agent re-derives all of them because they sit behind a growing transcript.

3. FLEET REPLICATION (weak). The same migration spec is run once per service in a multi-repo org. Artifacts differ almost entirely, so only the spec/plan layer is shareable. I do not count this as a strong reuse surface and it should not be used to justify the system.
run_cadence: Nightly during an active campaign (the Google design point), for 5-20 consecutive nights until the old-symbol count reaches zero. Plus 2-4 intra-run repair iterations per night. After the campaign, a much cheaper drift-guard variant runs per-commit in CI (grep-only, no model calls) to block reintroduction of the old signature — that CI variant is not this benchmark.

graph.description:
A wide fan-out sandwiched between a narrow root and a narrow, total-fan-in tail. Structurally: 6 discovery tool ops -> 1 planning model call (the root; everything depends on it) -> 90 independent per-candidate-file triage calls -> 26 selected files each get 3 independent edit attempts (78 model calls, mutually independent) -> deterministic static validation -> per-file necessity confirmation -> patch application -> then the graph collapses: one typecheck op consuming all 26 edits, then test ops consuming the typecheck plus every edit, then a repair layer that re-enters the per-file lane, repeated for 3 iterations, then Rosie-style owner sharding into ~15 PR-description calls.

The structural facts that decide whether cross-run reuse can pay:
(a) The wide middle (90 triage + 78 edit = 168 of 234 model ops, ~72%) is genuinely independent per file. This is the reuse surface and it is real.
(b) The tail is total-fan-in. The typecheck op and the test ops read every source file in the repo, so their reuse key changes if ANY file changed anywhere. They can never be reused across days in a live repo. They are also tool ops, so re-running them costs wallclock but zero tokens — state that honestly rather than counting it as a win.
(c) The root is single. If the human tweaks the target signature after review — which happens in most real campaigns at least once — the plan op's output hash changes and all 234 model ops invalidate transitively. Reuse for that run is ~0.
(d) THE BIGGEST STRUCTURAL THREAT is not in this graph, it is in the harness. A Claude-Code-style single-conversation agent linearizes this DAG into a chain: op N's inputs include the entire prior transcript, so fan-in is effectively 'everything upstream', and content-addressed reuse degenerates to 'reuse the whole run or nothing'. The DAG above only exists if the harness is built the way Google built it — stateless per-file sub-tasks with declared inputs. Half this benchmark's value is measuring that gap.

Measured grounding (I ran this on the real 1,117-file service repo in the working directory): the internal helper `record_usage` has 133 call sites across 26 files, 18 of them test files; per-file call-site count median 2, max 17. Python file sizes: median 7.1 KB (~1.8k tokens), p75 16.4 KB (~4.1k), p90 32.7 KB (~8.2k), with two god-files at 345 KB and 542 KB (~86k and ~135k tokens) that no agent can pass whole — those force window-scoped reads, itself reuse-relevant because a window hash is stable under edits elsewhere in the file.

layers.name: L1_discovery
layers.consumes: nothing (roots on the repo)
layers.reads_artifacts: ripgrep for the symbol name; ripgrep for the parameter keyword names; ripgrep for mock/patch/monkeypatch strings naming the symbol; `git ls-files`; a static import-graph / symbol-index query (Kythe at Google, pyright-index or ast-grep elsewhere) expanded to indirect references up to distance ~5; the API definition file itself. Output: candidate list of 90 files / ~310 candidate sites (133 direct, rest indirect and false-positive-heavy).

layers.name: L2_plan
layers.consumes: L1 (all 6 discovery ops)
layers.reads_artifacts: API definition file before/after (~1.2k tokens), 8 representative call-site windows sampled across packages (~4k), repo conventions/CLAUDE.md (~1.5k), candidate-count summary (~0.5k). Emits the mechanical rewrite rules, the triage rubric, and 3 worked before/after examples that become the cached prefix for every downstream call.

layers.name: L3_triage
layers.consumes: L2 (1 op) + L1 candidate list; 1 upstream model op each
layers.reads_artifacts: one candidate file each: the +/-60-line windows around every match in that file. Median 1.2k tokens, p75 3k, p90 7k (window-scoped, so the two god-files contribute ~2.5k each, not 100k). Classifies {needs_edit | no_change_needed | ambiguous}. Realistic split: 26 needs_edit, 58 no_change_needed, 6 ambiguous.

layers.name: L4_read
layers.consumes: L3 (1 triage op each)
layers.reads_artifacts: full file when < 8k tokens (20 files, median 1.8k), otherwise 3 line-ranges around the call sites plus the import block (6 files, ~6k each).

layers.name: L5_edit
layers.consumes: L2 (plan) + L3 (that file's triage) + L4 (that file's read) = fan-in 3. Three independent attempts per file because model output is non-deterministic — Google's actual production constant, not padding.
layers.reads_artifacts: same file content as L4 plus suggested line numbers. Emits a unified diff or full rewritten region.

layers.name: L6_static_validate
layers.consumes: L5 (1 edit attempt each)
layers.reads_artifacts: the proposed diff only. Cheap ladder: non-empty response, not whitespace-only, patch applies cleanly, `ast.parse` succeeds, no new undefined names via pyflakes. ~68 of 78 attempts survive; the per-file winner is picked deterministically (lowest surviving attempt index, so the choice is reproducible).

layers.name: L7_punt_confirm
layers.consumes: L5/L6 (that file's surviving attempts)
layers.reads_artifacts: the winning diff plus surrounding 40 lines. Asks the model to confirm the edit was required and semantics-preserving; a 'no' routes the file to the human queue. Google's 'Punt' validation step.

layers.name: L8_apply
layers.consumes: L7
layers.reads_artifacts: writes the patch to the worktree.

layers.name: L9_typecheck
layers.consumes: ALL 26 L8 ops (fan-in 26). Once per repair iteration.
layers.reads_artifacts: every .py file in the repo (348 files) — which is why its reuse key can never survive a day of unrelated churn. mypy/pyright, ~90s.

layers.name: L10_test
layers.consumes: L9 + all L8 (fan-in ~27). Four per iteration: 3 module-scoped runs over the 18 affected test files, then 1 full-suite run.
layers.reads_artifacts: the whole repo. Emits failure tracebacks. Iteration 1 typically fails 6-10 tests, iteration 2 fails 2-3, iteration 3 green.

layers.name: L11_repair
layers.consumes: L10 (the failing test op) + L4 (the implicated file) = fan-in 2. Eight per iteration x 3 iterations.
layers.reads_artifacts: failing traceback (~2.5k), implicated source window (~2k), failing test body (~1.5k). Emits a corrective diff that re-enters L8.

layers.name: L12_shard_and_describe
layers.consumes: L8 (the subset of edits owned by that team) + L10 (final green test result)
layers.reads_artifacts: OWNERS/CODEOWNERS mapping plus that shard's diff (~3k). Emits a PR title/body per owner shard. 15 shards = 595 changes / 39 migrations from the Google data.

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 3% on a quiet night with no shards merged, up to 100% when the target signature itself is revised after review (~1 run in 5-10). Ordinary range 8-20%.
change_rate.basis:
Mixed measured + sourced + estimated, separated explicitly.

MEASURED (by me, on the real 1,117-file service repo in the working directory, n=286 commits since 2026-05-01): files changed per commit median 4, p75 9, p90 21, mean 32 (mean inflated by merges). Unique files touched in the trailing 1 day: 33/1117 = 3.0%. Trailing 7 days: 69/1117 = 6.2%. Trailing 30 days: 773/1117 = 69% (that window contains a whole-dashboard redesign — the heavy tail is real, not an artifact).

SOURCED: 'Characterizing Commits in Open-Source Software' (~1M commits, 24 active Java projects) — commit size is heavy-tailed, most commits touch 1-10 files and 1-4 source files. An empirical study of GitHub Actions workflow evolution reports 7.3% of workflow files modified per week, 2.1% added — same order as my 6.2%/week measurement. Industry code-churn benchmarks put 15-25% of newly written lines rewritten within ~21 days.

ESTIMATED (stated plainly as such): the campaign's own conversion rate. If ~15 owner shards land over a 10-20 night campaign, roughly 8-12% of the still-open frontier changes per night BECAUSE OF THE BOT'S OWN MERGED WORK. No published number for this; it follows from 595 changes / 39 migrations plus typical review latency.

Combining: unrelated developer churn on the blast-radius set runs hotter than repo average (core APIs live in hot files), so ~4-8% of the 90 candidate files per night, plus ~8-12% converted by merged shards, gives ~13% of input artifacts differing between consecutive nightly runs. I would not defend 13% to better than +/-6 points.
change_rate.where_changes_land:
Overwhelmingly at LEAVES — the favorable case — but with a fat, campaign-fatal tail at the ROOT.

LEAF changes (~95% of runs): an individual call-site or test file was edited by an unrelated developer, or its shard merged. Each such change invalidates exactly one L3 triage, one L4 read, its 3 L5 edit attempts, 3 L6 validations, 1 L7 confirm, 1 L8 apply — about 9 ops, ~4 of them model ops. 13% of 90 files = ~12 files = ~110 invalidated ops out of 385. Everything else in the wide middle is theoretically reusable.

ROOT changes (rare, catastrophic): the migration spec or the API definition file changes. Not hypothetical — in a real campaign the reviewer of shard 1 says 'make it a dataclass, not a TypedDict' and the whole plan is re-derived. All 234 model ops invalidate. Frequency: at least once per campaign, so ~5-20% of runs.

TAIL ops (L9 typecheck, L10 tests) read the entire repo and therefore NEVER hit across days. They are tool ops, so re-execution costs wallclock but zero tokens — convenient for the reuse story and worth saying out loud rather than counting as a win.

One more asymmetry: window-scoped reads (L4 on god-files) are stable under edits elsewhere in the same file, whereas whole-file reads are not. On this repo, whole-file reading of `api/store.py` (542 KB) would invalidate its subtree on essentially every run; +/-60-line windows around 3 call sites survive almost all of them. The reuse rate of this workload is partly a property of how the harness slices files, not of the domain.

session_structure:
This is the baseline to beat and it is strong. A competent engineer builds it as follows.

1. ONE STABLE CACHED PREFIX FOR THE WHOLE CAMPAIGN. Block A = system prompt + repo conventions + language style rules (~2.5k tokens). Block B = the migration spec: old signature, new signature, mechanical rewrite rules, 3 worked before/after examples, the triage rubric, the "when to punt" rules (~6.5k tokens; this is the L2 output). Total ~9k tokens, byte-identical for every L3/L5/L7 call across the entire night. Put a cache_control breakpoint at the end of Block B. Per-call variable suffix = file window + line-number hints, 1-13k tokens.

2. ONE-TURN CALLS, NOT A CONVERSATION. Every per-file call is an independent single-turn request sharing the identical prefix. This is the single highest-leverage decision: an accumulating conversation makes the prefix diverge after the first file and destroys the shared cache entirely. Google's toolkit is built this way (per-file, three independent attempts), and this is why.

3. SERIALIZE ONE WARM-UP CALL BEFORE FANNING OUT. Concurrent fan-out is a trap: fire 90 triage calls at once and none sees a warm prefix, so all 90 pay the cache-write premium (1.25x on Anthropic) on 9k tokens. Issue call #1 alone, wait for it to return (the write is committed), then fan the remaining 89 out at concurrency ~8-16. Cost: one 9k write. Payoff: 89 reads at 0.1x.

4. ORDER FILES SO A SECOND BREAKPOINT PAYS. Group the 90 candidates by package, put that package's shared context (its API surface, its conftest.py) in a second cache_control block after the spec, and iterate all files of a package consecutively. On this repo that second block is worth ~2-4k tokens amortized over 8-17 files per package.

5. BATCH THE SMALL ONES. 20 of 26 edit targets are under 8k tokens; the median candidate window is 1.2k. Batching 4 small files per call amortizes per-call overhead and cuts prefix reads 4x. Do not batch large or high-call-site-count files — accuracy drops.

6. REPAIR LOOP KEEPS THE SAME PREFIX. L11 appends (traceback, file window) to the SAME 9k prefix rather than continuing the edit conversation.

7. TTL ARITHMETIC, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT. A full nightly run is 15-45 minutes of wallclock, so within a run the 9k prefix stays hot even on the 5-minute tier (refreshed by continuous traffic) and trivially so on the 1-hour tier. Across runs, 24 hours between sweeps blows past even the 1h tier, so the prefix is ALWAYS cold at the start of each run — one 9k write per night, which is noise.

NET BASELINE ECONOMICS: with this tuning the provider cache already removes ~90% of the cost of the 9k shared prefix on ~220 of 234 model calls. Per triage call the tuned cost is 9k x 0.1 + 2.2k at full rate = ~3.1k effective input instead of 11.2k — a 72% reduction, free. The reuse layer therefore cannot claim the prefix; it can only claim the ~2.2k variable suffix, the output tokens, and the wallclock of ops it skips entirely. That is a real but much smaller prize than the naive framing suggests, and any benchmark reporting savings against an uncached baseline is measuring the wrong thing.
grader:
Fully deterministic, no LLM, exact free ground truth via BACKWARD CONSTRUCTION.

SETUP (free, exact). Pin a real Python service repo at commit C with a green suite. Write a deterministic LibCST codemod that runs the migration IN REVERSE: given target symbol `f(Request)` at commit C, mechanically de-migrate it to `f(a, b, c)` across every call site, producing tree R0. The ORACLE is then the real upstream code at commit C — byte-exact, human-written, free, never model-generated. The agent's job is to get from R0 back to C without seeing C.

SEEDING. The codemod is parameterized by (symbol, arity, kwarg names, whether to leave a deprecation shim, whether to also de-migrate test fixtures/mocks, package subset). A seed picks the parameters, giving unlimited distinct instances with exact ground truth. Seeds also control instance size; the measured `record_usage` case (133 sites / 26 files / 18 of them tests) is one point on the curve.

CONSECUTIVE-RUN SIMULATION. To produce run N+1's inputs, replay the repo's ACTUAL next-day commits from git history onto R0 (excluding any that touch the target symbol, which get re-de-migrated). This yields a real, free, exactly-known change rate and a real distribution of where changes land — no synthetic churn model needed. Run the same harness twice and diff.

SCORING, in order, all mechanical:
1. HIDDEN-ORACLE TESTS (gate). Copy the ORIGINAL commit-C test files over the agent's tree, then `pytest -q`. Exit 0 or fail. Using the frozen original tests as oracle blocks the classic cheat of weakening assertions — the agent still edits its own copy of the tests, it just does not get to define the oracle.
2. RESIDUE (gate). LibCST/ast query over the agent tree: zero remaining Call nodes matching the old arity/kwarg pattern; exactly one FunctionDef for the new signature. Integer counts, must be 0 and 1.
3. FIDELITY (score). For each of the K files the reverse codemod touched, compare `ast.dump(ast.parse(src))` after stripping docstrings and comments, agent-tree vs oracle-tree. Score3 = (# AST-equal files) / K. Formatting-insensitive by construction, so black/ruff differences do not penalize.
4. COLLATERAL (score). Every file the reverse codemod did NOT touch must be byte-identical between the agent tree and R0-plus-replayed-commits. Score4 = 1 - (# unexpectedly modified files) / (# untouched files). This catches an agent that "helpfully" reformats the repo and thereby destroys everyone's reuse keys — a failure mode this benchmark specifically needs to see.

FINAL: pass = (1) AND (2) AND collateral == 0. Graded score = 0.5*gate + 0.3*Score3 + 0.2*Score4.

COST/REUSE METRICS reported alongside, measured not modeled: billed input tokens split into (uncached, cache-write, cache-read) from the provider response usage fields; output tokens; wallclock; ops executed vs served from store; and the same figures for run N+1. Headline number is run-N+1 dollars under the reuse layer divided by run-N+1 dollars under the tuned prefix-cache baseline above.
reuse_story:
168 of the 234 model calls (72%) live in the two wide, genuinely independent layers — per-file triage (90) and per-file edit attempts (78). Each one's true input set is small and explicit: the migration spec, one file's windows, nothing else. On a nightly campaign sweep ~87% of those files are byte-identical to last night, so ~145 model calls could in principle be served from the store at zero tokens and zero latency. The ops that must re-run — typecheck, tests — are tool ops costing zero tokens. The specific token prize the provider's own cache cannot touch: the per-file variable suffix (~2.2k triage / ~3.5k edit at full rate) plus all output tokens plus the 3x attempt multiplier, because the reuse key pins sampling params and attempt index, so an unchanged file's three attempts collapse to three store hits.

The sharpest sub-story is the triage layer. Index expansion to indirect references at distance 5 is deliberately over-inclusive: ~64 of 90 candidates get classified "no change needed". Those verdicts are pure repeated work on unchanged content, re-derived every night for the length of the campaign, and no provider mechanism helps because the file content differs per call. Ten campaign nights x 64 negative verdicts = 640 model calls whose answer was already known on night 1.

The second sub-story is the 3-attempts constant. Non-determinism forces 3x on every edit; content-addressed reuse makes nights 2..N free for unchanged files, a 3x multiplier landing on exactly the layer where reuse hits.
reuse_threats:
Five, in rough order of how much they worry me.

1. A FREE DOMAIN-SPECIFIC BASELINE ALREADY CAPTURES MOST OF IT. `rg old_symbol` costs nothing and exactly identifies the frontier. Any competent campaign bot already skips files that no longer match, and can trivially memoize triage verdicts keyed on (file sha, spec sha) in a 20-line JSON sidecar. The general content-addressed store must beat THAT, not a naive re-everything bot. My honest estimate: the sidecar captures 70-80% of the available prize, leaving the general system a marginal 20-30% plus "you didn't have to write the sidecar".

2. THE HARNESS LINEARIZES THE DAG. Real coding agents accumulate one conversation; op N's inputs include everything before it, so fan-in is total and op 40's key changes when op 3's output moves by a token. Under that harness reuse is ~0 regardless of how favorable the domain graph looks. The DAG above requires a Google-style stateless per-file orchestrator, which most customers do not have.

3. ROOT INVALIDATION IS FREQUENT ENOUGH TO MATTER. The migration spec gets revised after review in most campaigns; each revision zeroes the store for that run's 234 model ops. At 1-in-8 runs that alone knocks ~12% off expected savings, and it lands on exactly the runs where token spend is highest.

4. NON-DETERMINISM AND STALENESS ARE CORRECTNESS RISKS, NOT JUST MISSES. Serving a cached edit for file F is sound only if nothing outside F's declared inputs matters. But an edit's correctness depends on the new signature's semantics as finally landed — upstream state the key may not capture if the harness under-declares inputs. Under-declare and you ship wrong code that typechecks; over-declare (e.g. include the repo sha) and hit rate collapses to zero. The collateral and AST-fidelity checks exist precisely to catch a reuse layer that bought its hit rate with unsoundness.

5. THE PRIZE IS SMALLER THAN THE OP COUNT SUGGESTS. After the tuned prefix cache, a triage call bills ~3.1k effective input + 200 output. 145 reused calls at that rate is a few cents of Sonnet-class tokens per night. The defensible value here is wallclock and determinism (a 40-minute sweep becomes 8 minutes, and reruns are reproducible), not dollars. Selling this on dollars alone on THIS workload will be embarrassed by the arithmetic.
confidence:
Medium.

HIGH confidence: the graph SHAPE (narrow root, wide independent middle, total-fan-in tail) and the nightly-repeat cadence — both from a published production system doing exactly this (arXiv 2504.09691: 39 migrations / 595 changes / nightly loop / 3 attempts per file / whole-file prompt with suggested line numbers / 6-step validation ladder ending in build + regression tests). Also high confidence in call-site fanout and file sizes: measured on a real 1,117-file service repo rather than guessed (133 sites / 26 files / 18 tests; .py median 7.1 KB, p90 32.7 KB, two god-files > 300 KB).

MEDIUM confidence: the 13% inter-run change rate. The unrelated-churn half is measured (3.0%/day, 6.2%/week on this repo) and corroborated (7.3%/week workflow-file churn; commit-size heavy tail, most commits 1-4 source files). The campaign-conversion half is inferred from 595 changes / 39 migrations with no published per-night figure. Not defensible beyond +/-6 points.

LOW confidence: the candidate-expansion factor (90 candidates for 26 true targets, 3.5x, extrapolated from Kythe distance-5 expansion being described as "inaccurate yet practical"), the 15-shard PR count per migration, and the 8-failures-per-iteration repair volume. These move op counts by +/-30% but not the shape or the conclusion.

WHAT WOULD RAISE IT: (a) instrument one real nightly campaign and log per-op input hashes for 10 consecutive nights — turns the change rate from inference into measurement, a few days of work; (b) get per-file/per-call-count telemetry from a customer's migration bot to replace the 3.5x expansion guess; (c) run the grader above on 20 seeded instances against both a conversational harness and a stateless per-file harness, directly measuring threat #2 — the one I think actually decides whether this product works.

customer: A mid-market multi-brand retailer/distributor or marketplace aggregator: ~250,000 SKUs ingested from ~40 heterogeneous supplier feeds (CSV/XML/XLSX + spec-sheet PDFs + supplier image CDNs), published to own-site, Amazon, Google Shopping, and 1-2 marketplaces.
