Today they pay for (a) a PIM seat license (Salsify / Akeneo / Pimberly), (b) a feed-management layer (Feedonomics / GoDataFeed), and (c) the enrichment labor itself — historically 6-12 offshore data stewards, now an LLM pipeline that replaced most of them. The LLM pipeline is the line item in question: they pay per enriched SKU, and the thing they are actually buying is coverage (attributes filled per SKU), channel acceptance (feed rejection rate), and auditability. Reference production systems with the same shape: Shopify's two-step vision-LLM classify-then-extract over a ~12,000-node taxonomy at tens of millions of product updates/day; Zalando's ~50,000 attributes/week at ~75% accuracy; Amazon's multi-model consensus enrichment with a supervisor escalation path.
why_repeated: Two distinct repeat mechanisms, and conflating them is the main analytical trap. (1) NIGHTLY INCREMENTAL: supplier feeds land daily; new SKUs and revised supplier content must be enriched before the morning feed push. The work queue here is *by construction* the changed set, so a repeat run shares almost nothing with the last one. (2) FULL CATALOG RE-RUN: the entire 250k catalog is re-enriched because something shared changed — a prompt template was tuned, an attribute was added to a category schema, a new locale or sales channel was opened, the model was upgraded, the taxonomy was versioned, or a quality bug was found. This is the run where the same 250k products get processed again and again with mostly-identical inputs, and it is the only run where cross-run reuse has any surface at all. The benchmark unit must therefore be the full re-run, not the nightly.
run_cadence: Nightly incremental: every 24h, 600-2,500 SKUs out of 250k. Full-catalog re-run: 1-4x/month while the pipeline is being actively tuned, dropping to roughly 1x/quarter once stable, plus an unscheduled one whenever a channel rejects a feed en masse. The benchmark models a full re-run scaled to N=20,000 products.

graph.description: The honest shape is 20,000 independent shallow chains fanned out over a handful of shared root artifacts — NOT one deep graph. Per product the chain is depth ~10 and never touches any other product; the only cross-product coupling is the dedupe/match layer (a tool op reading a shared ANN index) and the shared roots every op reads (taxonomy, per-category attribute schema, style guide, banned-claims list, locale glossaries, channel mapping tables). This shape matters more than any other fact here: a changed supplier record is the root of exactly one chain out of 20,000, so it invalidates 0.005% of the graph, while a changed style guide or prompt template is read by every op in a layer and invalidates 100% of it. Reuse economics are entirely governed by which of those two kinds of change happened. Cost is heavily top-loaded: L4 (vision attribute extraction) alone is ~40% of run dollars, and the cheap bottom layers (alt text, translation) are ~55% of op count but ~18% of dollars — so a prompt edit to a bottom layer preserves most of the money, and a model upgrade or taxonomy bump preserves none. Tool ops (parse, retrieve, normalize, validate, map) are deterministic, cost no model tokens, and are worth keying only because they gate downstream keys. Note that images sit in the per-product suffix and are the single largest token line in L4/L9 — provider prefix caching can never touch them, but a reuse hit skips them entirely.

layers.name: parse_normalize
layers.consumes: nothing — this is the per-product root
layers.reads_artifacts: one raw supplier record (CSV row + HTML blob + spec-sheet text, ~4-9KB)

layers.name: dedupe_candidate_retrieval
layers.consumes: parse_normalize, 1:1
layers.reads_artifacts: shared ANN index over the existing catalog (embedding of title+brand+MPN)

layers.name: taxonomy_candidate_retrieval
layers.consumes: parse_normalize, 1:1
layers.reads_artifacts: taxonomy artifact — 5,200 leaf paths over 24 departments; returns top-30 candidates (the full taxonomy is ~180k tokens and cannot be sent per call)

layers.name: category_classification
layers.consumes: parse_normalize (1:1) and taxonomy_candidate_retrieval (1:1)
layers.reads_artifacts: canonical record ~600 tok; 30 candidate leaf paths with definitions ~1,100 tok; primary product image downsampled to 768px ~1,100 image tok; system+few-shot ~2,600 tok

layers.name: attribute_extraction
layers.consumes: parse_normalize (1:1) and category_classification (1:1 — the predicted category selects which attribute schema is loaded)
layers.reads_artifacts: canonical record ~600 tok; attribute schema for the predicted category (12-24 typed attributes + controlled vocabularies) ~900 tok; spec-sheet text chunk ~1,800 tok; up to 3 images ~3,300 tok; system+few-shot ~3,000 tok

layers.name: attribute_normalization
layers.consumes: attribute_extraction (1:1) and category_classification (1:1)
layers.reads_artifacts: controlled-vocabulary alias table and unit-conversion table for the category

layers.name: title_generation
layers.consumes: attribute_normalization (1:1) and category_classification (1:1)
layers.reads_artifacts: normalized attributes ~400 tok; brand style guide + title format rules ~1,400 tok; system+few-shot ~1,800 tok

layers.name: description_bullets
layers.consumes: attribute_normalization (1:1) and title_generation (1:1)
layers.reads_artifacts: normalized attributes ~400 tok; generated title; style guide ~1,400 tok; system + 3 exemplar descriptions ~2,900 tok

layers.name: seo_metadata
layers.consumes: title_generation (1:1) and description_bullets (1:1)
layers.reads_artifacts: channel keyword rules ~700 tok; system+few-shot ~1,200 tok

layers.name: image_alt_text
layers.consumes: category_classification (1:3 — one classification feeds 3 alt-text ops) and title_generation (1:3)
layers.reads_artifacts: one product image ~1,100 image tok; title; accessibility style rules ~500 tok; system ~300 tok

layers.name: compliance_claims_check
layers.consumes: description_bullets (1:1) and attribute_extraction (1:1)
layers.reads_artifacts: banned-claims list ~700 tok; category-specific regulatory rules ~500 tok; system ~900 tok

layers.name: locale_translation
layers.consumes: title_generation (1:4) and description_bullets (1:4) — 4 non-English locales
layers.reads_artifacts: title+description ~470 tok; locale glossary with required term substitutions ~600 tok; system ~800 tok

layers.name: validation
layers.consumes: attribute_normalization, description_bullets, seo_metadata, compliance_claims_check, locale_translation (fan-in 5)
layers.reads_artifacts: JSON schema + per-channel required-field rules

layers.name: channel_mapping
layers.consumes: category_classification (1:1) and attribute_normalization (1:1)
layers.reads_artifacts: 3 channel mapping tables (internal leaf -> Google product taxonomy / Amazon browse node / marketplace category)

layers.name: channel_mapping_llm_fallback
layers.consumes: channel_mapping (fires on the ~4% of products with no table entry)
layers.reads_artifacts: candidate channel nodes ~1,200 tok; product summary ~300 tok; system ~800 tok

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 4-12% of content-bearing artifacts between two full re-runs ~1 month apart; 0.15-0.5% between two full re-runs a day apart; ~80% if you naively hash the whole product row instead of only the fields each operation reads
change_rate.basis: ESTIMATE, not sourced. I searched specifically for published product-catalog churn data (PIM modification logs, GDSN trade-item update rates, Merchant Center feed deltas, retail assortment turnover) and no one publishes the number that matters — the rate at which *content-bearing* fields change. What I found and anchored on: (1) a feed-vendor claim that delta sync 'reduces API call volume by roughly 80% on catalogs where fewer than 20% of SKUs change daily' — weak marketing, and that 20% is dominated by price/stock; (2) Google Merchant Center guidance that price/availability need daily-or-faster refresh while a full content feed is required only once per 30 days — an implicit vendor statement that content is the slow-moving half; (3) SKULaunch's observation that manual enrichment runs '3 to 6 months behind new SKU arrivals', which no one would tolerate if content churned fast; (4) retail assortment turnover of 30-50%/yr in apparel and under 10%/yr in industrial/MRO, bounding the new-SKU rate at ~1.5-4%/month; (5) as a proxy for product-page content specifically, the web-change literature — Fetterly et al. (~150M pages, 11 weeks) found ~65% of pages had zero change; Cho & Garcia-Molina found ~23% changed daily; Adar et al. (55k URLs, 5 weeks) found ~2/3 changed but that most changes were minimal. E-commerce pages sit at the churny end of that distribution, but essentially all of that churn is price, stock, reviews, and recommendation modules — none of which any enrichment operation reads. Decomposing the estimate: price/availability differ on 60-95% of SKUs and are read by ZERO operations; new SKUs 1.5-4%/month (100% cold, no reuse possible); content revisions to existing SKUs (title, long description, spec table, images) 2-6%/month, typical 3.5%; discontinuations 1-3%/month (deletions, nothing to recompute). Content-bearing total ~5-9%, typical 6.5%. Confidence in the decomposition's *shape* is high; confidence in the 3.5% content-revision figure is low — it is the number I would most want a real PIM audit log to check.
change_rate.where_changes_land: Overwhelmingly at the leaves, and that is the reuse-friendly case — but the runs that cost money are triggered by root changes, which is the reuse-hostile case, and the two facts pull in opposite directions. LEAF SIDE: a revised supplier record is the root of exactly one of 20,000 independent chains, so it invalidates ~19 operations out of 380,800. At 6.5% content churn, 93.5% of chains are wholly reusable. ROOT SIDE: the shared artifacts (taxonomy, attribute schemas, style guide, banned-claims list, locale glossaries) plus the prompt templates and model ids are read by every operation in a layer. Nobody re-runs 250k products for fun — the full re-run is almost always triggered *because* a root changed. Trigger distribution, from how these pipelines are actually operated: prompt-template edit to one layer ~45% (e.g. 'descriptions read too salesy'); attribute-schema revision on 3-8% of categories ~20%; new locale or new sales channel ~15%; model upgrade ~12%; taxonomy version bump ~5%; tool-layer bug fix ~3%. The saving grace is that this graph is cost-top-loaded while prompt churn is bottom-loaded: an edit to description/SEO/translation preserves classification and vision attribute extraction, which are ~62% of model ops and ~76% of input tokens. A new locale preserves ~85% of tokens. But a model upgrade or taxonomy bump invalidates 100%. Expected reusable fraction of model ops on a randomly-drawn full re-run works out to roughly 60%, with brutal variance: exactly 0% on ~17% of runs, ~95% on ~20% of runs. Report the distribution, never just the mean.

session_structure: There is no conversation here — this is 260,800 independent single-turn calls — so the entire prefix-cache game is about making the shared preamble byte-identical and keeping it hot. A competent engineer does nine things. (1) SORT THE WORK QUEUE BY CATEGORY. All products in a category share an attribute schema, so sorting makes the L4 prefix byte-identical across consecutive calls instead of thrashing between 800 distinct schemas. (2) FREEZE THE PREFIX: layout is [tools] -> [system: instructions + few-shot + style guide + category attribute schema, with cache_control] -> [user: this product's record + images]. Nothing volatile above the breakpoint — no timestamp, no SKU, no run id — and JSON serialized with sorted keys so the bytes are stable. (3) TWO BREAKPOINTS, not one: one after the layer-global block (system + few-shot, ~2,600-3,000 tok, identical for every product in the layer, caches across the whole run) and one after the category-specific schema block (~900 tok, caches across that category's contiguous run of products). A single breakpoint at the end of everything would write a distinct entry per product and read nothing. (4) WARM BEFORE FANNING OUT — the one most engineers get wrong. A cache entry is readable only once the first response begins streaming, so firing 2,000 concurrent requests cold means all 2,000 pay the 1.25x write and none read. Send one max_tokens:0 warm request per distinct (layer, category) prefix, await it, then fan out. In a 20k-product run only ~800 distinct categories appear and only L4 is category-specific, so it's ~805 warm calls total. (5) USE ttl:"1h" on the layer-global block: a 20k run takes 30-90 minutes and a 5m TTL would lapse while traversing the long tail of categories. 2x write against 0.1x reads breaks even at 3 reads; we get ~20,000. (6) SPLIT THE PIPELINE BETWEEN STREAMING AND BATCH. Batches gives a flat 50% but you cannot control execution order, so warm-then-fan-out is unenforceable and the 24h window blows past even a 1h TTL. So: L3/L4 (big prefixes, high cache leverage, and L4 is 40% of spend) go through the streaming API with warm-then-fan-out; L7-L11 (small prefixes, huge volume) go through Batches for the flat 50%. (7) MODEL-TIER: Haiku for classification/alt-text/compliance/translation, Opus for vision attribute extraction, Sonnet for customer-facing copy. Caches are model-scoped, so this is 4 pools, but each is still large enough to amortize. (8) DOWNSAMPLE IMAGES to ~768px — white-background product shots do not need 2576px, and image tokens dominate L4 and L9. (9) THEIR OWN DELTA GATE: every mature pipeline already skips SKUs whose content_hash(title, description, specs, image_urls) is unchanged since last enrichment. MEASURED RESULT of all this: per-product cost falls from $0.1363 cold to $0.0691, a 49% reduction, entirely free. On a 20k full re-run that is $2,726 -> $1,382, or ~$995 with Batches on the bottom layers. Crucially, what prefix caching CANNOT touch is the per-product suffix — the supplier record, the spec text, and the images — plus all output tokens. For L4 that residue is 4,470 effective input + 380 output per product, and it is irreducible by construction because it is unique per product. That residue is exactly what a reuse store attacks, and on an unchanged product it goes to zero. The two mechanisms are close to orthogonal on this workload, which is unusual and is the strongest thing this scenario has going for it.
grader: Fully deterministic, no LLM in the loop, ground truth exact and free because a seeded generator computes it. GENERATOR (`catalogen --seed S --n 20000`): build a fixed taxonomy of 5,200 leaf paths over 24 departments from a seeded grammar; give each leaf 12-24 typed attributes, each with a controlled vocabulary of 6-20 canonical values plus 2-5 surface-form aliases per value and 2-4 unit variants for numerics. Per product: sample a leaf, sample a value per attribute, sample brand + model number matching ^[A-Z]{2,4}-\\d{3,5}[A-Z]?$, and render 1-8 procedural PNGs whose pixels ENCODE the sampled values (a rendered spec placard), so vision is genuinely load-bearing and gradeable rather than decorative. Then RENDER A MESSY SUPPLIER RECORD from that ground truth: abbreviated title with vendor codes, HTML description with junk markup, a spec table using alias surface forms and mixed units, 2-4 distractor attributes outside the schema, and 1-2 attributes deliberately omitted so recall is testable. Plant duplicate twins for 3% of products (same ground truth, different supplier phrasing, different SKU). Emit ground truth to a sealed JSON the pipeline never reads. SCORING: G1 category accuracy = exact string equality of predicted leaf path (report parent-level too). G2 attribute micro-F1 = canonicalize predictions through the generator's own alias table and unit-normalize to base SI, then exact-match the (attribute, value) set. G3 title hard constraints, pass/fail per product = length <= 70 chars AND contains brand AND contains model number verbatim AND zero hits against a fixed 180-token banned list AND every numeric+unit token extracted by regex must appear in the ground-truth value set after unit normalization — a fabricated spec is a hard fail, which makes this a deterministic hallucination detector. G4 description = valid against JSON schema AND 3-6 bullets AND every numeric claim traceable by the same subset test AND no banned-claims regex hit AND every attribute mentioned by name exists in ground truth. G5 dedupe precision/recall against the planted twins. G6 translation fidelity = every numeric value and unit survives unchanged AND the locale glossary's required term substitutions are present — pure string checks, no BLEU, no judge. G7 channel-mapping exactness against the generator-owned mapping table. G8 stability = for products unchanged between run 1 and run 2, outputs must be BYTE-IDENTICAL; any diff fails. MUTATION HARNESS (what makes this a reuse benchmark rather than a quality benchmark): `catalogen mutate --seed S --policy P` applies a seeded mutation and emits the ORACLE INVALIDATION SET — the exact set of (product, layer) operations whose correct output can differ — computable exactly because the generator knows what it changed and the layer spec declares what each op reads. Policies: `nightly` (0.4% new SKUs, 0.3% content revisions, 12% price-only, 40% stock-only; oracle invalidates only the 0.7% content-touched — a system keying on the whole product row invalidates 52% and is caught red-handed); `prompt-l7` (oracle: description/SEO/translation/validation only, classification and extraction reusable); `schema-drift` (5% of categories; oracle: extraction-and-downstream for those categories only); `new-locale` (oracle: 20,000 new translation ops, nothing else); `model-upgrade` (oracle: extraction and everything downstream); `image-reencode` (8% of images re-encoded to different bytes, identical pixels; oracle invalidates NOTHING — catches byte-hashing of images); `taxonomy-bump` (2% of leaves renamed/merged; oracle invalidates 2% of products, while a naive whole-artifact hash invalidates 100% — the sharpest test in the suite, separating field-level from artifact-level keying). REUSE METRICS: invalidation recall (below 1.0 means stale output shipped — G1-G8 independently catch it), invalidation precision (below 1.0 is wasted money, priced through the token model), and net dollars against three baselines: no caching, the tuned prefix-caching baseline specified above, and tuned prefix caching PLUS the customer's existing whole-product content-hash delta gate. The third is the only baseline that matters commercially.
reuse_story: This is the best-shaped domain I have seen for the Bazel model, for four specific reasons. (1) The graph is 20,000 independent shallow chains, so invalidation is naturally surgical — one changed supplier record touches 19 of 380,800 operations. There is no deep dependency spine to propagate through. (2) Cross-run reuse attacks exactly the cost that provider prefix caching cannot reach. Prefix caching removes 49% of spend by discounting the shared preamble; what survives is the per-product suffix (supplier record, spec text, and images) plus all output tokens, which is unique per product by construction and therefore permanently uncacheable at the prefix level. A reuse hit on an unchanged product skips the entire call, images included. Measured: $0.1363/product cold, $0.0691 with a fully tuned prefix cache, and ~$0.028 with reuse layered on top at a 60% hit rate. The two mechanisms are close to orthogonal, which is rare. (3) The cost distribution is top-loaded (vision attribute extraction is ~40% of dollars) while prompt churn is bottom-loaded (~45% of full re-runs are copy-tuning edits to description/SEO/translation). So the most common invalidation event preserves the most expensive layers — a prompt edit to L7 keeps 76% of input tokens reusable. (4) Byte-identical output for unchanged products is not just a cost win, it is a product requirement the customer already wants: retailers hate catalogs where descriptions churn every night for no reason, because it re-triggers channel review and SEO re-indexing. The reuse store delivers stability as a side effect, which converts a cost pitch into a quality pitch.
reuse_threats: Eight, roughly in order of how much they hurt. (1) THE CUSTOMER ALREADY HAS A DELTA GATE. Every mature pipeline skips SKUs whose content hash is unchanged. That is a coarse, hand-rolled version of this system, it is free, and on the nightly run it captures essentially the whole win. The marginal value of fine-grained reuse is confined to full re-runs and to partial-invalidation cases (price changed but description generator does not read price; description changed but image-derived attributes did not). Benchmark against the coarse gate or the result is meaningless. (2) ROOT CHANGES TRIGGER THE EXPENSIVE RUNS. ~17% of full re-runs are model upgrades or taxonomy bumps, which invalidate 100% and return exactly zero. These are precisely the runs an engineer most wants cheap, so the system is absent when most wanted. (3) PROMPT-TEMPLATE CHURN DURING DEVELOPMENT. In the weeks the pipeline is being tuned the template changes daily, and under strict keying every edit — including whitespace — nukes that layer's store. Keying on the rendered prompt with whitespace normalization mitigates it but is a deliberate correctness compromise. (4) BATCH API INTERACTION. Half the graph should run through Batches for a flat 50%, which means the reuse filter must run before batch submission — so you must materialize each layer completely before keying the next, serializing what is otherwise an embarrassingly parallel pipeline and costing wall-clock. (5) IMAGE RE-ENCODING. Supplier CDNs re-encode images constantly: different bytes, identical picture. Byte-hashing images produces phantom invalidations on the single most expensive layer. Perceptual hashing fixes the economics and breaks exactness — the `image-reencode` mutation policy exists to price this tradeoff explicitly. (6) THE CHEAP LAYERS ARE NOT WORTH CACHING. Alt text on Haiku at 1,900 in / 35 out costs ~$0.002; storing and indexing that key may exceed recompute. The system needs a value gate, and a value gate is itself an accuracy risk — marking a never-reused prefix costs real money, which is the same failure mode already documented in our ROI-gate work. (7) STORE OPERATIONS AT SCALE. 250k products x 13 model ops = 3.25M keys per run, ~4GB of outputs per snapshot, retained across months of runs. Storage is cheap; operating and garbage-collecting that index is not. (8) VARIANCE KILLS THE PITCH. Expected 60% hit rate with 0% on a sixth of runs is a hard thing to sell against a line item the CFO sees monthly. Quote the distribution, never the mean.
confidence: Medium overall, with the confidence unevenly distributed. HIGH on the graph shape and layer decomposition — the two-step classify-then-extract structure is confirmed by Shopify's published production architecture (12k categories, vision LLM, two calls because attributes are category-dependent, fuzzy-match repair on invalid taxonomy paths <2% of the time), and the downstream copy/translate/compliance layers are standard PIM practice. HIGH on the tuned-baseline analysis and the 49% figure — that follows from documented cache mechanics (0.1x reads, 1.25x/2x writes, prefix-match invariant, entries readable only once the first response begins streaming, which is what forces warm-then-fan-out). HIGH on the qualitative claim that price/stock churn is irrelevant because no enrichment operation reads those fields. MEDIUM on token sizes — they are engineering estimates from the artifact descriptions, not measured against a real pipeline; image token counts in particular swing 3x with resolution policy. LOW on the headline change rate. Nobody publishes content-field churn for product catalogs; I searched PIM vendor material, GDSN, Merchant Center guidance, feed-management vendors, and retail assortment research, and the closest anyone comes is a marketing claim about '<20% of SKUs change daily' that is dominated by price and stock. LOW-MEDIUM on the full-re-run trigger distribution, which is reasoned from how these pipelines are operated rather than counted. WHAT WOULD RAISE IT, in order of value: (1) a real PIM's audit log for 6-12 months, grouped by which field changed — this single artifact would move the change rate from estimate to measurement and is the highest-leverage thing to ask a design partner for; (2) one customer's enrichment job history showing full-re-run triggers, which converts the 60%-expected/0%-on-17%-of-runs figure into a real distribution; (3) token counts measured against an actual pipeline with real supplier records and real product images, which would firm up the cost split between the top-loaded and bottom-loaded layers.

customer: An IDP/AP-automation vendor (Rossum, Vic.ai, Stampli, Klippa, Ramp/BILL tier) or an enterprise AP shared-services org running its own pipeline. The tenant modelled here is a large enterprise processing ~40,000 invoices/month (~1,800 per business night). They pay per invoice processed, not per token: the vendor charges roughly $0.20–$1.00/invoice, and APQC benchmarks put fully-loaded cost per invoice at $2.07 (top performers) to >$10 (bottom). What they are buying is a touchless rate — Ardent Partners 2025 puts the average exception rate at 14% and says over 60% of invoices still require some human interaction, so every point of straight-through processing is the product. Model spend is roughly 1% of their cost per invoice, which matters enormously for the reuse pitch: a 40% token saving moves ~0.4% of their unit cost. The line items they actually feel are hosted-OCR page fees and the wall-clock of a re-extraction backfill.
why_repeated: Two structurally different reasons, and conflating them is the main way this domain gets analysed wrongly. (1) STREAMING: invoices arrive continuously — from vendor email, EDI, a supplier portal, and scanned mail — and the same pipeline runs against tonight's arrivals. The graph is repeated; the documents are not. (2) REPLAY: the same pipeline is re-run over documents it already processed. Replay is real and frequent in production and has four drivers — a schema/prompt change (a new field like "remit-to address" or "carbon surcharge" is added and the last 30–90 days are re-extracted so the ERP has it), a model upgrade, a partial-batch failure or OCR-provider outage requiring a rerun, and the 14% exception loop where a human corrects one field and the downstream validate/match/code ops re-execute over unchanged upstream results. There is also a small pure-duplicate channel: SAP Concur measured 1.29% of processed invoices as duplicates, and APQC puts duplicate-or-erroneous disbursements at 1–2.5%, so a fraction of documents are byte-identical resubmissions of ones already seen.
run_cadence: Nightly for the main batch (~1,800 documents), plus intra-day micro-batches every 15 minutes for rush/2-way-match invoices (same graph, N≈40). Replay runs are far rarer but far larger: roughly one prompt/schema-driven backfill every 3–8 weeks, each covering 30–90 days of history (50,000–160,000 documents, i.e. 30–90× a nightly run).

graph.description:
Honestly characterised: this is a thin shared root plus 1,800 near-identical independent per-document chains of depth 11, with a single aggregation op at the end. It is NOT a deep dependency graph and it is NOT one long chain. 34,560 of the graph's edges are intra-document; only 3,800 edges cross document boundaries (the 6 shared reference artifacts read by every chain, plus the final reconcile op's 1,800-way fan-in). Mean fan-in of 1.74 is the honest signature of a fan-out workload — most ops consume exactly one upstream result plus one config artifact.

The consequence for reuse is structural and worth stating up front: because the chains are independent, an invalidation never propagates sideways. A changed document invalidates 11 ops and nothing else. Conversely, a changed ROOT (the extraction schema or prompt pack) invalidates the same op in all 1,800 chains at once. So the graph has exactly two invalidation modes — 11 ops, or ~1,800×k ops — with nothing in between.

The second structural fact: the graph is 64% deterministic tool ops (12,690 of 19,891) and 36% model ops. The tool ops sit UPSTREAM of every model op. Layers 0–2 (fetch, rasterize, OCR — 6,120 ops) do not read the prompt pack or the schema at all, so a prompt change does not touch their reuse keys. OCR is also the dominant cost and latency in this pipeline (arXiv 2605.18818 reports OCR, not LLM parsing, accounts for the majority of end-to-end time in a production document-AI microservice at thousands of multi-page docs/hour), and hosted OCR is billed per page. That upstream-deterministic-expensive-layer / downstream-model-layer split is the single most important feature of this graph and is where the entire reuse case lives.

Document mix calibrated to DocILE (6,680 annotated real business documents, 1–3 pages, 55 field classes): 1.4 pages/document mean, 71% single-page, 24% two-page, 5% three-or-more. Line items: median 6.4, p90 18, p99 120+ (wholesale-distribution invoices can carry hundreds of SKU lines). 65% of invoices are PO-backed (the rest are non-PO and skip the match op, which is why layer 8 has 1,170 ops rather than 1,800).

layers.name: fetch_document
layers.consumes: nothing (graph root); one op per arriving document
layers.reads_artifacts: one invoice artifact: the raw PDF/TIFF/JPEG bytes from object storage or the AP mailbox attachment. Output is normalised bytes + sha256. This op is what binds a document's content hash into every downstream key in its chain.

layers.name: rasterize_and_normalize
layers.consumes: 1× fetch_document (its own)
layers.reads_artifacts: none beyond its upstream. Splits into pages, deskews, corrects orientation, denoises, crops non-textual margins, renders each page at 300 DPI. Emits a page list. Output is ~500 KB/page of image data — this is the storage cost centre for any reuse store.

layers.name: ocr_page
layers.consumes: 1× rasterize_and_normalize (one op per page; 1.4 pages/doc mean)
layers.reads_artifacts: none. Hosted OCR (Textract/Document AI/PaddleOCR-served) returning text tokens with bounding boxes and per-token confidence, plus CNN table-region detection. THE expensive layer — dominates latency and carries a per-page vendor fee. Reads no prompt and no schema, so its reuse key is immune to prompt-root changes.

layers.name: classify_document
layers.consumes: 1.4× ocr_page (all pages of its document)
layers.reads_artifacts: prompt_pack.md (the classification taxonomy section). Routes to one of 9 types: invoice / credit memo / receipt / statement / packing slip / remittance / PO ack / dunning / other. Runs on Haiku 4.5. System prompt is 4,180 tokens — deliberately above Haiku 4.5's 4,096-token minimum cacheable length, see session_structure. User payload is page-1 OCR text truncated to 600 tokens.

layers.name: resolve_vendor
layers.consumes: 1× classify_document
layers.reads_artifacts: vendor_master.csv (~1,900 active suppliers; note APQC-style benchmarks put mid-market at 30–150 active vendors, enterprise at low thousands). Deterministic fuzzy match of header text + tax ID + bank IBAN against the master, returning vendor_id + a layout-template id. This op is what makes the per-vendor prompt block in layer 5 addressable.

layers.name: extract_header_fields
layers.consumes: 1.4× ocr_page + 1× resolve_vendor
layers.reads_artifacts: extraction_schema.json (31 header fields) + prompt_pack.md + vendor_layouts.json (the resolved vendor's hint block). Haiku 4.5 with structured outputs. Input decomposes as: frozen system block 5,200 tok (instructions + 31-field JSON schema + 12 worked examples) | vendor layout hint block 480 tok | OCR text of all pages 850 tok median, 2,600 p90 | page images 1.4 × 1,600 = 2,240 tok on the standard-resolution tier. On the high-resolution tier (Opus 4.7+/Sonnet 5, 2576px long edge) the image term becomes 1.4 × 4,784 = 6,700 tok and input rises to ~13,200.

layers.name: extract_line_items
layers.consumes: 1.4× ocr_page + 1× extract_header_fields
layers.reads_artifacts: extraction_schema.json (line-item sub-schema) + prompt_pack.md. Separate call from the header because table extraction needs a different prompt, multi-page table-continuation rules, and a wider model — Sonnet 5 here. Input: system 3,100 tok | bbox-ordered OCR of the table region 1,900 tok | cropped table images 1.2 × 1,600 = 1,920 tok. Output scales with line count: median 6.4 lines × ~140 tok = 900; p95 (40 lines) = 5,600; p99 distribution invoices with 120+ SKU lines blow past 16,000 and must stream.

layers.name: validate_arithmetic
layers.consumes: 1× extract_header_fields + 1× extract_line_items
layers.reads_artifacts: tax_table.csv. Pure integer arithmetic in minor currency units: sum(line_total)==subtotal; qty×unit_price==line_total; subtotal+tax+freight−discount==total; tax rate legal for jurisdiction; dates sane and ordered; duplicate-hash lookup against the 24-month invoice ledger (this is the op that catches the 1.29% duplicate channel). Emits a per-field confidence vector.

layers.name: match_purchase_order
layers.consumes: 1× extract_header_fields + 1× extract_line_items + 1× validate_arithmetic. Only the 65% of invoices that are PO-backed.
layers.reads_artifacts: po_snapshot.parquet + goods_receipt.parquet. Deterministic 2-way (invoice↔PO) or 3-way (invoice↔PO↔receipt) match with tolerance bands on price and quantity. WARNING for reuse: po_snapshot is a LIVE table re-exported every run, so its content hash changes every night even when nothing relevant to a given invoice changed. See reuse_threats.

layers.name: code_to_gl
layers.consumes: 1× extract_line_items + 1× resolve_vendor
layers.reads_artifacts: gl_chart.csv (~600 accounts) + coding_rules.md + this vendor's trailing-90-day coding history. Assigns GL account, cost centre, and project code per line. Haiku 4.5. Input: system 2,300 tok + GL chart rendered inline 3,900 tok = 6,200 cached prefix (clears the Haiku floor comfortably) | header+lines JSON 1,150 tok | vendor coding history 620 tok.

layers.name: confidence_route
layers.consumes: 1× validate_arithmetic + 1× code_to_gl + (0.65×) 1× match_purchase_order
layers.reads_artifacts: routing_thresholds.yaml. Per-field confidence thresholds plus a rule engine decide auto-post vs exception queue. Produces the 14% exception rate (Ardent Partners 2025 average). Exceptions leave the graph, get a human touch, and re-enter as a partial replay — the human edits one field and only validate/match/code re-execute.

layers.name: batch_reconcile
layers.consumes: 1800× confidence_route (the only wide fan-in in the graph)
layers.reads_artifacts: control_totals.csv from the ERP. Sonnet 5. Reads run aggregates, the 252 exception summaries at ~110 tok each, and control totals; writes the nightly AP close memo. Input ~31,000 tok, output ~1,400.

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 97–100% in the streaming regime (the normal nightly run). 0–3% in the replay/backfill regime, where the documents are unchanged by construction and only 1 of the 6 config artifacts differs. Roughly 1 replay per 20–40 stream runs, but each replay is 30–90× larger, so replay is ~50–70% of all document-ops executed per quarter despite being a small minority of runs.
change_rate.basis: Explicitly mixed — here is exactly which parts are cited and which are mine. SOURCED: the duplicate-resubmission rate of 1.29% of processed invoices (SAP Concur, reported via Peakflo/Medius AP-duplicate literature), corroborated by APQC's 1–2.5% of annual disbursements being duplicated or erroneous and the Washington State Auditor's 0.8–2% range; the 14% exception rate driving the partial-replay loop (Ardent Partners, AP Metrics That Matter 2025, n=212 AP organisations); the >60%-of-invoices-need-human-interaction figure from the same report; the 1–3 page and 55-field-class document shape from DocILE (arXiv 2302.05658). ESTIMATED, not sourced: the ~0.5% batch-retry rate, and the replay frequency (one schema/prompt-driven backfill every 3–8 weeks). I could find no published data on IDP prompt-change or backfill cadence — nobody instruments and publishes it — so treat the replay-frequency number as an informed guess, and note that it is the single number the whole reuse economics is most sensitive to. The headline 98.7% is 100% minus the 1.29% duplicate channel, which is definitional rather than clever: an invoice stream is by construction a stream of documents never seen before.
change_rate.where_changes_land:
Overwhelmingly at the LEAVES, and this is the bad case for content-addressed reuse. 1,800 of the 1,806 input artifacts are per-document leaves; each changed leaf invalidates exactly its own 11-op chain and nothing else, because the chains are independent. There is no amplification and no sharing to recover.

The 6 shared artifacts are ROOTS and change on a completely different clock: extraction_schema.json and prompt_pack.md every 3–8 weeks, gl_chart.csv monthly, vendor_master.csv weekly (new supplier onboarding), tax_table.csv quarterly, po_snapshot.parquet EVERY RUN (it is a live ERP export). When a root does change, it lands simultaneously at the root of all 1,800 chains — but only on the layers that read it. That asymmetry is the whole story: a prompt_pack change invalidates all 7,201 model ops and ZERO of the 6,120 fetch/rasterize/OCR ops, because those layers never read the prompt. A gl_chart change invalidates only the 1,800 code_to_gl ops. A vendor_master change invalidates only the resolve_vendor ops of the affected vendors' documents.

So the practical summary: in the streaming regime changes land everywhere at the leaves and reuse recovers ~1.3%. In the replay regime nothing changes at the leaves, one root changes, and reuse recovers the 64% of the graph that is deterministic upstream tool work — including the layer that dominates cost and latency.

session_structure:
A competent engineer gets a lot out of provider prefix caching here, and this baseline is strong — the reuse layer has to beat all of it, not a naive one-call-per-invoice strawman.

MODEL SPLIT. Haiku 4.5 for classify, header extraction, and GL coding; Sonnet 5 for line items and the reconcile. Cheapest model that clears the accuracy bar per op, not one model for the whole graph.

THE FLOOR TRAP — the thing most engineers get wrong. Minimum cacheable prefix is per-model and NOT monotonic across generations: 4,096 tokens on Haiku 4.5, 1,024 on Sonnet 5, 512 on Opus 5. A 2,800-token extraction system prompt on Haiku 4.5 silently never caches — no error, just `cache_creation_input_tokens: 0` forever. So the engineer deliberately consolidates the classification prompt to 4,180 tokens and the header prompt to 5,200, both above the Haiku floor. Note the corollary: the 480-token per-vendor block is fine below the floor, because the floor applies to prefix length, not block length — it sits at the tail of a 5,680-token prefix.

PREFIX LAYOUT, three segments, two breakpoints. Render order is tools → system → messages, so: [deterministic tool list, sorted by name] → [system block A: frozen instructions + 31-field JSON schema + 12 worked examples, 5,200 tok, cache_control breakpoint 1] → [system block B: this vendor's layout hint block, 480 tok, breakpoint 2] → [user: OCR text + page images, no breakpoint, unique per document]. Nothing volatile above the last breakpoint — no `datetime.now()`, no run_id, no batch_id, no invoice number in the system prompt, and `json.dumps(schema, sort_keys=True)` so serialisation is byte-stable.

SORT THE BATCH BY VENDOR. This is the highest-leverage line of code in the baseline. With ~1,900 active vendors and 1,800 documents/night, an unsorted batch thrashes block B on nearly every call and it never pays back its write. Sorted by vendor_id, each vendor group is 5–20 consecutive documents and block B is written once and read 4–19 times.

1h TTL, not 5m. A 1,800-document batch runs 20–60 minutes; the global block A must survive the whole run, and 5m expires between vendor groups. Write premium is 2× vs 1.25×, break-even at ~3 reads, and every group clears that.

SERIALISE THE FIRST CALL OF EACH GROUP. The subtle one, and the one that separates a tuned baseline from a merely-configured one. A cache entry is readable only after the first response begins streaming, so N genuinely simultaneous callers with the same prefix ALL pay `cache_creation` and none read. Our own live probe measured this: at 0 ms inter-arrival skew, 5 of 5 concurrent callers were billed as writers; at ≥1 s skew, 1 of 5. So: (a) fire one `max_tokens: 0` pre-warm against block A at batch start and await it — prefill runs, cache is written, zero output tokens billed; (b) at each new vendor group, send the first document alone, await first token, then fan out the remaining 4–19 concurrently. Skipping (b) turns the vendor block from a saving into a 2× penalty on every group.

STRUCTURED OUTPUTS, not retry loops. `output_config.format` with the invoice JSON schema plus `strict: true` on any tool. This eliminates the parse-fail-and-retry loop, which is otherwise a hidden source of duplicate full-price calls that no caching strategy recovers.

BATCH API FOR THE NIGHTLY RUN. 50% off all token usage, prompt caching still applies, and the nightly run is not latency-sensitive. The 15-minute rush micro-batches stay on the synchronous path.

WHAT THIS BASELINE ACHIEVES, so the reuse layer knows what it must beat. On header extraction: 5,680 of ~8,770 input tokens cached ≈ 65% at 0.1×, giving effective input cost ≈ 0.65×0.1 + 0.35 = 0.415× of naive. On GL coding: 6,200 of 7,970 ≈ 78% cached → 0.30×. On line items: 3,100 of 6,920 ≈ 45% → 0.60×. On the high-resolution vision variant the per-document image term swells to 6,700 tokens and the cached share on header extraction falls to ~40% → 0.64×. Blended across the run the tuned baseline pays roughly 0.45× the naive input bill, and it does so for free, tonight, with no store to operate.

The critical point: this baseline captures essentially ALL of the streaming-regime opportunity. The only thing left over in the streaming path is the 1.29% duplicate channel — and even that is better served by the duplicate-hash lookup already sitting in `validate_arithmetic` than by a general reuse store.
grader:
Fully deterministic, no LLM in the loop, ground truth exact and free by construction — because the corpus is generated, not collected.

CORPUS GENERATOR. `gen_corpus(seed, n) -> [(doc.pdf, doc.png@300dpi, truth.json)]`. Forty seeded vendor templates vary the axes that actually break real extractors: label position and wording, date format (US/EU/ISO/written-month), currency and decimal separator, tax model (line-level VAT vs invoice-level sales tax vs reverse-charge), table column order, header/footer repetition, multi-page table continuation, and a stamped/skewed/low-contrast scan variant. Field-class count and page distribution calibrated to DocILE (55 classes, 1–3 pages) so the difficulty is realistic rather than toy. Regenerable from the seed, so nothing is stored, licensed, or PII.

TRUTH RECORD, per document: doc_id, vendor_id, invoice_number, invoice_date (ISO-8601), due_date (ISO-8601), currency (ISO-4217), po_number|null, subtotal_minor, tax_minor, freight_minor, discount_minor, total_minor, and line_items[] each with line_no, sku, description, qty_milli, unit_price_minor, line_total_minor, tax_rate_bp. All money in integer minor units and all quantities in integer milli-units, so no float comparison appears anywhere in the grader.

SCORING.
1. Canonicalise the prediction: dates → ISO-8601 (an ambiguous parse is scored wrong, not guessed); money strings → minor units via a fixed currency table; strings → NFKC + whitespace-collapse. Any canonicalisation failure marks that field wrong.
2. header_F1 = micro-F1 over (doc_id, field) exact matches across the 11 header fields.
3. lineitem_F1 = align predicted lines to truth by the explicitly rendered line_no, then exact-match all 6 sub-fields; micro-F1 over (doc_id, line_no, field). Unmatched predicted lines are false positives; unmatched truth lines are false negatives.
4. invariant_pass_rate, computed on the PREDICTION alone with no reference to truth: sum(line_total_minor)==subtotal_minor; qty_milli×unit_price_minor==line_total_minor×1000 (exact integer, no rounding slack); subtotal+tax+freight−discount==total. This is free self-consistency signal and it is exactly the check real AP pipelines run.
5. SCORE = 0.45×header_F1 + 0.45×lineitem_F1 + 0.10×invariant_pass_rate. Benchmark pass threshold SCORE ≥ 0.92, calibrated so a competent single-pass OCR+Haiku pipeline lands ≈ 0.94 and has room to regress visibly.

TWO HARD GATES SPECIFIC TO THE REUSE SYSTEM — these are the reason to prefer a generated corpus, and they cost nothing.

GATE A, reuse soundness (fail is absolute, independent of SCORE): run the identical corpus twice, once against an empty store and once against a warm one, and require sha256(canonical_json(output)) to be byte-identical per document. Any mismatch fails the benchmark outright regardless of how high SCORE is. This is the only check that catches a reuse layer serving a stale or mis-keyed result, and without it a reuse system can score well while being silently wrong.

GATE B, replay behaviour (this is the measurement the whole scenario exists to produce): mutate exactly one root artifact — append one field to extraction_schema.json — and re-run. Assert (a) tool_ops_executed across layers 0–2 (fetch, rasterize, ocr_page) == 0, i.e. all 6,120 deterministic upstream ops were served from the store; (b) SCORE over the unchanged 31 fields is identical to the last decimal. Report tool_ops_reused_pct, ocr_pages_reexecuted, and wall_clock_ratio vs the cold run. A reuse layer that cannot show tool_ops_reused_pct near 100 here has no case in this domain, because the streaming regime gives it nothing.
reuse_story:
There is exactly one mechanism, it is narrow, and it does not overlap with provider prefix caching at all.

Prefix caching is a discount on model input tokens. It cannot touch a tool op, because a tool op is not a prompt. In this graph 64% of operations are deterministic tool work, that work sits entirely upstream of every model call, and OCR — the single most expensive and slowest layer, billed per page by the hosted provider — is in it. A content-addressed store is the only mechanism that can serve `ocr_page` from a prior run.

The payoff arrives on replay, and the shape is precise. When the prompt pack or extraction schema changes and 60 days of history are re-extracted, the reuse key of every fetch/rasterize/OCR op is unchanged — those layers never read the prompt — while every model op's key changes. So a 100,000-document backfill re-executes 400,000 model calls and ZERO of the 340,000 OCR/rasterize/fetch ops. That eliminates the entire hosted-OCR page bill for the backfill and collapses its wall-clock, because OCR dominates end-to-end time. Prefix caching cannot contribute a cent to this; the two mechanisms are strictly complementary.

The second, smaller win is op-granular rather than prefix-granular invalidation. If only the line-item prompt changes, the 1,800 header-extraction model ops per run-equivalent still hit the store. Prefix caching cannot express this, because its unit of invalidation is a byte position in a prompt, not a node in a dependency graph. The same mechanism serves the 14% exception loop: a human corrects one field, and validate/match/code re-execute over unchanged OCR and extraction results.

Third and smallest: the 1.29% duplicate-resubmission channel gives whole-chain hits in the streaming path — though a duplicate-hash lookup already in `validate_arithmetic` gets most of that value more cheaply.

Net: the reuse layer's honest pitch here is "we make your backfills nearly free and much faster," not "we cut your token bill."
reuse_threats:
Seven, roughly in order of how likely each is to kill the case.

1. THE STREAMING REGIME OFFERS ~1.3%, AND IT IS MOST RUNS. On a normal night, 98.7% of input artifacts are documents never seen before, so the store serves ~290 of 19,891 ops. Writing and indexing 19,891 keys nightly to serve 290 hits is plausibly net-negative on storage and lookup alone. Worse, this repo already established that marking a never-reused prefix costs +25%, and the ROI gate would correctly decline to store almost this entire graph — which is the right call and also removes most of the surface area.

2. ONE VOLATILE ARGUMENT ZEROES THE REPLAY WIN. Real extraction ops pass today's date, because due dates are computed from payment terms relative to receipt. If that date is a literal argument to the op, every reuse key is unique and the replay hit rate is 0 even though nothing meaningful changed. Same for run_id, batch_id, or a correlation token threaded through for tracing. This is a one-line bug that silently converts the system into pure overhead, and it is extremely common in production pipelines.

3. po_snapshot.parquet CHANGES EVERY RUN BY CONSTRUCTION. It is a live ERP export. Every nightly re-export produces a new content hash, so all 1,170 `match_purchase_order` ops invalidate on every run and on every replay, regardless of whether any relevant PO moved. Fixing this means content-addressing at row granularity rather than file granularity, which is a different and much harder system than the one specified.

4. THE EXPENSIVE OPS ARE NOT ACTUALLY DETERMINISTIC. Hosted OCR is a versioned remote service with no pinned version exposed to the caller. The reuse key asserts that output is a pure function of (op type, arguments, artifact hashes), and for a hosted OCR endpoint that is simply false — the provider ships model updates silently. Serving a cached OCR result after a provider upgrade is serving a stale result while claiming soundness. The same applies more obviously to model ops, which are nondeterministic even at fixed inputs.

5. THE BUYER DOES NOT FEEL TOKENS. Model spend is ~1% of a $2.07–$10 fully-loaded cost per invoice. A 40% token reduction moves ~0.4% of unit cost — below the noise floor of their procurement. The pitch has to be denominated in OCR page fees avoided and backfill wall-clock, and those are the numbers I have the least confidence in, because I could find no published figure for how often real IDP shops actually backfill.

6. STORAGE IS DOMINATED BY THE THING THAT MAKES REPLAY WORK. The replay win requires retaining rasterized page images (~500 KB/page). At 2,520 pages/night that is 1.2 GB/night, ~440 GB/year per tenant, to serve a backfill every 3–8 weeks. Retaining only OCR text (~8 KB/page, 20 MB/night) is 60× cheaper but forfeits reuse of the rasterize layer and forces a re-render on any change to the image pipeline.

7. CROSS-USER SHARING IS PROHIBITED HERE, AND CROSS-DAY IS CONSTRAINED. The system's stated value includes reuse "across users." Invoices are financial records containing counterparty PII, bank details, and pricing that is frequently contractually confidential. A content-addressed store shared across tenants is a non-starter for this domain — it would let tenant A's key collide with tenant B's invoice bytes. Cross-day retention runs into 7-year records-retention rules pulling one way and GDPR erasure requests pulling the other, and an erasure request against a content-addressed store requires deleting a node plus every descendant key, which the design as specified has no mechanism for. So for invoice extraction, the store is realistically single-tenant and retention-bounded, which removes one of the three legs the value proposition stands on.
confidence:
Medium overall, with a sharp split by component.

HIGH confidence: the graph SHAPE (wide-independent fan-out, thin shared root, depth ~11 per chain, mean fan-in ~1.74) and the ordering of layers. This is consistent across every production description I checked — the microservice architecture paper (arXiv 2605.18818), the multi-stage OCR+VLM pipeline (arXiv 2510.23066), LlamaIndex/Rossum/BILL product documentation, and practitioner write-ups. Also high confidence in the streaming change rate being ≈99%: that is definitional, and the one component that pulls it below 100% (1.29% duplicates) is measured by SAP Concur and corroborated by APQC.

MEDIUM confidence: the per-op token sizes. These are constructed from documented per-image token costs (1,568px/~1,600 tok standard tier; 2,576px/4,784 tok high-res tier), documented cache minimums per model, DocILE's page and field-class distributions, and typical OCR text density — not from a real pipeline's telemetry. I would expect the true system-prompt sizes to vary ±50% across vendors, and the line-item output distribution to be heavier-tailed than I have modelled.

LOW confidence, and it is the number the entire conclusion hinges on: REPLAY FREQUENCY. My "one backfill every 3–8 weeks" is an informed guess. I searched specifically for published data on IDP prompt-change cadence, schema-migration frequency, and re-extraction volume and found none — vendors do not instrument or publish it. If the true figure is one backfill per quarter, the reuse layer is uneconomic here; if it is weekly, it is compelling. Everything in reuse_story is conditional on this.

WHAT WOULD RAISE IT, in order of value: (1) op-level telemetry from one real AP pipeline for 90 days — call counts, token histograms per op, and crucially a log of every prompt/schema deploy and the backfill it triggered; (2) a measured hosted-OCR cost per page for the specific stack, so the replay win can be denominated in dollars rather than in "OCR dominates latency"; (3) a determinism probe against the OCR provider — resubmit identical page bytes weekly for a quarter and measure how often output changes, which directly tests threat #4 and is cheap to run; (4) a survey of whether real extraction ops pass a wall-clock date as an argument, which decides threat #2 and could be answered by reading three open-source AP pipelines.

customer: Legal-ops / contract-intelligence function at a mid-to-large enterprise (2,000-20,000 executed agreements under management), either running its own pipeline or buying it from a CLM/contract-AI vendor (Evisort/Workday, Ironclad, Sirion, Luminance, Spellbook, LexisNexis). What they pay for is NOT "read one contract" — that is a $2-5 one-off. They pay for a maintained, queryable structured index over the whole executed portfolio: for every contract, which of ~40-230 clause types are present, the verbatim span and page cite for each, and whether that clause deviates from the company playbook. Downstream consumers are renewal/obligation calendars, revenue recognition (ASC 606 modification tracking), procurement risk dashboards, M&A due-diligence data rooms, and regulatory sweeps. Pricing is per-contract-under-management per year or per-seat, so the vendor eats the inference cost and margin is directly a function of tokens burned per portfolio re-scan. At the reference scale below a single full portfolio pass is ~45.5M input + ~5.6M output tokens per 510 contracts (~$220 at Sonnet-class rates), i.e. ~$5,200 per full pass over a 12,000-contract portfolio, run monthly plus ad-hoc — plus a comparable OCR bill.
why_repeated: Five genuinely distinct repeat drivers with very different reuse profiles — this is the crux of the scenario. (1) PERIODIC PORTFOLIO RE-SCAN: the extracted index is a system of record that must stay current; legal ops re-runs the full corpus monthly/quarterly because the source-of-truth is a DMS/SharePoint/Box sync that does NOT provide a trustworthy dirty-bit — documents get re-uploaded, re-OCR'd, re-exported with new file IDs and mtimes but identical content, and nobody trusts "unchanged since last run" enough to skip a compliance-relevant contract. So they re-run everything. (2) PLAYBOOK/TAXONOMY CHANGE: legal adds a clause type or rewrites a policy rule ("flag any AI-usage restriction", "flag any clause blocking subprocessor changes") and must backfill across the entire executed portfolio — the most common ad-hoc trigger, several times a year. (3) REGULATORY SWEEP: EU AI Act, LIBOR transition, tariff/force-majeure exposure, new data-residency rules — "which of our 12,000 contracts are exposed?" answered corpus-wide within days. (4) MODEL/PROMPT UPGRADE + CI EVAL: the vendor re-runs the pipeline over a 200-510 contract golden set on every prompt or model change, 5-20x/day, plus a full-portfolio re-baseline on model migration. (5) CRASH/RESUME: at 12,000 contracts a full pass is ~200k operations over 6-18 hours; partial failure (rate limits, OCR 5xx, a poison PDF, a gateway DNS flap) is routine and is handled today by a hand-rolled Postgres checkpoint table — which is a worse version of the reuse store. Drivers (1) and (5) are near-100% reuse. Drivers (2), (3), (4) are 0% model-layer reuse by construction and I will not pretend otherwise.
run_cadence: Headline: full-portfolio re-scan MONTHLY (some orgs quarterly; high-velocity procurement orgs weekly). Layered on top: daily/hourly incremental ingest of newly executed contracts (10-80 docs/day at 12k scale — new work, not a repeat run); ad-hoc playbook backfill 4-8x/year; regulatory sweep 2-4x/year; vendor CI eval over a 200-510 contract golden set 5-20x/day on weekdays; crash-resume roughly 1 in 5 full passes. The benchmark should model the monthly full re-scan as the primary run, with the playbook-change re-run and the CI-eval re-run as two adversarial variants a reuse layer must not claim credit for.

graph.description: Honest characterisation: 510 near-independent per-contract subgraphs (34 ops each, 10 deep) sitting under a tiny 27-op map-reduce tail. It is NOT one long chain, and NOT 500 flat independent calls either — inside each contract there is a real 10-deep dependency chain (OCR -> segment -> chunk/embed -> retrieve -> extract -> ground-verify -> classify -> rollup), and the middle fans out 12-wide per contract. The width is where the money is: 6,120 of 8,847 model ops and 83% of all input tokens live in one layer, L5 clause extraction. Cross-contract coupling is nil until the reduce tail, which is why leaf-level document churn gives near-linear reuse. The dangerous coupling is not between contracts, it is the shared context read by every extraction op (clause definitions + playbook slices) — artifact GRANULARITY at that root, not document churn, dominates the reuse economics. Reference corpus is CUAD v1 (510 real EDGAR commercial contracts, 9,283 pages = 18.2 pages/contract mean, ~11k tokens/contract, 13,101 lawyer-annotated spans, 41 categories, CC BY 4.0, free), so the graph is buildable and gradeable with zero data acquisition cost. Artifacts = 510 contract PDFs + 12 clause-group definition files + 12 per-group playbook rule slices = 534. The 41 CUAD labels are bucketed into 12 thematic groups: term/termination, IP/license, confidentiality, liability/indemnity, exclusivity+non-compete+MFN, assignment/change-of-control, payment/revenue-share, audit/insurance, warranty, governing-law/venue, data-privacy, restrictive-covenants. Scale factor to a real 12,000-contract portfolio is 23.5x on every per-contract layer; the reduce tail grows as N/20. Depth chain (10): L1 OCR -> L2 segment -> L3 chunk/embed -> L4 retrieve -> L5 extract -> L6 ground-verify -> L7 classify -> L8 contract rollup -> L9 batch rollup -> L10 final rollup. L11 warehouse write hangs off L8 at depth 9.

layers.name: L1 ingest_ocr_normalize
layers.consumes: nothing upstream; reads one contract artifact directly (fan-in 0)
layers.reads_artifacts: one contract PDF (mean 18.2 pages, ~1.6 MB); commercial OCR/document-AI at $0.01-0.05/page

layers.name: L2 section_segmentation
layers.consumes: L1, 1 op per op (its own contract's normalized text)
layers.reads_artifacts: none (pure function of L1 output); rule/regex heading+article splitter, ~60 sections emitted

layers.name: L3 chunk_and_embed
layers.consumes: L2, 1 op per op
layers.reads_artifacts: none; splits into ~30 windows of 450 tokens with 60-token overlap, one batched embedding call per contract (15,300 chunks corpus-wide)

layers.name: L4 clause_group_retrieval
layers.consumes: L3 (1 op) + L2 (1 op) = fan-in 2; 12 retrieval ops per contract, one per clause group
layers.reads_artifacts: the clause-group definition file for its group (used to build the query); returns top-8 chunks

layers.name: L5 clause_extraction
layers.consumes: L4 (1 op) + L2 (1 op) = fan-in 2; 12 model ops per contract
layers.reads_artifacts: the clause-group definition file for its group. Input breakdown: 2,000 static (system + output schema + few-shot + group clause definitions), 3,600 retrieved chunks, 600 section index + contract header. Output is JSON [{clause_type, verbatim_span, page, confidence}]. THIS LAYER IS 83% OF ALL INPUT TOKENS (37.9M of 45.5M).

layers.name: L6 span_grounding_verify
layers.consumes: L5 (12 ops) + L1 (1 op) = fan-in 13
layers.reads_artifacts: none; exact-substring-matches every returned verbatim span back into the normalized text, drops ungrounded spans, emits ~25.7 verified clause records per contract (13,101/510 CUAD mean)

layers.name: L7 playbook_classification
layers.consumes: L6, 1 op per op; ~4.3 batched ops per contract (25.7 clauses / 6 per batch)
layers.reads_artifacts: the per-group playbook rule slice (~1,500 tokens). Input = 1,500 playbook rules + 900 clause text batch. Output = {clause_id, label in [compliant|minor|material], rule_id, rationale} x6.

layers.name: L8 contract_risk_rollup
layers.consumes: L7 (4.3 ops) + L6 (1 op) = fan-in 5.3
layers.reads_artifacts: none; synthesizes per-contract risk summary, obligation list, deterministic risk score

layers.name: L9 portfolio_batch_rollup
layers.consumes: L8, 20 ops per op (ceil(510/20) batches) = fan-in 20
layers.reads_artifacts: none

layers.name: L10 portfolio_final_report
layers.consumes: L9, all 26 ops = fan-in 26
layers.reads_artifacts: none; emits the structured JSON portfolio report the grader scores in Part C

layers.name: L11 warehouse_upsert
layers.consumes: L8, 1 op per op (branches off at depth 9, not on the critical path)
layers.reads_artifacts: none; upserts ~26 clause rows + 1 contract row per contract into the index

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 0% to 8% depending on trigger. Monthly full re-scan: 2-4% of contract artifacts differ (typical 3%). Weekly incremental cadence: 0.1-0.5%. Quarterly: 6-10%. Playbook-change backfill, regulatory sweep, model upgrade, CI eval: EXACTLY 0% of contract artifacts differ (but 100% of model-op keys change). Crash-resume: 0% differ and 0% of keys change. Cumulative annual document turnover: 15-25%.
change_rate.basis: Partly sourced, partly estimated, and I want to be explicit about which. SOURCED: CUAD v1 gives exact corpus geometry (510 contracts, 9,283 pages, 13,101 labeled spans, 41 categories, ~10% of each contract clause-labeled, ~0.25% per individual label) — arxiv.org/abs/2103.06268, zenodo.org/records/4595826. Customer/contract renewal rates of 85-95%/yr are corroborated by two PRIMARY SEC filings (GEO Group 10-K: facility management contract renewal ~90%; CoStar 10-Q FY2026: ~89% subscription renewal for >=1yr terms), bounding annual portfolio churn-out at ~5-15%/yr with roughly matching new-execution inflow, i.e. ~1%/month of the portfolio replaced. ESTIMATED / WEAKLY SOURCED: the widely-repeated figure that ~40% of commercial contracts are amended at least once during term, and that enterprise software agreements average ~2.3 amendments over a 3-year initial term, surfaced attributed to Deloitte Contract Analytics 2024 — I tried three separate searches to locate the primary Deloitte publication and could NOT verify it; treat it as folklore. Taking it at face value gives ~13%/yr amendment rate = ~1.1%/month. Replacement (~1%/mo) + amendment (~1.1%/mo) + amended-and-restated reissues gives the 2-4%/month figure. This is an ESTIMATE anchored on one verified and one unverified source; it could plausibly be 1% or 6%. Also weakly sourced: a legal-tech engineering source puts the average US commercial contract at 'at least 12 pages', consistent with but lower than CUAD's primary 18.2. NOT SOURCED AT ALL, field intuition only: observed FILE-level churn in a DMS-synced corpus is far higher than CONTENT churn — re-exports, re-OCR passes and connector resyncs produce new file IDs and mtimes for byte-identical documents at rates I would put at 10-40% per sync. That gap is the entire practical argument for content-hash keying over path/mtime keying, and it is why the customer cannot skip unchanged work today. It is load-bearing and unverified.
change_rate.where_changes_land: Overwhelmingly at the LEAVES, which is the good case. A changed or new contract PDF is the root of its own 34-op subgraph and touches nothing else, so a 3% document change invalidates ~3% of ops plus the 27-op reduce tail (0.15% of ops) — roughly 96-97% of the graph is legitimately reusable on a monthly re-scan. Amendments are ADDITIVE rather than mutative about 75-85% of the time (a new amendment PDF is filed alongside an untouched base agreement), which is better still: the base contract's 34 ops stay valid and only the amendment's subgraph plus the affected contract-level rollup recompute. The 15-25% of long-running agreements that get amended-and-restated are true mutations and invalidate the whole subgraph. THE OTHER PLACE CHANGES LAND IS THE KILLER: the 12 clause-definition files and 12 playbook rule slices are read by all 6,120 extraction ops and all 2,190 classification ops. One word changed in a playbook invalidates that entire slice's model ops while 0% of documents changed — and playbook edits are the single most common reason this customer re-runs. If the playbook is modelled as ONE artifact, realistic average reuse collapses from ~96% to roughly 40%, because about half of real re-runs are playbook-triggered. Sliced into 12 per-group artifacts (as specified in the layer spec), a typical single-group edit invalidates 1/12 of the extraction layer (~8%) instead of all of it. That structural choice is worth more than every other reuse consideration in this workload combined, and any honest benchmark MUST include a playbook-edit variant to expose it.

session_structure: A competent engineer builds this as CONTRACT-MAJOR full-document prefix caching, not retrieval, and it is a genuinely strong baseline. Concretely: (a) DROP the retrieval layer for extraction — at 11k tokens a contract fits trivially in context and the cached-read rate (10% of input) is cheaper than the accuracy loss from chunk retrieval. Issue all 12 clause-group calls for one contract back-to-back against a shared prefix. (b) Prompt order, strictly: [static system + output schema + global few-shot, ~1,200 tok] -> cache_control breakpoint -> [full normalized contract text + section index, ~11,600 tok] -> cache_control breakpoint -> [this group's clause definitions + question, ~600 tok]. Two invariants at the front; only the last ~600 tokens vary across the 12 calls. (c) WARM THE CACHE BEFORE FANNING OUT. Issue group 1 alone, await the response (which writes the 12,800-token prefix at the 1.25x write premium), THEN fan out groups 2-12 concurrently. Firing all 12 concurrently makes every one of them pay the write premium — a measurable 20-30% own-goal on exactly this shape. (d) Use the 1-HOUR cache TTL, not the 5-minute default: a contract's 12-call pass plus its downstream classify calls span more than 5 minutes under realistic queue depth and retry, and the shared 1,200-token global prefix wants to survive across contracts for the whole run. (e) Order the classify layer PLAYBOOK-MAJOR: put the full playbook slice (1,500 tok) in the cached prefix and stream all clause batches for the same clause group across all contracts against it, keeping that prefix hot for hundreds of calls. (f) Batch 6 clauses per classify call — output-token amortisation, not cache. (g) Reduce tail is a plain map-reduce with a shared cached instruction prefix; it is 0.3% of ops and does not matter. ECONOMICS, per contract, extraction layer: naive = 12 x 11,300 = 135,600 input token-equivalents; tuned = 12,800 x 1.25 (one write) + 12 x (12,800 x 0.1 + 600) = 16,000 + 22,320 = ~30,550 token-equivalents — a 77% cut. Classify layer gets ~56%. So the tuned baseline removes roughly three quarters of the input bill WITHIN a run. WHAT IT STRUCTURALLY CANNOT DO: carry anything across runs. Runs are 30 days apart, max TTL is 1 hour, so next month's pass pays that same 30,550/contract again for the 97% of contracts that did not change by a single byte. It also cannot dedupe the OCR layer, which at 18.2 pages/contract and $0.01-0.05/page is $90-450 per 510-contract pass — comparable to the whole LLM bill and 100% redundant on a re-scan. The reuse layer's entire claim is the across-run axis plus the tool layer, where the provider cache is not a competitor at all. Caveat: the customer's existing hand-rolled checkpoint table already captures part of the crash-resume case, so that portion is not incremental value.
grader: Fully deterministic, no LLM, exact and free ground truth, in three independently-scored parts. GROUND TRUTH SOURCE: CUAD v1 (Zenodo 4595826, CC BY 4.0) — 510 contracts as PDF and pre-extracted TXT, 13,101 lawyer-annotated verbatim clause spans across 41 categories, distributed as SQuAD-style JSON with exact answer strings. Free, no annotation cost. PART A — EXTRACTION F1 (grades L1-L6). System emits per contract a list of {clause_type from the fixed 41-label vocabulary, verbatim_span string, page_int}. Grader: (1) normalize predicted and gold spans by NFKC, lowercase, collapse whitespace runs to a single space, strip leading/trailing punctuation; (2) locate the predicted span in the normalized CUAD .txt by exact substring search — if not found it scores as a false positive AND increments a separate hard 'ungrounded/hallucinated span' counter which is reported and must be zero for a run to be valid; (3) a prediction matches a gold span iff same clause_type AND character-interval Jaccard >= 0.5, with greedy one-to-one assignment in descending Jaccard order so matching is deterministic; (4) report micro-F1 over all (contract, clause_type, span) triples. PART B — PRESENCE MATRIX (same layers, zero span-boundary noise). 510 x 41 = 20,910 binary cells: did the system correctly assert present/absent for each clause type in each contract? Gold is a direct read of the CUAD annotation file. Score = balanced accuracy and Matthews correlation coefficient; the matrix is ~94% empty so raw accuracy is useless and must not be reported. PART C — PLAYBOOK COMPLIANCE + ROLLUP (grades L7-L10 without an LLM judge; this is where the task had to be designed for gradeability). CUAD has no deviation labels, so supply a SEEDED, MACHINE-CHECKABLE playbook: a versioned YAML of ~30 rules that are pure functions of extracted spans. Examples: GOV-01 'material iff the Governing Law span names a jurisdiction outside {Delaware, New York, California}' (regex over a fixed 60-entry jurisdiction gazetteer); MFN-01 'material iff a Most Favored Nation span is present'; ASSIGN-02 'material iff Anti-Assignment present AND Change of Control present'; CAP-01 'material iff the Cap on Liability span contains a numeric multiplier < 1.0 per a fixed regex'; TERM-03 'minor iff Notice Period to Terminate Renewal exceeds 90 days per a fixed duration parser'. A ~200-line Python reference implementation runs these same rules over the GOLD spans to produce exact ground truth for every (contract, rule) pair, free, in under a second. The system under test must produce the same labels having seen only the raw PDF. Score = macro-F1 over the 3-way {compliant, minor, material} label across all populated (contract, rule) cells. The portfolio rollup is graded as a STRUCTURED artifact, never prose: the final report must be JSON containing (i) a count per clause type, checked by exact integer equality; (ii) the sorted list of contract IDs with any material deviation, checked by set equality with Jaccard reported; (iii) the top-10 contracts by a fully specified deterministic risk score (sum of per-rule weights given in the playbook YAML), checked by exact ordered-list equality with ties broken by contract ID ascending. All three parts are exact, free, reproducible, with no model in the loop. DETERMINISM CAVEAT THAT MATTERS FOR THE REUSE EXPERIMENT: LLMs are not bit-deterministic even at temperature 0, so the reuse layer must NOT be validated by byte-comparing outputs against a fresh run — validate by SCORE PARITY: score_with_reuse >= score_baseline - epsilon, with epsilon set from measured run-to-run variance of the no-reuse pipeline (empirically ~0.5-1.5 F1 on this task; measure over 5 baseline runs before setting it). Report cost alongside every score in one table — input tokens at full rate, at cached-read rate, at cache-write rate, output tokens, and OCR pages — because a reuse layer that saves 90% of tokens while dropping 4 F1 is a failure and the harness must make that visible.
reuse_story: Three mechanisms, in descending order of how much I believe them. (1) THE TOOL LAYER IS PURE WIN AND NOBODY DISPUTES IT. 8,670 of 17,517 ops are deterministic functions of file bytes: OCR/text extraction, section segmentation, chunking, embedding, span grounding, warehouse upsert. OCR alone at commercial rates ($0.01-0.05/page x 18.2 pages) is $90-450 per 510-contract pass — comparable to the entire LLM bill — and on a monthly re-scan ~97% of it recomputes an identical answer. Provider prefix caching does not touch this at all, and nothing in the customer's stack does either, because the DMS gives them no trustworthy dirty-bit. Content-hash keying turns an O(N) pass into O(dN) here with essentially no correctness risk, and it survives the file-ID/mtime churn that defeats path-based skipping. Crucially this benefit persists even when the prompt or model changes — exactly when the model-layer benefit is zero. (2) THE MONTHLY MODEL-LAYER RE-SCAN. ~97% of contracts are byte-identical month to month; with per-clause-group playbook artifacts and an unchanged playbook, ~96% of the 8,847 model ops hit the store. The tuned prefix-cache baseline achieves 77% within-run but structurally 0% across-run (1-hour TTL vs 30-day cadence), so this axis is uncontested — the reuse layer competes against full price, not against the provider cache. Because keys compose transitively, an unchanged contract with an unchanged playbook slice produces ZERO calls, not cheap calls: that is a 100% saving on that subgraph versus the baseline's 77%. (3) CRASH-RESUME AND CI. A 12,000-contract pass is ~200k ops over 6-18 hours and partially fails routinely; CI eval over a 200-contract golden set runs 5-20x/day. Both are 0%-artifact-change scenarios where the tool layer reuses 100%, and for crash-resume the model layer reuses 100% too. Honest discount: the customer usually already has a checkpoint table for the crash case, so this is a generality-and-quality win more than a pure cost win.
reuse_threats: Five, two of them severe. (1) THE PLAYBOOK ROOT — the dominant threat. Roughly half of all real re-runs are triggered by a playbook or clause-taxonomy edit, and every extraction and classification op reads that context. If the playbook is one artifact, those runs deliver exactly 0% model-layer reuse while superficially looking like 0%-document-change (i.e. maximally cacheable) runs. A benchmark that only measures the monthly document-churn case overstates this workload's value by roughly 2x. The fix is artifact slicing (12 per-group files), a real engineering win that must be earned, not assumed. (2) MODEL UPGRADES INVALIDATE EVERYTHING BY DESIGN. The model id is in the key; this customer migrates models 2-4x/year and A/B tests continuously. Every such run is 0% model-layer reuse — and the customer WANTS that invalidation: silently serving a Sonnet-4.5 answer for an Opus-5 request would be a correctness bug in a compliance product. (3) PROMPT DRIFT IS CONTINUOUS AT THE VENDOR. Contract-AI vendors tune extraction prompts weekly; every tweak to a shared system prompt fully invalidates the layer it sits in, so model-layer reuse in vendor CI is near zero no matter what. (4) THE 77% BASELINE IS ALREADY VERY GOOD WITHIN A RUN, so incremental win on a FIRST run is zero — and can be NEGATIVE if the reuse layer's key computation or store lookup perturbs prompt ordering, splits the call stream, or reorders the queue in a way that breaks contract-major prefix locality. The two mechanisms must be composed deliberately, not stacked naively. (5) NON-DETERMINISM AND LEGAL DEFENSIBILITY. This is a compliance artifact. Serving today an answer computed last month is defensible only if OCR text, clause definitions, playbook, model, and sampling params are provably identical — which the reuse key does establish — but "we did not actually look at that contract this quarter, we reused a hash" is a procurement conversation, not a technical one. Some regulated buyers (financial services, healthcare, government) will refuse it for attestation-bearing runs, and expect a per-rule or per-run force-recompute flag that customers over-use. NET HONEST ASSESSMENT: high reuse on the tool layer always; high reuse on the model layer for the monthly-rescan and crash-resume cases only; near-zero model-layer reuse for the playbook/model/prompt-change cases, which are roughly half of real re-runs. A blended real-world number is plausibly 55-70% of ops served from store, not the 96% the monthly case alone suggests.
confidence: Medium overall, unevenly distributed. HIGH confidence in graph shape, operation counts and token sizes: CUAD v1 gives exact primary numbers (510 contracts, 9,283 pages = 18.2 pages/contract, 13,101 spans, 41 categories, ~10% of each contract labeled, ~0.25% per label), and the 12-clause-group fan-out over full-document context is how these pipelines are actually built. HIGH confidence in the tuned baseline: contract-major full-document prefix caching with a serialized warm-up call and 1-hour TTL is a specific, correct, non-straw-man design and I stand behind the ~77% figure. HIGH confidence in the grader: CUAD plus a seeded machine-checkable playbook gives exact free ground truth with no LLM in the loop. MEDIUM-LOW confidence in the 3%/month change rate — the renewal half rests on two primary SEC filings, but the amendment half rests on a widely-repeated ~40%-amended-during-term figure I attempted three times to trace to Deloitte and could not verify; treat 3% as a defensible estimate, not a measurement (plausible range 1-6%). LOW confidence in my claim that DMS file-level churn (new IDs/mtimes for identical bytes) runs 10-40% per sync — field intuition, unpublished, and load-bearing for the 'they cannot skip unchanged work today' argument.
