WHAT WOULD RAISE CONFIDENCE, in priority order: (a) one real customer's contract-repository event log over 6 months giving actual per-run counts of documents added / content-modified / re-uploaded-identical — this single artifact settles both weak numbers at once; (b) one CLM vendor's re-processing job history showing the real distribution of re-run triggers (document-churn vs playbook-edit vs model-upgrade), which sets the blend between the 96% and 0% reuse regimes and is the highest-variance unknown in the whole estimate; (c) a measured OCR-vs-LLM cost split from a production contract pipeline, to confirm the tool layer is as economically significant as I claim; (d) five baseline no-reuse runs over CUAD to empirically set the score-parity epsilon before any reuse claim is made.

customer: A US acute-care hospital's mid-revenue-cycle function, or the autonomous-coding/CDI vendor that serves it (Fathom, CodaMetrix, Nym, AKASA, Iodine, Regard class). They pay per inpatient encounter coded — roughly $2–$6/chart for autonomous inpatient coding, or a per-bed/PMPM subscription for concurrent CDI review. What they are buying is (a) coder FTE displacement, (b) DRG/CC-MCC capture they would otherwise miss, and (c) an auditable rationale trail, because the deliverable is a billed claim that a RAC auditor or payer can claw back. Denial rates hit 11.6% in 2025 ($48.4B), outpatient coding-related denials rose 26% YoY, and coding errors are 25% of audit triggers — so accuracy is priced, not just throughput.
why_repeated: Two independent repeat drivers, and it matters which one you pick. (1) CONCURRENT REVIEW — the real one. CDI/autonomous-coding platforms re-process every currently-admitted patient's chart on a nightly cadence, because the working DRG drives length-of-stay management, physician queries, and expected reimbursement while the patient is still in the bed. A 4.9-day-ALOS encounter is therefore processed ~5 times, and each night's run reads the same signed notes as last night's plus the ~7 filed in the last 24h. This is where the reuse surface lives. (2) LIFECYCLE RE-CODING — the same encounter is re-run after a CDI query response lands (12–40% of reviewed inpatient charts get a query per ACDIS benchmarks, 65–85% physician response rate), after a pre-bill audit, and after a coding-related denial or appeal. Plus corpus-wide re-runs on every engine/prompt release and on the quarterly regulatory updates. NOTE THE HONEST CAVEAT: hospitals that do discharge-only coding (one pass per encounter after the discharge summary is signed) have essentially NO cross-run reuse surface — each run reads a fresh chart. The entire reuse thesis in this domain rests on the concurrent-review cadence being the customer's actual workflow.
run_cadence: Nightly batch, ~02:00 local, over the full inpatient census plus the prior day's discharges — sized so the coding manager's morning worklist is ready. Latency-insensitive (a multi-hour window is fine), which makes the Batch API the correct baseline. Some vendors run a second intraday pass at ~14:00 for high-acuity units. Regulatory root updates land on a fixed calendar: ICD-10-CM/PCS + MS-DRG grouper annually Oct 1 (FY2026 = v43.0), a mid-year grouper update Apr 1 (v43.1), and NCCI PTP/MUE edits quarterly (Jan/Apr/Jul/Oct 1).

graph.description: One run = one nightly batch over a 350-bed hospital's inpatient census (~300 encounters at 85% occupancy, ALOS 4.9d, ~61 admits and ~61 discharges/day). It is a wide layered DAG, not a chain and not N independent ops: ~300 near-identical per-encounter subgraphs of ~110 ops each, fanning out over documents at the bottom and funneling hard into a single per-encounter principal-diagnosis + DRG decision at the top, with one cross-encounter reconciliation op at the very end. Counts below are PER RUN; divide by 300 for per-encounter. Average encounter on census is at day 3.4 of stay with 26.3 cumulative coding-relevant documents (~25k tokens of chart text at discharge for a med-surg stay; 60–100k for ICU). Document mix per encounter-day: ~2.4 physician progress notes, ~3 radiology reports, ~0.6 consult notes, 1 rendered structured digest (labs/meds/vitals), plus a one-time H&P (1,400 tok), 0–1 operative note (900 tok), a prior-encounter problem-list/HCC blob (1,200 tok), and a discharge summary on the final day (1,800 tok — MIMIC-IV: 600M tokens across 330k discharge summaries = ~1,820 each). Uncached, the model layers burn ~127M input / 4.7M output tokens per night = ~$450 at Sonnet-class rates = ~$1.50/encounter against a $2–6 price point, which is exactly why the caching design is load-bearing rather than a nicety.

layers.name: L0_chart_fetch
layers.consumes: nothing — graph root; args are (encounter_id, as_of_timestamp)
layers.reads_artifacts: the EHR FHIR/HL7 endpoint for one encounter; emits a manifest of document IDs with per-document content hashes. This op is where the external mutable world enters the graph.

layers.name: L1_doc_normalize
layers.consumes: L0 — 26.3 ops per encounter, one per document in the manifest
layers.reads_artifacts: one raw clinical document. Does de-identification/surrogate mapping, HL7-CDA section segmentation (CC/HPI/ROS/PE/Assessment-Plan/meds), and copy-forward block detection. Deterministic given document bytes + normalizer version. THIS OP DECIDES THE REUSE GRANULARITY: emit one artifact per document and the 54% copy-forward redundancy is invisible to a content hash; emit one per section/block and it becomes harvestable.

layers.name: L2_evidence_extract
layers.consumes: L1 — one op per normalized document, fan-in 1
layers.reads_artifacts: one normalized document plus a frozen 6,000-token shared prefix (extraction schema, negation/uncertainty/historicity/subject rubric, section taxonomy, ICD-10-CM chapter-level guidance excerpt). Emits structured clinical entities — conditions, procedures with laterality/approach/device, POA-relevant timing — each with a verbatim source character span. This is the highest-count model layer and where most raw document tokens are spent.

layers.name: L3_candidate_lookup
layers.consumes: L2 — ~1.3 ops per extracted entity
layers.reads_artifacts: SNOMED-CT→ICD-10-CM map, the FY2026 ICD-10-CM Alphabetic Index + Tabular List, the ICD-10-PCS tables, and the billable-leaf code file. Deterministic given entity text + code-set version. A single reference-file version bump re-keys all 10,200 of these and everything downstream.

layers.name: L4_code_adjudicate
layers.consumes: L2 + L3 — 18 ops per encounter, one per deduped candidate code, fan-in ~4.5 (evidence spans for the same diagnosis pulled from multiple notes)
layers.reads_artifacts: a 6,000-token frozen guidelines prefix + a 4,000-token per-encounter evidence bundle + the candidate code and its supporting/refuting spans. Decides: is it documented to coding-guideline standard, is it a reportable secondary dx under clinical-significance criteria, what is the POA flag, does a chapter-specific rule apply (sepsis sequencing, HIV, obstetrics, combination codes). The cross-document fan-in here is what makes this layer fragile to reuse.

layers.name: L5_principal_dx_select
layers.consumes: L4 — 1 per encounter, fan-in 18
layers.reads_artifacts: all adjudicated codes plus the full Assessment/Plan narrative across the stay. Applies the 'condition established after study chiefly responsible for the admission' rule. Single highest-dollar decision in the graph and a total funnel point — any new note anywhere in the encounter re-keys it.

layers.name: L6_procedure_code_pcs
layers.consumes: L1 + L2 — 1 per operative/procedure note, fan-in ~3
layers.reads_artifacts: the operative note plus a 4,000-token ICD-10-PCS reference prefix. PCS is 7-character combinatorial (section, body system, root operation, body part, approach, device, qualifier) and needs its own pass; a wrong root operation moves the DRG by thousands of dollars.

layers.name: L7_grouper
layers.consumes: L5 + L4 + L6 — 1 per encounter, fan-in 19
layers.reads_artifacts: the CMS ICD-10 MS-DRG Grouper + Medicare Code Editor v43.1 (free Java reference implementation from cms.gov, FOIA-released). Inputs principal dx, up to 24 secondary dx with POA flags, up to 25 PCS codes, age, sex, discharge status. Outputs MS-DRG, MDC, CC/MCC tier, relative weight, and MCE edit flags. Fully deterministic — and the op whose output the customer actually gets paid on.

layers.name: L8_edit_check
layers.consumes: L7 — 1 per encounter
layers.reads_artifacts: NCCI PTP pair file + MUE file (quarterly), payer LCD/medical-necessity policy set, POA validity rules. April 2026 alone added 3,750+ PTP pairs and deleted 4,800+.

layers.name: L9_cdi_query_gen
layers.consumes: L4 + L7 — fires only when a documentation gap with DRG impact is detected (~30% of encounters, matching ACDIS query-rate benchmarks of 12–40%)
layers.reads_artifacts: the evidence bundle, the working DRG, and the AHIMA/ACDIS compliant-query template set. Drafts a non-leading physician query. Its answer becomes a NEW signed document tomorrow — this op is the mechanism by which the pipeline mutates its own future inputs.

layers.name: L10_rationale_and_gate
layers.consumes: everything upstream for the encounter — fan-in 21
layers.reads_artifacts: the full adjudicated code set, spans, and grouper result. Emits the auditable rationale (code → evidence span → guideline citation) and the auto-bill vs. route-to-human-coder decision. Vendors quote 85%+ direct-to-bill rates, so this gate is what the pricing model rests on.

layers.name: L11_batch_reconcile
layers.consumes: L7 + L10 across all 300 encounters — fan-in 300
layers.reads_artifacts: the hospital's rolling case-mix-index baseline and DRG distribution. Flags CMI drift and statistical outliers for the coding manager's morning worklist. One op, but it re-keys on every single encounter, so it never reuses.

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 18–45% night-over-night for concurrent review; ~100% if the customer runs discharge-only coding; 100% on 4+ scheduled regulatory-update days per year
change_rate.basis: Partly sourced, partly computed from sourced inputs — I'll separate them. SOURCED: (a) Signed clinical notes are immutable by regulation — CMS/AHIMA amendment guidance requires the original entry remain retrievable, so corrections arrive as addenda or versioned amendments (NEW artifacts), never as in-place edits. This is the single most important fact for reuse in this domain and it is a legal fact, not an estimate: yesterday's documents are byte-identical today. (b) Copy-forward redundancy is 54% of progress-note text duplicated from prior notes in the same admission (multiple studies converge here; a UCSF study of 23,630 Epic progress notes decomposed a typical note as 18% manually entered / 46% copied / 36% imported; outpatient median redundancy rose 47.9%→58.8% between 2009 and 2018). (c) Discharge summary length ~1,820 tokens (MIMIC-IV-Note: 330k summaries, ~600M tokens; the MIMIC-IV-Ext-BHC subset averages 2,267). (d) Regulatory root churn: ICD-10-CM FY2026 = 487 new / 38 revised / 28 deleted codes effective 2025-10-01, i.e. 0.75% of a ~74,000-code file, once a year; MS-DRG grouper v43.1 effective 2026-04-01 added 80 PCS codes mid-year; NCCI updates quarterly (April 2026: 3,750+ new PTP pairs, 4,800+ deletions, 121 new MUEs). (e) ACDIS query rates 12–40% of reviewed charts, 65–85% physician response. ESTIMATED, and I could not find published data for it: the number of coding-relevant documents filed per patient-day (~7). I could find cumulative chart sizes (a 2006–2023 study of 730,968 ED visits found general-admission patients had a median 541 prior notes / 95,411 words available in 2022 — but that is the patient's whole historical chart, not the current encounter's documentation) and I could not find a per-encounter-day note-count distribution. My 27.4% is computed as (61 new encounters × 7 docs + 178 mid-stay × 7 new docs + 61 discharging × 8 new docs) ÷ (300 encounters × 26.3 cumulative docs) = 2,161 / 7,890. Treat the 7 as the load-bearing estimate; the ratio moves roughly linearly with it. The range endpoints come from ALOS: an LTAC/rehab census (ALOS 25d) has a much larger cumulative denominator and lands near 18%; a short-stay/observation-heavy hospital (ALOS 2.5d) has most of its census new each night and lands near 45%.
change_rate.where_changes_land: Split, and the split is the whole story. CLINICAL DOCUMENTS CHANGE AT THE LEAVES: new notes are appended, prior notes are frozen by regulation. ~72% of document artifacts are byte-identical night to night, and those unchanged leaves feed L1/L2/L3, which are 26 of ~47 model ops per encounter and carry most of the raw document tokens. That is a genuinely favorable shape. REFERENCE ARTIFACTS CHANGE AT THE ROOTS: the ICD-10-CM code file, the PCS tables, the MS-DRG grouper, the MCE edit lists, the NCCI PTP/MUE files, and the Official Coding Guidelines are each one artifact consumed by every candidate lookup and every adjudication. A 0.75% content change to the code file is a 100% hash change to the artifact, which re-keys all 33,121 ops. So the year looks like ~361 nights at 27% change and ~4 nights at 100%, plus a full flush on every prompt or model version bump. THE THIRD PLACE — AND THE ONE THAT QUIETLY DESTROYS MOST OF THE WIN: the funnel ops. L5 (principal dx), L7 (grouper), L8 (edits), L10 (rationale/gate) each consume the entire encounter, so a single new progress note anywhere re-keys all of them. ~80% of the census gains at least one note each night. Worse, L4 adjudication fans in across documents, and a routine progress note restates the active problem list — so one new note re-keys roughly 60% of that encounter's adjudications too. Netting it out honestly: ~76% of L2 ops reuse, ~40% of L4 ops reuse, and 0% of L5–L11 reuse on any encounter with a new note. That is ~60% of model ops, weighted toward the cheaper ones.

session_structure: A competent engineer gets most of this workload's shared-token cost to 0.1× with provider-native caching alone, and the reuse layer has to beat THAT, not a naive baseline. Concretely: (1) FREEZE A PER-LAYER PREFIX. L2's prefix — sorted tool definitions, then a system block holding the extraction schema, negation/historicity rubric, section taxonomy, and guidance excerpt — is ~6,000 tokens and byte-identical across all 7,890 L2 calls in a run. One `cache_control` breakpoint on the last system block covers tools+system (render order is tools → system → messages). L4 gets its own ~6,000-token guidelines prefix, L6 a ~4,000-token PCS reference prefix. (2) TWO-LEVEL BREAKPOINTS. For the 18 L4 calls belonging to one encounter, the ~4,000-token evidence bundle is shared across all of them: breakpoint 1 at the end of the global prefix, breakpoint 2 at the end of the encounter bundle, then the ~1,200-token candidate rides uncached after it. That is 10,000 of an 11,400-token request served at 0.1×, using 2 of the 4 allowed breakpoints. (3) NOTHING VOLATILE ABOVE A BREAKPOINT — no run date, no encounter ID, no `datetime.now()` in the system prompt, deterministic JSON serialization, sorted tool list. A single interpolated timestamp at the front discards everything after it. (4) SERIALIZE THE FIRST CALL OF EACH PREFIX, THEN FAN OUT. This is the one most teams get wrong and it is decisive here: a cache entry only becomes readable once the first response BEGINS STREAMING, so firing 7,890 L2 calls concurrently means all 7,890 pay the 1.25× write and none reads — the cache is a net loss. The right shape is a `max_tokens: 0` pre-warm per distinct prefix (runs prefill, writes the cache, returns immediately, bills zero output tokens), then fan out. (5) LAYER-MAJOR BATCH ORDERING — run all L2 calls, then all L4, rather than walking each encounter down through the layers, so one prefix stays hot instead of thrashing between three. (6) 1h TTL on the global L2/L4 prefixes (2× write amortized over thousands of reads is free), 5m default on the per-encounter bundle (18 reads in seconds). (7) BATCH API — this is a nightly, latency-insensitive job, so everything runs at 50% off, and batches support caching. (8) PIN THE MODEL — caches are model-scoped, a mid-run switch is a total flush. WHAT THIS BASELINE ALREADY CAPTURES: essentially all of the shared-prefix input cost. An L2 call drops from ~7,000 full-price input tokens to ~1,600 effective (6,000 read at 0.1× + 1,000 uncached document), and halves again under batch pricing. WHAT IT STRUCTURALLY CANNOT CAPTURE, and therefore the reuse layer's entire opening: (a) the per-document content itself, which varies per call and must sit after every breakpoint; (b) OUTPUT tokens — provider caching never saves a generated token, while a reuse hit saves 100% of both sides; (c) anything across runs — with a 1h max TTL, last night's cache is stone cold 24 hours later, and the 24-hour gap is exactly the interval this workload repeats on.
grader: Fully deterministic, no LLM, ground truth free and exact because the corpus is generated from a seed. GENERATOR (`gen_encounters.py --seed N`): (1) Pick a target MS-DRG from the CMS ICD-10 MS-DRG v43.1 Definitions Manual, then sample a principal diagnosis from that DRG's principal-dx list plus k secondary diagnoses drawn from the CMS FY2026 ICD-10-CM code-descriptions file (`icd10cm_codes_2026.txt`, free from cms.gov, no license), deliberately choosing some from the CC list and some from the MCC list so the severity tier is a controlled variable. Procedures sampled from the ICD-10-PCS order file. (2) Draw LOS from a seeded lognormal (median 4), then render each day's documents from Jinja templates plus a seeded phrase bank, expressing each gold code in exactly one of N documented surface forms at a recorded (document_id, char_start, char_end). (3) Inject labeled distractors that mirror the actual failure modes of this task: negated findings ("no evidence of pulmonary embolism"), history-of ("h/o MI 2019" → I25.2, not I21), ruled-out ("PE excluded by CTA"), family history, symptoms integral to a definitive diagnosis (not separately reportable), and abnormal labs with no physician statement (not codeable). (4) Generate day d's progress note by applying a seeded edit to day d−1's that retains a target 54% of tokens verbatim, so the corpus's redundancy structure matches the sourced field measurement rather than an idealized one — this is what makes the reuse-vs-baseline comparison honest. (5) Emit a manifest: gold principal dx, gold secondary set with POA flags, gold PCS set, gold DRG (computed by running the gold codes through the grouper), and every evidence span. GRADER (`grade.py`), four tiers, all exact: TIER 1 — hard validity gates, any failure scores the encounter 0: every returned code is a billable leaf in the FY2026 file; principal dx is not on the MCE unacceptable-principal-diagnosis list; no MCE age or sex conflicts; POA flags in {Y,N,U,W,1}. TIER 2 — accuracy: principal-dx exact match (0/1), secondary-dx set micro-F1 (order-insensitive exact string match), PCS set F1. TIER 3 — the money metric: run both the predicted and the gold code set through the CMS MS-DRG Grouper + Medicare Code Editor v43.1 (free Java reference implementation, FOIA-released on cms.gov), score DRG exact match (0/1) and dollar error as |RW_pred − RW_gold| × $6,500 fixed base rate. Report BOTH mean absolute dollar error and NET signed dollar bias — net bias is the metric that catches systematic upcoding, which is what gets a hospital sued and which F1 is completely blind to. TIER 4 — evidence grounding: every returned code must carry a character span that intersects the manifest's recorded span for that code; correct-but-ungrounded codes are scored separately as lucky guesses. Deterministic offset intersection. WHY NOT MIMIC-IV BILLED CODES: PhysioNet credentialing is friction, not free; the labels are billing labels with known undercoding noise rather than gold labels; and there are no evidence-span annotations, so Tier 4 is impossible. Every artifact this grader needs — code files, grouper, MCE tables, DRG relative weights — is a free download from cms.gov.
reuse_story: The mechanism is narrow but real, and it rests on one regulatory fact: signed clinical notes are immutable. Once yesterday's H&P, progress notes, consults, and radiology reports are signed, they are byte-identical tonight — corrections arrive as new addenda, never as edits. So on a concurrent-review cadence, ~72% of the documents a nightly run reads it already read last night, and the L2 evidence-extraction op over each of those documents is a pure function of (document bytes, extraction prompt, model id, ICD-10-CM version). Those keys hit. That is ~6,000 of 7,890 L2 model calls skipped outright — and skipped means both the ~1,000 uncached input tokens AND the 350 output tokens, where provider prefix caching saves neither the document nor any output at all. The second, sharper edge is the time axis: the repeat interval here is 24 hours and the longest provider TTL is 1 hour, so the tuned prefix-cache baseline is structurally cold on every single one of these repeats. There is no configuration of `cache_control` that reaches across a night. Cross-run reuse is the only mechanism that can. A third, more speculative lever: L1 could emit section-level rather than document-level artifacts, at which point the sourced 54% copy-forward redundancy inside progress notes becomes addressable — today's note is a new artifact but half its blocks are not.
reuse_threats: Eight, roughly in order of how much damage they do. (1) THE FUNNEL OPS NEVER REUSE. L5 principal-dx, L7 grouper, L8 edits, L10 rationale each consume the whole encounter, so one new progress note re-keys all of them — and ~80% of the census gains a note nightly. Worse, L4 adjudication fans in across documents and routine progress notes restate the active problem list, so a single new note re-keys ~60% of that encounter's adjudications. Net achievable is ~60% of model ops, and they are the cheaper ones; the expensive high-fan-in decisions are exactly the ones that always recompute. (2) ROOT INVALIDATION IS TOTAL AND SCHEDULED. The ICD-10-CM file, PCS tables, MS-DRG grouper, MCE lists, NCCI PTP/MUE files, and the Official Guidelines are each one artifact under every op. FY2026's 487 new codes are 0.75% of the file and 100% of its hash. Four scheduled flushes a year (Oct 1, Jan 1, Apr 1, Jul 1), plus a flush on every prompt or model version bump. (3) DE-IDENTIFICATION KILLS IT SILENTLY. If L1 injects per-run randomized surrogate names/dates (a standard HIPAA safe-harbor pattern), every document hash changes every run and reuse is exactly zero with no error surfaced. Same for a rendered structured digest stamped "vitals as of 23:47". These are easy to ship and hard to notice. (4) COPY-FORWARD IS NEAR-DUPLICATE, NOT DUPLICATE. The sourced 54% redundancy is completely invisible to a document-level content hash. Harvesting it needs sub-document artifact granularity, which is not free: clinical significance and POA determination depend on cross-section context, so block-level extraction degrades the thing being sold. (5) PHI LAW REMOVES THE CROSS-USER HALF OF THE PITCH. A (reuse key → output) store of extracted clinical entities is a PHI datastore: BAA, encryption, access logging, and a retention policy that honors HIPAA amendment and deletion requests. Cross-tenant sharing of anything PHI-derived is effectively unavailable, so "across days AND users" collapses to "across runs, within one hospital." (6) THE WORKLOAD REWRITES ITS OWN INPUTS. L9 drafts physician queries; 12–40% of charts get one and 65–85% get answered, and each answer is a new signed document that re-keys the encounter's funnel. The pipeline manufactures its own invalidations. (7) THE BASELINE IS ALREADY CHEAP. Batch API 50% × prefix caching at 0.1× on the shared 10k tokens takes this from ~$1.50 to roughly $0.35/encounter. The reuse layer is fighting over a shrunken pot, and it must also beat its own storage, lookup, and hashing cost at 33,121 ops per run. (8) AUDIT EXPOSURE FROM FROZEN OUTPUTS. L2/L4 are sampled, not deterministic. A reuse store freezes whichever output was sampled first, which is fine operationally but gives an auditor a question the customer must answer: why did this chart yield code X in June and code Y in July from identical documentation? In a domain where the deliverable is a claim and 25% of audit triggers are coding errors, that is a real objection, not a theoretical one.
confidence: Medium-high on the graph shape, the operation inventory, the token sizes, and the tuned baseline; medium on the change rate; high on the grader being buildable exactly as specified. The graph structure, the layering, and the funnel-op behavior follow from how DRG coding actually works (principal-dx selection and grouping are definitionally whole-encounter operations) and match the published agentic-ICD-coding pipelines. Token sizes for discharge summaries and the 54% copy-forward figure are directly sourced. The regulatory change rates are exact figures from CMS. THE WEAK LINK IS THE ~7 CODING-RELEVANT DOCUMENTS PER PATIENT-DAY: I searched for a published per-encounter-day note-count distribution and could not find one — the available literature reports cumulative chart size (median 541 notes / 95,411 words available at a general admission in 2022), which is the patient's entire history, not the current stay. The 27.4% change rate moves roughly linearly with that estimate. WHAT WOULD RAISE CONFIDENCE, in order of value: (1) a single real hospital's document-metadata export — one row per (encounter, document_id, type, signed_at, char_count) for 90 days — which pins the change rate exactly and costs the customer nothing to produce; (2) confirmation of whether the target customer actually runs concurrent nightly review or discharge-only coding, because discharge-only collapses the reuse surface to near zero and that single fact decides whether this scenario is worth benchmarking at all; (3) whether their de-identification is deterministic or per-run randomized, which decides whether measured reuse is ~60% of model ops or exactly 0%.

customer: A platform/developer-productivity team at a ~350-engineer SaaS company running one polyglot monorepo (Go + TypeScript + Python), ~45,000 test cases in ~6,200 test files, sharded across 24 CI jobs on GitHub Actions + Buildkite, ~1,400 CI runs/day. Equivalently: a CI-triage vendor (Trunk, Aviator, Graphite, Datadog CI Visibility class) selling this as a service. What they pay for today is build-cop hours, not tokens: the Apache study of unrelated build failures found developers spend a MEDIAN OF 4 HOURS deciding whether a failure was even caused by their patch (arXiv 2605.05564, 77,354 failures across 7 ASF projects). The agent's job is to collapse that to a machine-generated triage comment on the PR within ~90 seconds of the red build: for every failing test, a label in {new_regression, pre_existing, flaky, infra, dependency}, the suspect file/commit, and a runnable repro command. They pay for tokens as a cost of goods; at the volumes below it is ~240M input tokens/day, i.e. a real six-figure annual line item, which is why the caching question is live at all.
why_repeated:
Three independent repetition drivers, and they have very different reuse consequences — this distinction is the whole story of the scenario.

(1) MECHANICAL: the agent is wired to the CI webhook. It fires on every failing run, forever, with no human deciding to invoke it. Published failure rates: median CI success 79.5% for commits and 75.9% for PRs on TravisTorrent (arXiv 1512.01862), so roughly 1 in 4-5 runs is red. There is no "run it once" option.

(2) SAME-DEFECT REPETITION (the real reuse surface): the overwhelming majority of failures the agent triages are not novel. SAP HANA's pre-submit CI: 87% OF TEST FAILURES ARE FLAKY (An et al., arXiv 2310.06298). Google: when a test flips pass->fail in post-submit, 84% of the time it is flakiness, not a regression. Apache: 13.3% of all build failures are entirely unrelated to the patch (infra, environment, concurrent commits, non-reproducible). A broken main compounds this — one bad merge makes every subsequent push on every branch re-triage the identical failure until it is reverted. So the same underlying defect is triaged tens to hundreds of times.

(3) SAME-BRANCH ITERATION: a developer pushes a fix, CI goes red again on a partly-overlapping failure set. Roughly 45% of consecutive triage invocations are the next push on a branch already triaged minutes earlier.

Driver (2) is the only one that yields cross-run reuse of a model result, and it yields it only for the CHEAP half of the graph. Driver (3) yields overlap in the artifacts but not in the answers, because the diff — the thing the answer is about — is exactly what changed.
run_cadence: ~1,400 CI runs/day on the monorepo; the triage agent fires only on red runs, ~21% of them, so ~300 triage runs/day, ~9,000/month. Clustered in working hours: median inter-run gap of roughly 2-3 minutes during the 09:00-19:00 window, with an overnight dead zone. That cadence matters for the baseline: the gap between consecutive triage runs is comfortably inside the provider's 1h cache tier and usually inside the 5m tier, so any prompt component that is genuinely constant across runs is already free at the provider without any reuse layer.

graph.description:
Three structurally different regions stitched together, and conflating them is how people get this workload wrong.

REGION 1 - wide, shallow, deterministic ingest (layers A1-A8, 75 tool ops, depth 2-3). Almost embarrassingly parallel: fetch run metadata, pull all 24 JUnit shard artifacts, pull raw logs for the 6 failing jobs, get the diff, read the changed files, and for each of the ~12 failing tests read its source, its git history, and its pass/fail history from the test-results warehouse. Zero model calls. High artifact count, near-zero token cost, trivially parallel.

REGION 2 - the narrow waist (layers B1-B4 + C, 24 tool ops + 5 model ops). This is where the graph contracts and where the interesting reuse lives. Failing tests are NOT triaged one-per-test. Their stack traces and error messages are abstracted (mask numbers, addresses, timestamps, temp paths, thread ids) and then clustered by signature. SAP HANA's measurement of exactly this step: 102,529 raw failure symptoms collapse to 16,345 abstracted ones, a 84% reduction, and one single abstracted symptom matched 1,522 failures across 120 test cases. So 12 failing tests become ~5 clusters, and the model fans out over CLUSTERS, not tests. Five single-shot triage calls, ~33k input tokens each, run concurrently.

REGION 3 - the deep chain that holds the money (layer D, 10 model turns + 14 interleaved tool ops, depth 10). Only clusters labelled new_regression get a deep-dive agent: read the suspect files, grep for the symbol, narrow the culprit hunk, run the single test locally, propose the fix. On a typical run 1 of the 5 clusters earns this. It is a growing single conversation, ~62k average input per turn, and it is 620k of the run's 795k input tokens - 78% of the workload sits in a 10-deep sequential chain with fan-in 2.

The honest summary: 115 of 131 operations are deterministic tool calls that cost nothing in tokens, 5 model calls sit in a genuinely wide fan-out, and 10 model calls sit in a long chain that dominates the bill. Any reuse claim has to say which of those three regions it is talking about.

One op count that surprises people: the agent must read ALL 24 JUnit shards, not just the failing ones, because the shard-to-test mapping is decided at runtime by the test splitter and you cannot know which shard holds a failure without parsing it.

layers.name: A1_run_metadata
layers.consumes: nothing - this is the root of the whole graph (CI webhook payload)
layers.reads_artifacts: GitHub Actions run object: run_id, head_sha, base_sha, branch, PR number, workflow file, conclusion, job list

layers.name: A2_fetch_junit_shard
layers.consumes: A1 (1 upstream op each; the job list tells you which artifacts exist)
layers.reads_artifacts: one JUnit/CTRF XML artifact per CI shard, ~1,875 testcase elements each

layers.name: A3_fetch_job_log
layers.consumes: A1 and A2 (2 upstream ops each - A2 identifies which jobs actually hold failures)
layers.reads_artifacts: raw stdout/stderr log of one failing CI job. SOURCED SIZE: LogDx-CI (arXiv 2605.28876) measured real GitHub Actions failure logs at median 5,000 lines, max 200,000; at ~12 tok/line that is ~62k tokens median, ~2.4M at the tail

layers.name: A4_git_diff
layers.consumes: A1 (1 each) - one call for --name-status, one for the unified patch
layers.reads_artifacts: diff of head_sha against merge-base. SOURCED SIZE: median change is 24 lines at Google, 25 Apache, 32 Linux, 44 Android/AMD, 78 Chrome; a PR-branch push aggregating 2-3 commits lands near 120 lines

layers.name: A5_read_changed_file
layers.consumes: A4 (1 each)
layers.reads_artifacts: full contents of each changed source file at head_sha. SOURCED COUNT: commit size is heavy-tailed but most commits touch 1-10 files and 1-4 source files (Characterizing Commits in OSS, SBQS 2022); 6 is a PR-push aggregate

layers.name: A6_git_log_test_file
layers.consumes: A2 (1 each) - one per distinct failing test
layers.reads_artifacts: `git log -n 20 --format=... -- <test_file>` : last 20 commits touching the failing test's file

layers.name: A7_flake_history_query
layers.consumes: A2 (1 each)
layers.reads_artifacts: test-results warehouse: last 50 runs of this test id on main - pass/fail, duration, shard, runner. This is the single most decision-relevant artifact in the graph and it changes on EVERY run because a row is appended every run

layers.name: A8_read_test_source
layers.consumes: A2 (1 each)
layers.reads_artifacts: source of the failing test function plus its fixtures/setup

layers.name: B1_abstract_failure_symptom
layers.consumes: A3 (1 each) - extracts this test's stack trace + error message from its job log
layers.reads_artifacts: none external; pure regex normalization - mask integers, hex addresses, timestamps, tmp paths, thread/pid, UUIDs, line numbers in vendored frames

layers.name: B2_cluster_signatures
layers.consumes: all 12 B1 ops (fan-in 12)
layers.reads_artifacts: none; union-find over abstracted symptom equality + edit distance threshold. Emits ~5 clusters from 12 failing tests

layers.name: B3_log_reduce
layers.consumes: A3 (1 each)
layers.reads_artifacts: none external. SOURCED: LogDx-CI found a hybrid grep+tail router matches raw-grep diagnostic quality at 4.5x fewer tokens, so 62k -> ~13.8k per job. This step is not optional; raw logs blow the context window

layers.name: B4_impact_lookup
layers.consumes: B2 and A4 (2 each) - one per cluster
layers.reads_artifacts: per-test coverage/impact index (Bazel-style rdeps or a stored coverage map): which of the 6 changed files are reachable from this cluster's tests

layers.name: C_cluster_triage
layers.consumes: B2 (its cluster), B3 (reduced log slice), B4 (impacted files), A4 (diff), A5 (changed files), A6+A7 (history), A8 (test source) - fan-in ~7
layers.reads_artifacts: composition of the ~33.2k input: system+tool defs+triage playbook 3.5k | CODEOWNERS-derived ownership/routing map 4.0k | flake registry, top 2,000 known signatures with verdicts 12.0k | reduced log slice for this cluster 3.0k | abstracted symptoms + test names 0.6k | diff patch 1.8k | changed-file hunks with context 5.0k | test source 2.5k | flake-history rows 0.8k. Output is strict JSON: label, confidence, culprit_file, culprit_line, repro_command, rationale

layers.name: D_deep_dive_turn
layers.consumes: the one C op labelled new_regression, then each turn consumes the previous turn plus its tool result (fan-in 2)
layers.reads_artifacts: a growing conversation. Turn 1 starts at ~35k (the C context plus the deep-dive system prompt); by turn 10 it is ~90k because every file read, grep result and test rerun output is appended. Average across the 10 turns is ~62k input

layers.name: D_deep_dive_tool
layers.consumes: the preceding D model turn (fan-in 1)
layers.reads_artifacts: ad-hoc: read_file on suspect sources, ripgrep for a symbol, `git log -S`, and 1-2 targeted single-test reruns in the CI container

layers.name: E_synthesis
layers.consumes: all 5 C ops + the final D turn (fan-in 6)
layers.reads_artifacts: the 5 cluster verdicts, the deep-dive conclusion, the diff summary, and the agent's own prior triage comment on this PR if one exists

layers.name: F_publish
layers.consumes: E (1 each)
layers.reads_artifacts: none read; writes - one POST of the markdown comment to the PR, one INSERT of the structured triage record into the warehouse (which becomes an A7 artifact for future runs, closing a feedback loop)

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 35-55% with aggressive canonicalization; 92-100% without it. The canonicalization decision, not the world, sets this number.
change_rate.basis:
MIXED - the underlying rates are sourced, the composition into a per-artifact percentage is my arithmetic over the 75-artifact list. Walking the artifact classes:

- Code churn is genuinely tiny and this is well sourced. Median change size 24 lines at Google, 25 Apache, 32 Linux, 44 Android/AMD, 78 Chrome; most commits touch 1-10 files and 1-4 source files (Characterizing Commits in OSS, SBQS 2022). Against 6,200 test files plus ~30,000 source files, that is roughly 0.02% of the repo per push. If the workload read the repo, reuse would be ~99.98%.

- But the workload does NOT read the repo. It reads the 75 artifacts implicated by the failure, and those are adversarially selected to be the changed ones. This is the load-bearing point. A5 (changed files) is 100% changed BY DEFINITION. A4 (diff) is 100% changed. A1 (run metadata) is 100% changed, new sha every time.

- A2, the 24 JUnit shards: byte-identical never, because every XML carries per-test durations, timestamps, hostname and shard ordering. Canonicalized to a sorted set of (test_id, status) tuples, 20-22 of 24 shards are bit-identical run to run and only the 2-4 shards containing failures differ. So this class swings from 100% to ~12% purely on whether you canonicalize.

- A3, the 6 job logs: 100% changed raw. After B1 abstraction the picture inverts and this is the best-sourced number in the whole answer: SAP HANA's 6-month CI history collapsed 102,529 raw failure symptoms to 16,345 abstracted ones (-84%), and matching a new failure's abstracted symptom against that history achieved 76% RECALL at 96% PRECISION (An et al., arXiv 2310.06298). Read as a cache statistic: 76% of flaky failure symptoms have been seen before.

- A7, the 12 flake-history queries: 100% changed, unavoidably, because F_publish appends a row every run. Bucketing (e.g. 'failed 7 of last 50') pulls it down to ~30%.

- A6 (git log of test files) and A8 (test sources): the CONTENT is ~99% unchanged, but the SET of 12 differs run to run because different tests failed. Keyed per-file these reuse beautifully; they are also the cheapest artifacts in the graph.

- CI config: changes on well under 1% of pushes (An et al., Evolution of GitHub Actions Workflows, arXiv 2602.14572).

Weighting by artifact count over the 75: raw ~97%, canonicalized ~46%. I would not defend 46 to better than +/-10.
change_rate.where_changes_land:
AT THE ROOTS, and this is the single most important fact about this scenario. A1 (head_sha), A4 (the diff) and A2 (the JUnit result set) are all depth-1 or depth-2 roots and all three change on 100% of runs. Because reuse keys compose transitively through upstream output hashes, a naive Bazel/Nix-style keying of this graph gets EXACTLY ZERO REUSE. Not low reuse - zero. Every one of the 131 operations is a descendant of a sha that is new every time.

The consequence is that reuse here is not a property of the graph, it is a property of a deliberately NARROWED key. The layer-C triage verdict for a flaky or infra cluster is genuinely a function of only (abstracted_failure_signature, test_id, flake_history_bucket) - it does not depend on the sha, does not depend on the diff, does not depend on 23 of the 24 JUnit shards. If you key on that narrowed tuple you get the 76% hit rate SAP measured. If you key on the honest transitive closure you get nothing. So the reuse layer's real engineering content is a per-operation key-narrowing policy, and every narrowing is a correctness bet that the excluded inputs really were irrelevant.

The secondary consequence is worse: the changes concentrate precisely in the region that is expensive. Layer D, the deep-dive, is 78% of the tokens and fires only on clusters labelled new_regression - i.e. only on the failures whose cause is by construction novel and whose diff has never existed before. The cheap wide region reuses; the expensive deep region cannot.

session_structure:
A competent engineer does five specific things here, and together they capture most of the available saving before any reuse layer exists. Figures below are measured against the Anthropic API on this repo's own probe key (docs/ANTHROPIC_CACHE_MAP.md, docs/FIELD_CACHE_MEASUREMENT.md), not from vendor prose.

1. ORDER THE LAYER-C PROMPT BY VOLATILITY, NOT BY READABILITY. Emit strictly: [system + tool defs + triage playbook 3.5k] [CODEOWNERS ownership map 4.0k] [flake registry 12.0k] [run-shared: diff + changed-file hunks 6.8k] [cluster-specific: reduced log slice, symptoms, test source, history 6.9k]. This matters because invalidation is breakpoint-granular and brutal inside a block: with a single breakpoint, ten separate perturbation axes - leading space, trailing space, CRLF, NFC/NFD, case flip, and single-token insertion at head, MIDDLE and TAIL - all gave 0% recovery. Position inside a cached block is irrelevant; any byte kills all of it. Only moving volatile content past the last breakpoint protects the earlier blocks.

2. SPEND 3 OF THE 4 BREAKPOINTS. Breakpoint 1 after the ownership map (7.5k), 2 after the flake registry (19.5k), 3 after the run-shared diff (26.3k). Four is the hard ceiling - a 5th cache_control returns HTTP 400. Note the floor trap: the minimum cacheable prefix was measured at 4,094 tok (no) / 4,351 tok (yes) for claude-haiku-4-5, so on Haiku the 3.5k playbook CANNOT get its own breakpoint and must be merged with the ownership map. The floor is per-model.

3. SKEW THE FAN-OUT. The 5 layer-C calls are the obvious place to parallelise, and naive parallelism destroys the benefit: under genuinely simultaneous fan-out at 0ms skew, all 5 callers were billed cache_creation and zero were billed cache_read - the cached arm pays 5x the 1.25x write premium and collects nothing. At >=1s skew it is cleanly 1 writer and 4 readers. So: issue cluster call 1, await its first token, then launch clusters 2-5. One line of code, and it is the difference between 5 writes and 1.

4. PUT ttl:"1h" ON BREAKPOINTS 1 AND 2. The playbook + ownership map + flake registry (19.5k) is identical across every triage run in the org. At ~300 red runs/day the inter-run gap is 2-3 minutes in working hours; measured field arrivals on an agent workload of this exact shape give P(gap <= 300s) = 93.7%, and buying the 1h tier moves the practical expiry cliff from 300s to 3600s (median prefix recovery goes 100% -> 0% exactly at the tier boundary). So that 19.5k stable block is warm essentially always, cross-run and cross-PR, for free, from the provider. A reuse layer that proudly caches this block is charging for something already free.

5. RUN LAYER D AS ONE CONVERSATION, NEVER AS 10 RECONSTRUCTED PROMPTS. This is where the tokens are and it is where the provider is already strongest. Measured over 112 real long-context agent sessions, 9,224 billed requests, 2.49 BILLION prompt tokens: 97.47% of prompt tokens billed at the 0.10x read rate, 84.1% saving versus the no-cache counterfactual, and 99.86% of all realized cache value came from within-session growing-prefix continuation. The 78% of this workload that lives in the deep-dive chain is therefore already ~97% cached for free.

NET TUNED BASELINE, one run: raw 795,000 input tokens -> ~162,000 cache-weighted equivalent. Layer C falls from 166k to ~55k (33% of list), layer D from 620k to ~99k, synthesis ~8k. THE PROVIDER'S OWN CACHE, COMPETENTLY DRIVEN, ALREADY REMOVES 79.6% OF THIS WORKLOAD AT ZERO COST. Any reuse layer is competing for the remaining 162k, not the 795k. One more thing a competent engineer knows: marking a prefix that is then never reused costs +24.8% versus not caching at all (it pays the 1.25x write and collects zero reads), and flips negative only at the second call - so on runs with a single failure cluster the correct action is to NOT set breakpoint 3.
grader:
Fully deterministic, no LLM anywhere, ground truth free and exact because it is INJECTED rather than observed.

CORPUS GENERATOR (this is the trick that makes the domain gradable). Take a real OSS repo with a real, fast, hermetic suite - apache/commons-lang plus a Go and a TS package to make it polyglot. Start from a green commit. Then generate a seeded sequence of 400 consecutive CI runs on a synthetic branch history whose composition matches the sourced field rates: 45% same-branch follow-up pushes / 55% different-PR interleaving; 87% of injected test failures flaky, 13% real (SAP HANA rate); 13.3% of runs carrying an additional unrelated infra failure (Apache rate). Each run applies one or more seeded mutations drawn from a catalog with KNOWN consequence:

- regression: a standard mutation operator (conditional-boundary, negate-conditional, return-value, math) applied to source file F line L. Ground truth = (label=regression, culprit_file=F, culprit_line=L, expected_failing_tests=T), where T is obtained by ACTUALLY RUNNING the suite in the container, not predicted.
- flaky: inject seeded nondeterminism into test T - `if xxhash(SEED, RUN_INDEX, TEST_ID) % 5 == 0: fail` - so failure is reproducibly non-reproducible under a controlled RNG. Ground truth = (label=flaky, culprit_test=T).
- infra: kill a service container, point a dependency at a dead port, or fill the runner disk in a setup step. Ground truth = (label=infra, culprit_step=S).
- dependency: bump a pinned dep to a version with a known breaking change. Ground truth = (label=dependency, culprit_pkg=P).
- pre_existing: a regression mutation injected at run R and deliberately left unfixed for the next 6-40 runs. Ground truth = (label=pre_existing, first_seen_run=R).

Every run is really executed, so JUnit XML and job logs are REAL artifacts with real timestamps, real durations, real stack traces and real shard ordering - which is essential, because the canonicalization question in the change-rate section is exactly what a synthetic-XML corpus would beg.

GRADER. The agent must emit strict JSON against a fixed schema (schema violation = 0). Then, pure code:

S1 LABEL MACRO-F1: over the 5 labels, comparing the agent's cluster labels to the generator's injected causes. Arithmetic only.
S2 CULPRIT LOCALIZATION: for regression and pre_existing clusters, is the named culprit_file in the ground-truth mutated-file set? Exact set membership, top-1 accuracy.
S3 CLUSTERING QUALITY: Adjusted Rand Index between the agent's partition of failing tests into clusters and the generator's ground-truth cause partition. Closed-form, deterministic.
S4 REPRO EXECUTES: the grader takes the agent's repro_command string, runs it in the pinned container with a 120s timeout, and checks that the named tests fail (for regression/pre_existing) or that the command is correctly marked non-reproducing (for flaky). Free, exact, and it is the one metric an agent cannot bluff.
S5 NO HALLUCINATED PATH (gate): every file path cited must satisfy `git cat-file -e <sha>:<path>`. Any miss zeroes the entire run.

COMPOSITE = 0.35*S1 + 0.25*S2 + 0.15*S3 + 0.25*S4, gated by S5.

COST SIDE, measured not modelled: the harness records the provider's own usage receipt per call - input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens split by ephemeral_5m/ephemeral_1h - and prices them at list. The reuse layer must beat the tuned baseline on $/run at EQUAL OR BETTER composite. Reporting a token saving without the composite score is disqualifying, because the cheapest possible agent is one that labels everything 'flaky' from the store.

THE ADVERSARIAL CASE THE GENERATOR MUST PLANT, because it is the actual failure mode of the reuse layer: take a signature that has been flaky for 200 consecutive runs and then make it a genuine regression with the identical abstracted symptom. A store keyed on the narrowed tuple (signature, test_id, history_bucket) WILL serve the stale 'flaky' verdict and be wrong. S1 and S4 both catch it, for free, and the score delta on those planted runs is the honest price of key-narrowing. Plant them at ~4% of runs, matching the SAP-measured 96% precision ceiling of symptom matching.
reuse_story:
The mechanism is narrow, real, and much smaller than it first appears.

WHERE IT WORKS. Layer C, the 5 per-cluster triage calls. For any cluster whose cause is a recurring flaky test, an infra fault or a pre-existing broken-main failure, the correct verdict is a function of the abstracted failure signature and the test's history - and NOT of the head_sha or the diff. Key the operation on that narrowed tuple and it hits across runs, across branches, across PRs and across developers. The hit rate is directly measurable and already published: SAP HANA matched new failure symptoms against six months of abstracted flaky history at 76% RECALL / 96% PRECISION. Multiply by the share of clusters that are recurring rather than novel - 87% of pre-submit failures flaky at SAP, 84% of pass->fail transitions flaky at Google - and the expected layer-C reuse rate is 0.85 * 0.76 = ~65%.

WHAT THAT IS WORTH, honestly, against the tuned baseline of ~162k equivalent tokens/run: 65% of layer C removes ~29.5k, and the avoided deep-dives (a cluster confidently resolved from the store no longer earns a layer-D investigation, which happens on perhaps 15% of runs) remove another ~15k. Total ~27% off the tuned baseline. Against the raw 795k it looks like 94%, but 79.6 of those 94 points belong to the provider's free cache. The reuse layer's genuine contribution is the ~27%.

THE STRONGER ARGUMENT IS NOT TOKENS. It is avoided work and avoided latency. The Apache study puts a median of 4 hours of developer time on deciding whether a failure was even related to the patch. A store that answers 'this exact abstracted signature has been seen 341 times in 6 months, always flaky, tracked as JIRA-1234' does not merely serve a cached model output - it deletes the entire layer-D deep-dive that an uncertain classifier would otherwise have launched, and it returns in milliseconds instead of 90 seconds. On this workload the reuse layer is better sold as a determinism-and-latency mechanism with a token dividend than as a caching mechanism.

CROSS-USER REUSE IS THE ONE PLACE THIS BEATS THE PROVIDER OUTRIGHT. A flaky signature first triaged on Alice's PR at 09:14 is served to Bob's unrelated PR at 16:40. That is a 7-hour gap across two different conversations with no shared prefix - structurally impossible for provider prefix caching, whose practical cliff is 3600s even on the 1h tier. This is the one mechanism the provider cannot replicate, and the whole defensible case rests on it.
reuse_threats:
Six, roughly in order of how much damage they do.

1. THE BASELINE IS ALREADY AT 79.6%. Measured, on real traffic of this exact shape: 97.47% of prompt tokens billed at the 0.10x read rate across 2.49B tokens, 84.1% saving versus no-cache. The 78% of this workload that lives in layer D's growing conversation is essentially fully served by the provider for free. The reuse layer's addressable market is one fifth of the bill, and it must not double-charge for the four fifths it did not save.

2. TRANSITIVE KEYING GETS EXACTLY ZERO. Every operation in this graph descends from a head_sha that is new on 100% of runs. A faithful Bazel/Nix key composition returns no hits at all. Every hit requires deliberately DROPPING real inputs from the key, and each drop is an unproven correctness bet. This is not a caching system with a soundness caveat; it is a heuristic matcher wearing a content-addressing costume, and it should be described that way.

3. STALE VERDICTS ARE THE EXPENSIVE FAILURE. SAP's 96% precision means ~1 in 25 symptom matches is wrong, and the wrong direction is catastrophic: serving a cached 'flaky, ignore' for a signature that has become a genuine regression is precisely how a real bug reaches main. The customer's tolerance for that is near zero, which caps how aggressively keys can be narrowed - and the tighter the key, the closer the hit rate falls back toward zero.

4. NOVELTY CONCENTRATES IN THE EXPENSIVE REGION. Layer D fires only on new_regression clusters. Those are, by construction, the failures whose diff has never existed before. 78% of the tokens have a structural reuse ceiling of approximately zero. No amount of key engineering changes this.

5. THE STORE IS ZIPFIAN AND THE TAIL IS ENORMOUS. Even after 84% collapse, SAP still had 16,345 distinct abstracted symptoms over 6 months, most of them singletons; the paper explicitly notes a flakiness that manifests only once cannot be matched at any threshold. Reuse is concentrated in a few hot signatures, which are also the ones a customer will simply add to a suppression list once they notice them - at which point the hottest, most valuable cache entries stop being requested at all. The mechanism partly destroys its own demand.

6. THE FAN-OUT IS NATURALLY CONCURRENT AND CONCURRENCY INVERTS THE ECONOMICS. Layer C wants all 5 clusters in flight at once for latency. Measured at 0ms skew: 5 writers, 0 readers, the cached arm strictly worse than uncached. And at k=1 reuse depth, marking a prefix at all costs +24.8%. A reuse layer that sits in front of a naively-parallel triage agent can make the bill go UP while reporting a healthy hit rate. Whatever fixes this (>=1s skew) is a one-line change the customer's own engineer can make for free.

7. Minor but worth stating: the whole benefit can be captured without any LLM caching at all. Deterministic symptom matching against a flake registry - a database lookup - already delivers the 76%/96% result. That is BuildSheriff (ICSE 2022) and it is what Trunk and Datadog CI Visibility ship today. The reuse layer has to explain what it adds over a SELECT.
confidence:
MEDIUM overall, with sharply uneven internals.

HIGH confidence (published, multi-source, industrial scale): the flakiness rates (87% SAP HANA pre-submit, 84% Google pass->fail transitions, 13.3% Apache unrelated failures); the symptom-collapse and matching figures (102,529 -> 16,345, 76% recall / 96% precision over 6 months of SAP HANA CI); CI failure rates (~20.5% commits, ~24.1% PRs, TravisTorrent); log sizes (median 5k lines, max 200k, real GitHub Actions failures); commit sizes (median 24-78 lines across Google/Apache/Linux/Android/Chrome, 1-10 files heavy-tailed); the 4-hour median investigation cost.

HIGH confidence, first-party measured: every provider-cache number in the baseline - the 4,094/4,351 token floor, the 4-breakpoint ceiling, the (300,330]s cliff, the 1h tier moving the field cliff to 3600s, the 0ms-skew 5-writer inversion, the +24.8% k=1 penalty, the 97.47%/84.1%/99.86% field figures over 2.49B tokens.

MEDIUM confidence: the 131-operation count and the layer structure. Nobody publishes the operation graph of a proprietary CI-triage agent. The clustering waist, the 5-cluster fan-out and the 10-turn deep-dive are my reconstruction from BuildSheriff's architecture, LogDx-CI's agent-loop findings and the shape of shipped products. The topology I would defend; the exact counts (24 shards, 12 failing tests, 5 clusters, 10 turns) are a plausible instantiation, not a measurement.

MEDIUM-LOW confidence: the token split inside layer C (33.2k decomposed into 9 named components) and the resulting 79.6% baseline / 27% incremental figures. These are arithmetic on estimated component sizes. I would defend the ORDERING of the conclusions - provider cache >> reuse layer, layer D >> layer C, roots change 100% - much more strongly than the specific percentages, which I would not defend to better than +/-10 absolute.

LOW confidence: the 46% canonicalized change rate. It is a weighted composition over artifact classes whose individual rates are sourced but whose weights are mine, and it is extremely sensitive to a canonicalization policy that a real implementation may or may not adopt.

WHAT WOULD RAISE IT, in descending order of value: (a) instrument ONE real production triage agent for two weeks with per-operation receipts - operation counts, artifact hashes before and after canonicalization, and the provider's cache_read/cache_creation split per call; that single dataset would move nearly everything to high. (b) Build the seeded-mutant corpus above and actually run the tuned baseline against a narrowed-key reuse layer, since the 79.6%/27% split is currently arithmetic and should be a measurement. (c) Get the distribution of failing tests per red build from a real large suite - I am extrapolating from Chromium's fault-revealing tests per failing build (mean 2.7, sd 14.9, max 579), which counts only fault-revealing failures and therefore understates total failing tests by roughly the flakiness multiple.

customer: A platform / developer-productivity team at a mid-size engineering org (150–600 engineers, 40–120 services in separate repos or 40–120 service directories in one monorepo). Concretely: fintech, infra-SaaS, or a healthcare platform with a Go/Python/Java fleet. Today they pay for (a) Renovate/Dependabot Enterprise or Mend (~$20–60k/yr) which opens the PRs but does NOT fix breakages, and (b) engineer time: a "fleet upgrade campaign" for one major dependency across 60 services is a 2–4 week project for 1–2 engineers, ~$25–60k of loaded cost, run 4–10 times a year (framework majors, JDK/Go/Node runtime bumps, CVE-forced majors, internal-SDK majors). What they would pay an agent for is specifically the part Renovate cannot do: the ~13% of routine bumps and ~40% of major bumps where the build breaks and someone has to read a compiler error and rewrite call sites in a service they do not own. Secondary buyer: the security team, who needs a hard SLA on time-to-remediate a CVE across the whole fleet.
why_repeated:
Four independent repeat mechanisms, all real:
(1) SAME-CAMPAIGN DAILY RE-RUN — the dominant one. A 60-service sweep is not merged atomically. Services' main branches move under you, some PRs merge and change their own manifest, some conflict, CI infra flakes, a service owner rejects a patch. The campaign driver is re-run every night until the fleet is green. That is 10–20 re-runs of substantially the same graph, with the ROOT (target version, changelog, API diff) held constant.
(2) NEXT-VERSION SWEEP — grpc-go, aws-sdk, k8s libs, protobuf all cut releases every 2–6 weeks; the identical sweep runs again against a new version. Root changes, service trees mostly do not.
(3) CVE RE-SWEEP — a security advisory forces re-bumping a library that was already swept weeks ago, on largely unchanged services.
(4) AGENT ITERATION — the platform team changes the system prompt, the repair strategy, or the model, and re-runs the whole sweep to compare pass rates. This is the purest repeat: zero input artifacts changed, only the prompt.
Note that (4) invalidates every model op under strict keying (prompt is an input) but leaves every tool op (grep, build, test, lock resolution) reusable — which is the opposite of where the token dollars are.
run_cadence: Two nested cadences. CAMPAIGN: a major-version fleet sweep is launched 4–10 times/year and, once launched, its driver re-runs nightly for 5–20 nights until the fleet is green. ROUTINE: on top of that, a Renovate-style patch/minor sweep runs weekly or nightly across the same 60 services (~100–400 individual bumps/week fleet-wide), of which ~13% break something and enter the same repair subgraph. So the benchmark's "repeat run" is a nightly re-run, 5–20 consecutive times, and then a version-shifted re-run 2–6 weeks later.

graph.description: A narrow shared root (5 ops: fetch changelog/migration guide/module tarballs, compute a machine-readable API diff, synthesise a migration brief) fanning out to 60 near-independent per-service subgraphs. Each service subgraph is a short chain — inventory -> triage -> apply -> lock -> build -> test — with a bounded repair loop hanging off it that fires only for services that actually break. It closes with a single fleet rollup that fans in from all 60. This is NOT one long chain and it is NOT 500 fully independent ops: it is 60 independent chains of depth ~8 sharing one root of depth 3, plus a repair loop of depth up to 12 on a minority of services. Two structural facts dominate any reuse analysis. FIRST: the build and test ops read the ENTIRE service tree (~410 tracked source+config files per service), not the 6 files the model looked at. Of the 24,700 external artifacts, only ~490 (60 manifests + 60 lockfiles + ~360 matched source files + 3 upstream docs) are read by model-facing ops; the other ~24,200 are read exclusively by build/test. Any content-hash key over what build actually read is therefore a key over the whole repo. SECOND: the repair loop is where all the value and all the cost concentrate — 40% of services in a major sweep, 13% in a routine sweep — and it is the layer least likely to be reusable because its inputs include a compiler error log produced by the run itself. Sizing anchors, measured: across 350 real dependency-bump commits in two production Go services (argo-rollouts, prometheus/alertmanager), 87% changed ZERO non-test source files (93% and 79% respectively); the 13% that did needed a median of 2–4.5 and a mean of 5–8 non-test files. A major-version campaign is selected precisely because it breaks things, so the benchmark sets the breakage rate to 40% rather than 13% — build the graph with breakage rate as a tunable so both regimes can be measured. Compile-error counts per breaking update are sourced: median 5 errors for MAJOR bumps (max 100), median 2 for MINOR (max 35) [arXiv 2606.24446]. Wall clock for one full run: 40–90 minutes with concurrency 8–12, dominated by builds and test suites, not by model latency. Cost of one full run at Sonnet-class pricing with NO caching: ~3.44M input tokens + ~200k output ~= $13; with the tuned prefix-cache baseline below, ~$5–6. CI compute for the same run: 60–200 build+test minutes, i.e. $2–15 of runner time. Note that the model spend and the compute spend are the same order of magnitude here — that matters for what a reuse layer is actually selling.

layers.name: upstream_fetch
layers.consumes: nothing — graph roots. (a) release notes / CHANGELOG for the full version range being crossed, (b) the library's migration guide if one exists, (c) source tarballs of the OLD and NEW module versions.
layers.reads_artifacts: 3 external artifacts: upstream CHANGELOG/release-notes page, migration guide page, and the two module tarballs from the registry (proxy.golang.org / PyPI / npm / Maven Central).

layers.name: api_diff
layers.consumes: upstream_fetch (the two module tarballs) — fanin 2.
layers.reads_artifacts: the two extracted module trees. Runs a real differ: `apidiff` (Go), `griffe check` (Python), `japicmp` (Java), or `api-extractor` (TS). Deterministic, no model.

layers.name: migration_brief
layers.consumes: api_diff (1) + upstream_fetch (3) — fanin 4.
layers.reads_artifacts: none directly; consumes upstream op outputs. Emits a structured symbol map: removed_symbol -> replacement + rewrite recipe + a grep pattern per symbol group.

layers.name: svc_manifest_read
layers.consumes: nothing — 60 independent roots, one per service.
layers.reads_artifacts: 2 per service: the manifest (go.mod / pyproject.toml / package.json / pom.xml) and the lockfile (go.sum / uv.lock / package-lock.json). 120 artifacts total.

layers.name: svc_dep_resolve
layers.consumes: svc_manifest_read (1) + migration_brief (1) — fanin 2. Runs `go list -m all` / `pip-compile --dry-run` / `npm ls --json` to find whether the target library is direct, transitive, or absent, and what else pins it.
layers.reads_artifacts: the lockfile plus the live package registry index — NOTE this op is not a pure function of local artifacts, see reuse_threats.

layers.name: svc_callsite_grep
layers.consumes: migration_brief (grep patterns) — fanin 1. Three greps per service, one per symbol group in the brief.
layers.reads_artifacts: the whole service source tree as a search corpus (~410 files/service) but returns only matching lines.

layers.name: svc_file_read
layers.consumes: svc_callsite_grep — fanin 1. Median 6 matched files per service (grounded: 150/401 argo-rollouts Go files import client-go, but only a median of ~6 contain the specific removed symbols).
layers.reads_artifacts: 1 source file each; 360 distinct artifacts, ~350 lines / 2,500 tokens each.

layers.name: svc_triage
layers.consumes: migration_brief (1) + svc_manifest_read (1) + svc_dep_resolve (1) + svc_callsite_grep (3) + svc_file_read (6) — fanin 12. Decides: not-affected / lockfile-only / needs-code-change, and emits the intended edit plan.
layers.reads_artifacts: none directly.

layers.name: svc_apply_bump
layers.consumes: svc_triage — fanin 1. Edits the manifest to the target version.
layers.reads_artifacts: the manifest (rewrites it).

layers.name: svc_lock_regen
layers.consumes: svc_apply_bump — fanin 1. `go mod tidy` / `uv lock` / `npm install --package-lock-only`.
layers.reads_artifacts: manifest + lockfile + LIVE REGISTRY STATE (transitive deps may have published new versions since the last run).

layers.name: svc_build
layers.consumes: svc_lock_regen — fanin 1.
layers.reads_artifacts: THE ENTIRE SERVICE TREE — ~410 source+config files per service, ~24,600 artifacts fleet-wide, plus the resolved dependency closure. Output is empty on success; on failure, median 5 compile errors for MAJOR / 2 for MINOR, ~1,500 tokens.

layers.name: svc_test
layers.consumes: svc_build — fanin 1. Only runs for services that compiled (60 attempted, ~48 compile on first try in a major sweep).
layers.reads_artifacts: entire service tree plus test fixtures and golden files. Output ~400 tokens on pass, 3,000–30,000 on failure, truncated to 8,000.

layers.name: repair_patch
layers.consumes: svc_build or svc_test error output (1) + migration_brief (1) + svc_file_read (up to 6) + prior repair_patch attempt if any (1) — fanin ~9. 24 services break (40% of 60 in a MAJOR campaign; set to 13% for the routine regime, which is the measured rate) x mean 1.8 iterations = 43 calls.
layers.reads_artifacts: may pull 1–3 additional files not in the original grep set (roughly 30% of iterations do).

layers.name: repair_apply_build_test
layers.consumes: repair_patch — fanin 1. Three tool ops per repair iteration: apply patch, rebuild, retest.
layers.reads_artifacts: entire service tree again on each rebuild.

layers.name: pr_body
layers.consumes: final diff (1) + svc_triage (1) + migration_brief (1) — fanin 3.
layers.reads_artifacts: none.

layers.name: pr_open
layers.consumes: pr_body — fanin 1. `gh pr create` against the forge API.
layers.reads_artifacts: none (side-effecting; must be excluded from the reuse store or keyed to a dry-run).

layers.name: fleet_rollup
layers.consumes: all 60 pr_body + all 60 svc_triage — fanin 60 (summaries only).
layers.reads_artifacts: none.

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 1–3% for the dominant regime (nightly re-run of the same campaign, measured on file count). 5–25% for the next-version regime 2–6 weeks later, where in addition 100% of the 120 manifests/lockfiles change. 0% for the prompt-iteration regime, where no artifact changes at all but every model key still changes.
change_rate.basis: MEASURED BY ME, not asserted. I cloned four real production repos and computed distinct source files touched per 7-day window over the last 8 weeks, divided by total tracked source files. prometheus/alertmanager (374 Go files): 0.53, 2.14, 0.00, 2.41, 4.81, 2.41, 6.15, 2.94 %/week; 5.88% over 30 days. argoproj/argo-rollouts (457 Go files): 0.00, 0.44, 7.00, 3.50, 5.47, 0.00, 3.72, 4.38 %/week; 10.07% over 30 days. fastapi (1,140 py files): 0.26, 0.96, 2.02, 0.00, 0.61, 0.00, 0.35, 1.05 %/week; 3.07% over 30 days. getsentry/sentry-python (499 py files, high-velocity outlier with mechanical sweeps): 15.8, 11.0, 20.4, 25.9, 14.0, 3.2, 10.8, 6.8 %/week; 45% over 30 days. Files per commit: median 1–2, mean 2.2–4.2, p90 3–8 — consistent with the published heavy-tailed finding that most commits touch 1–4 source files (Characterizing Commits in Open-Source Software, SBQS 2022, dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3571473.3571508). Dividing the weekly figures by ~5 working days gives 0.3–1.5%/day/service for normal repos, hence the 2% typical (I round up because enterprise service repos with 10–30 committers churn faster than these OSS repos, which is my main generalisation risk). SEPARATELY MEASURED, and more important than the churn number: how often a dependency bump requires ANY source edit. I walked every commit touching go.mod in two production services. argo-rollouts: 200 bump commits, 186 (93%) changed zero non-test .go files; the 14 that did had median 4.5, mean 7.9, max 34. alertmanager: 150 bump commits, 119 (79%) changed zero non-test .go files; the 31 that did had median 2, mean 5.1, max 38. Pooled: 87% of real dependency bumps are manifest-and-lockfile-only. This is corroborated by Alfadel et al., who found only 3.2% of manually examined Dependabot security PRs across 2,904 JS projects suffered build breakages, and by GitHub's own compatibility-score data where the vast majority of scores with enough candidates are above 90%. Counter-anchor for the major-version case: Raemaekers et al. found ~one third of Maven releases introduce at least one breaking change, identically for minor and major, and 32.9% of clients were hit by at least one breaking change — which is why a campaign sweep, not a routine sweep, is the right benchmark. Estimated rather than measured: the per-service probability of ANY commit landing overnight (I estimate 60–80% of 60 actively-developed services on a weekday) and the number of PRs merging mid-campaign per night (I estimate 10–20).
change_rate.where_changes_land: This is the whole story and the two regimes are opposites. REGIME A (nightly campaign re-run, ~2% artifact change): changes land almost entirely AT THE LEAVES — individual service source files, deep in the graph, downstream of the shared migration brief. The expensive root (fetch, api_diff, migration_brief) is byte-identical for the full 2–6 week campaign life. That is the friendly case, and it is the common case. REGIME B (next-version sweep, 2–6 weeks later): the change lands AT THE ROOT — new version string -> new changelog -> new api_diff -> new brief -> every one of the 1,229 downstream keys changes, even though 95%+ of the service source is byte-identical. Transitive keying converts a 1-artifact change into a 100% cache miss. REGIME C (prompt iteration): zero artifacts change, but the model-op keys all change and the tool-op keys all hit — which is exactly backwards from where the money is. AND THE STRUCTURAL KILLER, which applies inside regime A: leaf changes are diluted at the file level but concentrated at the SERVICE level. 2% of files changing fleet-wide does not mean 98% of services are reusable; it means 60–80% of services had at least one commit, and because svc_build and svc_test read the entire ~410-file tree, one commit anywhere in a service destroys its build key, its test key, and every repair key downstream. Measured file-level churn of 2% therefore produces service-level build/test invalidation of 60–80%. The reusable slice is the 20–40% of services that were genuinely untouched overnight. I also checked whether the specific files that matter churn more slowly than average — they do not: 150/401 argo-rollouts Go files import k8s.io/client-go and 44 of those 150 (29%) changed in 90 days, roughly the repo-wide rate. There is no free lunch from 'the call sites are stable'.

session_structure:
A competent engineer gets a LOT out of provider prefix caching here, and any reuse layer must beat this, not a naive baseline.

WHAT GOES IN THE CACHED PREFIX (identical for all 60 services and every repair iteration in the campaign, ~15–18k tokens): system prompt and repair policy (~3k); the fleet's coding conventions and forbidden-edit rules (~1.5k); the migration_brief symbol map (~2.5k); the raw api_diff output (~4k); 2–3 few-shot exemplars of a correct call-site rewrite for this specific library (~4k); tool schemas (~1.5k). One `cache_control` breakpoint at the end of that block, with the 1h TTL, not the 5m — the sweep's wall clock is 40–90 minutes, which straddles the 5m tier constantly and sits inside the 1h tier cleanly. This is the single highest-leverage choice in the baseline.

WHAT VARIES PER CALL, strictly after the breakpoint: the service's manifest and lock excerpt (~1.2k), the 3 grep result sets (~2.7k), the 6 matched file bodies (~15k), and the task instruction (~200). Static-first ordering is non-negotiable; putting the manifest before the brief would destroy the shared prefix.

DO THE 60 CALLS SHARE A CONVERSATION? No — they share a PREFIX, not a conversation. Putting 60 services in one thread would serialise them and blow past context. They are 60 independent requests with a byte-identical first 15–18k tokens.

CONCURRENCY RAMP — the detail most people get wrong. Issue ONE triage call first and wait for it to return, so the prefix is written to the cache exactly once. Then fan out the remaining 59 at concurrency 8–12. If you fan out all 60 concurrently from a cold prefix, every one of them misses and every one of them pays the cache-write premium (1.25x for 5m, 2x for 1h) — turning a saving into a loss. On a 15k prefix at 1h TTL that mistake costs roughly +$0.30 per run versus -$0.55 for doing it right.

WITHIN A SERVICE, the repair loop IS one conversation. Turn 1 triage, turn 2 the build error log, turn 3 the patch, turn 4 the next error. Place a SECOND `cache_control` breakpoint at the end of the per-service file dump (after the 15k of file bodies) and roll a third breakpoint to the end of each assistant turn. Repair iteration 2 then re-reads ~35k tokens of which ~32k is already cached. Since mean iterations is 1.8 and the tail goes to 4, this is where most of the repair-layer token cost evaporates.

KEEP THE 1h WINDOW WARM by ordering the sweep so calls are continuous — never let the fleet-rollup wait 20 minutes after the last PR body.

DON'T use the Batch API for the 60 triage calls even though it is 50% off: batch scheduling is opaque, breaks the warm-up-then-fan-out ordering, and can strand calls past the TTL. Ordinary streaming calls at concurrency 8–12 with a warm 1h prefix beat batch-without-cache on this shape.

WHAT THIS BASELINE ALREADY ACHIEVES: triage calls ~15k of 22k input cached => ~68% of triage input at 10% rate. Repair iterations 2+ ~90% cached. PR bodies ~55% cached (brief + template shared). Rollup ~10% cached. Weighted over the 3.44M input tokens, the tuned baseline serves roughly 62–72% of all input tokens at the cached rate, cutting the run from ~$13 to ~$5–6. THAT is the number to beat. It is also worth stating plainly what this baseline does NOT touch: it does nothing for the 1,069 tool operations — the greps, the lock resolutions, the 189 builds and 48+ test runs that account for 60–200 minutes of CI compute per run.
grader:
FULLY DETERMINISTIC, NO LLM, EXACT AND FREE GROUND TRUTH — achieved by generating the fleet from a seeded template generator that emits both the "before" tree and the reference "after" tree.

GENERATOR. `gen_fleet.py --seed S --services 60 --lib jwt --from v4 --to v5` emits 60 self-contained Go modules (or Python packages). Each service is assembled from a fixed catalogue of ~40 code templates that exercise a real library whose real major bump removed/renamed real symbols — `github.com/golang-jwt/jwt/v4 -> /v5`, `pydantic v1 -> v2`, or `com.fasterxml.jackson 2.x -> 3.x`. The seed decides, per service: which subset of ~12 affected API symbols it uses (0–7 of them), how many call sites per symbol (1–9), which of ~15 distractor libraries it also imports, and ~350 lines of generated business logic per service so the tree is realistically sized (~400 files). Crucially the generator ALSO emits, for every service, the reference "after" tree with the correct rewrite already applied, because it knows which template produced which call site. Dependencies are vendored and the registry is served from a local file-backed proxy, so lock resolution is hermetic and the graph is a pure function of local artifacts.

FOUR CHECKS PER SERVICE, all exit-code or byte-diff, no judgment:
1. PIN — the manifest, parsed with the ecosystem's own parser, resolves the target library to exactly the requested version. Fail otherwise. Catches "agent downgraded to make it compile".
2. COMPILE — `go build ./...` (or `mypy`/`python -c "import pkg"`/`mvn -q compile`) exits 0.
3. TEST-INTEGRITY THEN TEST — first assert that the sha256 of every `*_test.go` / `test_*.py` file is UNCHANGED from the generated original; hard-fail the service if any test file was touched. Then `go test ./...` must exit 0. The tests are generated alongside the code from the same templates, are seeded, and contain no clocks, no network, no randomness, so they are exactly reproducible.
4. BEHAVIOURAL EQUIVALENCE — the generator also emits a golden-IO harness: 200 seeded input vectors per service and the exact expected outputs, computed by running the harness against the REFERENCE "after" tree at generation time. The agent's tree must produce a byte-identical output file. This is the check that catches an agent that stubbed a function to make the compiler happy.
Plus a SCOPE guard: `git diff --name-only` must be a subset of (reference edit set) ∪ (manifest, lockfile), with at most K=2 extra files. Catches deleting code to pass.

SCORE. Primary: services_passing_all_four / 60 — an integer over an integer, exact. Secondary, reported alongside and equally deterministic: total operations executed, total operations served from the reuse store, billed input tokens (uncached), billed input tokens (cached), billed output tokens, and total build+test seconds. The benchmark is only meaningful as a pair (pass rate, cost) — a reuse layer that raises cache hits while dropping pass rate from 55/60 to 48/60 has lost.

REPEAT-RUN DRIVER. To grade the reuse claim rather than the fix claim, the harness generates run N+1 by applying a seeded mutation script to run N: pick a target churn fraction c, select ceil(c * 24600) files uniformly at random from the fleet, apply a semantics-preserving-but-hash-changing edit (rename a local variable, reorder independent statements), and regenerate the golden outputs so correctness is unaffected. Sweep c over {0, 0.005, 0.02, 0.05, 0.25} to trace the reuse-vs-churn curve, and separately run the ROOT-CHANGE regime by re-targeting `--to v6` with c=0.02. Both regimes must be reported; a system that only reports the c=0.005 leaf-change number is cherry-picking the friendly half of the real distribution.
