OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION VALIDATION SET, also free and exact: BUMP (arXiv 2401.09906), 571 reproducible breaking dependency updates from 153 real Java projects, each frozen in a Docker image with a guaranteed-reproducible build failure. Ground truth is the build exit code — free, exact, no LLM. These are single-service cases so they do not exercise the fan-out or the reuse surface, but they prove the synthetic fleet's repair difficulty is not a toy.
reuse_story:
Four mechanisms, in descending order of how much money they actually move.

1. WHOLE-SERVICE SKIP (the big one, ~20–35% of a nightly re-run). In regime A, 20–40% of services had zero commits overnight. For each such service, every op in its subgraph — 2 manifest reads, 1 resolve, 3 greps, 6 file reads, 1 triage model call (22k input), apply, lock, build, test, and any repair iterations — keys identically and is skipped wholesale. That is ~22k of model input AND 1–4 minutes of build+test compute per skipped service. Skipping 18 of 60 services saves ~400k input tokens and ~40 CI-minutes. The provider prefix cache gives you none of this: it discounts the shared 15k prefix, but you still pay full rate on the 7k of per-service content and full compute on the build.

2. CROSS-TENANT ROOT SHARING (structurally the most interesting). The migration_brief for `grpc-go 1.72->1.75` or `pydantic v1->v2` is a function of nothing but public artifacts — two published module versions and a public changelog. It is byte-identical for every customer on earth who bumps that pair. So is the api_diff. So, largely, are the rewrite recipes. One tenant's computation of the root serves everyone else's, with no privacy exposure, because the inputs are public by construction. This is the one reuse surface in this domain that a provider prefix cache can never touch and that a single-tenant cache cannot reach either. The catch: it is only ~35k input tokens and two tool calls per run — real, but small in absolute dollars unless you are serving thousands of tenants.

3. REPAIR-ITERATION REPLAY under prompt iteration (regime C). When the platform team re-runs a sweep after changing only the repair prompt, all 1,069 tool ops key identically — the greps, the resolves, the initial builds. Model ops all miss. So the saving is entirely compute, not tokens: ~60–200 CI-minutes reclaimed per experiment, which is why this only matters to a customer who is paying for the runners.

4. FLEET-WIDE DEDUPLICATION OF IDENTICAL SERVICE SHAPES. In a real fleet built from a service template (which is how most 60-service fleets got to 60), many services have byte-identical dependency stanzas and near-identical call-site patterns. Their resolve and grep ops key identically today, within a single run. The cross-project-transfer result in arXiv 2606.24446 — 33.3% overall, above 80% where API usage is uniform — is direct evidence this class of sharing is real at the fix level too, not just the lookup level.
reuse_threats:
Six reasons this might not pay, listed honestly and roughly in order of severity.

1. WHOLE-TREE READS COLLAPSE THE KEY GRANULARITY. svc_build reads ~410 files; svc_test reads those plus fixtures. A measured 2% file-level change produces 60–80% service-level invalidation of exactly the ops that cost the most compute. Bazel gets around this with declared per-target inputs; an agent that shells out to `go build ./...` has no such declaration and must key on the tree. Fixing this means teaching the reuse layer the build system's own dependency graph, at which point you have rebuilt Bazel — and the customers who would benefit most already have it.

2. TRANSITIVE KEYING TURNS A ONE-BYTE ROOT CHANGE INTO A TOTAL MISS. Regime B — the next-version sweep — changes one version string. Under the stated key composition that invalidates the api_diff, the brief, and therefore all 1,229 downstream keys, despite 95%+ of the fleet's source being byte-identical. This is the single most common repeat mode after the nightly re-run, and the design as specified gets zero from it. A content-addressed layer only wins here if it can key some ops on a SUBSET of the brief (e.g. "this service uses none of the changed symbols") rather than the brief's hash — which is a semantic weakening of the key, not the Nix model.

3. IMPURE OPS. svc_lock_regen and svc_dep_resolve read the live package registry, whose state changes hourly as transitive dependencies publish. Include registry state in the key and you never hit; exclude it and the cache is unsound — you will serve a lockfile that omits a patch released this morning, which in a CVE sweep is precisely the failure that gets you fired. pr_open is side-effecting and must be excluded outright. That is ~180 of 1,234 ops that are either unsafe or unhittable.

4. THE TUNED BASELINE ALREADY TOOK MOST OF THE TOKEN PRIZE. 62–72% of input tokens are already served at 10% rate by a correctly-structured 1h-TTL prefix. The reuse layer's incremental token headroom is the remaining ~30% plus the skipped services. On a $13 gross run that means competing for roughly $2–4, of which whole-service skip delivers maybe $1.50. Meanwhile the same layer delivers 40+ CI-minutes — genuinely more valuable, but it is compute on the customer's runners, a different budget line, and one you cannot bill as a share of token savings.

5. SAMPLING BREAKS THE FUNCTIONAL ASSUMPTION. At temperature > 0 a model op's output is not a function of its inputs. Serving a stored repair patch is a behaviour change, not an optimisation — and in this domain teams specifically WANT a fresh attempt after a failed one. Caching triage (a classification) is fine; caching repair_patch (a generation the human may have already rejected) is arguably wrong. That removes the single most expensive model layer (43 calls x 35k = 1.5M tokens, 44% of all input) from the safely-reusable set.

6. SILENT STALENESS THAT IS ACTUALLY INCORRECT. Service A's tree is unchanged, so its key hits — but service A depends on internal library B whose version floats via a range constraint, and B shipped a breaking change overnight. The key over A's tree misses that entirely unless the fully-resolved lock closure is in the key, and putting the lock closure in the key reintroduces threat 3. In a fleet with internal shared SDKs, which is the exact customer described, this is not hypothetical.
confidence:
MEDIUM-HIGH overall, with the components varying a lot.

HIGH confidence: the bump-breakage rate (I walked 350 real dependency-bump commits in two production Go services and counted; 87% required zero source edits, and this agrees with Alfadel et al.'s independently-derived 3.2% build-breakage figure on JS Dependabot PRs); the weekly file-churn range (measured on four repos, 32 repo-weeks); the graph SHAPE (a shared root fanning out to N near-independent short chains with a bounded repair loop is not a modelling choice, it is what Renovate + a repair agent structurally is); and the whole-tree-read problem, which is a fact about build tools rather than an estimate.

MEDIUM confidence: the token sizes per operation (engineering estimates, I would hold them to +/-40%, most uncertain on the repair_patch input of 35k which could plausibly be 20k or 60k depending on how much surrounding file context the agent pulls); the 40% breakage rate for a MAJOR campaign (interpolated between my measured 13% for routine bumps and the ~33% of Maven releases that carry a breaking change, but the number is a design choice for the benchmark and should be a tunable, not a constant); and the tuned-baseline cache-hit figure of 62–72%, which I computed from the token layout rather than measured.

LOW confidence: the generalisation of OSS churn to enterprise service repos. My four repos are OSS with modest committer counts; a 20-engineer service repo may churn 2–3x faster, which would push per-service overnight invalidation from 60–80% toward 90%+ and materially shrink the whole-service-skip prize. Also low: the 20–40% of services with zero overnight commits, which is the single number the entire reuse case rests on and which I estimated rather than measured.

WHAT WOULD RAISE IT, in priority order: (1) instrument one real customer fleet for two weeks and measure, per service per night, whether ANY tracked file changed — this converts the load-bearing 20–40% estimate into data and costs nothing but a cron job; (2) run one real 60-service major sweep with full token accounting under the tuned baseline to replace my computed 62–72% with a measured figure; (3) log actual context sizes from a real repair agent on 20 BUMP cases to pin the repair_patch input distribution; (4) measure how often lock regeneration produces a different lockfile from the same manifest 24h apart, which directly sizes threat 3.

customer: A ~$180M-revenue, PE-backed multi-entity SaaS/services company on NetSuite: 6 legal entities, 3 currencies, an 8-person accounting team under a Controller, a 6-business-day close, and a Big-4-adjacent annual audit with PCAOB AS 2401 journal-entry testing. They already pay for a close-management platform (BlackLine / FloQast / Numeric class, $40-120K/yr) and have bolted an LLM agent onto it — either the vendor's AI module or an internal agent on the NetSuite SuiteQL API. What they pay for is NOT cheaper tokens. They pay for (a) days off the close calendar, (b) an audit-ready evidence trail per account, (c) the Controller not personally writing 72 flux narratives at 9pm on day 4. Token cost is a rounding error to them: the full graph below is ~6.7M input tokens, ~$20 uncached per run, ~$1,700/yr at 84 runs. The buyer for a token-reuse layer is therefore NOT this company — it is the CAS firm / BPO / outsourced-controller shop running this identical graph across 40-80 client entities with one shared policy spine, where the same layer is $70-140K/yr of provider spend and the prompt spine is literally shared across tenants.
why_repeated: Three independent repetition axes, and they are NOT equally important. (1) INTRA-CLOSE RE-RUNS — the dominant one. A close is not a single pass. Recs and the flux pack are generated on day 2 against incomplete data, the Controller reviews, adjusting entries get posted, and the pack is regenerated. Every posted top-side entry, late vendor invoice, or corrected FX rate triggers "re-run it now that I've booked the accrual." This is not sloppiness; it is the designed workflow, which is why every close product ships a refresh button and why the literature describes preparing a series of adjusted trial balances before closing. (2) MONTH BOUNDARY — 12x/yr, same graph, same policy pack, same 420 accounts, entirely new transactions. (3) CROSS-TENANT — a CAS firm runs a structurally identical graph per client, differing only in COA mapping and entity config; the policy pack, rec templates, JE risk rules and flux thresholds are the firm's, not the client's. Axis 1 supplies ~86% of consecutive-run pairs and holds nearly all the reuse surface. Axis 2 is where the surface is most fragile. Axis 3 is where the dollars are.
run_cadence: Full-graph runs: ~7 per monthly close (day 2 draft, day 3 post-AP-cutoff, day 4 post-adjustments, day 4 late, day 5 review, day 5 re-review, day 6 final) x 12 closes = ~84 full runs/yr per entity set. Partial-graph runs: the cash slice (L0 bank fetch -> L1 matcher -> L2d) runs DAILY under a continuous-close regime, ~250 runs/yr. Quarter-end adds a heavier variant 4x/yr; year-end one heavier still. HONESTY FLAG: "~7 re-runs per close" is the single weakest load-bearing number in this spec. It is my estimate from the documented iterative adjusted-trial-balance cycle and from every close product shipping a re-run affordance; I found no vendor or benchmark publication of an actual re-run distribution. If the true number is 2 rather than 7, the blended change rate roughly triples and the reuse case weakens materially.

layers.name: L0_extract
layers.consumes: nothing (graph roots): 3 TB pulls (current, prior period, prior year), 12 GL-detail chunk queries sharded by entity x account-range, 9 subledger extracts, 14 bank-statement fetches, 8 policy/config reads
layers.reads_artifacts: NetSuite saved-search exports (TB, GL detail), subledger extracts (AR aging, AP aging, fixed-asset register, prepaid schedule, deferred-revenue waterfall, payroll register, inventory, intercompany, accrual schedule), BAI2/CSV bank statements, COA-with-owners, materiality memo, rev-rec and accrual policy, close checklist, FX rate table

layers.name: L0_5_shred
layers.consumes: L0_extract (all 46)
layers.reads_artifacts: none beyond L0 outputs; splits the monolithic TB and GL exports into one content-addressed shard per (entity, account) with canonical row ordering, stripped export timestamps and integer-cent formatting. PREREQUISITE, NOT AN OPTIMIZATION: without it every downstream key is a function of two whole-file hashes and one posted journal entry invalidates all 419 model ops.

layers.name: L1_deterministic_gates
layers.consumes: L0_5_shred (2) and ~7 L0_extract ops each
layers.reads_artifacts: shards only. The eight gates: auto-certification rule engine (zero balance / no activity / balance unchanged MoM / matches approved amortization schedule), JE risk scorer over the full 2,400-header population (round dollar, weekend or after-hours, post-date beyond period end, unusual account pair, preparer equals approver, seldom-used account, generic or missing memo), flux threshold calculator (5-10% AND $25-50K dual threshold), bank auto-matcher, intercompany pair matcher, FX revaluation calculator, prior-open-item carryforward resolver, close-checklist dependency resolver. This layer removes ~58% of balance-sheet accounts and ~93% of journal entries BEFORE any model call. Omitting it inflates model-op count 2.4x and lets a reuse layer claim credit the free rule engine already banked.

layers.name: L2a_account_reconciliation
layers.consumes: L1 auto-certification manifest (1) + 3 L0_extract ops (subledger extract, TB shard, GL shard). ADDITIONALLY 32 of the 176 consume exactly 1 other L2a op via an explicit adjacency list: deferred revenue <- revenue, accrued payroll <- payroll register, accrued bonus <- payroll register, income tax payable <- essentially the entity roll-forward, intercompany due-from <- due-to. Wire this adjacency list explicitly; it is what makes max_depth 8 and where root changes propagate furthest.
layers.reads_artifacts: prior-period certified workpaper for this account, the account's GL activity shard (median 40 lines, p90 4,000+ lines for cash/AR/AP), the supporting subledger extract, the rec template, the policy pack

layers.name: L2b_je_adjudication
layers.consumes: L1 JE risk scorer (1) + 1 L0 GL chunk
layers.reads_artifacts: the flagged journal entry header and lines, its rule-hit vector, the target account's normal-pattern summary, attached supporting-document text where present. 140 of 2,400 headers reach the model (~6%); the other 94% are cleared by rules. In the tuned baseline these are batched 10 per provider call (14 calls) but remain 140 logical operations with independent reuse keys.

layers.name: L2c_flux_explanation
layers.consumes: L1 flux threshold calculator (1) + 3 L0 TB pulls + 1 L0 GL chunk
layers.reads_artifacts: current, prior-period and prior-year balances for the account, the top-20 driver transactions by absolute amount, last month's narrative for the same account, the budget line

layers.name: L2d_bank_exception
layers.consumes: L1 bank auto-matcher (1) + 1 L0 bank statement + 1 L0 GL chunk
layers.reads_artifacts: the residual unmatched items for one bank account (90%+ of lines auto-match, so ~40 items survive across all 14 accounts), prior-period open items, the cash policy. This is the layer that also runs standalone daily.

layers.name: L2e_intercompany_tieout
layers.consumes: L1 intercompany pair matcher (1) + 2 L2a reconciliations (both sides of the pair)
layers.reads_artifacts: both entities' due-from/due-to detail, the FX rate table, the intercompany policy. 9 active pairs out of 15 possible across 6 entities.

layers.name: L3_entity_review
layers.consumes: ~51 upstream ops each: ~29 L2a + ~12 L2c + ~2 L2d + ~2 L2e + 6 L2b batches
layers.reads_artifacts: the entity trial balance, last month's entity close memo, the entity's checklist state

layers.name: L4_consolidated_package
layers.consumes: all 6 L3_entity_review outputs
layers.reads_artifacts: consolidated TB, materiality memo, prior close memo, elimination schedule. Two documents: the Controller close memo and the audit exception packet.

layers.name: L5_writeback
layers.consumes: L4_consolidated_package (2)
layers.reads_artifacts: none; posts certifications and workpapers back to the close platform and renders PDF evidence

graph.description:
A wide-independent middle sandwiched between a narrow extraction root and a narrow consolidation apex. 419 of 476 ops are model calls and 411 of those sit in one embarrassingly-parallel band (L2a-L2e) with no dependency on each other beyond 32 explicit intra-band edges. This is close to the best-case topology for operation-level reuse: the wide band is 98% of model ops, each band op touches a small account-scoped slice of state, and only 8 ops (L3+L4) genuinely depend on everything.

CRITICAL STRUCTURAL FACT that determines the whole result: the wide band's ops LOOK account-scoped but the ERP hands you two monolithic root artifacts — the TB export and the GL-detail export, each one saved-search CSV. Keyed on those files as delivered, one posted journal entry changes both hashes and invalidates all 419 model ops, and measured reuse is exactly zero regardless of how little actually changed. Hence L0_5_shred. That shredder is a prerequisite, not an optimization, and it must itself be byte-stable forever.

Also note L1. In production the deterministic gates run BEFORE any model call and already remove the easy 58% of accounts and 94% of journal entries. The 176 accounts reaching L2a are the residual that a free, domain-specific 'nothing changed' cache has already failed to eliminate. Do not build the benchmark without L1.

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 3-8% for an intra-close re-run (86% of consecutive-run pairs); 42-100% across a month boundary depending entirely on artifact sharding and prior-workpaper normalization; ~1-3%/month for policy and config artifacts
change_rate.basis:
PARTLY SOURCED, PARTLY ESTIMATED — separated explicitly.

SOURCED, and the strongest number available in this domain: BlackLine reports that clients auto-certify 58% of balance-sheet reconciliations using three rules — zero balance, no activity, and matches-an-approved-amortization-schedule (Revelwood citing BlackLine; other sources give a 40-65% typical range and a 43-85% client spread). Two of those three rules ARE a change-rate measurement: 'no activity' and 'no change in account balances month over month' are the vendor with the largest sample in the category asserting that a clear majority of balance-sheet accounts are input-identical between consecutive MONTHLY runs. Separately sourced: 90%+ of bank-reconciliation lines auto-match, so bank inputs are ~90% invariant at line level. Also sourced for context: mid-market close is 6-10 business days (PwC 2023 average 6.4), and mid-market flux thresholds are 5-10% with $25-50K minimums, which sets the 72-account flux population.

ESTIMATED — the intra-close figure. Between re-run k and k+1 what changes is the adjusting entries posted in between: realistically 4-20 JEs touching 8-30 of 420 (entity, account) combos, i.e. 2-7% of account-scoped artifacts, plus the ~32-edge intra-band dependency closure. I could not find published data on adjusting-entry counts per close iteration; this is calibrated from typical manual close-entry volume (~180/month for this profile spread over ~7 iterations) rather than measured.

ESTIMATED — reference churn. COA gains or loses a handful of accounts per year; materiality annual; rev-rec and accrual policy roughly quarterly; checklist a couple of tasks a month. 1-3%/month, low confidence but low stakes given the small artifact count.

CERTAIN — the transactional layer month-over-month is 100% new. Every GL chunk, bank statement and subledger extract is a different file every month, unconditionally. No research needed.

BLENDED: 84 full runs/yr of which 12 cross a month boundary, so 0.86 x ~5% + 0.14 x ~60% = ~12.7% raw. I report 6% rather than 12.7% because the distribution is sharply bimodal, not centered, and a single mean misrepresents both modes. The honest statement is: 86% of consecutive-run pairs change ~5% of inputs, and 14% change ~60%.
change_rate.where_changes_land:
PHYSICALLY AT THE ROOT, SEMANTICALLY AT THE LEAF — reconciling those two facts is the entire engineering problem in this domain.

Every real change is a journal entry, and a journal entry lands in exactly one place: the GL, exported as one file that is transitively read by all 419 model ops. At the granularity the ERP actually gives you the data, 100% of changes land at the root and blast radius is total: one $4,000 accrual posted on day 4 invalidates the entire graph including the 380 accounts it did not touch.

Semantically the same change touches 1-3 accounts. After the deterministic (entity, account)-sharded shred with canonical ordering, it becomes leaf-local: 8-30 of 420 shards change, ~94-97% of L2a and L2c ops keep their keys, and only the 32-edge intra-band closure (revenue -> deferred revenue, payroll -> accrual) and the tax-payable rec propagate further.

The apex genuinely never survives. L3 (6 ops, ~51 children each) and L4 (2 ops, 6 children each) change keys if any single child changes. These 8 ops recompute on every run forever, and they are the most expensive per op (26K and 29K input). That is ~194K input tokens per run permanently non-reusable, ~3% of run input — a real floor, not a fatal one, but a disproportionate share of latency-critical output.

The month boundary is different in kind. There, changes land at the root AND at every leaf simultaneously — new GL, new bank statements, new subledger extracts, AND a freshly regenerated prior-period workpaper feeding every single L2a op. Month over month, without prior-workpaper normalization, reuse is structurally zero even for a dormant account whose balance has not moved in 14 months. The sourced 58% invariance is real but is not reachable by byte-hashing workpaper text.

session_structure:
A competent engineer gets very far here with no cross-run store at all. This baseline must be beaten as specified, not as a straw man.

1. FIXED PREFIX, ONE BREAKPOINT. Order every call as [tool definitions | system role | accounting policy pack (rev-rec, accrual, capitalization, FX) | COA with account owners and rec-required flags | materiality memo | rec/flux output schema | 4 few-shot exemplar workpapers] = 12,000-14,000 tokens, byte-identical across all 419 calls in a run, all 7 re-runs in a close, all 12 closes in a year (policy churn 1-3%/mo) and, for a CAS firm, across all 40 tenants. Cache breakpoint here. Largest single lever, costs nothing.

2. SECOND BREAKPOINT AFTER THE ENTITY BLOCK — entity TB, entity FX table, entity policy overrides, ~2,400 tokens. Order the fan-out ENTITY-MAJOR so all ~35 accounts of entity 3 execute contiguously and the block stays hot. Never interleave entities.

3. THIRD BREAKPOINT AFTER ACCOUNT-STABLE CONTEXT — prior certified rec plus the account's normal-pattern summary, ~1,300 tokens. Pays only across intra-close re-runs, where it is genuinely unchanged. MUST be floor-checked: this repo measured (docs/FIELD_CACHE_MEASUREMENT.md, X4) that the surviving prefix at a breakpoint must independently clear the model's minimum cacheable length or the segment silently caches nothing — a 2,194-token survivor gave 0% recovery where the staircase predicted 25%. At 12K+2.4K the third breakpoint clears; a naive design that put the volatile GL slice second would not.

4. VOLATILE TAIL LAST. The account's current-period GL activity (900 tokens median, 24K at p90 for cash/AR/AP) goes strictly after the last breakpoint. This repo's X3/X4 result: position WITHIN a cached block is irrelevant, any byte kills the whole block, so the only thing that matters is being past the last breakpoint.

5. BUY THE 1h TTL, NOT 5m. Re-runs are 40 minutes to 4 hours apart. This repo's field data: 88.8% of writes already go to the 1h tier and the observed TTL cliff is at 3600s, not 300s. The 1h tier covers the intra-close refresh loop natively, free, with no warming layer on top.

6. STAGGER THE FAN-OUT — highest-value non-obvious move. This repo's X1 probe measured that at 0ms skew all 5 concurrent callers are billed cache_creation; the one-writer/N-readers identity only recovers past ~1s of skew. Firing 411 account ops in parallel means 411 callers each pay 1.25x on a 14K prefix and none of them read. The tuned baseline issues ONE warm-up call, waits for completion, then fans out with >=1s jitter. On this repo's own numbers that is the difference between +24.8% and -77.8%.

7. KEEP EACH ENTITY'S CALLS IN ONE CONVERSATION so the prefix grows monotonically. This repo's 112-session field measurement found 99.86% of realized cache value is within-session continuation and 0.14% is cross-session sharing — the win comes from conversation structure, not from hoping a cold call hits a shared prefix.

8. BATCH THE SUB-FLOOR OPS. The 140 JE adjudications carry ~1,400 tokens of genuinely per-item content against a 14K prefix. Batch 10 per call -> 14 calls.

NET BASELINE: ~6.7M input tokens/run, ~6.0M of it repeated prefix served at 0.10x. Uncached ~$20/run; tuned ~$4.30-4.60/run — the provider's free mechanism alone delivers ~77-78%, matching this repo's measured -77.84% at reuse depth 10. Any operation-reuse layer must beat $4.50/run, not $20/run, and must beat it on the RESIDUAL: the volatile per-account tail plus all 216K output tokens, which no provider cache touches. The theoretical prize is real — prefix caching still pays full freight for the account's GL slice, its prior workpaper, its subledger extract and every output token, whereas serving the whole operation from a store eliminates all 17,800 input and 700 output for a dormant account. On a 5%-change re-run that is ~$4.50 -> ~$0.55 (the 8 apex ops plus the changed band), a further ~88% off a well-tuned baseline — provided the shred is hermetic.
grader:
FULLY DETERMINISTIC, NO LLM, EXACT AND FREE GROUND TRUTH — because the ledger is generated, not found.

GENERATOR (seeded, ~600 lines of Python, deterministic from one integer seed): emits a complete internally-consistent multi-entity ledger — 6 entities, 3 currencies, 420 balance-sheet and 300 P&L (entity, account) combos, ~2,400 JE headers / ~140,000 JE lines for the month — plus matching subledger extracts (AR aging, AP aging, FA register, prepaid schedule, deferred-revenue waterfall, payroll register, inventory, intercompany), 14 BAI2 bank statements, an FX rate table, and last month's 420 certified workpapers. By construction every control account ties to its subledger and the consolidated balance sheet sums to zero.

DEFECT INJECTION: the generator then injects exactly N=37 defects from a closed 10-type catalogue, recording a ground-truth tuple (entity, account, defect_type, amount_cents, source_je_ids) for each. Types: UNBALANCED_JE, SUBLEDGER_GL_VARIANCE, DUPLICATE_JE, PERIOD_CUTOFF_ERROR, FX_RATE_ERROR, INTERCOMPANY_MISMATCH, UNREVERSED_ACCRUAL, UNSUPPORTED_TOPSIDE_ENTRY, BANK_UNEXPLAINED_DIFFERENCE, PREPAID_OFF_SCHEDULE. Amounts are drawn to straddle the materiality threshold so the grader also tests threshold discipline.

AGENT CONTRACT: the run emits exceptions.jsonl — {entity, account, defect_type (closed vocab), amount_cents (integer), je_ids: [string]} — plus recs.jsonl {entity, account, gl_balance_cents, subledger_balance_cents, open_items_cents} and flux.jsonl {entity, account, prior_cents, current_cents, variance_cents}.

GRADER (pure Python set and integer comparison, zero model calls):
Four arithmetic gates, exact to the cent against generator state, all free —
 G1 every recs.jsonl gl_balance_cents equals the generated TB for that (entity, account).
 G2 sum of recs.jsonl balances equals the generated TB control total.
 G3 the consolidated balance sheet assembled from agent output sums to zero.
 G4 every flux.jsonl variance_cents equals current minus prior computed from the generated TB.
One hallucination gate —
 G5 every je_id cited anywhere exists in the generated ledger. A free, exact, zero-false-positive fabricated-evidence detector, and the gate I expect to fail most often.
Detection scoring — a predicted exception matches iff (entity, account, defect_type) match exactly AND amount_cents matches exactly. Recall and precision over the 37 injected defects; F1 is the ranking score.
PASS iff G1-G5 all hold AND recall >= 0.90 AND precision >= 0.80 (false exceptions cost controller time and are a real product failure, so precision is graded, not just recall). Ranking within passes: F1, tie-broken by total provider cost in cents.

REUSE-SPECIFIC SECOND METRIC — what makes this benchmark diagnostic rather than merely scored. To produce run k+1 the harness posts a seeded set of adjusting entries (e.g. 12 JEs touching 22 combos) and regenerates. Because the harness knows exactly which shards changed, it computes the transitive closure over the declared dependency graph and therefore knows the EXACT count of operations whose complete input set provably did not change. Then:
 reuse_efficiency = ops served from the store / ops provably unchanged
 false_reuse_count = ops served from the store whose inputs DID change — must be exactly 0; any nonzero value is an automatic benchmark failure, because in this domain it means certifying an account against stale data
 wasted_recompute = ops provably unchanged but recomputed anyway
This separates "the domain has reuse surface" (a property of the generator, computable in advance) from "your keying captured it" (the thing under test), and catches non-hermetic shredding immediately: if the export carries a timestamp or unstable row order, reuse_efficiency collapses to ~0 while the correctness score stays perfect — exactly the silent failure to instrument for.

Everything above is a seeded generator plus integer arithmetic. Ground truth costs nothing, is exact, and is reproducible from the seed alone.
reuse_story: 411 of 419 model ops sit in one flat band, each scoped to a single (entity, account) slice of state, and between the dominant pair of consecutive runs — an intra-close re-run — only 8-30 of 420 slices actually move. A dormant prepaid, a fully-amortized intangible, a quiet intercompany pair: their reconciliation input set is byte-identical between run k and k+1, so the entire operation leaves the bill, not merely its prefix. Provider prefix caching can only discount the repeated 14K policy spine to 0.10x; it still pays full freight for the account's GL slice, its prior workpaper, its subledger extract, and every one of its 700 output tokens. Operation-level reuse eliminates all of it. On a 5%-change re-run the tuned baseline's ~$4.50 falls to roughly $0.55 — the 8 always-recompute apex ops plus the genuinely changed band — ~88% below a properly tuned prefix-cached baseline. The gap exists because the two mechanisms attack orthogonal parts of the bill: prefix caching attacks the shared head, operation reuse attacks the per-op tail and the output. Output tokens alone are 216K/run and are untouched by any provider cache. Structurally this is the most favourable shape I would expect in any business-document domain: wide, shallow, account-partitionable, re-run many times against slowly-moving state, with a vendor-published 58% month-over-month invariance figure sitting in the incumbent tooling. The CAS-firm axis makes it better still — the 14K policy spine and rec templates belong to the FIRM, so cross-tenant operation reuse can fire on template-driven ops even when no two clients share a transaction.
reuse_threats:
Ranked by how likely each is to kill it outright.

1. THE INCUMBENT ALREADY ATE THE EASY 58%, FOR FREE. BlackLine's auto-certification rules — zero balance, no activity, balance unchanged month-over-month, matches an approved amortization schedule — are a domain-specific implementation of exactly this cache, they run before any model call, they cost nothing, and they clear a reported 58% of balance-sheet reconciliations. The 176 accounts that reach the model are precisely the residual that "nothing changed" already failed to catch. A reuse layer measured against a pipeline WITHOUT that gate will report spectacular and entirely fake savings. This mirrors this repo's own finding that the caching wedge is commoditized: the free thing is already in the box.

2. NON-HERMETIC ERP EXPORTS. NetSuite saved searches do not guarantee row order, exports carry a generation timestamp in the header, and decimal formatting varies by locale. Any of these makes byte-hashes differ on semantically identical data and drives reuse_efficiency to zero while every correctness metric stays green — a silent failure. The canonical shred is real engineering that must be built and must stay byte-stable forever.

3. AUDITABILITY MAY FORBID IT ENTIRELY, AND THIS IS NOT A TECHNICAL PROBLEM. Under SOX 404 and PCAOB AS 2401 the evidence required is that the control was PERFORMED for the period under audit. A reconciliation conclusion served from a store keyed on a prior run is, to an external auditor, a conclusion that was not performed this period. Some auditors will accept a cryptographic input-equivalence proof; some will not, and a Controller told "your rec might get challenged" will disable the feature at zero cost to themselves. Largest adoption risk, entirely outside the technology's control.

4. THE PRIOR-PERIOD WORKPAPER DESTROYS MONTH-OVER-MONTH REUSE. Every L2a op reads last month's certified rec, regenerated in full every month even for an account that has not moved in a year. Byte-hashed, this alone zeroes the sourced 58% invariance. Fixable only by normalizing that input to its semantic content (closing balance, open-item set, conclusion code) — which means the reuse key stops being a hash of what the operation read and becomes a hash of a domain-specific projection of it. That is a correctness liability, not a free win.

5. PROMPT AND MODEL CHURN. Finance teams tune close prompts constantly through the first two or three quarters of adoption, and any edit to the 14K policy spine invalidates 100% of the store — every entry, every account, every tenant. Same for a model upgrade. Empirically this is the standard way Bazel-style caches fail in practice, and this domain's prompts are unusually volatile early because the output is being negotiated with a Controller and an audit firm.

6. THE ABSOLUTE DOLLARS ARE SMALL. ~$1,700/yr uncached, ~$380/yr after competent prefix caching, per entity set. Capturing 88% of the residual saves ~$335/yr for this customer — that does not buy a procurement cycle at a company with an 8-person accounting team. The economics only close on the CAS/BPO axis at 40+ tenants, or at true enterprise scale — where the close runs on SAP with a different graph shape and a much larger deterministic-rule footprint.

7. THE APEX NEVER REUSES. L3 and L4 are 8 ops but 194K input tokens and the highest-value output; they change on every run by construction, setting a hard ~3% floor on input tokens and a much larger share of latency-critical output.

8. P90 SKEW. Cash, AR and AP GL slices run 24K+ tokens against a 900-token median, and those are exactly the accounts that change every run. The reuse surface is concentrated in the cheap ops and absent from the expensive ones, so token-weighted reuse will land materially below op-weighted reuse. Report both, or the benchmark flatters itself.
confidence:
MEDIUM on graph shape and token sizes; MEDIUM-LOW on the change rate; LOW on the re-run cadence, which is the number the whole case rests on.

Solid ground: the topology (wide band between a narrow root and a narrow apex), the existence and placement of the deterministic gate layer, the artifact inventory, and the tuned-baseline construction — all of which follow from how these products are documented to work and from this repo's own measured cache behavior (floor truncation, breakpoint granularity, concurrent-fan-out write premium, 1h tier). Token sizes are engineering estimates calibrated to real artifact types, accurate to maybe +/-40%; they will not change any conclusion.

Weak ground, in order: (a) the ~7 intra-close re-runs — unsourced, and if it is really 2 the blended change rate roughly triples and the reuse case degrades from "best-in-class domain" to "marginal"; (b) the 8-30 changed shards per re-run, inferred from manual-JE volume rather than observed; (c) the 176/140/72 op counts, calibrated to a specific $180M profile and scaling non-linearly with entity count and industry; (d) APQC's journal-entry-line-item quartiles, the right sourced anchor for op counts, are paywalled and I could not retrieve them.

What would raise confidence, cheapest first: (1) two consecutive trial-balance snapshots from ONE real NetSuite or Intacct tenant taken hours apart during a close — a 20-line diff gives the intra-close account-level change rate directly and replaces the BlackLine 58% inference with a measurement; (2) the refresh/re-run event log from any close-automation vendor for one customer for one close, which settles cadence; (3) APQC membership for the gated general-accounting quartiles; (4) one conversation with an external audit senior on whether an input-equivalence proof constitutes evidence of control performance — if the answer is no, threats 1-8 are moot and this domain is closed to operation-level reuse regardless of how well the technology works.

Sources used: BlackLine auto-certification 58% figure via https://revelwood.com/auto-certification-rules-for-balance-sheet-reconciliations-in-blackline/ ; 90%+ bank auto-match and Brex 6->4 day case via https://www.numeric.io/blog/ultimate-guide-to-blackline-account-reconciliation ; mid-market close 6-10 days / PwC 6.4-day average via https://www.eaglerockcfo.com/blog/research/month-end-close-benchmarks ; flux thresholds 5-10% and $25-50K via https://nordavix.com/blog/flux-analysis-example and https://ramp.com/blog/flux-analysis ; AS 2401 full-population JE scoring and high-risk criteria via https://pcaobus.org/resources/staff-publications/audit-focus-journal-entries and https://www.rillet.com/blog/journal-entry-testing ; iterative adjusted trial balances via https://www.accountingtools.com/articles/what-is-a-post-closing-trial-balance.html ; continuous/daily reconciliation cadence via https://www.numeric.io/blog/cash-reconciliation-guide ; APQC measures exist but are paywalled at https://www.apqc.org/what-we-do/benchmarking/open-standards-benchmarking/measures/average-number-journal-entry-line ; internal cache mechanics from /Users/jamesyang/Documents/GitHub/Brevitas-Systems/docs/FIELD_CACHE_MEASUREMENT.md

customer: A 200–800 engineer product company (fintech / healthtech / B2B SaaS) with a 6–12 person AppSec team, paying today for (a) a SAST/SCA platform seat-priced per developer — Semgrep Code + Supply Chain, Snyk, GitHub Advanced Security, or Endor — typically $30–60/dev/yr for the scanner and a separate AI-triage add-on, and (b) the AppSec engineers' own time. The thing they actually buy is not detection: raw scanners are cheap or free (semgrep OSS, CodeQL, trivy, gitleaks all cost $0). They buy (1) *suppression* of the 60–90% of findings that are false positives, (2) an auditable trail showing a human-or-machine adjudicated every finding, for SOC2/PCI/FedRAMP evidence, and (3) a patch they can merge. Published economics: a mid-sized codebase produces ~500 findings per scan, ~60% of them noise, at ~10 min of engineer time per finding to adjudicate. That is the line item the AI triage layer is billed against.
why_repeated: Three independent forces make this run again rather than once. (1) The code changes: every merge to the default branch re-runs the full-repo scan, because a diff-scoped scan cannot see a vulnerability introduced by a *callee* change three files away from the sink. (2) The rule pack changes: Semgrep registry / CodeQL query packs ship new and revised rules continuously; a rule added today must be evaluated against code written last year, so the whole repo is re-analyzed with the rules as the changed input. (3) The advisory database changes: ~131 new CVEs/day in 2025, running ~221/day in 2026 — an unchanged lockfile becomes vulnerable overnight with no code change at all, which is precisely why nightly SCA re-runs exist. On top of that, compliance regimes require a dated scan artifact on a fixed cadence regardless of whether anything changed, so the run happens even on a quiet week.
run_cadence: Three overlapping cadences on the same repo, and the benchmark should model all three because they have very different change rates. (a) Full-repo SAST+SCA scan on every merge to the default branch — measured mainline merge rate on the repos I sampled: django ~3/day, rails ~6/day, next.js ~14/day, kubernetes ~9/day; an active product monorepo is 10–40/day. (b) A nightly cron full scan (GitHub code scanning's default schedule is push-to-default plus a weekly cron; Semgrep's recommended config is full scan on default-branch merge plus scheduled). (c) A weekly deep CodeQL pass, because the interprocedural database build takes 20–90 min on a repo this size. Separately, per-PR diff-scoped scans run 50–200×/day, but that is a different and much smaller graph (0–5 findings, and Semgrep caps autotriage at 10 new findings per diff scan) — I am specifying the full-repo graph, which is where the operation count and the reuse question live.

graph.description: A wide layered DAG with a very thin neck. The shape is: a handful of monolithic whole-repo tool ops at the root (checkout, inventory, CodeQL database build, SARIF merge/baseline), then a hard fan-out to ~500 independent per-finding subgraphs that never talk to each other, then a thin fan-in to a report. Concretely: 5,166 operations, of which 1,602 are model calls and 3,564 are tool calls; 9,109 external input artifacts (8,000 scannable non-test source files at ~110 LOC median, 6 lockfiles, ~1,100 Semgrep rule YAMLs from the registry rulesets, 1 advisory-DB snapshot, 1 org security-policy doc, 1 triage-baseline/fingerprint state file). Repo profile calibrated to the real repos I measured: ~8,000 non-test source files, ~900k LOC, polyglot TS/Python/Go. TOKEN CONVENTION FOR TOOL LAYERS: input_tokens=0 (no model involved); output_tokens = the size in tokens of the artifact the op emits, so an engineer can size what downstream model ops read. THE ONE STRUCTURAL FACT THAT DOMINATES EVERYTHING: the graph is bimodal. The 5,100 leaf operations each read 1-3 files and are trivially memoizable. The ~6 root operations each read all 8,000 files and are invalidated by literally any change. And the expensive-in-wall-clock ops (CodeQL: 20-90 min) are in the root group, not the leaf group. A reuse system that keys ops on 'the content hash of every artifact it read' gets ~99% hit rate on the leaves and 0% on the roots, forever. Second structural fact, and the one that makes this domain intellectually interesting: the TRUE input set of a per-finding triage op is not enumerable without doing the analysis. Whether `db.query(userInput)` is a real SQL injection depends on whether some sanitizer three call-hops away is still applied — a file the triage op never read and whose hash is therefore not in the key. So a sound key must either over-approximate (hash the whole reachable subgraph -> almost no hits) or under-approximate (hash the snippet -> stale WRONG answers, not just stale expensive ones). This is a correctness question, not a cost question, and the grader below is built to catch it.

layers.name: checkout
layers.consumes: nothing (root; input is a commit SHA)
layers.reads_artifacts: the git pack for one commit

layers.name: file_inventory
layers.consumes: checkout, 1 op
layers.reads_artifacts: path + content hash of all 8,000 source files, 6 lockfiles

layers.name: sast_shard
layers.consumes: file_inventory, 1 op each (each shard is assigned ~250 files)
layers.reads_artifacts: ~250 source files + the ~1,100 rule YAMLs; semgrep is per-file-parallel internally so this sharding is faithful to how the tool actually works. Secrets scanning (gitleaks/trufflehog) is folded into the same shard.

layers.name: codeql_analysis
layers.consumes: file_inventory, 1 op
layers.reads_artifacts: ALL 8,000 source files. This op is genuinely whole-program — interprocedural taint tracking cannot be sharded — and takes 20-90 min wall clock. Include it and do not pretend it shards; it is the honest 'no reuse surface' node in this graph.

layers.name: sca_resolve
layers.consumes: file_inventory, 1 op each (6 lockfile ops); 1 advisory-DB fetch op consumes nothing
layers.reads_artifacts: one lockfile each (package-lock.json, go.sum, poetry.lock, ...) resolving to ~1,900 transitive deps total; plus one op that fetches the OSV/NVD advisory snapshot

layers.name: finding_normalize
layers.consumes: all 32 sast_shard + codeql_analysis + 7 sca_resolve = 40 ops
layers.reads_artifacts: the triage-baseline/fingerprint state file from the previous run. Merges SARIF, computes partialFingerprints, diffs against baseline, dedupes. Cold output: ~500 SAST-class findings + 120 SCA findings + 15 secrets. Warm output (see reuse_threats): 5-50 NEW findings.

layers.name: context_assembly
layers.consumes: finding_normalize, 1 op each; 4 ops per SAST finding
layers.reads_artifacts: per finding: (a) read the enclosing function plus 10 lines either side — this is exactly Semgrep Assistant's real recipe, 'lines that are part of the finding plus 10 lines of context on each side'; (b) read each file in the taint trace, mean 2.1 hops; (c) grep for callers of the enclosing function; (d) git blame the line for author and age. 50-300ms each.

layers.name: sast_triage
layers.consumes: finding_normalize + its own 4 context_assembly ops = 5 ops
layers.reads_artifacts: indirectly: the finding's file, the taint-trace files, the rule definition, the org policy doc, the per-project 'memories' file. Input breakdown: system+rubric+org policy 3,500; rule block (rule source YAML + rule doc + 3 previously-adjudicated exemplars for this rule) 2,200; code context block (enclosing function + 10 lines each side + taint trace excerpts + caller snippets) 4,800; finding-specific suffix 600.

layers.name: triage_selfcheck
layers.consumes: its sast_triage op, 1 each; fires only on findings labelled false-positive (~55% of a cold corpus). Semgrep runs a distinct self-evaluation chain for exactly this reason.
layers.reads_artifacts: same context block as the parent triage op, plus the parent's verdict

layers.name: sca_reachability
layers.consumes: finding_normalize, 1 op each; 2 ops per SCA finding
layers.reads_artifacts: (a) grep the repo for the advisory's affected symbols; (b) walk the dependency graph for the transitive path to the vulnerable package

layers.name: sca_triage
layers.consumes: finding_normalize + its 2 sca_reachability ops = 3 ops
layers.reads_artifacts: one advisory record, the lockfile region, the grep results. Question answered: is the vulnerable symbol actually reachable from an entrypoint. Input: advisory text 900 + affected-symbol list 400 + grep results 3,000 + manifest context 600.

layers.name: fix_generate
layers.consumes: its triage op (+ selfcheck if present) = 2 ops; fires on findings labelled real (~225 SAST + ~42 SCA = 267 findings) at a 1.6x attempt rate after failed validation
layers.reads_artifacts: the WHOLE file, not a window — a fix needs imports, helpers, and the surrounding class, which is why this layer's token profile is 3x the triage layer's. Input: shared prefix 3,500 + full file 9,000 + rule/fix guidance 1,500 + prior verdict 500.

layers.name: fix_selfeval
layers.consumes: its fix_generate op, 1 each. Semgrep explicitly runs 'secondary prompts to review diffs for potential failure modes' — this layer is that.
layers.reads_artifacts: the generated patch + the original file region + the rule intent

layers.name: fix_validate
layers.consumes: its fix_generate op, 1 each; 3 ops per fix attempt
layers.reads_artifacts: (a) re-run the triggering rule against the patched file; (b) type-check / compile the affected module; (c) run the tests that cover the patched file. Failures feed the 1.6x retry factor on fix_generate.

layers.name: cluster_and_report
layers.consumes: 1 clustering op consuming all 500 triage verdicts; 12 PR-body ops consuming ~40 ops each
layers.reads_artifacts: the verdict set; the org's PR template

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 0.03% – 7% depending on cadence and repo age. Per-merge on a mature repo: 0.03–0.2%. Nightly on an active repo: 0.29–0.85% mean, p90 0.64–1.90%. Nightly on a young startup repo: 2.6% mean, 7.0% p90. Weekly: 1.7–4.4%. 30-day cumulative unique churn: 8.1–27.4% on mature repos, 58.7% on the young one. Plus one artifact — the advisory DB — that changes 100% of the time, every run.
change_rate.basis: MEASURED, not estimated. I cloned four large OSS repos (django, rails, kubernetes, next.js) plus one private startup repo and computed, over a 180-day window on first-parent mainline history, the number of distinct non-test source files touched per merge / per hour / per day / per week, as a fraction of the scannable file count at tip. Script at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-jamesyang-Documents-GitHub-Brevitas-Systems/30a08619-bfdd-4d15-a8c6-1c8b59d5d979/scratchpad/secscan_churn_measure.py. Raw results — files-per-mainline-merge (median/mean) and %-of-repo-per-day (mean): django 946 files, 1/1.9 per merge, 0.29%/day; rails 1,558 files, 1/2.2, 0.63%/day; kubernetes 11,450 files, 3/8.7, 0.49%/day; next.js 6,947 files, 3/7.6, 0.85%/day; private startup repo 271 files, 2/6.0, 2.60%/day. The 0.9% headline is the mean of the per-day means across those five. This is corroborated by published PR-size data — median lines changed per PR is ~20 across many GitHub repos; median change size is 24 lines at Google, 44 at AMD, 25 for Apache, 32 for Linux, 78 for Chrome — and by commit-characterization studies finding a median of 1 file per commit with a heavy right tail. TWO CAVEATS that make the effective rate worse than the raw number. First, changes are highly concentrated: I measured that 2.4–9.9% of files account for 50% of all file-touches. The same hot files change over and over. Second, and this is the one that bites, churn is the single best-established predictor of defect density (Nagappan & Ball 2005, Windows Server 2003, 89% accuracy discriminating fault-prone binaries) — so findings live disproportionately in exactly the files that keep changing. A sibling measurement on this machine found that files an agent actually chose to read churn 2.45x the repo-wide mean. Multiply the naive 0.9% by ~2.5x and the effective per-run invalidation rate on FINDINGS is ~2-3%, not 0.9%. Reuse on the triage layer is therefore ~97%, not ~99%.
change_rate.where_changes_land: Overwhelmingly at the LEAVES, and concentrated — but the graph has two roots that make that fact matter much less than it sounds. (1) LEAVES: per-finding context_assembly, sast_triage, fix_generate ops each read 1-3 files. ~97% of them are byte-identical run to run. This is where all the reuse is. (2) SOURCE-FILE ROOTS: codeql_analysis reads all 8,000 files, file_inventory reads all 8,000 hashes, finding_normalize consumes all 40 upstream scanner ops. Under a transitive-hash key these are invalidated by ANY of the 0.9% — that is, on essentially 100% of runs. The single most expensive operation in the graph by wall clock (CodeQL, 20-90 min) has a structurally guaranteed 0% hit rate, and it is not shardable, because interprocedural dataflow is what you are paying it for. (3) THE ADVISORY-DB ROOT is the sharpest edge: ~131 CVEs/day in 2025 and ~221/day in 2026 means the advisory snapshot's content hash changes every single run. It is 1 artifact out of 9,109 by count, but every SCA op descends from it. Key it naively on the whole-snapshot hash and you destroy 100% of SCA reuse daily; key it per-CVE-record and you invalidate only the ~0.5% of packages with a new advisory. That single encoding decision swings the SCA subtree's hit rate from 0% to 99.5%, and no amount of change-rate measurement tells you which one the implementation chose. (4) THE RULE-PACK ROOT: registry rulesets bump weekly-to-monthly, changing 1-3% of the ~1,100 rule files. A rule bump is a root change for every finding under that rule — small in artifact count, wide in blast radius, and it is the one change that legitimately requires re-triaging code nobody touched.

session_structure: A competent engineer gets a great deal out of provider prefix caching here, and this is a strong baseline, not a straw man. The workload is close to ideal for it: hundreds of calls, a huge shared preamble, a small varying suffix, all inside one short wall-clock window. Concretely, with Anthropic's 4-breakpoint limit: BREAKPOINT 1 (~3,500 tok) system prompt + triage rubric + org security policy + output schema + generic few-shot exemplars — frozen, byte-identical across every call and every run of every repo in the org. BREAKPOINT 2 (~2,200 tok) the rule block: rule source YAML, rule documentation, known-FP patterns for this rule, and 3 previously-adjudicated exemplars *for this rule*. The engineer sorts the 500 findings by ruleId so all findings under one rule go consecutively; with ~40 distinct rules firing that block is amortized ~12x. BREAKPOINT 3 (~4,800 tok) the file block: within a rule group, sub-sort by file, and put the full enclosing file in the prefix — multiple findings in one file share it. BREAKPOINT 4 the accumulated conversation for multi-finding-per-file calls. Then the ~600-token finding-specific suffix varies and is charged at full rate. Three further things a good engineer does. (i) WARM THEN FAN OUT: a cache entry is only readable once the first response *begins streaming*, so N concurrent identical-prefix calls all pay the 1.25x write. The engineer fires one call, awaits first token, then fans out 20-way. (ii) TTL: a 500-finding scan at ~2s/call with 20-way concurrency completes in under a minute, comfortably inside the default 5-minute TTL; the 1h TTL at 2x write cost is only worth it if the org runs several repos back to back within the hour, which for a nightly fleet scan it often does. (iii) FROZEN PREFIX HYGIENE: no scan timestamp, no run UUID, no commit SHA in the system prompt; deterministic JSON ordering of the rule metadata; tools list sorted and never mutated mid-run. NET RESULT OF THE TUNED BASELINE: of ~11,100 input tokens per triage call, ~10,500 are served at 0.1x and ~600 at 1.0x. Effective input cost per triage call falls to roughly 1,650 token-equivalents — an ~85% reduction — before the reuse layer does anything at all. THIS IS THE NUMBER THE REUSE LAYER MUST BEAT, and it beats it only on the axis provider caching cannot touch: cross-run. Provider caching turns a repeat run from 1.0x into 0.1x; a correct reuse key turns it into 0.0x plus the store lookup. That is a real 10x on the cached portion — but it is 10x on a portion that has already been discounted 90%, so the end-to-end saving on the triage layer is ~7-8% of the untuned cost, not ~90%. The fix_generate layer is where the reuse layer has a genuinely better story: its 9,000-token full-file block is per-file, not shared, so prefix caching amortizes it poorly (only across the 1.6 retry attempts), while a content-hash key on (file content, rule, verdict) reuses it perfectly across runs.
grader: Fully deterministic, zero LLM, exact and free ground truth, built from a seeded generator so every run has a manifest. CORPUS CONSTRUCTION: take a real OSS repo skeleton (django/next.js scale) and inject V=600 findings from a template bank of ~60 vulnerability templates across CWE-89/79/78/22/502/327. Each template ships four artifacts: (a) a VULNERABLE form, (b) a SAFE LOOKALIKE that the same SAST rule also fires on — the guaranteed, by-construction false positive, (c) a canonical FIX diff, (d) an EXPLOIT-WITNESS unit test that fails on the vulnerable form and passes on the fixed form. Ground truth per finding is a row in the generator's manifest: {finding_id, ruleId, file, line, is_real: bool, canonical_fix}. Nothing is inferred; nothing is judged. TIMELINE CONSTRUCTION: generate a sequence of R=30 commits by replaying a real repo's measured commit-size distribution (median 1-3 files, mean 2-9, p90 16, heavy tail to 128 — the distributions I measured above), so run N+1 differs from run N at a realistic rate. Also replay one rule-pack bump and one advisory-DB append during the timeline. FOUR PROGRAMMATIC METRICS, all computed by a script: (1) TRIAGE CORRECTNESS — per finding, compare emitted label to manifest.is_real; score = Matthews correlation coefficient over the run's findings. Exact, free. (2) FIX CORRECTNESS — a fix scores 1 iff all four booleans hold: the triggering rule no longer fires at that site (re-run semgrep), the exploit-witness test flips fail->pass (run pytest/jest), the repo's full pre-existing test suite still passes, and the patch touches only the declared file. Four subprocess exit codes. No LLM. (3) COST — from provider usage records, summed per run: uncached input tokens, cache-read tokens, cache-write tokens, output tokens, plus reuse-store hit count. Headline metric is dollars-per-correctly-adjudicated-finding, reported separately for run 1 (cold) and runs 2..30 (warm), because the whole question is the warm number. (4) STALENESS — the anti-cheat, and the reason this design exists. THE ADVERSARIAL MUTATION SET, which is what actually makes this a benchmark rather than a demo: the generator must include three mutation classes that flip a finding's ground truth WITHOUT changing the finding's own file. (a) SANITIZER-AT-DISTANCE: a sanitizer is added or removed in a callee 2-4 files away; the sink line and its whole enclosing file are byte-identical, but is_real flips. (b) ENTRYPOINT REWIRE: a route registration in a config file changes whether the vulnerable path is reachable at all; the SCA and taint answers flip with zero change to any source file the triage op read. (c) LOCKFILE-SILENT ADVISORY: a new CVE lands in the advisory DB against an unchanged pinned version; every SCA finding for that package flips from not-real to real with no repo change whatsoever. Grading: any finding whose ground truth flipped but whose emitted label matches the PREVIOUS run's label is scored as a CORRECTNESS FAILURE, not merely a cache miss, and is reported as a separate 'stale-wrong' count alongside MCC. This is the honest test of the whole premise. A reuse key that hashes only the artifacts the operation actually read will be confidently, silently wrong on every one of these — and they are not exotic; class (c) happens ~200 times a day in the real world. A key that over-approximates by hashing the whole reachable subgraph will be correct and will have a near-zero hit rate. The benchmark's real output is the Pareto frontier between stale-wrong count and warm-run cost, and I would expect no configuration to dominate.
reuse_story: The mechanism, if it works, is this. 5,100 of the 5,166 operations are per-finding leaves reading 1-3 files each. At a measured 0.9% daily file-change rate concentrated in hot files, ~97% of those leaves are byte-identical between two consecutive nightly runs. Under a content-addressed key they are served from the store at zero model cost — versus 0.1x under the tuned provider-cache baseline, and versus 1.0x untuned. Three places the reuse layer beats provider caching on its own terms rather than marginally: (1) THE fix_generate LAYER. Its 9,000-token full-file block is per-file and therefore amortizes badly across a prefix cache — it is shared only across the 1.6 retry attempts on the same finding. A key on (file content hash, ruleId, verdict) reuses it perfectly across runs. This is the single largest token layer in the graph (427 ops x 14,500 input) and the one where prefix caching is weakest. (2) CROSS-TENANT / CROSS-REPO SHARING. SARIF fingerprints are per-repo by construction; a reuse key is not. The same vulnerable log4j 2.14.1 gets triaged independently in 400 customer repos today. The same vendored file, the same framework-idiom FP under the same rule, the same advisory-to-reachability judgment — all of it is identical work being paid for N times. This is the one reuse surface the incumbents structurally cannot offer, because their dedup is scoped to a repo's finding identity. (3) THE TTL WALL. Provider prefix caches live 5 minutes to 1 hour. Nightly scans are 24 hours apart, weekly CodeQL passes 168 hours apart. Every scheduled run starts stone cold under the provider mechanism and warm under the reuse store. On a nightly cadence the provider cache contributes exactly nothing across runs — its entire benefit is intra-run, across the 500 concurrent triage calls.
reuse_threats: Five, in descending order of how much they worry me. (1) THE DOMAIN ALREADY SHIPS THIS, FREE AND EXACT. GitHub code scanning matches results across runs via SARIF partialFingerprints so an alert appears once; Semgrep persists triage state across scans and branches; and — decisively — Semgrep Assistant autotriage runs on NEW findings only, capped at 10 per diff scan. So in production the AI layer never sees the 97% of findings that are unchanged; the tool's own baseline diff already suppressed them. The cold graph I specified above is 1,602 model ops; the WARM production graph, with fingerprint dedup already doing its job, is 5-50 model ops. The reuse layer's honest claim is not 'we save 97%' — it is 'we save the residual after a free, exact, domain-native dedup already took 97%.' Any benchmark that measures the reuse layer against a no-baseline scanner is measuring a strawman, and I would not trust a result that does not implement fingerprint baselining in the control arm. (2) CORRECTNESS, NOT COST, IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT. The true input set of a triage op is not enumerable without doing the analysis (see the graph description and the grader's mutation classes). Fingerprints have the same flaw, but they are honest about it — they are explicitly a heuristic for 'same alert', and the tool re-runs the analyzer every time, so the *analysis* is always fresh even when the *triage state* is carried forward. A reuse key that skips the model call is asserting something stronger and can be silently wrong in a security tool, which is the worst domain in which to be silently wrong. (3) THE EXPENSIVE ROOT IS UNREUSABLE. CodeQL's 20-90 minute whole-program build reads all 8,000 files and is invalidated by any of them. It is the single largest cost in wall clock and often in compute dollars, and it has a structural 0% hit rate. The reuse layer only ever addresses the cheap-per-op, many-op half of the graph. (4) CHURN CONCENTRATES WHERE FINDINGS LIVE. Churn is the best-known defect predictor (Nagappan & Ball); I measured 2.4-9.9% of files carrying 50% of all touches, and agent-read files churning 2.45x repo-wide. Findings are not uniformly distributed over files — they cluster in the churny ones. The effective invalidation rate on findings is ~2.5x the raw file-change rate, so 0.9% file churn buys ~2-3% finding invalidation, not 0.9%. (5) THE PROVIDER BASELINE IS ALREADY VERY GOOD INTRA-RUN. With 4 breakpoints, rule-then-file sorting, and a warm-then-fan-out schedule, ~95% of the triage layer's input tokens are already charged at 0.1x. The reuse layer's incremental win on that layer is the last 10% of an already-90%-discounted quantity. Its real edge is fix_generate, cross-tenant sharing, and the TTL wall — and a benchmark that does not isolate those three will report a number that is mostly the strawman baseline.
confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH on the change rate; MEDIUM on the graph; HIGH on the threats. What is solid: the change-rate numbers are computed, not asserted — five real repos, 180 days, first-parent mainline, script retained; they agree with published PR-size and commit-size literature. The provider-cache baseline arithmetic is solid (4 breakpoints, 5m/1h TTL, 1.25x/2x write, 0.1x read, 512-4096 token minimum by model, cache readable only once the first response starts streaming). The threat that the domain already ships free exact dedup is documented, not inferred — Semgrep's own docs state autotriage applies to new findings only, capped at 10 per diff scan. What is softer: (a) the 500-findings-per-scan figure is an industry-blog number ('a mid-sized codebase producing 500 findings per scan') rather than something I measured; real volume varies 5x with ruleset tuning, and the false-positive rate spread in the literature is enormous (30-70% per NIST SATE, 71-88% per vendor sources, 91% in one Ghost Security study over ~3,000 repos). (b) The per-finding operation counts in the context_assembly and fix layers are reconstructed from Semgrep's published architecture — 'finding lines plus 10 lines of context each side', taint dataflow for taint-mode rules, named guidance/autofix/self-evaluation/dependency-filtering/diff-filtering chains — but Semgrep explicitly does not publish token budgets, model names, or retry thresholds, so my 11,100/14,500 input-token figures and 1.6x retry factor are engineering estimates fitted to that architecture, not disclosed numbers. (c) Whether real deployments run 1 or 3 model calls per finding varies by vendor. WHAT WOULD RAISE CONFIDENCE, in order of value: (1) one week of a real customer's scan telemetry — findings per run, new vs carried-forward, and the model-call count per finding — which would collapse (a) and (c) at once and would settle the single most important open number, the warm-run model-op count; (2) instrumenting an actual Semgrep Assistant or GHAS Copilot Autofix deployment to count tokens per finding; (3) running the adversarial mutation set from the grader against a real fingerprint-based baseline, to measure how often the INCUMBENT is already stale-wrong — if fingerprints are frequently stale-wrong on sanitizer-at-distance mutations, the reuse layer's correctness bar is lower than I have assumed and the whole story improves.

customer: A regional health plan / TPA (~1.2M covered lives, ~40,000 claims/day received on 837P+837I). Their core claims system (Facets / HealthEdge / QNXT) auto-adjudicates ~82% of volume; ~7,200/day pend. Most pends clear on deterministic rules. The subset that needs a human to read a policy and a medical record — coverage determination, medical-necessity, modifier/edit override, benefit-exclusion calls — is ~2,000/day and is what the LLM triage system runs on. They pay today for adjuster/nurse-reviewer labor: a manually touched claim costs a payer roughly $20 (some sources put fully-loaded payer cost at $40-50/submission), so 2,000/day of clinical review is a $10-40M/yr line item. They buy the AI system to cut minutes-per-touch and to raise effective auto-adjudication toward 90%, and they buy auditability because state AI-in-utilization-review laws and the CMS Interoperability & Prior Authorization rule (effective 2026-01-01) require an immutable record of which policy version and which record version produced each adverse determination.
why_repeated: Three genuinely distinct repeat modes, and they have opposite reuse properties — conflating them is the main way this domain gets mis-sold. (A) The nightly/hourly production batch: same graph, same policy corpus, but 2,000 brand-new claims. The claim artifacts are new by construction, so this repeats the *program*, not the *inputs*. (B) Retro reprocessing / policy-change replay: when a medical policy is revised, corrected, or a state DOI or a settlement mandates it, the plan re-adjudicates the affected historical claims. Same claims, same records, one policy differs. (C) Regression / drift evaluation: every prompt edit, model version bump, or policy compile change requires re-running a frozen gold set (2,000-20,000 historical claims with known dispositions) to prove decisions did not drift — this is now effectively mandatory under the state AI-review statutes and is run on every deploy. Modes B and C are byte-for-byte repeats of the inputs; mode A is not.
run_cadence: Mode A: continuous, batched hourly, with a nightly corpus-refresh cycle (the run specified below = one nightly cycle, 2,000 claims). Mode B: 1-4 times a month, triggered by the ~18.7 policy revisions/month, with a large spike every January 1 when the annual code update lands. Mode C: per deploy — realistically 2-8 times a month, plus a scheduled monthly full-suite run for the compliance file.

graph.description: Two graphs welded together, and their difference is the whole story. (1) A shared, slowly-changing CORPUS layer at the root: 468 medical/drug policies ingested, compiled into structured criteria trees, and embedded; 140 benefit-plan documents compiled into benefit grids; one code/edit table build (CPT, HCPCS, ICD-10-CM, NCCI PTP, NCCI MUE). ~1,545 ops, enormous fan-out — a single compiled policy feeds thousands of claim subgraphs. (2) 2,000 INDEPENDENT per-claim subgraphs hanging off it, each ~23 ops and ~8 deep, with zero edges between claims. It is embarrassingly parallel in the claim dimension: N=200 or N=20,000 has identical shape. Max depth 11 runs policy_ingest -> policy_compile -> policy_embed -> retrieve_policy -> load_policy_criteria -> policy_applicability -> criteria_evaluation -> disposition -> rationale_and_letter -> citation_verify -> write_back. Token realism, measured where possible: real UHC policies extract to a median ~18k tokens, p90 ~55k, with a genuine 210k-token monster (Omnibus Codes, 240 pages, revised in 4 of the 7 months I sampled). 837P claims serialize to 2k-6k tokens (median 3.2k); 837I institutional with 40-200 revenue lines runs 6k-25k. Attachments (OCR'd records) are present on ~35% of pended clinical claims: median ~14k tokens (~25 pages), p90 ~65k, inpatient itemized-bill outliers >200k. SPD/EOC documents are 55k-130k tokens (median ~78k). Compiled artifacts are small and stable by design: criteria object 1.5k-9k (median 2.5k), benefit grid ~1.8k. The honest summary: ~91% of operations and ~97% of model ops live in the per-claim half, whose reuse keys contain a claim content hash that is novel every run. The reuse surface is 3% of the ops.

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 94-97% run-over-run for the whole artifact set. Decomposed: claim-instance artifacts (8,126 of 8,263 — claims, attachments, eligibility snapshots, history bundles, auth records) change 96-100%; corpus artifacts (137 of 8,263 — policies, benefit docs, code tables, fee schedules, letter templates) change 0.10-0.20% on an ordinary day, ~10% on January 1. On a mode-B policy-change replay or a mode-C regression run the figure inverts completely: 0.1-0.3% of artifacts differ.
change_rate.basis: MIXED — the corpus half is sourced by direct measurement, the claim half is arithmetic, one component is estimated. SOURCED: I downloaded and parsed seven consecutive UnitedHealthcare Commercial Medical Policy Update Bulletins (Jan-Jul 2026 quick views) and counted status rows: 12, 22, 20, 18, 20, 22, 17 = mean 18.7 policy changes/month, against a published commercial medical + medical-benefit-drug library of roughly 450-500 policies. That is 4.2%/month = 0.13%/day. I also parsed the full January and April bulletins: April's quarterly CPT/HCPCS refresh touched only 9 policies (I had expected a library-wide blast radius and was wrong), while January's annual CDT/CPT/HCPCS update touched ~34 policies on top of the 12 semantic revisions — a genuine ~10% single-night spike. Underlying code churn is also sourced: CPT 2026 = 418 changes (288 new, 84 deleted, 46 revised) on ~11,100 codes = 3.8%/yr; ICD-10-CM FY2026 = 487 new + 38 revised + 28 deleted on ~74,000 = 0.7%/yr. ARITHMETIC, not estimated: a production claims batch processes claims that did not exist yesterday, so ~100% of claim artifacts are new — this is definitional, not empirical. ESTIMATED, and my weakest number: (a) the share of a day's pended claims that are re-entries of a claim already adjudicated (corrected claims with 837 frequency code 7, resubmissions after a records request, adjustments) — I could not find a clean published figure and put it at 8-12% of pended volume, of which maybe a third are byte-identical re-runs; (b) eligibility-snapshot churn, which I put at 35-45%/day because deductible/OOP accumulators tick whenever any claim for that member pays; (c) benefit-document renewal churn — I know 55-65% of commercial group renewals land January 1 from benefits practice, but found no published percentage. Cross-check on appeal-driven repeats: KFF found <1% of the ~85M denied in-network HealthCare.gov claims in 2024 were appealed by consumers, so member appeals are a negligible repeat source; provider-initiated reconsideration is much larger but I have no number for it.
change_rate.where_changes_land: At BOTH extremes simultaneously, and this bimodality is the single most important structural fact. (1) LEAVES, constantly: every claim, attachment, eligibility snapshot and history bundle is a fresh root feeding an 8-deep chain that has no ancestor in common with any other claim. ~91% of operations and ~97% of model operations sit downstream of an artifact that is new this run. Their reuse keys are novel by construction. No amount of key discipline recovers them. (2) ROOTS, rarely but with violent fan-out: a policy revision lands at policy_ingest, whose compiled output is consumed by load_policy_criteria for every claim routed to that policy. Fan-out is extremely uneven — pended clinical volume concentrates in maybe 25 policies (spine/pain, sleep studies, advanced imaging site-of-service, DME, genetic testing, infusion drugs, skin substitutes), so revising Omnibus Codes (revised in 4 of my 7 sampled months) or Bariatric Surgery invalidates a large slice of the run, while revising a tail policy invalidates ~3 claims. The mean of 0.13%/day badly understates the variance; the distribution is spiky and the spikes are correlated with the high-traffic policies, because high-traffic policies are exactly the ones that get revised most. (3) A trap in the middle: eligibility accumulators and 24-month history bundles are high-churn artifacts that sit UPSTREAM of the expensive model ops. If normalize_claim or disposition ingests a whole accumulator record for context, a field that ticks whenever any unrelated claim pays will invalidate the chain for no semantic reason. Whether the reuse layer hashes the fields it actually reads, or the record it was handed, decides whether the corpus-layer reuse survives at all.

session_structure: A competent engineer does five things here, and together they are a strong baseline. (1) SORT CONTENT BY STABILITY, VOLATILE LAST. Every prompt is assembled as [invariant system + task instructions] + [invariant reference block] + cache_control breakpoint + [volatile claim content]. (2) BATCH BY POLICY, NOT BY CLAIM. This is the key move and it is not obvious. Instead of walking claims in arrival order, group the night's 2,000 claims by retrieved policy id and process all claims for policy X consecutively. Because clinical-review volume concentrates in ~25 policies covering an estimated 60-70% of the queue, this produces long runs of byte-identical prefixes. (3) EXPLOIT THE PER-OP PREFIX RATIO HONESTLY — it varies enormously and only two ops actually pay. policy_applicability: prefix = 1,000 instructions + 2,500 criteria = 3,500 cached against 1,200 unique claim summary, i.e. 74% of input cached, ~67% input saving, and that same prefix serves 3 candidate policies x every claim in the policy group. criteria_evaluation, the token-dominant op: prefix = 2,000 instructions + 3,000 policy-specific few-shot criteria-walk exemplars + 2,500 criteria object = 7,500 of ~22,500 input tokens, i.e. 33% cached, ~30% input saving — the 13,800-token clinical narrative is unique and cannot be prefixed, so this op is structurally capped. disposition: 3,000 (decision policy + CARC/RARC code book + state rules) of 8,000 = 40% cached. normalize_claim: only a 1,500-token instruction block against a 9,600-token input = ~9% cached, and after the write premium it is roughly break-even; mark it anyway because it is reused thousands of times, but expect ~8% net. edit_adjudication and benefit_application: ~25-30%. (4) MANAGE TTL DELIBERATELY, TIERED. Policy-sorted batching keeps the top policy's prefix hit roughly once every 2.7 minutes (180 claims spread over 8 hours), inside a 5-minute TTL that refreshes on each hit. For the long tail — a policy with 3 claims all night — the 5m window always misses, so put the top ~40 policies' criteria prefixes on the 1-hour tier and accept cold writes on the tail rather than paying the 1h write premium 400 times. Do not warm speculatively on top of the 1h tier; measured internally, that is net-negative. (5) BYTE-STABILITY DISCIPLINE. One long-lived process per shift; canonical JSON serialization with sorted keys; no timestamps, request UUIDs, or wall-clock in any prefix; pinned model id; temperature 0; the code/edit tables and CARC/RARC book hoisted into the shared system prefix so they are written once per shift rather than per claim. Any byte drift in the prefix silently zeroes every hit and looks identical to a healthy run. Net effect of this tuned baseline: roughly 30-40% of total input tokens served at 10% rate, weighted across the model layer. Output tokens — ~19,976 model ops averaging ~800 output tokens — are charged in full and prefix caching cannot touch them. That is the bar, and note what it implies: on a mode-B or mode-C replay run, prefix caching still charges 10% of every input token and 100% of every output token, so the reuse layer's headroom on those runs is the entire remaining bill.
grader: FULLY PROGRAMMATIC, NO LLM IN THE LOOP, GROUND TRUTH COMPUTED FROM A SEED SO IT IS EXACT AND FREE. Generator (seeded, deterministic from an integer seed): (1) Emit P=468 synthetic policies. Each is generated from a criteria tree first: a boolean expression over typed predicates drawn from a fixed schema — age>=N, bmi>=X, failed_conservative_therapy_months>=N, dx in {code set}, cpt in {code set}, place_of_service in {...}, not tobacco_use_within_days<=N, prior_procedure_count<=N. The tree is then RENDERED into prose in the real house style ('...is proven and medically necessary when all of the following criteria are met:' with nested bullets), padded with a Clinical Evidence section and a References section sampled from a fixed pool so the token distribution matches what I measured on real policies (median 18k, p90 55k, one 210k-token Omnibus-style monster), and finished with an Applicable Codes table. (2) Emit G=140 benefit grids: covered categories, exclusion list, visit/dollar limits, cost-share tiers, accumulator state. (3) Emit an NCCI-style edit table: PTP pairs and MUE unit caps over the synthetic code set. (4) Emit F fee schedules mapping code -> allowed_amount_cents. (5) Emit N=2000 claims.
