For each: sample member/provider/plan, sample a target policy, sample a TRUTH ASSIGNMENT over that policy's predicates, then render a clinical record as narrative prose (H&P, progress notes, op note, labs, ~14k tokens median) that encodes exactly those predicate values, plus distractor facts that bear on no predicate. GROUND TRUTH IS COMPUTED, NEVER LABELLED: evaluate the criteria tree against the sampled assignment, then apply benefit grid, edit table and fee schedule in a fixed precedence (eligibility -> benefit exclusion -> code edit -> medical necessity -> cost-share). The generator writes, per claim, the exact expected tuple: (disposition in {PAY, DENY, PEND_RECORDS, ROUTE_MD}, denial_code from the CARC set, allowed_amount_cents as an integer, set_of_unmet_criterion_ids, set_of_cited_policy_ids, policy_version_hash). SCORING, all exact string/integer/set operations: (a) disposition exact match; (b) denial_code exact match when disposition==DENY; (c) allowed_amount_cents exact integer match — off by one cent is a fail, and this is the field that is actually money; (d) unmet_criterion_ids exact set equality (report Jaccard for diagnostics, but pass requires ==) — this is the real test of criteria walking and cannot be faked by guessing the disposition; (e) cited_policy_ids exact set equality AND every quoted span must be a verbatim substring of the cited policy's rendered text at the pinned version hash (plain substring check); (f) determinism: run the batch twice, require byte-identical tuples. Run-level score = fraction of the 2,000 claims whose full tuple matches exactly; run-level PASS = 2000/2000. THE REUSE-SPECIFIC PROTOCOL, which is the part that matters: Run 1 = cold run over seed S, record all tuples. Then a seeded mutation script advances the corpus one simulated day at the measured rate — flip 0.13% of policies by editing exactly ONE predicate in the criteria tree and re-rendering the prose; a --annual-update flag flips 10% at once to reproduce the January 1 spike; a --hot-policy flag forces the mutation onto a top-25-by-traffic policy to reproduce the high-fan-out case. Recompute ground truth from the mutated trees — free, because it is a tree evaluation. Run 2 = the SAME 2,000 claims against the mutated corpus. CORRECTNESS GATE: run 2's tuples must equal the recomputed ground truth exactly. Any operation served from the store whose true output should have changed surfaces immediately as a tuple mismatch, so under-invalidation — the failure mode that actually matters and the one a hit-rate metric hides — is caught deterministically. EFFICIENCY METRIC: total billed dollars for run 2 from provider receipts, against the tuned-prefix-cache baseline running the identical run 2; report store hit rate, and separately report the fraction of claims whose ground-truth tuple actually changed (expect ~0.1% for a tail-policy mutation and 5-15% for a hot-policy mutation — the generator must report those two cases separately or the headline number is meaningless). WHAT I DROPPED TO GET GRADEABILITY, stated plainly: fraud/SIU judgment, genuinely ambiguous clinical documentation, and provider-intent inference are not programmatically gradeable and are excluded. Those are also the parts payers keep humans on, so the excluded set is roughly the set the production system does not automate either.
reuse_story: Not in the nightly batch — there, essentially nothing. The story is entirely in modes B and C. (1) POLICY-CHANGE REPLAY. 18.7 policies are revised per month (measured). When one is, the plan must re-adjudicate the historical claims that touched it — sometimes voluntarily, sometimes because a DOI or a settlement mandates retro reprocessing. Artifacts are ~99.9% identical; exactly one policy differs. Transitive keying computes the affected claim set exactly rather than by a hand-written SQL guess, and recomputes only those subgraphs. Today this is done either as a full-price re-run of the whole cohort or, more often, not at all because it is too expensive — which is itself a compliance exposure. (2) REGRESSION / DRIFT SUITE. Every prompt edit, model bump, or compile change requires re-running a frozen gold set to prove no decision drift; the state AI-in-utilization-review statutes have made this near-mandatory. Same claims, same policies, one changed input. This is where the reuse layer wins outright and prefix caching cannot compete at all: prefix caching still bills 10% of every input token and 100% of every output token, and this workload emits ~19,976 model outputs averaging 800 tokens. A store hit bills zero. On a prompt change to a single layer, transitive keying recomputes that layer and its descendants and serves everything upstream free — roughly a 60-85% cut depending on which layer moved. (3) THE AUDIT RECORD IS THE PRODUCT. Payers are already required to keep an immutable record binding each disposition to the input snapshot, the retrieved policy context, the model id, and the reviewer. The reuse key IS that record — a content hash over exactly those inputs. For this buyer that provenance is plausibly worth more than the token saving, and it is the one thing here that a competent engineer's hand-rolled memo table does not give them, because that table is invalidated by a manually maintained policy_version column that drifts. (4) CROSS-TENANT CORPUS COMPILE. The same ~468 UHC policies (and the Aetna, Cigna, Anthem equivalents) are compiled by every payer, TPA, provider RCM vendor and UM vendor in the country, from identical public PDFs. policy_compile on public policy documents is the one operation with genuine cross-user reuse — 468 ops x ~19,500 input tokens, repeated across hundreds of tenants.
reuse_threats: Seven, roughly in order of how much they hurt. (1) THE DOMINANT ARTIFACT CLASS IS NEW EVERY RUN. 96% of artifacts differ run-over-run; ~97% of model ops have a claim content hash in their key and can never hit on the nightly batch. This is not a tuning problem, it is what a claims run is. Any pitch that quotes a reuse rate without separating mode A from modes B/C is measuring the wrong run. (2) THE REUSE SURFACE IS ALREADY MEMOIZED. Nobody recompiles a 210k-token policy PDF per claim; every real deployment stores the compiled criteria object in Postgres keyed by policy id + version. The corpus layer's dollars are already saved by ordinary application-level caching, so the reuse layer's marginal win there is correct invalidation, not tokens — a real benefit, but a much smaller and harder-to-price one. (3) HIGH-CHURN ARTIFACTS SITTING UPSTREAM OF EXPENSIVE OPS. Eligibility accumulators tick whenever any claim for that member pays (~35-45%/day churn); the 24-month history bundle changes daily by construction. If either is hashed as a whole record rather than as the fields actually read, they poison the keys of the very ops that would otherwise hit. Field-level key hygiene is load-bearing here and it is easy to get wrong silently. (4) NONDETERMINISM AND DELIBERATE KEY CHURN. Temperature>0 breaks the determinism gate. Worse, mode C exists precisely to re-run with a NEW model version or a NEW prompt — the customer is deliberately changing the key on the runs where reuse would otherwise be perfect. Reuse only pays on the unchanged fraction of those runs, which is why the transitive-composition property, not the flat hit rate, is the thing being sold. (5) REGULATORY PROHIBITION ON THE HIGHEST-VALUE PATH. Several states now require an adverse determination to be made by a licensed reviewer on the current record. Serving a DENY from a store — even on a technically valid key — is a hazard counsel will likely forbid, and the deny path is the token-heaviest path because it is the only one that runs rationale_and_letter. Expect the reuse layer to be switched off on ~28% of claims, and specifically the expensive 28%. (6) FAN-OUT VARIANCE, CORRELATED THE WRONG WAY. Policy revisions concentrate in high-traffic policies (Omnibus Codes was revised in 4 of the 7 months I sampled and is the single most-cited policy). So the rare root changes land disproportionately on the roots with the largest fan-out, and the mean change rate systematically overstates surviving reuse. The January 1 event invalidates ~10% of the corpus at once, on the day of peak volume. (7) THE BASELINE IS STRONG WHERE IT COUNTS. policy_applicability — 6,000 ops, the highest-count model layer — is already 74% prefix-cached under policy-sorted batching. Reuse must beat 10%-of-input on exactly the ops where the prefix is most favourable, and its clean win is on output tokens and on runs where the inputs genuinely repeat.
confidence: MEDIUM overall, with the components varying a lot. HIGH on the policy-corpus change rate: I parsed seven consecutive primary-source UHC bulletins and counted rows rather than asserting a number, and I corrected one wrong prior along the way (I expected the quarterly CPT/HCPCS refresh to touch the whole library; April touched 9 policies). HIGH on the two measured policy token sizes (56 pages/~48k tokens and 240 pages/~210k tokens, extracted directly). MEDIUM-HIGH on the operation sequence and graph shape — it matches published payer AI architectures, the CMS 2026 prior-auth rule shape, and the standard pend-reason taxonomy, but it is a composite of documented practice rather than one named customer's pipeline. MEDIUM on claim and attachment token sizes, which are estimated from 837 structure and typical record page counts, not measured. LOW-MEDIUM on the corrected-claim / resubmission share of pended volume (I searched and found no clean published figure) and on eligibility-accumulator churn. LOW on benefit-document renewal churn beyond the well-known January 1 concentration, and LOW on the retrieval concentration curve — my '~25 policies cover 60-70% of clinical reviews' claim is inference from pend-reason mix, and it is the single assumption the entire prefix-cache baseline rests on. WHAT WOULD RAISE IT, in priority order: (1) one real payer's pend-reason distribution plus the retrieval concentration curve — how many distinct policies actually cover 80% of clinical reviews — because that number alone sets the tuned baseline and therefore the bar; (2) an 837 payload size distribution from a clearinghouse; (3) frequency-code-7/8 corrected-claim share of volume, also from a clearinghouse; (4) whether any payer's counsel has actually approved cache-served adverse determinations, which decides whether threat (5) removes 28% of the value or none of it.

customer: A medical-device manufacturer's regulatory/clinical-evidence function, or (more often) the CRO that does it for them — Celegence, Cytel, Certara, RWS/Vitalink, Evidera. The paid deliverable is a periodic literature review that is a legal artifact: EU MDR Annex XIV Part B post-market surveillance / PMCF literature review, refreshed annually for class III and implantable devices, biennially below that. The same customer profile also buys HEOR systematic literature reviews for HTA dossiers (NICE/CADTH/IQWiG), which are refreshed per-submission and per-annum. Today they pay for DistillerSR or EPPI-Reviewer seats plus analyst hours; the analyst hours dominate. Published estimates put a full SLR at roughly $141k and on the order of 1,000+ person-hours end-to-end (Michelson & Reuter 2019; Borah et al. 2017 BMJ Open) — I could not re-verify these two figures in this session, treat them as recalled not sourced. Title/abstract screening is the single largest labour line inside that, and it is the part being handed to models. Crucially, this is a regulated deliverable: the protocol is under change control, screening is dual-independent with documented conflict resolution, and every decision needs an audit trail — which is why customers accept a slow, expensive, one-abstract-per-call pipeline rather than the cheap batched one.
why_repeated: Three independent reasons, and they have opposite consequences for reuse. (1) Statute. EU MDR requires the PMS literature search to be re-executed on a schedule for the life of the device — a device family on the market 10 years generates 10 near-identical runs. The search string is frozen in the PMS plan; changing it requires a documented justification, so the root is genuinely stable. (2) Corpus growth. New papers appear; the review must cover them. (3) Protocol iteration during the build. In the 6–12 weeks that a new review is being constructed, the criteria get amended after a pilot screen of 100–200 records, then again after full-text screening reveals ambiguity — typically 2–6 full re-runs, each triggered by a root change. So the run population is bimodal: a minority of re-runs are root-changed (reuse ≈ 0) and a majority are scheduled frozen-root refreshes (reuse ≈ 95%). Over the multi-year life of a PMS programme the scheduled refreshes dominate by count; during the first quarter of a review's life the root-changed ones dominate.
run_cadence: Bimodal. Build phase: 2–6 full re-runs over 6–12 weeks, mostly root-triggered. Steady state: annual (class III/implantable PMS, HTA dossier refresh) or biennial (lower-risk devices). The living-review and pharmacovigilance variants of the same pipeline run monthly or weekly respectively — the Cochrane-style living review case study I checked ran 30 search updates over ~2 years with monthly searches and weekly automated feeds of 100–200 new records. So the cadence range across the domain is weekly to biennial, with annual as the modal regulated case. Note the tension this creates: the longer the gap, the larger the reuse prize and the higher the probability the pinned model was deprecated in between.

graph.description:
Structurally this is the single most reuse-friendly workload I can imagine, and it has exactly two chokepoints that can destroy that. 94% of all operations (8,200 of 9,774) live in one enormous wide-independent layer: dual-independent title/abstract screening of ~4,100 deduplicated bibliographic records. Each of those ops reads exactly one record artifact plus a shared frozen criteria block, and consumes exactly one upstream op. Record 3,001 arriving new does not perturb record 12's key. That is the textbook case for content-addressed reuse.

The two chokepoints: (a) DEDUPLICATION. As actually implemented in every tool I know of, dedup is one operation that ingests all search pages and emits one deduplicated library. Under the stated keying rule — a downstream op's key includes its upstream's OUTPUT hash — a single new record changes the dedup output hash and therefore invalidates all 8,200 screening ops and everything below them. Reuse goes from 95% to 0% on that one modelling choice. The store must support per-output keying: dedup must emit 4,100 individually-hashed record artifacts and each screening op must key on its own record only. An engineer building from this spec must implement it that way or the benchmark measures nothing. (b) PRISMA COUNTING and narrative synthesis fan in over the entire graph and will always recompute — that is fine, they are 3 ops.

Below the wide layer the graph narrows hard and becomes a shallow tree: ~6% of records pass to full text (246 fetches, 211 successfully retrieved — paywalls and non-English kill the rest), dual full-text screening, then ~63 included studies each getting one structured extraction and one risk-of-bias appraisal, then a fan-in to evidence tables and synthesis. Depth 11 root-to-leaf but the deep path carries <1% of the ops and <15% of the tokens.

Token mass is bimodal too: the T/A layer is 8,200 ops × ~5.4k input each ≈ 44M input tokens (before any caching), the full-text layer is ~520 ops × ~14k ≈ 7M. Total run cost at Sonnet-class pricing with provider prefix caching working properly is roughly $55–70. That is the honest dollar prize per run and it is small — see reuse_threats.

layers.name: search_page_fetch
layers.consumes: nothing — these are graph roots. One frozen Boolean query string per database (PubMed E-utilities esearch+efetch, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, ClinicalTrials.gov), paginated at 200 records/page; ~6,200 raw hits across 4 sources
layers.reads_artifacts: the frozen query string artifact for its database, plus the live database index (the one genuinely non-hermetic input in the whole graph — the same query re-executed returns a superset)

layers.name: dedup_and_canonicalize
layers.consumes: all 38 search_page_fetch ops. Deterministic: DOI match, then PMID match, then fuzzy title+first-author+year. ~34% duplicate rate across 4 databases, 6,200 raw -> 4,100 unique
layers.reads_artifacts: the prior run's included/excluded library (for carry-forward matching) — this is what real tools do and it is why an incremental design is natural here

layers.name: record_project
layers.consumes: dedup_and_canonicalize, one record each. THIS IS THE SHARD THAT MAKES REUSE POSSIBLE — it emits one individually content-hashed artifact per record containing only the screening-relevant projection: title, abstract, publication type, language, year. It deliberately EXCLUDES MeSH headings, indexing status, citation counts and record revision dates, all of which churn without changing any screening-relevant fact
layers.reads_artifacts: none beyond its slice of the dedup output

layers.name: ta_screen_primary
layers.consumes: exactly one record_project op (fan-in 1)
layers.reads_artifacts: the PICOS criteria block (~2,200 tok), the 20 labelled few-shot exemplars from the pilot screen (~2,400 tok), the output schema (~400 tok) — a ~5,000-token block identical across all 4,100 ops

layers.name: ta_screen_secondary
layers.consumes: exactly one record_project op (fan-in 1). Independent second screener — a different model id and a differently-worded criteria rendering, because regulated review requires dual independent screening and an ensemble of two prompts to one model is not defensible as independent
layers.reads_artifacts: the same PICOS criteria, re-rendered (~4,800 tok stable block)

layers.name: ta_conflict_resolve
layers.consumes: two upstream screening ops plus the record (fan-in 2). Disagreement rate ~12% of records, which matches human dual-screening disagreement rates
layers.reads_artifacts: criteria block plus the conflict-adjudication instructions

layers.name: fulltext_fetch
layers.consumes: one resolved include decision. 6% T/A pass rate
layers.reads_artifacts: the publisher/Unpaywall/institutional-proxy PDF — a genuinely external, genuinely unstable artifact (paywall state, version-of-record replacing accepted manuscript)

layers.name: fulltext_parse
layers.consumes: one fulltext_fetch. 35 of 246 unobtainable (paywall, non-English, conference abstract only)
layers.reads_artifacts: PDF bytes

layers.name: ft_screen_dual
layers.consumes: one fulltext_parse (fan-in 1), run twice per paper by two independent screeners
layers.reads_artifacts: criteria block plus the full-text-stage exclusion hierarchy (reason codes required for the PRISMA flow diagram)

layers.name: ft_conflict_resolve
layers.consumes: two ft_screen_dual ops (fan-in 2). ~8% disagreement
layers.reads_artifacts: criteria, adjudication instructions, both full texts

layers.name: data_extraction
layers.consumes: one ft decision plus its parse (fan-in 2). 63 studies included
layers.reads_artifacts: the extraction template — ~40 fields: population, N, device, comparator, endpoints, adverse events, follow-up duration, funding

layers.name: risk_of_bias
layers.consumes: one fulltext_parse (fan-in 1)
layers.reads_artifacts: the RoB instrument — Cochrane RoB2 for RCTs, ROBINS-I or MINORS for observational, selected by study design

layers.name: evidence_table_assemble
layers.consumes: all 63 data_extraction ops (fan-in 63). Deterministic table build
layers.reads_artifacts: table format spec

layers.name: prisma_count
layers.consumes: the dedup op and every screening and conflict op — fan-in ~9,200. Produces the PRISMA 2020 flow diagram counts. This op always recomputes and always will; it is the one place where a full-graph dependency is genuinely required, and it costs nothing
layers.reads_artifacts: PRISMA 2020 template

layers.name: narrative_synthesis
layers.consumes: evidence_table_assemble plus all 63 risk_of_bias ops (fan-in 64). Two ops: clinical-benefit narrative and safety/adverse-event narrative
layers.reads_artifacts: the prior period's review text (for a change-since-last-period section), the device IFU claims list

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 0.5–20% for a scheduled frozen-protocol refresh, scaling with the gap: ~0.5% month-over-month, ~6% year-over-year, ~12% biennial. Effectively 100% of the 9,276 model ops for the ~1-in-3 re-run triggered by a criteria amendment or a model-id change.
change_rate.basis:
Partly sourced, mostly derived — I am calling it ESTIMATED overall and want that on the record.

Sourced anchors I actually pulled: (1) NLM's own citation-count-by-year page gives MEDLINE at ~28.2M citations total with ~0.98M–1.06M added per publication year 2019–2022 — a ~3.5%/yr corpus growth rate. (2) The living-SR practical guide (PMC10474670) gives per-update record counts for a real Cochrane-style living review: 89 records (Mar 2020), 230 (Apr 2020), 688 (Jun 2020), 4,213 (Feb 2021), 3,018 (Jul 2021), and a steady-state automated feed of '100–200 new records per week' against a review that ultimately included 146 studies. The second is a pandemic topic and therefore a high-churn outlier; I use it as an upper bound, not a central estimate.

What I could NOT find and did not fabricate: a published measurement of the fraction of a FROZEN Boolean query's hit set that is new when the identical query is re-executed 12 months later. That is the number this benchmark actually needs. My 6% comes from MEDLINE's 3.5%/yr baseline adjusted upward because topic-specific device/clinical queries index an actively-growing literature and because indexing backfill retroactively adds records with older publication dates to the hit set. I would put a factor-of-two error bar on it.

One measurement subtlety that matters more than the headline number: PubMed records are MUTABLE. Ahead-of-print records acquire MeSH headings 2–6 months later, indexing status flips from 'Publisher' to 'Indexed for MEDLINE', abstracts get corrected, records get retracted or amended. If the reuse key hashes the WHOLE record, I estimate 15–20% of a hit set shows a byte difference year-over-year even though the title and abstract — the only fields a T/A screener reads — are identical. That is a 3x inflation of the change rate created entirely by hashing the wrong projection. This is why the graph spec has a dedicated record_project layer that hashes title+abstract+pubtype+language+year and nothing else. Any implementation that skips it will report ~80% reuse where the true ceiling is ~94%, and will look like the reuse layer underperforms when in fact the harness is broken.

The HTA/PMS variant has a second, non-corpus change source: the search string itself. Regulatory feedback (an NICE evidence-review-group critique, a notified-body deficiency letter) forces a query amendment maybe once every 3 years. That is a root change of the worst kind — it changes which records exist at all.
change_rate.where_changes_land:
Overwhelmingly at the LEAVES, which is the best possible answer for this system. New records are new leaves in the wide screening layer; each one adds exactly one primary screen, one secondary screen, an expected 0.12 conflict resolutions, and an expected 0.06 full-text branches. Nothing about an existing record's screening decision is perturbed. Downstream closure from one new leaf is ~2.5 model ops. So a 6% leaf change rate implies a ~6% recompute rate and ~94% reuse — IF the dedup chokepoint is sharded per-record as specified.

But the changes that matter most land at the ROOT, and they are all-or-nothing. Three root artifacts sit in the key of every one of the 8,200 screening ops: the criteria block, the few-shot exemplar set, and the model id. Any edit to any of them — a single word added to an exclusion criterion, one exemplar swapped after a pilot disagreement, a model version bump — invalidates the entire wide layer. There is no partial invalidation and no graceful degradation. In real SLR practice criteria are amended 2–6 times during the build phase, and each amendment is precisely the event that causes someone to hit re-run. So the runs most likely to happen are disproportionately the runs where reuse is worth zero.

The full-text sub-tree has its own leaf churn that is easy to miss: publisher PDFs are replaced (accepted manuscript -> version of record), which changes the parse hash and invalidates that paper's screening, extraction and RoB ops. Small in absolute terms (~5–10 of 211 papers/year) but it is real and it is not corpus growth.

session_structure:
A competent engineer gets a great deal out of provider prefix caching here, and the reuse layer must be measured against this, not against a naive baseline.

THE WIDE LAYER. The screening prompt decomposes cleanly into a large invariant head and a tiny variable tail. The engineer puts, in this order: system prompt, the PICOS criteria block, the 20 labelled few-shot exemplars from the pilot screen, and the JSON output schema — ~5,000 tokens — behind a cache_control breakpoint. The variable suffix is one record's title+abstract, ~400 tokens, plus a one-line instruction. Cache hit rate approaches 100% for all 4,100 primary screens. Effective input cost per call falls from 5,400 tokens to 5,000×0.1 + 400 = 900, i.e. the provider's free mechanism already removes ~83% of input cost. Output is ~120 tokens and is never cached, so the true per-call floor is 900 input + 120 output, and output is ~40% of the marginal cost at Sonnet ratios. That is the number to beat.

CONCURRENCY DISCIPLINE. Fan out 4,100 calls at once and every in-flight caller misses the cache and pays the 1.25x write premium — with 30-way concurrency that is ~30 wasted writes at ~6,250 billed tokens each. The tuned baseline issues one warm-up call sequentially, confirms cache_creation_input_tokens > 0, then fans out. Cheap, free, and it is what a careful engineer does.

TTL. The whole 8,200-op layer completes in single-digit minutes at 30–50-way concurrency, so the 5-minute tier suffices and the 1-hour tier is not needed. Every call refreshes the TTL, so there is no expiry risk mid-layer. This is the part that must be said plainly: within a run, provider caching is near-perfect and free. Across runs separated by a year, it is worth exactly zero — the TTL is an hour at the outside. The two mechanisms are orthogonal and they do not compete.

TWO PREFIXES, NOT ONE. The secondary screener uses a different model, so it gets its own cached prefix; the engineer does not try to share. Conflict resolution gets a third, smaller prefix (492 calls, still worth caching). Full-text screening gets a fourth — but here the invariant head (~1,500 tokens of criteria) is small relative to a ~13,000-token paper, so caching buys almost nothing on that layer; the engineer caches anyway because it is free, and does NOT bother restructuring for it.

WHAT THE ENGINEER DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO. Batching 20 abstracts per call would cut call count 20x and amortize the prefix a further 20x, dropping effective per-abstract input from 900 tokens to ~650. The 2025 literature on batch size in T/A screening reports sensitivity degradation as batch size grows, and a regulated review cannot trade recall for cost — a missed relevant study is a finding at audit. So the tuned regulated baseline is batch size 1. An unregulated academic customer would batch at 10–20 and their token spend is ~30% lower, which shrinks the reuse prize proportionally.

CROSS-RUN. The strongest thing the engineer can do across runs is not a caching trick at all: it is a date-limited update search plus dedup against the prior EndNote/DistillerSR library, which is standard practice and free. See reuse_threats — this is the real competitor.
grader:
Fully deterministic, no LLM in the loop, ground truth free and exact. Built on the SYNERGY dataset (ASReview, 2023): 26 real systematic reviews, ~169k bibliographic records, each with title, abstract, OpenAlex/DOI identifier and a binary gold `label_included` derived from the published reviews' actual inclusion decisions; openly licensed. Fallback if SYNERGY is unavailable: CLEF eHealth TAR 2017–2019 technology-assisted-review topics, which ship PMID-level qrels at both abstract and content level.

HARNESS. Freeze one SYNERGY review's record set behind a local mock PubMed E-utilities server so the search and fetch layers are hermetic, reproducible and free. Split the record set by publication year at a cut point T chosen so ~6% of records fall after it. Run 1 screens records with year <= T. Run 2 screens the full set. Both runs use the identical criteria block, model id and sampling params, so run 2's only legitimate recompute is the new records plus their downstream closure. Additionally, for a controlled mutation arm, deterministically perturb a seeded 2% of pre-T records in a screening-IRRELEVANT field (append a MeSH term, bump the record revision date) and a seeded 0.5% in a screening-RELEVANT field (replace the abstract with a different record's abstract, which flips the correct label). The seed makes the changed-set exactly computable.

THREE EXACT METRICS, all computed by set arithmetic and integer comparison.

G1 CORRECTNESS (free ground truth, no LLM): recall and specificity of run 2's final include set against SYNERGY's gold `label_included`. PASS requires recall >= 0.95 on the gold includes — the sensitivity floor regulated screening actually operates at — and this is computed by comparing two ID sets, nothing more.

G2 STALENESS, the safety metric: compute the changed-set C = {records whose screening-relevant projection hash differs between run 1 and run 2} ∪ {new records}, then take its downstream closure D under the declared dependency edges. Read the run-2 execution log. PASS requires executed_ops ⊇ D — every op that should have recomputed did. This is a subset test on integers. A reuse layer that serves a stale decision for a record whose abstract was swapped fails here deterministically and without any model being consulted. The 0.5% relevant-field mutation arm exists specifically to make this metric bite: those records' gold labels change, so a stale serve also shows up as a G1 recall drop, giving two independent detections of the same bug.

G3 EFFICIENCY, the thing being benchmarked: executed_ops on run 2 divided by |D|, the oracle-minimal count. 1.0 is perfect. Report alongside billed input tokens, billed output tokens, and cache_creation vs cache_read token counts from the provider response, so the reuse layer's saving is measured net of what provider prefix caching already delivered rather than on top of an uncached strawman. Also report the same three numbers for the tuned baseline (full re-execution with prefix caching and sequential warm-up) so the comparison is apples-to-apples.

ROOT-CHANGE ARM (mandatory, or the benchmark flatters the system): re-run the whole thing with one word changed in an exclusion criterion. |D| = every model op. Any implementation scoring above ~0.05 reuse on this arm is serving stale results and fails G2. Weight the reported headline by the real run mix — I would use 1 root-changed run per 2 scheduled runs for a review in its first year, 1 per 6 thereafter.
reuse_story:
The mechanism is clean and the topology is close to ideal. 94% of operations are mutually independent leaves, each reading exactly one small artifact and one shared invariant block. Year-over-year, ~6% of those artifacts are new and the rest are byte-identical under a correctly chosen projection. Downstream closure of one new record is ~2.5 ops. So a frozen-protocol annual refresh should execute ~600 of 9,276 model ops and serve the rest, for ~94% reuse — and that reuse is on the axis the provider cache structurally cannot touch, because the runs are twelve months apart and the TTL is an hour.

The compounding argument is stronger than the single-review argument. A CRO runs this pipeline over hundreds of device families whose search sets overlap heavily (same device class, same clinical indication, same journals). A record already screened for device family A under criteria C is not reusable for family B under criteria C', because the criteria are in the key — but the full-text FETCH and PARSE ops are, and so is any criteria-independent enrichment (study design classification, population extraction, RoB appraisal). Those are the expensive per-token ops: full-text parse and RoB are ~13k input tokens each versus 5.4k for a screening call. Cross-customer reuse of the parse/enrich layer over a shared corpus is the only version of this story with real scale in it.

The second real benefit is not money at all: determinism and auditability. A regulated review must be able to demonstrate that the same record under the same criteria received the same decision this period as last. A content-addressed store gives that property by construction, where re-executing a temperature>0 model does not. That is a compliance feature the customer will pay for independent of tokens saved, and it is the strongest commercial angle here.
reuse_threats:
Five, roughly in descending order of how much they worry me.

1. THE DOMAIN ALREADY SOLVED THIS, FOR FREE. Standard practice for an update search is a date-limited re-run (`AND 2025:2026[dp]`, or an EDAT window) deduplicated against the prior review library. That is manual incremental computation and it captures nearly the whole prize at zero cost and zero new vendor. This is the same shape as the finding already in this repo's memory about warming losing to the 1h tier: the free incumbent mechanism is most of the win. The counter-argument is real but narrow — date-limited searches are known to miss records because of indexing lag and EDAT/DP divergence, and rigorous guidance for regulated updates is to re-run the full undated search and dedup against the prior library. That is precisely the workflow the reuse layer accelerates. So the addressable slice is the subset of customers who run undated full searches for validity reasons, which is the regulated subset, which is smaller than the whole market.

2. THE DOLLAR PRIZE PER RUN IS SMALL. With provider prefix caching tuned as specified, a full run costs roughly $55–70 in tokens. Saving 94% of that is ~$60. A CRO with 300 device families running annually saves ~$18k/yr in tokens. That is not a business on its own. The value has to come from the analyst hours the pipeline displaces (thousands of dollars per review) or from the compliance/determinism property — and neither of those is a token-reuse story. I would not build a pricing model on the token line here.

3. ROOT CHANGES ARE FREQUENT AND TOTAL. Criteria amendment invalidates all 8,200 screening ops with no partial credit. Amendments happen 2–6 times during a review's build phase, and an amendment is exactly what causes a re-run. So the runs are adversarially selected against reuse in the phase where compute is heaviest.

4. MODEL PINNING VS CADENCE, a direct structural contradiction. The model id is in the key. Annual cadence means a 12-month gap; provider deprecation cycles run 12–18 months. The runs with the largest reuse prize are the runs most likely to straddle a model change that zeroes it. Regulatory validation practice pins the model, which helps, but pinning to a deprecated endpoint is not an option — you get forced onto a new id and revalidate anyway.

5. THE HASHING-PROJECTION TRAP, which will silently break naive implementations. Hash the whole PubMed record and 15–20% of an unchanged hit set looks changed because of MeSH backfill and indexing-status flips, cutting measured reuse from ~94% to ~80% for no real reason. Related and worse: implement dedup as one op emitting one library and reuse drops to 0%, because one new record changes the dedup output hash and every screening op keys on it. Both failures look like the reuse layer underperforming rather than like harness bugs.

6. (minor) Auditor acceptance. A notified body may or may not accept a carried-forward screening decision as an independent screen for the current period. Humans do exactly this carry-forward, so it is defensible, but it is not tested and a single adverse finding would force full re-execution regardless of cost.
confidence:
Medium overall, and unevenly distributed.

HIGH confidence in the dependency graph shape: the wide-independent screening layer, the ~6% T/A pass rate, dual screening with ~10–15% conflicts, the narrowing to ~50–80 included studies. These match published PRISMA flow diagrams across hundreds of reviews and I would defend the order of magnitude on any of them. High confidence too in the two structural findings — the dedup fan-in chokepoint and the record-projection hashing trap — because those follow from the stated keying rule, not from empirical claims.

MEDIUM confidence in the token sizes. Abstract ~350–450 tokens and criteria block ~5,000 tokens I am comfortable with; full-text at ~13k input tokens is right for a clinical trial report but has a long tail (registry studies and pooled analyses with large tables run 25k+).

LOW confidence in the headline change rate. The 6% is derived from MEDLINE's ~3.5%/yr corpus growth, not measured. I searched for a direct measurement of frozen-query hit-set turnover at 12 months and did not find one; my web-search budget ran out before I could try the CLEF/Cochrane update-search literature, which is where I would look next. Factor-of-two error bar.

LOW confidence in the run mix between root-changed and frozen-root re-runs, which is the single most decision-relevant number in this whole spec and is pure judgement.

WHAT WOULD RAISE IT: (a) measure the change rate directly — re-execute five real published SLR search strings against PubMed today, diff against the PMIDs in each review's PRISMA diagram, and compute both whole-record and projected-field turnover per elapsed year. That is a half-day of work with E-utilities and it converts the weakest number here into a sourced one. (b) Get one CRO to tell you how many times they amended criteria on their last ten reviews. (c) Instrument one real DistillerSR-based pipeline for a single annual refresh and count how many records were carried forward versus re-screened — the tools already log this, so the ground truth exists inside a customer today.

customer: A Series-B developer-tools company (~60 engineers) that sells an SDK + HTTP API and whose docs site is a lead-gen and support-deflection asset. Today they pay for: (a) a CI job on every PR that flags docs invalidated by the diff, and (b) a nightly full sweep over the whole docs corpus that opens "doc drift" issues and drafts patches. Before this was automated they paid two technical writers to do it by hand and still shipped stale docs. What they are actually buying is precision-gated auditability: a per-claim ledger of "this sentence is still true / no longer true, and here is the code that proves it," because a false flag costs an engineer 20 minutes and destroys trust in the bot faster than a miss does. Scale used throughout: 4,200 tracked source files (~1.1M LOC), of which ~600 are "public surface" (SDK exports, API handlers, CLI commands, config/env schemas, error enums); 380 doc pages averaging ~1,900 tokens, split into ~1,200 doc sections; ~40 PRs merged per weekday.
why_repeated: Doc staleness is a monotonically accruing liability, not a one-time cleanup. Every code-only commit adds drift and the corpus never self-heals. I measured the accrual rate directly in this repo: of 299 non-merge commits, 178 (60%) touch source code and no markdown at all, while only 57 (19%) touch both. So roughly three out of five commits are pure drift-generating events. The sweep must re-run because the question it answers ("is every documented claim still true of HEAD?") has a different answer after every merge. It is also re-run because it is a gate, not a report: the per-PR variant blocks merge on newly-introduced staleness, so it runs once per PR by construction, ~40x/day. The arXiv study of 3,000+ GitHub projects found most projects contain at least one outdated code-element reference at some point in their history, which is the industry-wide version of the same accrual.
run_cadence: Two cadences against one graph. (1) Per-PR incremental: ~40x per weekday, triggered on push, gating merge, must finish in under 4 minutes. (2) Nightly full sweep on main: 1x/day, ~15 minutes wall-clock at 40-way concurrency, opens issues and drafts patches. The nightly sweep is the one that establishes the store; the 40 daily PR runs are the ones that harvest it, since each PR branch shares ~99.8% of its input artifacts with the main commit the nightly just processed. A weekly "deep" variant re-runs with a stricter prompt for release notes.

graph.description: A wide, shallow, fan-out-then-fan-in DAG, emphatically not a chain. Two independent fan-out wings (source files -> surface extraction; doc pages -> claim extraction) converge in a single wide adjudication layer, which then funnels through a narrow patch/rollup/report tail. 57% of operations (4,580 of 7,984) are deterministic tool ops costing microseconds and no money; the entire economic question lives in the 3,024 model ops, and really in the 1,200 adjudicate ops which carry 47% of all input tokens. Depth is only 6 and the tail is 24 ops wide, so there is almost no serial critical path -- this workload is embarrassingly parallel and latency is set by concurrency limits, not by the DAG. The linking structure is the important part: adjudicate ops fan in from a mean of 3.1 surface_extract ops, and inverting that edge set gives a mean of 6.2 doc sections per surface file with a heavy tail (measured in this repo: mean 9.7 docs per documented source file, p50=3, max=84 for api/serve.py). That tail is the amplifier that decides whether reuse pays. Cold-run totals: ~11.3M input tokens, ~2.0M output tokens.

layers.name: symbol_index
layers.consumes: nothing (leaf). One op per tracked source file.
layers.reads_artifacts: exactly one source file. Tree-sitter parse emitting a symbol table: exported names, signatures, param defaults, decorators, docstring spans, file-relative line numbers.

layers.name: doc_parse
layers.consumes: nothing (leaf). One op per doc page.
layers.reads_artifacts: exactly one .md/.mdx page. Splits into sections at H2/H3, extracts code fences with language tags, and regex/AST-extracts candidate code-element references (backticked identifiers, import paths, CLI flags, HTTP routes, env var names).

layers.name: ref_resolve
layers.consumes: its own doc_parse op (1) plus the symbol_index ops of every source file its references resolve into (mean 9, heavy-tailed). Fan-in ~10.
layers.reads_artifacts: none directly; pure join over upstream outputs. Emits resolved/unresolved reference lists. Unresolved = the deterministic staleness signal (the arXiv 2212.01479 'deleted code element' class) and it is caught here for free, with no model.

layers.name: surface_extract
layers.consumes: the symbol_index op for its own file (1). Only runs for the ~600 public-surface files, selected by path globs plus export analysis.
layers.reads_artifacts: its one source file, in full (median 280 LOC ~= 3,400 tokens). Emits structured JSON: every public symbol with signature, param defaults AND their units, raised errors, deprecation markers, side effects, and behavioral contracts the AST cannot see. This is the layer that catches 'the default changed from 30s to 30000ms', which no static index can.

layers.name: claim_extract
layers.consumes: the doc_parse op of its page (1). One op per doc section.
layers.reads_artifacts: one doc section (~1,100 tokens) plus its page-level heading context (~300). Emits 3-8 atomic, individually-checkable claims as JSON with stable claim_ids and exact line spans, e.g. {'claim_id':'auth-3','span':[41,43],'assertion':'POST /v1/keys returns 201 with a body containing key_id'}.

layers.name: adjudicate
layers.consumes: its section's claim_extract (1) + its page's ref_resolve (1) + the surface_extract of every source file its claims link to (mean 3.1). Fan-in 5.1. THE EXPENSIVE LAYER: 1,200 ops x 4,450 input tokens = 5.34M tokens, 47% of the run.
layers.reads_artifacts: the raw doc section again (~1,100) for verbatim-quoting of evidence. Emits per-claim verdict {fresh|stale} plus a citation to the exact surface field that proves it.

layers.name: patch_generate
layers.consumes: one adjudicate op (1). Runs only for sections with >=1 stale verdict. Count is STEADY-STATE nightly (14); on a cold first sweep of a never-audited corpus this is ~180 ops, a 13x difference that dominates first-run cost and must not be used to size steady state.
layers.reads_artifacts: the stale doc section plus the linked surface JSON. Emits a unified diff rewriting the section.

layers.name: page_rollup
layers.consumes: all patch_generate ops for that page (mean 1.6).
layers.reads_artifacts: none. Merges per-section patches into one coherent page-level diff, resolving overlapping edits and keeping voice consistent.

layers.name: run_report
layers.consumes: all page_rollup ops (9) plus aggregate counters from ref_resolve and adjudicate.
layers.reads_artifacts: none. Emits the human-facing drift summary and the GitHub issue bodies. Always recomputes -- its key embeds every downstream hash, so it is cold on every run by construction.

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 0.2% per-PR run (9 files of 4,580); 4-7% nightly; 18-30% after a weekend or a merge-heavy week. Cold/first run and any prompt edit = 100%.
change_rate.basis: MEASURED, in this repository, not asserted -- then cross-checked against published work. I ran git archaeology over 340 commits: files per non-merge commit p50=4, p75=9, p90=21 (mean 31.3, skewed by vendor drops); unique files touched per active day p25=10, p50=30, p75=59, p90=138, against 744 tracked source files -> 30/744 = 4.0% of source artifacts per day. Published corroboration for the per-commit half: characterization studies of ~1M commits across 24 Java projects find commit size heavy-tailed with most commits touching 1-10 files and most touching 1-4 source files -- my p50=4 sits exactly there. Scaling to the specified 4,200-file customer with 40 PRs/day at ~9 files/PR with overlap gives ~250 unique source files/day = 6%; doc pages change far less (I measured only 19% of commits touching both code and markdown), ~6 of 380 pages/night = 1.6%. Combined: (250+6)/4,580 = 5.6%. HONEST CAVEAT: the artifact rate is well-supported, but the number the economics actually turn on is the amplification from artifact churn to invalidated adjudicate ops, and that is a single-repo measurement (n=1) extrapolated. I could not find published data on doc-section-to-source-file link density.
change_rate.where_changes_land: Entirely at the leaves -- source files and doc pages are the DAG's inputs, and every change enters at depth 0. Nothing ever changes in the middle. That sounds ideal for reuse and it is not, because of a concentration effect I measured and initially got wrong. My first estimate assumed churn was uniform across files. It is not: files with the most documentation churn 2.1x the repo average (top-25 most-documented files: 8.1 commits/90d; random sample: 3.8; undocumented files: 2.4). Documentation and churn are positively correlated, because teams document what they are actively building. Combined with a heavy-tailed link graph (mean 9.7 doc references per documented file, p50=3, max=84), a 5.6% artifact change rate amplifies to roughly 12.5% of surface files changing (75 of 600) and ~35% of the expensive adjudicate layer invalidating (~420 of 1,200) -- an amplification factor of ~6x from artifact rate to expensive-op invalidation rate, not the ~2x I assumed before measuring. Concretely, this repo's api/store.py is referenced by 64 docs and is modified in the working tree right now; a one-line change to it re-runs 64 pages' worth of adjudication. The per-PR cadence is the opposite and is where reuse shines: 9 changed files -> ~1.3 surface files -> ~13 adjudicate ops, ~99.5% of the graph reusable from the prior nightly.

session_structure: Assume a competent engineer who has read the caching docs and is not leaving anything free on the table. Six things they do, all of which the reuse layer must beat: (1) Layer-stable prefixes. Each model layer has a frozen system prompt + JSON schema + 3 few-shot examples, marked with a cache breakpoint: surface_extract ~2,000 tokens of the 5,400, claim_extract ~800 of 2,200, adjudicate ~1,000 of 4,450. Across 600/1,200/1,200 calls the prefix is written once and read at 0.1x thereafter. (2) A shared repo-context block -- glossary, module map, naming conventions, ~3,000 tokens -- placed at the absolute front of EVERY call in every layer behind its own breakpoint, so all 3,024 calls in the run share one cached prefix. (3) Suffix-sorted call ordering, the big one for adjudicate. Sort the 1,200 adjudicate calls so that all sections referencing source file X run consecutively, and lay out each prompt as [repo block][system][surface JSON of linked files][doc section last]. Because mean doc-fan-in per surface file is 6.2, the ~1,900-token surface payload is then a cache hit on 5 of every 6 calls -- pushing cached prefix to ~65% of adjudicate input. (4) Batch 4 doc sections per adjudicate call, cutting 1,200 calls to 300 and amortizing the prefix 4x. (5) Schedule the whole sweep in one tight window at 40-way concurrency so it completes in ~15 min, comfortably inside the 1h tier and continuously refreshing the 5-min tier, so nothing ever expires mid-run. (6) Route claim_extract to a cheap small model since it is near-mechanical, reserving the frontier model for adjudicate. Net effect: roughly 55-65% of input tokens served at 0.1x, giving ~0.46x of naive cost. Critically this 0.46x is free, applies to the cold run too, and repeats identically every single night -- so the reuse layer's real hurdle is 0.46x naive, not 1.0x. Against that hurdle: reuse executes ~18% of model tokens at nightly cadence, and those still pay the tuned 0.46 rate, landing at ~0.098x naive = a genuine but unspectacular ~4.7x over the tuned baseline. At per-PR cadence the same arithmetic gives ~100x, which is where the actual money is.
grader: Fully deterministic, no LLM, ground truth exact and free because it is GENERATED rather than discovered -- the mutation script knows precisely what it broke. Setup: vendor a real repo snapshot at commit C into the benchmark, run the pipeline once, and FREEZE run-0's claim_extract output as part of the benchmark fixture. Every subsequent run therefore adjudicates the same enumerated claim_ids, which removes claim-extraction variance and reduces grading to pure binary classification. Then generate commit C' by applying K seeded AST-level mutations, each logged to a ground-truth ledger. Stale-inducing mutations: rename_symbol (update all code call sites but NOT docs -> every doc reference to the old name is stale; ground-truth set computed exactly by AST/grep over the doc corpus); change_default (param default 30 -> 60 where a doc literally contains that param and value; exact by regex); delete_function (the arXiv outdated-code-element class); add_required_param (every doc code fence calling that function is now stale; verified by parsing fences with the real language parser and checking arity); change_http_status (201 -> 200 in a handler; docs asserting 201 are stale). Distractor mutations, ground truth NOT stale: reformat_only (whitespace/comment reflow, zero semantic change -- this one specifically punishes whole-file hashing and any system that flags on diff presence); rename_internal_symbol (referenced by no doc); move_function (symbol survives at a new path -- docs citing it by name are fresh, docs citing it by import path are stale, and the ledger distinguishes them). Required output: JSON array of {doc_path, line_start, line_end, claim_id, verdict in {stale,fresh}}. Scoring, exact: F1 against the ledger's stale set, with a HARD GATE of precision >= 0.90 AND recall >= 0.90 (fail otherwise) -- precision is gated at least as hard as recall because a false flag is what actually kills these products in production. Plus a second deterministic gate, the reuse-safety check: for every claim whose ground truth is fresh AND whose complete transitive upstream artifact set is byte-identical to the previous run's, the emitted verdict AND evidence string must be byte-identical to the previous run's output; any divergence fails the run outright. That directly tests the property the reuse layer claims and costs nothing to check. Cost is reported alongside, never as part of the score, taken from the provider's own usage fields (uncached input / cache-read input / cache-write input / output) rather than estimated, with the tuned-baseline arm run on the identical seed. Sweeping K reproduces the whole cadence range -- K tuned to 0.2% for per-PR, 5.6% for nightly, 25% for weekly -- which is exactly how you find the change rate at which reuse stops paying.
reuse_story: Two mechanisms, very unequal, and the obvious one is the weaker one. The weak story is nightly-over-nightly: 5.6% of artifacts change, so 82% of model ops and ~79% of model tokens are reusable, giving ~4.7x over the tuned baseline. Real but not thrilling, and it degrades fast because churn concentrates on the most-documented files. The strong story is branch-over-main, and it is strong because of the workload's cadence structure rather than anything clever. Each of ~40 daily PR branches differs from the main commit the nightly already processed by ~9 files, i.e. 0.2% of artifacts. A PR run therefore executes ~1.3 surface_extract and ~13 adjudicate ops out of 3,024 -- roughly 0.3M input tokens against 11.3M cold, about 100x over the tuned baseline, and it converts a 4-minute CI gate into a ~10-second one, which is the difference between a check engineers tolerate and one they disable. Today those 40 runs each either pay full freight or, more commonly, are scoped down to "only look at the diff" precisely because full freight is unaffordable -- and that scoping is what makes them miss the drift class where an unchanged doc page references a changed symbol. Cross-run reuse is what makes the full-corpus check affordable per-PR, which is a capability change and not merely a discount. Secondary: the deterministic layers (57% of ops) also cache, which does not save money but does cut wall-clock, and wall-clock is what gates merge.
reuse_threats: Six, ordered by how much damage they do. (1) THE MEASURED AMPLIFIER, the biggest and the one I got wrong before measuring. Churn and documentation density are positively correlated -- 2.1x in this repo -- and doc fan-in is heavy-tailed (max 84 pages for one file). So 5.6% artifact churn amplifies ~6x into ~35% invalidation of the expensive adjudicate layer. If a customer's tail is fatter than this repo's, amplification goes higher and the nightly story collapses toward break-even. (2) WHOLE-FILE GRANULARITY OVER-INVALIDATES, and it is the largest recoverable loss. A one-line edit to a 3,400-token source file invalidates its entire surface_extract and then every downstream adjudicate, even when the edit touches nothing any doc mentions -- which, given that ~60% of commits are code-only refactors, is the common case. The fix is a two-level key: recompute the cheap surface_extract on file-hash miss, then key adjudicate on the surface JSON's hash, which is frequently byte-identical after an unrelated edit. With it, adjudicate reuse goes from ~65% to ~85%; without it, this workload is close to a wash at nightly cadence. Whether the system supports "recompute cheap, short-circuit expensive" decides the whole result. (3) PROMPT AND SCHEMA EDITS ARE ROOT CHANGES. The layer system prompts are input artifacts; editing one invalidates 100% of that layer. Teams iterating on a docs bot edit prompts far more often than nightly, so during active development every run is cold and the 82% figure describes a steady state that may not exist yet. (4) NON-DETERMINISM MAKES STORED OUTPUTS SAMPLES, NOT VALUES. Even at temperature 0 providers do not guarantee bitwise reproducibility. The DAG stays internally consistent because downstream keys hash the stored sample, but the run's answer now depends on when each op was first executed -- so two engineers can see different verdicts on the same commit. That is an audit problem, not a cost problem, and it is what gets these systems rejected in exactly the compliance-doc pipelines that would pay most. My grader's byte-identity gate exists to surface it rather than hide it. (5) ZERO CROSS-TENANT SHARING. Every key embeds a private source-file hash, so this is single-tenant reuse only; none of the cross-user pooling that makes other workloads attractive applies here. (6) 57% OF OPS ARE FREE ANYWAY. Caching 4,580 microsecond tool ops saves no billable dollars; the entire economic case rests on 1,200 adjudicate ops, so any accounting that quotes an op-level hit rate over all 7,984 ops is inflating by ~2.4x.
confidence: MEDIUM, and specifically: high on the graph shape and the artifact change rate, low on the amplification factor that the economics actually turn on. High confidence: the layered-DAG shape, depth 6, the fan-out/fan-in structure, and the fact that adjudicate carries ~47% of tokens -- these follow from how the task decomposes and would look the same at any customer. High confidence on the 4-7% nightly artifact churn: I measured it (p50=30 unique files/day of 744) and published commit-characterization studies corroborate the per-commit distribution (p50=4 files, heavy tail). Also high confidence the grader is sound, because generated mutations give exact free ground truth with no LLM anywhere. LOW confidence on the amplification factor (~6x, artifact churn -> adjudicate invalidation), which is a single-repo extrapolation and which I revised sharply upward the moment I measured rather than assumed it -- that is a warning sign that it could move again. It is also the number that decides whether nightly reuse is 4.7x or roughly break-even. Medium confidence on token sizes (engineering estimates, probably +/-40%) and on the 0.46x tuned baseline (depends on batch size and how well suffix-sorting holds up under real link skew). WHAT WOULD RAISE IT: instrument 3-5 real repos at the target scale and, for each, actually build the doc-section-to-source-file link graph and measure the JOINT distribution of (file churn, doc reference count) instead of assuming independence -- that single measurement resolves the dominant uncertainty. Second, run the two-level surface-hash keying against real commit sequences to find what fraction of surface_extract outputs are byte-identical after a code-only refactor; if that fraction is high (I would guess 50-70%, untested), threat (2) is recoverable and the nightly case is comfortably positive. Third, measure how often a real team edits the pipeline's own prompts, since that sets the ceiling on steady-state reuse.

customer: A platform/developer-productivity team at a company with a large monorepo (10k-100k source files, 50-500 engineers) running an internal "ask the codebase" + CI-triage agent. Two production surfaces, same engine: (1) a CI bot that, on every red build or flaky-test alert, opens a session and produces a localization ("this failed because commit X changed `src/foo/bar.ts:412`") plus a candidate patch; (2) an internal Q&A endpoint where engineers ask "where is auth enforced for route R", "what does config key K resolve to in staging", "who calls this deprecated function". They pay per seat for the product (Cursor/Sourcegraph/Glean/Devin-class tooling, $20-40/seat/mo) or, when self-built, they pay the raw provider bill — which for this workload is dominated by input tokens: measured 2.49B prompt tokens vs ~47M output tokens across 112 sessions of a long-context coding agent, i.e. input is ~98% of billed volume even before rate differences. What they are actually buying is time-to-localization on a codebase no single human holds in their head.
why_repeated:
Three distinct repeat mechanisms, only one of which is a true "same work twice":

(1) FIXED QUESTION BANK, MOVING REPO. The CI triage bot runs the same triage procedure against the same test suite every night and on every PR. When a test is flaky or a bug is not fixed for a week, literally the same question ("why does `test_billing_settlement` fail") is re-asked against a repo that has advanced by ~82 commits/day. This is the genuine repeat.

(2) SAME COMMIT, MANY ASKERS. On a busy day, dozens of engineers ask questions against the same pinned HEAD. Different questions, shared repo state — so the shared *artifacts* repeat, not the operation sequence.

(3) SAME QUESTION, DIFFERENT ASKERS. Onboarding and on-call: a long tail of canonical questions ("how does the request get from the gateway to the worker") gets asked by a new person every few weeks. Real, but low volume relative to (1) and (2).

The honest framing: this workload is not re-run because anyone wants the same answer twice. It is re-run because the trigger (a failing test, a new engineer, a PR) recurs while the codebase moves underneath it. That distinction is what makes the reuse story hard here.
run_cadence:
Two cadences worth benchmarking, and they behave completely differently:
- PER-COMMIT / PER-PR: at vscode scale I measured 574 commits in a 7-day window = ~82/day, so a per-PR triage bot fires tens to low-hundreds of times per day. Gap between consecutive runs of the *same* question: minutes to hours. This is inside the provider's 1h cache TTL.
- NIGHTLY BATCH: the full question bank (I benchmark Q=200) replayed once per night against that night's HEAD. Gap: 24h. This is *outside* every provider cache TTL, and it is the cadence where a persistent reuse layer has an opening the provider cache structurally cannot serve.
I specify the benchmark at the nightly cadence and recommend running the per-PR cadence as a second arm, because the two give opposite answers and quoting only one is how this domain gets mis-sold.

layers.name: repo_pack
layers.consumes: nothing — this is the run root, executed once per commit and shared by all 200 questions
layers.reads_artifacts: `git ls-files` over all 17,926 tracked paths, the 12 top-level READMEs/OWNERS/build configs, and a generated symbol index (tree-sitter or ctags) over ~2.5M LOC. Its content hash is a function of the ENTIRE repo tree, which is the single most important fact about this layer.

layers.name: question_intake
layers.consumes: repo_pack (1 per op) + the question text. One op per question in the bank.
layers.reads_artifacts: none directly; consumes repo_pack's output

layers.name: scoped_search
layers.consumes: the single model op (question_intake or reason) that issued it; 1 per op. Issued in waves of 1.4 tools per acting model call (measured mean 1.4, max 2-3, 40% of acting turns issue more than one).
layers.reads_artifacts: one file or one directory subtree each. MEASURED over 5,314 real bash tool calls: 95.5% of searches name an explicit path or filename, 3.4% are genuinely repo-wide, 1.1% are type/glob-scoped. Search is the dominant tool: median 12 search calls vs 1-4 file Reads per session. Implemented as grep/rg/git-log/find, NOT as a dedicated search tool.

layers.name: file_read
layers.consumes: the model op that issued it; 1 per op
layers.reads_artifacts: exactly one file, usually a line range of it. Median 4 distinct files read per question at this repo scale (measured median 1-6 on a 1,117-file repo; scaled to 4-16 for an 18k-file monorepo).

layers.name: reason
layers.consumes: EVERY prior operation in its own question's chain — the full growing transcript. Mean 20 upstream ops. 20 per question, serial. This cumulative fan-in is the defining property of the graph.
layers.reads_artifacts: none directly; all artifact content arrives via upstream tool outputs already in the transcript

layers.name: verify_exec
layers.consumes: the reason op that issued it; 1 per op. 2 per question.
layers.reads_artifacts: the working tree plus the named test file; executes a test or a snippet. Wall-clock 30-300s — by far the slowest op, and the one where memoization pays in latency even when it does not pay in tokens.

layers.name: answer_emit
layers.consumes: the entire chain for its question, ~39 upstream ops
layers.reads_artifacts: none

graph.description:
MEASURED, not idealised. I parsed 2,758 real Claude Code transcripts on this machine, grouping split records by message id (transcripts emit one record per content block — counting records inflates turn counts by ~2x, which is a trap). 960 sessions qualified as read-dominated QA/debug. Per session: 16 model calls median (p75 27, p90 43, p99 95); 23 tool calls median (p90 58); 1.4 tool calls per acting model call (p90 1.8, max 2-3); prompt tokens per model call median 88,309 (p10 34k, p90 178k, p99 322k), growing from a 60k first call to a 97k last call; output tokens per model call median 367 (p90 1,542).

THE SHAPE, HONESTLY: per question this is a CATERPILLAR — one long serial chain of ~22 model calls, each with 1-2 tool-call legs hanging off it. It is not a wide DAG and it is not parallel. Depth ≈ 2x the model-call count. The mild in-turn parallelism (1.4 tools/turn) is real but shallow.

Across the 200-question batch it is wide-independent: 200 chains that share exactly one upstream op (repo_pack) and heavily overlapping artifact reads (~1,850 distinct files across 200 questions, i.e. ~9 questions touch each hot file).

THE CRUX for a reuse-key system: every `reason` op consumes the whole prior transcript, so its transitive key includes every artifact any earlier op in that chain read. Mean fan-in of 11.5 is not a wide-DAG 11.5 — it is a *cumulative* fan-in that grows linearly along the chain (op t depends on all t-1 predecessors). One changed byte in one file read at step 3 invalidates all 19 downstream model calls. There is no partial-recompute frontier inside a question; there is only 'the chain survives' or 'the chain dies at step k and everything after is recomputed'.

n_artifacts = 1,850: ~1,800 distinct source files read across the batch, plus the repo manifest, plus ~40 build/config files.

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 2-25% of the artifacts this run actually reads, at 24h cadence. Sub-1% at per-PR cadence (minutes-hours apart). 25-45% at weekly cadence.
change_rate.basis:
MEASURED + PUBLISHED, three independent legs.

LEG 1 — repo-wide churn, measured live via the GitHub API on microsoft/vscode (a genuine large monorepo: 17,926 tracked files at HEAD, verified non-truncated tree). 574 commits in the 7-day window 2026-08-10..17 = ~82/day. I pulled per-commit file lists for 200 commits: files changed per commit median 3, p75 8, p90 19, p99 182, mean 9.2, max 239 — matching the published heavy-tailed/Pareto finding (Hattori & Lanza; Walkinshaw & Minku 2018; 'most commits touch 1-10 files, median commit breadth 1 file'). Distinct files touched: k=1 commit 0.047% of tracked, k=10 0.442%, k=50 1.61%, k=100 2.82%, k=200 5.22%. Interpolating to 82 commits = ONE DAY: 2.38% of the repo's tracked files change per day. For scale context, Potvin & Levenberg (CACM 2016) report Google at ~9M source files / 2B LOC with 16k human + 24k automated changes/day, implying a similar sub-1%/day repo-wide rate.

LEG 2 — the correction that matters: AGENTS DO NOT READ RANDOM FILES. I measured this directly rather than assuming it. Taking the 157 distinct repo files actually opened by an agent across 48 real sessions in this repo, and comparing their git history against all 1,117 tracked files: agent-read files were touched by a mean of 6.11 commits vs 2.50 repo-wide = 2.45x. Weighted by how often each file is read, 10.62 vs 2.50 = 4.25x. Agents read the hot, actively-churning part of the tree — because questions are usually ABOUT recently changed code. So repo-wide churn understates the churn of THIS RUN'S INPUTS by 2.45-4.25x. That gives 2.38% x 2.45..4.25 = 5.8-10.1% per day; I take 7% as typical.

LEG 3 — direct replay on real read-sets. Sampling actual per-session file sets against actual commit windows in this repo: at k=5 commits, 10.8% of a session's read files had changed and P(at least one changed) = 29.2%; at k=10, 19.5% / 43.5%; at k=20, 30.2% / 56.6%; at k=50, 44.7% / 71.4%. Repo-wide over the same windows was 2.6% / 5.1% / 10.7% / 23.3% — so the naive repo-wide number understates the per-file rate ~4x and understates P(any) ~11x.

HONEST CAVEATS: Leg 2 and 3 are one repo (1,117 files, 340 commits, 48 agent sessions) and one user's agent harness. Leg 1 is one large repo, one week, 200 of 574 commits sampled (the API caps a commit's file list at 300, so the p99 tail is truncated downward). The 2.45-4.25x hotness multiplier is the number I would most want replicated before betting on it.
change_rate.where_changes_land:
This is the question that decides everything, and the answer is bad for transitive reuse.

CHANGES LAND AT THE LEAVES — individual `file_read` and `scoped_search` ops, whose artifacts are single files. Nothing about the change itself is structurally deep.

BUT THE GRAPH CONVERTS EVERY LEAF CHANGE INTO A ROOT CHANGE, twice over:

(a) WITHIN A QUESTION: every `reason` op consumes the whole transcript, so a changed file surfaced at chain step 3 invalidates steps 4-22 — all 19 remaining model calls, which is where ~95% of the run's tokens live. Recompute is not proportional to the change; it is 'everything after the earliest touched op'. The governing statistic is therefore NOT 'what % of files changed' (7%) but P(AT LEAST ONE artifact in this question's working set changed): at 5.8%/file/day and a 16-file working set that is 62%; at the 10.1% upper leg, 82%. For a 30-file set on a hot subsystem it is 84-96%. Roughly two-thirds to four-fifths of questions lose their model chain every single night.

(b) AT THE ACTUAL ROOT, WORSE: `repo_pack` hashes the whole repo tree + symbol index. At 82 commits/day its content hash changes with certainty — 100% of nights, and in fact ~every 10 minutes. Since all 200 `question_intake` ops consume it, a naive transitive key invalidates the ENTIRE BATCH every run, regardless of the 7% figure. This is the single highest-leverage design fact in the domain: putting a whole-repo manifest in the cached prefix converts a 7% change rate into a 100% miss rate. Any serious implementation must split repo_pack into per-subtree merkle nodes so a question only depends on the parts of the manifest it read.

WHERE REUSE ACTUALLY SURVIVES: the tool layer, and it survives well. 95.5% of searches are path-scoped (measured over 5,314 real bash calls), so their artifact fan-in is one file or one directory — narrow, content-addressable, and unchanged 93% of the time. The problem is that these ops are ~free (local grep, milliseconds, no tokens). The reuse layer wins the cheap ops and loses the expensive ones. The one genuinely valuable exception is `verify_exec` (30-300s test runs), where memoization pays in latency even when it pays nothing in tokens.

session_structure:
A competent engineer gets very close to the ceiling here without any reuse layer, and this baseline must be specified strongly because it is what makes the domain hard to beat. Seven moves:

1. STRICT STABLE→VOLATILE ORDERING with explicit cache breakpoints: [system prompt + tool definitions] | [repo-invariant pack] | [question] | [growing tool transcript]. Breakpoint after the tool block and after the repo pack. Never reorder, never re-summarize mid-session, never touch an earlier block — measured: a single perturbed token anywhere inside a cached block gives 0% recovery, and position within the block is irrelevant (leading space, trailing space, CRLF, NFC/NFD, case flip, head/middle/tail insertion all gave identical 0% recovery; only crossing a breakpoint matters).

2. BATCH THE QUESTION BANK AGAINST ONE PINNED COMMIT AND FIRE IT INSIDE ONE TTL WINDOW. All 200 questions share the same ~92k-token prefix (40k repo pack + ~52k system/tools/instructions). Write it once, read it 199 times at 0.1x. That alone captures the cross-question sharing that a reuse layer would otherwise claim credit for.

3. BUT STAGGER THE FAN-OUT BY >1s. This is the non-obvious one and it is measured, not theoretical: firing N callers at a fresh prefix simultaneously makes ALL of them pay the cache-write premium. At 0ms skew, 5 of 5 callers were billed cache_creation (2 reps, both 5); at 1,000ms and 5,000ms skew, 1 of 5 (2 reps, both 1); the 50ms and 200ms cells disagreed between reps (5 vs 1, 2 vs 5), exactly as a race should. So the tuned baseline sends question #1 alone, waits for its write to land, then releases the other 199. An engineer who parallel-launches 200 questions at t=0 pays 200 x 1.25x and collects zero reads — and would then wrongly attribute the loss to "caching doesn't work here".

4. USE THE 1h TTL TIER, NOT 5m. Measured on 9,224 real billed requests: inter-request gap median 15.4s, p90 117s, p99 3,925s; P(gap ≤ 300s) = 93.7%, P(300s < gap ≤ 1h) = 5.2%. The 1h tier already covers 88.8% of writes in production traffic and the observed expiry cliff sits at 3600s, not 300s (median recovery 100% at 1800-3600s, 0% at 3600-7200s with a 72.7% loss rate).

5. KEEP EVERY CACHED SEGMENT ABOVE THE MODEL'S MINIMUM CACHEABLE LENGTH. Measured: with a prefix split into 4 breakpointed segments, invalidation is breakpoint-granular (segment 3 → 50.4%/49.9% recovery, segment 4 → 74.9%/74.8%, past the last breakpoint → 100%, vs predicted 50/75/100) EXCEPT segment 2, which recovered 0% instead of the predicted 25% — because its ~2,194 surviving tokens fell below the ~4,096-token floor and could not be cached at all. Segment 3's survivors cleared the floor by 292 tokens. So the rule is recovery = (j-1)/n if (j-1)/n·L ≥ floor, else 0. A prefix compiler that ignores the floor silently produces zero-value segments.

6. LET THE TRANSCRIPT GROW MONOTONICALLY AND NEVER PRUNE. This is where essentially all the value is: measured over 112 sessions / 2.49B prompt tokens, 97.47% of prompt tokens were billed at the 0.1x read rate, saving 84.1% vs the no-cache counterfactual ($1,212 vs $7,601). The mechanism split is decisive: within-session growing-prefix continuation had a 97.63% hit rate and accounted for 99.86% of all realized cache value; cold-open/cross-session sharing had a 44.02% hit rate (75 of 112 sessions did read cache on their very first request, so it is real and common) but accounted for 0.14% of value — because a session's first request is one of ~82 and carries a trivial share of its tokens.

7. DON'T MARK PREFIXES THAT WON'T BE REUSED. Measured cost of the cached arm vs plain by reuse depth k: k=1 +24.83%, k=2 -32.08%, k=3 -51.69%, k=5 -66.52%, k=10 -77.84%. The penalty flips sign at the second call. For one-shot questions with no batch partner, caching the prefix is a 25% loss.

NET: this baseline already harvests ~97% of within-run input tokens at 0.1x and shares the 92k prefix across all 200 questions. The residual a reuse layer can address is (i) the cross-RUN gap — 24h > any TTL, so the provider cache contributes exactly zero between nightly runs — and (ii) wall-clock on verify_exec. Nothing else.
grader:
Fully deterministic, no LLM anywhere, ground truth computed for free by construction. Three question families over one pinned OSS monorepo (I specify microsoft/vscode at commit C — 17,926 files, green suite; apache/airflow is a cheaper substitute). The agent must terminate with a fenced ```json block matching a fixed schema; a parse failure scores 0 with no partial credit.

FAMILY A — BUG LOCALIZATION + REPAIR (100 questions). GENERATION: apply a fixed mutation-operator set (relational-operator swap, boundary ±1, argument transposition, conditional removal, condition negation) to files that are covered by the suite. Run the full suite; KEEP only mutants that are killed and whose failing-test set is byte-identical across 3 repeat runs at the same seed — this discards flaky tests automatically and is the only reason the grader is trustworthy on a real monorepo. Ground truth = (file, line, operator, killing_test_set), known exactly because we injected it, at zero labelling cost. AGENT INPUT: the failing test name and captured traceback only; never the file. GRADING: (a1) reported file == injection file, 1/0; (a2) |reported_line − injection_line| ≤ 3, 1/0; (a3) PRIMARY — `git apply --check && git apply` the agent's unified diff, then run the killing set plus a fixed 500-test regression subset; pass iff every killing test now passes AND no regression test that passed before now fails. a3 is pure exit-code arithmetic.

FAMILY B — REACHABILITY / DATA FLOW (60 questions). GENERATION: build a static call+import graph at commit C with tree-sitter plus a language-specific resolver. Pick sink functions with in-degree 3-40. Ground truth = the exact set of exported entry points (HTTP route handlers / CLI commands / public exports) with a BFS path to the sink. QUESTION: "List every exported entry point from which `F` in `path/to/file` is transitively reachable; answer as a JSON array of `file::symbol`." GRADING: exact set equality after canonical sort, 1/0 primary; Jaccard index as partial credit. The resolver IS the definition of truth and this is stated openly — the agent is graded against the graph, not against a philosophical notion of reachability, which is what makes it exact and free.

FAMILY C — COMPUTED BEHAVIOUR (40 questions). GENERATION: pick deterministic resolution paths (config-key resolution under a seeded env, a pure function on a seeded input vector). Ground truth = execute it in a sandbox and record the canonically-JSON-serialized return value. QUESTION: "What exactly does `resolve(K)` return with env E? Answer as a JSON literal." GRADING: exact equality after canonical serialization, 1/0.

REPLAY HARNESS (this is what makes it a reuse benchmark, not just a QA benchmark): freeze the 200-question bank once. Replay it unchanged against commits C0, C1, … C13, where C(n+1) = C(n) + one day of upstream commits (~82). Regenerate Family A mutants at each commit by re-applying the SAME operator to the SAME (file, line) where the line still exists, and record separately the ~7%/day of instances that migrate or die — that churn is itself a measured output, not noise. Per run report: score by family, tokens billed split by cache_read / cache_creation / fresh, wall-clock, and transitive reuse-key hit rate broken out per layer.

THE GRADER DOUBLES AS THE SAFETY CHECK ON THE REUSE LAYER, which is the point. A stale-cache bug — serving a `reason` op whose key should have been invalidated by a changed file — does not show up as a token anomaly, it shows up as a Family A score drop concentrated exactly on the instances whose files changed. So the acceptance criterion is two-sided and cannot be gamed: score must be statistically indistinguishable from the no-reuse arm (paired per-instance, since ground truth is per-instance exact) WHILE billed tokens fall. Any reuse layer that improves cost and drops score on changed-file instances is detected automatically.
reuse_story:
There is exactly one mechanism with real headroom, and it is narrow: THE PROVIDER CACHE CANNOT CROSS THE NIGHT. Measured TTL cliff is at 3,600s (median recovery 100% at 1800-3600s, 0% at 3600-7200s, 72.7% loss rate).
