A nightly batch runs 24h after the last one, so between runs the provider baseline delivers precisely zero. A persistent store keyed on content is the only thing that can carry anything across that gap. Within the 24h window the reuse layer has nothing to add — the tuned baseline already books 97.47% of prompt tokens at 0.1x.

What could actually be carried across, ranked by honest value:

1. `verify_exec` MEMOIZATION — the strongest case, and it is a latency story, not a token story. Test runs are 30-300s of wall-clock and zero tokens. Keyed on (test id, merkle hash of the test's transitive source closure), ~93% of them are unchanged night to night. This is Bazel's actual value proposition and it is real. It just does not show up on the provider bill at all.

2. `repo_pack` / SYMBOL-INDEX MEMOIZATION — deterministic, expensive to build, shared by all 200 questions. Genuinely worth storing, but per-subtree merkle nodes are mandatory: as one whole-repo blob its hash changes ~every 10 minutes at 82 commits/day and it is never a hit.

3. `scoped_search` and `file_read` REPLAY — 95.5% of searches are path-scoped so their keys are narrow and ~93% survive a day. High hit rate, near-zero value: these are local grep calls costing milliseconds and no tokens. Their real contribution is indirect — a cheap tool op that key-hits does not change the transcript, which is what would let a downstream model op key-hit.

4. THE ONE PATH TO MODEL-OP REUSE: for the ~35% of questions where NOTHING in their working set changed overnight (measured P(no artifact changed) = 38% at a 16-file working set, 5.8%/file/day), the entire 22-model-call chain is bit-reproducible and can be served whole from the store. That is not incremental recomputation — it is whole-chain replay, essentially a memoized answer. It skips ~2.1M prompt tokens per question. At 200 questions/night x 35% x 2.1M tokens, that is ~147M tokens/night of the run's ~420M avoided, i.e. roughly a third — but only against the *already 84%-discounted* baseline, so the marginal dollars are ~a third of the residual 16%, not a third of gross.

That is the whole story. It is a real but modest win concentrated in whole-chain replay of unchanged questions, plus a genuine latency win on test execution.
reuse_threats:
Six, roughly in order of how likely each is to kill the thesis:

1. THE CATERPILLAR SHAPE HAS NO PARTIAL-RECOMPUTE FRONTIER. Every `reason` op consumes the entire transcript, so its transitive key covers every artifact any earlier op read. There is no "recompute the 7% that changed" — there is only "the chain dies at the earliest touched op and everything after it is recomputed". Since ~95% of tokens sit in the model chain, a question is effectively all-or-nothing. The governing number is P(any artifact in the working set changed) = 62-82%/day, not the 7% file change rate. Bazel's model works because build graphs are wide with narrow fan-in; this graph is the opposite.

2. WHOLE-REPO ROOTS CONVERT 7% INTO 100%. `repo_pack` hashes the entire tree; at 82 commits/day it changes with certainty. Any implementation that does not shard it into per-subtree merkle nodes gets a 0% hit rate on all 4,400 model ops and will look catastrophically worse than the baseline. This is an implementation landmine, not a theoretical one.

3. AGENTS READ HOT FILES — measured 2.45x repo-wide churn, 4.25x read-weighted. Every naive change-rate estimate in this domain (including "the repo only changes 2%/day, so we get 98% reuse") is wrong by 2.5-4x on files and ~11x on P(any). If someone sizes this business on repo-wide churn they will overstate reuse by roughly an order of magnitude.

4. THE BASELINE IS ALREADY EXCELLENT AND THE MARGIN IS THE RESIDUAL, NOT THE GROSS. Measured: caching already saves 84.1% ($1,212 vs $7,601 over 2.49B tokens) and 97.47% of prompt tokens already bill at 0.1x. A reuse layer competes for the remaining ~16%, and only in the cross-run slice. Quoting "we save 35% of tokens" against a no-cache counterfactual would be dishonest by construction.

5. MODEL NON-DETERMINISM MAKES THE KEY OVER-STRICT AND THE HIT OVER-TRUSTED SIMULTANEOUSLY. Even at temperature 0, provider-side batching and kernel non-determinism mean two runs of the same `reason` op can differ, so op 3's output hash differs, so ops 4-22 all miss even with a frozen repo — the key composes transitively over a value that is not reproducible. Working around this by keying model ops on their *inputs* only (ignoring upstream output hashes) restores hit rate but reintroduces exactly the staleness the transitive key existed to prevent. This tension has no clean resolution and it is the deepest problem with applying Bazel semantics to model calls.

6. THE HIGH-HIT-RATE OPS ARE FREE AND THE EXPENSIVE OPS ARE LOW-HIT-RATE. Searches and reads: ~93% hit, ~$0 value. Model chains: ~35% hit, ~all the value. Test runs: ~93% hit, real latency value but zero token value. The distribution of value across the hit-rate spectrum is precisely inverted from what you would want. Anyone reporting an aggregate "operation-level cache hit rate" for this workload will get a flattering number (~75-85%, dominated by tool ops) that is almost entirely decoupled from dollars saved.

7. (minor but real) CONCURRENT FAN-OUT INVERTS THE ARITHMETIC. If the 200-question batch is launched simultaneously, all 200 pay the 1.25x write premium and collect zero reads — measured 5/5 writers at 0ms skew vs 1/5 at ≥1s. A reuse layer benchmarked against a badly-parallelised baseline will look great for a reason that has nothing to do with reuse.
confidence:
MEDIUM, and unevenly distributed — I would separate the four asks.

HIGH confidence: the graph shape and token sizes. These come from 2,758 real transcripts / 960 QA-like sessions / 21,012 model calls with the provider's own usage counters attached, and the per-layer numbers (16 model calls median, 1.4 tools per acting turn, 88k prompt tokens median, 367 output tokens median, 95.5% path-scoped searches) are direct measurements, not estimates. The caterpillar-with-cumulative-fan-in structure is not a modelling choice; it is what the transcripts show.

HIGH confidence: the tuned baseline. Every number in it (97.47% at 0.1x, 84.1% saving, 99.86% of value from within-session continuation, the 3,600s cliff, the k=1 +24.83% inversion flipping at k=2, the 0ms-skew 5/5-writers result, the min-cacheable-length floor truncating the breakpoint staircase) is live-measured or field-measured, several with clean replication.

MEDIUM confidence: the change rate. The repo-wide leg is solid (live GitHub API, 17,926 files, 574 commits, verified untruncated tree, and it matches the published Pareto commit-size literature). The 2.45-4.25x agent-hotness multiplier — the number that actually drives the conclusion — rests on 48 sessions / 157 files in ONE 1,117-file repo with ONE user's harness. It is the weakest load-bearing number in this spec and it is doing a lot of work.

LOWER confidence: the repeat rate itself. I have no measurement of how often a production codebase-QA system genuinely re-asks an identical question. I reasoned it structurally (CI re-triages the same red test; question banks recur) and did not find data. If the true identical-question rate is low, the whole-chain-replay win in the reuse story shrinks toward zero regardless of everything else.

WHAT WOULD RAISE IT, in order of value per unit effort:
1. Replicate the hotness multiplier across 5-10 repos and 3+ users' agent transcripts. One week of work, and it is the number most likely to move the answer.
2. Instrument a real production codebase-QA product for identical-question rate and inter-arrival time. This is the only way to settle the repeat question, and I currently have nothing on it.
3. Actually run the replay harness: 200 questions x 14 daily commits x {no-reuse, tuned-baseline, reuse} arms, and report transitive key hit rate PER LAYER alongside dollars. My prediction, stated in advance so it can be falsified: aggregate op-level hit rate 75-85%, model-op hit rate 30-40%, marginal dollar saving over the tuned baseline in the 3-8% range, and a large wall-clock win on verify_exec that shows up nowhere on the bill.
4. Re-run the floor/breakpoint probes per model — floors and TTL tiers are per-model, and the X4 floor interaction was measured on exactly one model.

customer: A multi-source residential listing aggregator / portal (the shape of Zumper, HotPads, an apartment ILS, or a mid-size CRE data vendor; the same graph applies to CarGurus-style dealer-inventory aggregation and to hotel room-type mapping). They ingest ~40 upstream feeds: RESO Web API / MLS Grid / Trestle MLS feeds, PMS exports from Yardi / RealPage / AppFolio, broker XML+CSV drops on SFTP, and a few partner APIs. Contractually they must publish ONE canonical listing per physical unit, with correct beds/baths/sqft/price/fees/pet-policy/parking, no duplicates, and no fair-housing-violating copy. What they pay for today: (a) the LLM bill for free-text extraction and duplicate adjudication — the single largest line item in their data-platform budget after storage; (b) a 4-8 person data-ops team whose job is chasing "same unit listed three times at three prices" tickets and feed-partner regressions. Duplicates and wrong prices are directly revenue-affecting: a portal that shows the same apartment three times loses the lead-gen auction, and a stale price triggers a chargeback from the advertiser. They are not paying for "AI"; they are paying to keep a duplicate rate under ~1.5% and a field-accuracy SLA above ~97% at a per-listing cost that stays under their per-listing ad revenue.
why_repeated: The corpus is a live, continuously-mutating population, not a one-shot job. Every night the pipeline must re-derive the published corpus because: (1) feeds deliver deltas but the *cluster* structure is global — a new listing arriving tonight can merge two clusters that were separate yesterday, so cluster assembly and golden-record reconciliation cannot be purely incremental; (2) upstream feeds regress constantly (a partner changes a column, drops unit designators, or starts sending m² instead of sqft) and the nightly full pass is how that is caught; (3) the prompt, amenity taxonomy, or model gets edited every week or two and the affected slice has to be re-derived; (4) SLA/audit: advertisers can demand a re-derivation of any published record from source, so the pipeline is designed to be re-runnable end to end. Crucially, the same ~97% of listings are semantically identical night over night — this is the same computation over an almost-identical corpus, repeated ~365 times a year per shard, and the customer already knows it, which is why nearly all of them have hand-rolled a memo table.
run_cadence: Nightly full reconcile (typically a 01:00-05:00 local window, sharded by metro, ~10-30 shards); plus hourly-to-15-minute incremental delta passes during the day that run L1/L2 and a shard-local subset of L3-L6 but skip the global reconcile. The benchmark run is one nightly full reconcile for one metro shard. Additionally: an unscheduled full re-run of the whole corpus on every prompt / taxonomy / model change (~2-4 times per month) and on every feed-partner schema regression (~1-2 times per month).

graph.description:
One nightly full reconcile of a single metro shard: 8,000 active raw listing records arriving from 5 source feeds, resolving to ~5,600 unique physical units (mean 1.43 renderings per unit; ~26% of units appear in 2+ feeds). Production runs 10-30 such shards per night, so multiply everything by ~20 for the customer's real nightly bill (~53M input tokens and ~6.9M output tokens per shard, ~1.1B input tokens per night corpus-wide).

The 8,017 artifacts are: 8,000 raw listing records (JSON/XML/CSV rows, 4-40 KB each including up to 24 photo URLs and 120-400 words of free-text remarks), 5 feed manifests, and 12 config artifacts (RESO Data Dictionary field-schema subset ~180 fields; canonical amenity taxonomy ~1,800 terms; 5 per-source mapping-rule files; 3 prompt templates; a 60-example labelled exemplar bank; a source-trust/field-precedence table). The 12 config artifacts are the graph ROOTS: any one of them changing invalidates every model op in the run.

Structure in one line: 8,000 independent per-listing chains of depth 2 (normalise -> extract), then a genuinely relational middle (blocking -> pairwise scoring -> LLM adjudication of the gray zone -> union-find clustering), then a per-cluster tail (golden record -> canonical copy -> validate -> repair). It is NOT one long chain and it is NOT 500 independent ops: it is a wide-independent head (16,000 ops, no cross-talk) welded to a relational waist that couples listings pairwise within a blocking shard, with exactly ONE global aggregation node (L6b, fan-in 512) that sits above 42% of the model ops. That single node is the most important structural fact for any reuse system: unless its output can be keyed per-cluster rather than per-run, everything below it recomputes every night no matter how little changed.

The LLM is deliberately NOT used for pairwise comparison at O(n^2). Real production uses deterministic blocking + a gradient-boosted scorer and escalates only the ~11% gray band to a model. Anyone who benchmarks 'LLM compares every pair' is benchmarking a system no one runs.

layers.name: L1_record_normalise
layers.consumes: no upstream ops; each op reads exactly one external artifact
layers.reads_artifacts: one raw listing record + its source's mapping-rule file + the field schema. Does: libpostal parse + USPS/CASS standardisation, geocode to geohash-9, price/area unit coercion (annual->monthly, m²->sqft, concession-adjusted rent), enum coercion to RESO values, pHash of up to 24 photos, and — critically — PROJECTION: it strips DaysOnMarket, CumulativeDaysOnMarket, ModificationTimestamp, photo ordering, rotating CDN URL tokens, denormalised agent/office fields and float-formatting noise. ~6 ms per op. This layer is what makes reuse keys stable; its output hash is the honest content identity of a listing.

layers.name: L2_freetext_extraction
layers.consumes: L1, exactly 1 upstream op per op
layers.reads_artifacts: shared/prefix: amenity taxonomy excerpt (~140 relevant of 1,800 canonical terms), field-schema subset, per-source mapping rules, 8 few-shot exemplars, output JSON schema (~3,400 tokens, identical across all 8,000 calls within a source). Variable: the L1-normalised free-text bundle — public remarks, private remarks, unit description, raw amenity blob (~700 tokens). Extracts facts that exist ONLY in prose: unit designator hidden in the description, pet policy exceptions, included utilities, parking count, lease-term floor, fee disclosures, plus beds/baths/sqft when the structured fields are null. Emits strict JSON with per-field confidence.

layers.name: L3_blocking_shard
layers.consumes: L1, ~15.6 ops per shard (8,000 / 512)
layers.reads_artifacts: geohash-5 / zip3 partition table. Builds candidate pairs within a shard on (normalised street number+name, zip), geohash-7 proximity, and pHash bucket. Emits ~23 candidate pairs per shard, ~11,800 total. Sharding is deliberate: the naive design is ONE global blocking op with fan-in 8,000, which invalidates on any single listing change. 512 shards is the finest partition that still catches ~99.4% of true duplicate pairs.

layers.name: L4_pair_scorer
layers.consumes: 1 L3 shard output + the 2 L1 outputs + the 2 L2 outputs of the pair (fan-in 5)
layers.reads_artifacts: GBDT model file + string-similarity config. Features: Jaro-Winkler on street, unit-token exact/prefix match, haversine metres, price ratio, sqft ratio, pHash Hamming distance, listing-date overlap, source-pair prior. Bands the pair: auto-match >=0.93 (~31% of pairs), auto-reject <=0.55 (~58%), gray zone (~11%, 1,300 pairs). ~1 ms per op, no model.

layers.name: L5_pair_adjudication
layers.consumes: 1 L4 scorer output + the 2 L2 extractions (fan-in 3)
layers.reads_artifacts: shared/prefix: match policy (what makes two renderings the same physical unit vs. adjacent units, same building different floor, model unit vs. real unit) + 6 adjudication exemplars (~2,600 tokens). Variable: two normalised listing summaries side by side (~380 tokens each) + the scorer's feature vector rendered as text (~120 tokens). Outputs {same_unit: bool, distinguishing_evidence[], rationale <=40 words, confidence}. Fan-in 2 on listings means transitive invalidation bites hard here: a pair op dies if EITHER listing changed.

layers.name: L6a_cluster_shard
layers.reads_artifacts: none. Union-find over accepted edges within the shard; emits shard-local clusters plus the set of edges that cross shard boundaries.

layers.name: L6b_cluster_global
layers.consumes: all 512 L6a outputs (fan-in 512)
layers.reads_artifacts: none. Stitches cross-shard edges (units on a shard boundary street, or matched by pHash across geographies) and emits the final ~5,600 clusters. THIS IS THE POISON NODE: fan-in 512 means P(invalid) ~= 1.0 on every real run, and 12,391 ops below it (6,790 of them model ops, 42% of all model ops) inherit that invalidation unless the reuse system can key its consumers on individual cluster membership rather than on the whole L6b output hash.

layers.name: L7_golden_record
layers.consumes: 1 L6b cluster slice + the 2-4 member L2 extractions (fan-in ~3.9)
layers.reads_artifacts: shared/prefix: source-trust ranking, field-precedence and recency rules, conflict-resolution policy (~2,100 tokens). Variable: 2-4 member records with provenance and timestamps (~1,500 tokens). Fires only for multi-member clusters (~1,700) that have at least one MATERIAL conflict (price differs >1%, sqft differs, beds differ, amenity sets disagree, descriptions contradict) — ~62% of them. Emits merged record + per-field chosen source + a conflict log used by data-ops.

layers.name: L8_canonical_copy
layers.consumes: 1 L7 output for conflicted clusters, else 1 L6b cluster slice + 1 L2 (fan-in 2)
layers.reads_artifacts: shared/prefix: style guide, canonical phrasing rules, fair-housing forbidden-phrase list (~1,400 tokens — note this is BELOW the 2,048-token cache minimum on Haiku-class models, so it will silently not cache if the team routes this cheap layer to a cheap model). Variable: the golden record (~700 tokens). Emits the deduplicated public description + SEO title. Optional layer — some portals template it instead — but where it exists it is the largest single token consumer (11.8M input, 2.35M output per shard) and the cleanest reuse surface, because it is a pure function of the golden record.

layers.name: L9_validate
layers.consumes: 1 L8 each, plus one aggregate report op over all 5,600
layers.reads_artifacts: JSON Schema, invariant config, zip-level comp statistics. Checks: schema conformance, price within 3σ of zip comps, sqft>0, beds<=12, unit-designator regex, no PII or fair-housing trigger phrase in public copy, cluster size <= 6. ~2.5% fail.

layers.name: L10_repair
layers.consumes: 1 L9 failure (fan-in 1)
layers.reads_artifacts: shared/prefix: repair instructions + violated-rule catalogue (~1,800 tokens). Variable: the failing record and the specific violated rule text (~650 tokens). One shot; a second failure is routed to a human queue, not retried.

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 2.5% (content-relevant projection, i.e. L1 output hash) — 8-15% (raw-record bytes on a well-behaved RESO delta feed) — ~100% (PMS/broker full-snapshot feeds that regenerate timestamps, ids and float formatting every night). Config-root artifacts change on ~15-20% of nightly runs.
change_rate.basis:
PARTLY SOURCED, PARTLY ESTIMATED — I am splitting it explicitly.

SOURCED (the semantic components):
• Inventory turnover: NAR pegged unsold US inventory at 1.56M in June 2026 at a 4.6-month supply, which is ~21.7% of the active corpus exiting per month => ~0.72%/day going pending/sold/withdrawn/expired. Steady state implies a matching ~0.8-0.9%/day of new listings entering (NAR/ShowingTime reported new listings +10.9% YoY for single-family, -2.4% for townhouse-condo).
• Price changes: Redfin's Data Center reports ~20.2% of active listings carry a price cut in a given month (down from 21.0% a year prior), with a >=1% threshold and a mean cut of 4.0% => ~0.67%/day, but CLUSTERED — price cuts are pushed disproportionately Thursday/Friday, so a Friday-morning run sees ~1.0-1.2% and a Sunday run ~0.3%.

ESTIMATED (no published data found; I searched for MLS/RESO per-day record-change statistics and for Google Merchant Center delta-feed churn rates and neither is published — vendors say 'much fewer records' and refuse to quantify):
• Free-text remark edits: agents edit public remarks on maybe 12-18% of listings over a ~90-day listing life => ~0.2%/day. Media/photo edits ~0.5%/day.
• Non-semantic feed noise: MLS deltas advance ModificationTimestamp for DaysOnMarket increments, photo reordering, rotating CDN URL tokens, and denormalised agent/office fields. My estimate is 8-15%/day of raw records differ byte-wise for reasons no model op cares about. For PMS full-snapshot exports it is effectively 100%.

So: semantic change ~2.5%/day (range 1.5-4.5% by weekday and market heat); raw-bytes change ~9%/day typical. The headline 9.0 is the literal answer to 'what fraction of input artifacts differ', and it is roughly 3.6x the fraction that MATTERS. That gap is the single most consequential number in this spec: a reuse key over the raw artifact gets ~91% hit rate on a good feed and ~0% on a snapshot feed; a reuse key over the L1 projection gets ~97.5% on both. The benchmark must have a knob for this.

WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS SOURCED: pull two consecutive nightly snapshots of a single MLS RESO feed and diff them at both the raw and projected level. That is a half-day of work and it replaces both estimated components with a measurement. I did not have feed access here.
change_rate.where_changes_land:
Real changes land almost entirely at the LEAVES of the listing sub-DAG — individual listing records, scattered roughly uniformly across metro geography and therefore across blocking shards. That is the favourable case in isolation, but this graph amplifies leaf churn twice and has a root hazard on top:

(1) DIRECT, no amplification: L1 and L2 (16,000 ops, 8,000 of them model ops = 50% of all model ops) invalidate at exactly the artifact rate — 2.5% if keyed on the projection, 9% if keyed on raw bytes.

(2) FIRST AMPLIFICATION — blocking shards. With 512 shards averaging 15.6 listings, P(shard untouched) = 0.975^15.6 = 0.674, so ~33% of L3 shard ops invalidate from a 2.5% listing change rate, and every L4/L5/L6a op below them inherits it. A 13x amplification purely from aggregation granularity. Shard finer (per blocking bucket, ~2.5 listings) and it drops to ~6%.

(3) SECOND AMPLIFICATION — the global node. L6b has fan-in 512 and invalidates with probability ~1.0 every single run. Everything below it — L7 (1,050), L8 (5,600), L9 (5,601), L10 (140), i.e. 6,790 model ops = 42% of all model ops and ~55% of the token spend — recomputes every night unless the reuse layer is expressive enough to key L7/L8 on their cluster's membership set rather than on L6b's monolithic output hash. This is not a hypothetical: it is the default shape and it is where naive content-addressed reuse silently delivers half the savings it promises.

(4) ROOT HAZARD. The 12 config artifacts (prompts, amenity taxonomy, source-trust table, model id) change on an estimated 15-20% of nightly runs — prompt edits 2-4x/month, taxonomy edits 1-2x/month, model id ~1x/quarter. On those runs 100% of model ops recompute. Averaged over a month this alone caps achievable reuse at ~82% before any other effect. Root changes are rare but total; leaf changes are constant but local.

NET: a well-engineered reuse layer keyed on projections with per-cluster keys should serve ~85-90% of model ops on a median night. A naive one keyed on raw artifacts with a monolithic global node serves ~30-45%, and on a snapshot-feed customer, ~0%.

session_structure:
A competent engineer tuning THIS workload for Anthropic-style prefix caching does the following, and this is a strong baseline, not a straw man:

1. LAYER-HOMOGENEOUS BATCHES, NOT INTERLEAVED. Run L2 to completion, then L5, then L7, then L8. Never interleave layers, because each layer has a different prefix and interleaving thrashes the cache. Within L2, sort calls by SOURCE FEED so the ~600-token source-specific mapping rules also sit inside the cached prefix.

2. PREFIX ORDERED LONGEST-STABLE-FIRST, with an explicit cache breakpoint at its end: tool/output JSON schema -> RESO field schema subset -> amenity taxonomy excerpt -> field-precedence rules -> few-shot exemplars -> "now process:" . Variable payload strictly last. No run id, timestamp, shard id, or listing id anywhere above the breakpoint. Prefix sizes: L2 3,400 tok, L5 2,600, L7 2,100, L8 1,400, L10 1,800 — all above the 1,024-token minimum for Sonnet-class, but L8's 1,400 is BELOW the 2,048 minimum for Haiku-class, so if the team routes the cheap copy layer to a cheap model the cache silently does not engage. A tuned engineer either pads L8's prefix past 2,048 or keeps it on a Sonnet-class model.

3. WARM THE CACHE BEFORE OPENING THE FAN-OUT. At cold start with 40 concurrent workers, all 40 in-flight callers pay the 1.25x cache-WRITE surcharge because none of them sees the others' entry yet. Fire one warm-up call per prefix, await it, then open concurrency. This is worth ~5-8% of the L2 bill on its own and most teams get it wrong.

4. USE THE 1-HOUR TTL, NOT THE 5-MINUTE ONE. An 8,000-listing shard at ~8 calls/s takes ~17 min for L2 alone and ~35-40 min for the full run; the 5-minute TTL would expire between layers, the 1-hour TTL spans the whole nightly window. Cache reads refresh the TTL, so a continuously-running layer keeps itself warm.

5. BATCH 4-8 LISTINGS PER L2 CALL. This is the single biggest baseline win: it amortises the 3,400-token prefix over 8x more variable payload and cuts call count 8x. At batch=8, L2 becomes 1,000 calls of (3,400 cached-read + 5,600 variable in + 3,600 out) instead of 8,000 calls of (3,400 + 700 + 450). Effective input tokens drop from 32.8M to ~5.9M — an ~82% reduction in L2 input cost from the free mechanisms alone. NOTE THE CONFLICT: batching is directly adversarial to content-addressed reuse, because it welds 8 independent artifacts into one reuse key, raising effective invalidation from 2.5% to 1-(0.975^8) = 18.3%. Any honest evaluation must run BOTH arms at batch=1 and batch=8; a reuse layer that only wins at batch=1 is winning against a detuned baseline.

6. SORT L5 PAIRS BY BLOCKING SHARD so shard-local context (street-level priors, comp stats) is prefix-stable too, adding a second breakpoint.

7. USE THE BATCH API for the entire nightly run. It is not latency-sensitive (a 4-hour window), it composes with prompt caching, and it is a flat 50% discount on top.

8. DON'T SEND WHAT THE MODEL DOESN'T READ. Send only the L1-projected free-text bundle to L2, not the raw record. This halves the variable payload and is also, not coincidentally, exactly the discipline that makes reuse keys stable.

WHAT THIS BASELINE LEAVES ON THE TABLE — and therefore what the reuse layer is actually competing for: the provider prefix cache only ever discounts the SHARED prefix. After the tuned baseline at batch=8, the remaining bill is ~85% variable-payload input plus 100% of output tokens, and output is ~6.9M tokens per shard at 5x the input rate. The reuse store attacks precisely that residue. So the honest framing is COMPLEMENTS, NOT SUBSTITUTES: prefix caching removes the instruction cost, content-addressed reuse removes the per-listing recompute. But it also means the naive "we save 90%" pitch double-counts — the 82% that batching plus prefix caching already delivered on L2 is not the reuse layer's to claim.
grader:
FULLY PROGRAMMATIC, NO LLM ANYWHERE IN THE GRADER, ground truth exact and free because the corpus is generated and the generator IS the truth.

CORPUS GENERATOR (seeded, deterministic, reproducible from a single integer seed):
1. Draw K = 5,600 ground-truth physical units. Address components come from OpenAddresses / Census TIGER (free, downloadable, versioned, deterministic); beds/baths/sqft/price/amenity-code-set/lease-terms come from seeded distributions calibrated to a real listing sample.
2. For each unit emit 1-4 SOURCE RENDERINGS (mean 1.43, so ~8,000 renderings) by applying an enumerated corruption grammar with seeded parameters: street-type abbreviation swaps (Street/St/St.), directional swaps (N/North), unit-designator RELOCATION (structured field <-> buried in prose <-> dropped entirely), sqft rounding and unit swap (sqft <-> m²), price expressed monthly / annual / net-of-concession / with a fee bundled in, amenity set rendered as free-text prose with 0-3 synonyms per canonical code, 0-2 injected factual contradictions each tagged with a declared TRUE source, photo sets with a specified overlap fraction, and typo injection at a seeded rate.
3. Inject 5% deliberate HARD NEGATIVES: unit 3A vs 3B in the same building, same street number in an adjacent city, a model unit vs a real unit, two identical floorplans in the same complex. These are what separate a real grader from one that any string matcher passes.
4. Emit the answer key alongside: true cluster id per rendering, true canonical value for each of 14 typed fields, true amenity code set.

GRADER (pure code, runs in seconds, costs nothing):
• DEDUP: pairwise precision / recall / F1 and Adjusted Rand Index of predicted clusters against true cluster ids. GATE: pairwise F1 >= 0.965 AND pairwise precision >= 0.985 (asymmetric on purpose — over-merging two real units is the expensive error; it publishes one listing where two should exist and loses a whole lead).
• NORMALISATION: exact-match rate over 14 typed canonical fields — beds (int), baths (half-step float), sqft (±1), price_monthly_cents (exact int), unit_designator (casefolded string exact), pets_allowed (enum), pet_deposit_cents, parking_spots (int), lease_term_months (int), utilities_included (sorted code set), sqft_source, deposit_cents, available_date (ISO), fee_total_cents. Plus Jaccard on the canonical amenity code set. GATES: typed-field exact-match >= 0.97, amenity Jaccard >= 0.92.
• REUSE CORRECTNESS: run the pipeline twice with the reuse layer on, applying the seeded run-2 perturbation. Assert BYTE-IDENTICAL golden records for the exact set of clusters the generator knows was not perturbed. Any divergence there is either a reuse-correctness bug or model nondeterminism — the harness distinguishes them by also running the no-reuse arm twice and reporting the delta-of-deltas. A reuse layer that improves cost while failing this check has not saved money, it has silently changed the published corpus.
• COST/LATENCY: total uncached-input, cache-write, cache-read and output tokens read from the provider's own usage fields (never estimated), plus wall-clock, per layer.

RUN-2 PERTURBATION, applied by the same seeded generator to match the measured change profile: 0.9% of renderings removed (off-market), 0.9% new renderings added, 0.7% price change, 0.2% remark rewrite, 0.5% photo-set edit. Plus the decisive knob: FEED_NOISE ∈ {0%, 12%, 100%} rewrites purely non-semantic bytes (ModificationTimestamp, DaysOnMarket counter, photo URL tokens, float formatting) in that fraction of records. Sweeping that knob is the whole experiment — a reuse layer that keys on raw artifacts collapses from ~91% to ~0% hit rate across the sweep while a projection-keyed one holds at ~97.5%, and the quality gates must stay green throughout.

SECOND KNOB: BATCH_SIZE ∈ {1, 8} on L2, so the reuse arm is measured against the genuinely tuned prefix-cache baseline and not against a detuned one.

REALISM ANCHOR (one-time, offline, does not touch the benchmark's cost or determinism): fit the corruption grammar's parameter vector to a held-out sample of ~2,000 real listings by matching the observed distributions of inter-source edit distance, missing-field rate, unit-designator location, and duplicate rate. The benchmark itself stays 100% synthetic and free.
reuse_story:
~97.5% of listings are semantically unchanged night over night, and half of all model ops (L2, 8,000 of 16,090) are pure per-listing functions of a single listing's projected free text. Those are trivially content-addressable: hash(L1 projection + prompt version + model id) -> extraction JSON serves ~97.5% of them for free, and L2 is ~34% of the shard's token spend. L8 canonical-copy generation (5,600 model ops, ~40% of output tokens, the biggest single line item) is a pure function of the golden record, so it reuses whenever that record is unchanged — which for a singleton cluster means whenever its one listing is unchanged.

Three additional reuse surfaces the customer cannot easily hand-roll:
• TRANSITIVE CORRECTNESS. When a taxonomy term or a source-trust rule changes, exactly the affected slice must be re-derived and nothing else. Hand-rolled memo tables get this wrong in both directions — they either flush everything (wasting the whole night) or forget to flush and publish stale records for weeks. The transitive key is the part that is genuinely hard to build in-house.
• CROSS-SOURCE DUPLICATION WITHIN A RUN. Broker copy-paste and syndication mean identical remark text appears verbatim across feeds; the same L2 extraction is requested 1.43 times on average, so ~30% of L2 calls are same-run duplicates that a pure-function store collapses at zero risk.
• CROSS-TENANT. A data vendor serving 40 portal customers normalises the same physical unit for many of them. The extraction is a pure function of public listing text, so one store could serve all of them — nominally a 40x multiplier on the biggest layer.

Compounding: with 2.5%/day semantic churn, the store's working set converges and the marginal fresh work per night is ~2.5% of L1/L2 plus whatever the DAG amplifies. Over a 30-day window the store pays for itself many times over IF the amplification is controlled.
reuse_threats:
Ordered by how likely each is to kill the deal, most lethal first.

1. THE CUSTOMER ALREADY BUILT THE LEAF CACHE. Every serious listing pipeline built after 2024 has a `hash(remark_text + prompt_version) -> extraction_json` table in Postgres or Redis, because per-listing LLM cost forced it in month two. That table already captures L2 and L8 — which is where ~75% of the theoretical savings live. The reuse layer's genuinely incremental value is the transitive/relational part (L3-L7), which is the harder half to build and the smaller half of the money. Any pitch that quotes the L2 saving as new value is quoting a saving the customer already banked. This is the single biggest threat and it should be measured, not argued: the honest comparison arm is "customer's hand-rolled leaf memo + tuned prefix cache", not "no cache".

2. FEED HYGIENE DESTROYS NAIVE KEYS. Raw-record bytes differ ~9%/day on a good RESO delta feed and ~100%/day on PMS/broker full-snapshot exports that regenerate timestamps, ids and float formatting. Keying on the raw artifact yields near-zero hit rate on a meaningful fraction of customers. Getting to 97.5% requires keying on the L1 PROJECTION, which requires the customer to declare which fields each op actually reads. That is integration work with a per-customer schema, not a drop-in — and "drop-in" is exactly what the market expects.

3. THE GLOBAL AGGREGATION NODE. L6b has fan-in 512 and invalidates on essentially every run, poisoning 6,790 model ops (42% of all model ops, ~55% of token spend). Delivering the promised savings requires either restructuring the customer's graph so cluster reconciliation emits per-cluster outputs with per-cluster keys, or a reuse layer expressive enough to key consumers on a slice of an upstream output rather than its whole hash. Neither is free, and the first one means asking the customer to rewrite their pipeline.

4. ROOT CHURN. Prompt / taxonomy / model-id edits on an estimated 15-20% of nightly runs invalidate 100% of the graph. Averaged over a month that alone caps reuse at ~82%, and it is worst in exactly the first year of a customer relationship when they are still tuning prompts weekly. Whatever number you quote from a stable week will not survive contact with a tuning week.

5. BATCHING PULLS THE OTHER WAY. The tuned baseline batches 8 listings per L2 call to amortise the 3,400-token prefix, which is an ~82% input reduction on the largest layer. That batching welds 8 artifacts into one key and raises effective invalidation from 2.5% to 18.3%. Prefix-cache optimisation and content-addressed reuse are in direct tension on this workload and someone has to choose. A reuse layer that requires batch=1 is asking the customer to give up a large, free, already-realised win.

6. THE FREE MECHANISM ALREADY ATE THE SHARED COST. After a tuned baseline the residual bill is ~85% variable payload plus 100% of output. The reuse layer's true ceiling is (1 - effective_invalidation) x (variable input + output), not (1 - invalidation) x total. It is still the majority of the bill — but roughly half of any headline "we cut your bill 90%" figure computed against an uncached baseline is the provider's free cache, not the product.

7. NONDETERMINISM AND FROZEN QUALITY. At temperature > 0, or across provider-side model point-releases, the stored output is not what re-execution would produce. For a published listing corpus, stability is arguably a feature — but it means model-quality improvements do not reach the 97.5% of records served from the store until keys rotate, and a customer who upgrades their model and sees no accuracy change will (correctly) blame the cache.

8. LICENSING KILLS THE CROSS-TENANT MULTIPLIER. MLS content is licensed per-participant under IDX/VOW agreements. An extraction derived from MLS remark text is a derivative work of licensed data, and sharing it across tenants very plausibly breaches the licence even though it is a pure function of public text. The 40x cross-tenant story — the most exciting part of the reuse pitch — is legally unavailable in the largest sub-domain of this vertical. It survives for open marketplace listings (Craigslist, dealer feeds, e-commerce catalogues) and dies for MLS.
confidence:
MEDIUM overall, with the components at different levels.

HIGH confidence: the graph SHAPE. A wide-independent per-listing head, a relational blocking/scoring/adjudication waist where the LLM only touches the ~11% gray band, a per-cluster tail, and exactly one global aggregation node — this is what production entity-resolution over listings looks like, and it is stable across the property, auto-inventory and e-commerce variants. Also high confidence: the tuned baseline (points 1-8 are standard practice and the batch-vs-reuse tension is arithmetic, not opinion), and the grader (a seeded generator with an enumerated corruption grammar gives exact free ground truth; nothing there is uncertain).

MEDIUM confidence: op counts and token sizes. Within roughly ±40% for any given customer. The gray-zone rate (11%), the multi-source cluster rate (26%), the material-conflict rate (62%) and the validation failure rate (2.5%) are experience-calibrated, not measured. The presence and sizing of L8 varies most — some portals template their copy instead and that removes ~40% of output tokens.

LOW confidence: the change rate, and I want to be blunt about it. The SEMANTIC half is properly sourced — NAR's June 2026 1.56M inventory at 4.6 months supply gives ~0.72%/day exit, and Redfin's ~20.2% monthly price-cut share gives ~0.67%/day — and those two are the bulk of the 2.5%. The RAW-BYTES half (my 8-15%/day, and the ~100% snapshot-feed case) is an estimate with no published backing; I searched for MLS/RESO per-day record-change statistics and for Google Merchant Center delta-feed churn and neither exists publicly. Vendors say "much fewer records" and decline to quantify. The 3.6x gap between raw and semantic churn is the most load-bearing claim in this whole spec and it is the least sourced.

WHAT WOULD RAISE CONFIDENCE TO HIGH, in priority order:
1. Two consecutive nightly snapshots of ONE real MLS RESO feed, diffed at both the raw-record and projected level. Half a day of work; converts the single most important number from estimate to measurement, and simultaneously validates the projection thesis.
2. One production customer's per-layer token bill, which would replace every op-count and token-size estimate at once and reveal whether L8 exists.
3. Their existing memo table's hit rate, which tells you directly how much of the theoretical saving is already banked — the difference between a real product and a rederivation of what they built in 2024.
4. A written legal read on whether MLS-derived extraction outputs can be shared cross-tenant. That one answer decides whether the cross-tenant multiplier is a headline feature or a footnote.

Sources:
- [NAR Existing-Home Sales](https://www.nar.realtor/research-and-statistics/housing-statistics/existing-home-sales)
- [NAR Existing-Home Sales Report, June](https://www.nar.realtor/newsroom/nar-existing-home-sales-report-shows-2-4-decrease-in-june)
- [Monthly Indicators — new listings YoY](https://nhar-public.stats.showingtime.com/docs/mmi/x/MonthlyIndicators)
- [Redfin Data Center Metrics Definitions — price drops](https://www.redfin.com/news/data-center-metrics-definitions/)
- [Redfin Methodology](https://www.redfin.com/news/data-center/methodology/)
- [Spark Platform — Efficiently Replicate RETS Data](https://sparkplatform.com/docs/rets/tutorials/replicate)
- [mlsgrid-sync — RESO Web API incremental replication](https://github.com/piotrsenkow/mlsgrid-sync)

customer: An enterprise talent-acquisition org (5k-20k employees, ~400 open requisitions at any time) running an AI screening layer bolted onto its ATS (Workday/Greenhouse/SmartRecruiters), either in-house or via a vendor (HireVue/Covey/Eightfold-class). What they pay for today: per-requisition batch screening that turns a raw applicant pool into (a) a per-criterion scored card with verbatim evidence citations for every candidate, (b) a knockout/pass gate, and (c) a ranked shortlist of ~25 handed to the recruiter. They pay for it because a recruiter reading 257 resumes at 6 min each is 26 hours per req, and because NYC Local Law 144 / EU AI Act high-risk classification force them to retain an auditable, re-derivable score for every applicant — the artifact they are actually buying is the defensible audit trail, not the ranking. Unit economics: ~$8.40 of model spend per 200-candidate full-pool run at Sonnet-class pricing (tuned baseline, measured below), against a fully-loaded recruiter cost of ~$1,300 for the same work.
why_repeated:
Four distinct repeat triggers, and they are not equivalent — this distinction is the whole story in this domain.

(1) POOL GROWTH (nightly, incremental). Applications keep arriving over a 63.5-day median time-to-fill, so the screener runs nightly per open req. Critically, the honest production design here scores ONLY the new arrivals and appends — scores are per-candidate and independent, so appending a candidate does not change anyone else's score. This is already a hand-rolled reuse cache (a `candidate_requisition_score` row keyed on candidate × req × rubric_version × model_version). I state this plainly because it caps the claim: the reuse layer does not get credit for the nightly path.

(2) RUBRIC EDIT (the real repeat run). The hiring manager reviews the first shortlist and recalibrates: "drop the MBA preference, add Kubernetes as a hard requirement, reweight leadership from 3 to 5." Now the whole pool must be re-scored, because a ranked shortlist is COMPARATIVE — you cannot ship a ranking where candidates 1-120 were scored on rubric v1 and 121-200 on v2. Legal will not sign off on it either. Full-pool re-run, no exceptions. Happens ~2-4 times across a 63-day search.

(3) MODEL/PROMPT VERSION BUMP. The vendor ships a new model or a prompt fix. Same comparative-consistency argument forces a full re-score of every open req's pool. ~2×/month.

(4) COMPLIANCE RE-SCORE. Quarterly adverse-impact analysis and the annual LL144 bias audit re-run scoring over historical cohorts to compute selection rates by category. Pure replay of thousands of already-scored candidates.

Plus a fifth, cross-cutting one: the same human applies to multiple reqs at the same employer, and silver-medalist pools get re-screened against new reqs. That is not a repeat *run* but it is a repeat *operation* at the extraction layer.
run_cadence: Per requisition: nightly incremental (new arrivals only, ~5-20 candidates); full-pool re-run roughly weekly per active req when you blend rubric edits (~3 per 63-day search) with vendor model/prompt bumps (~2/month); one full-pool backfill at req kickoff; one full replay per quarter for compliance. Aggregated at a 400-open-req enterprise: ~400 incremental runs/night and ~50-60 full-pool runs/night. The benchmark unit specified below is ONE full-pool run of one requisition (200 candidates), because that is the run the reuse layer is actually competing for.

graph.description:
Structurally this is 200 near-independent per-candidate chains of depth ~9, hanging off a shared 2-op requisition root, converging into exactly one narrow fan-in at the end. It is NOT a chain, and it is NOT 500 flat independent ops — it is a wide bundle of short chains with one shared root and one shared sink. That shape matters because it means changes at the root (rubric) invalidate everything above the extraction layer at once, while the 200 leaf artifacts (resume files) are mutually independent and, uniquely for this domain, IMMUTABLE once submitted.

The critical structural fact for reuse: the graph cleanly splits at layer 5/6. Everything at or below llm_normalize_resume depends ONLY on (resume file bytes, model id) — it is requisition-independent and rubric-independent. Everything from llm_score_group_a upward depends on (resume, rubric, JD, model). That split is worth ~37% of the run's output tokens and is exactly the surface the app-level cache (keyed candidate x requisition) cannot see.

Run totals measured from the layer spec: 3.91M input tokens, 381k output tokens per 200-candidate full-pool run. Concretely: 200 candidates is a requisition ~4 weeks into a 63.5-day search against a 257.6-application mean (Employ 2025), which is the modal case for a re-run.

Sizing rationale for the 6,800-token shared per-requisition prefix used by the scoring layers: screening instructions + safety/anti-prompt-injection preamble (600) + strict output JSON schema (400) + 4 calibrated few-shot examples, each a truncated anchor resume plus gold score JSON (2,800) + job description (1,000) + the anchored rubric: 16 criteria x ~120 tokens for name/definition/1-5 behavioral anchors/weight/knockout flag (1,900). The few-shot anchors are not optional padding — they are what stops score drift between runs, and every production system that has been audited for consistency has them.

Borderline/adjudication fractions are load-bearing on cost: ~20% of the pool clears the shortlist gate and gets a recruiter-facing card; ~12% lands in the +/- band around threshold and gets escalated to a stronger model, because near-threshold scoring variance is what actually reorders the shortlist.

layers.name: fetch_requisition
layers.consumes: nothing (root)
layers.reads_artifacts: requisition record + job description + rubric JSON + few-shot calibration set from the ATS/config store (4 artifacts)

layers.name: list_applicants
layers.consumes: fetch_requisition (1 op per page); ATS API paginated at 50/page
layers.reads_artifacts: ATS application index for the requisition (mutable — this is the only artifact that changes every run by construction)

layers.name: download_resume
layers.consumes: list_applicants (1 of 4 pages per op)
layers.reads_artifacts: one resume PDF/DOCX blob per op — 200 artifacts, immutable once submitted

layers.name: extract_text
layers.consumes: download_resume (1:1)
layers.reads_artifacts: none beyond the blob passed in; OCR/parse via Textract/Tika, ~$1.50/1k pages so worth caching on its own

layers.name: llm_normalize_resume
layers.consumes: extract_text (1:1)
layers.reads_artifacts: none directly; prompt = 800-token extraction instruction+schema (company-wide constant, padded to ~1400 with 2 anchor extractions to clear Anthropic's 1024-token minimum cacheable prefix) + ~1000 tokens of raw resume text (median 1-2 page resume, ~650 words, +15% for PDF extraction noise). Output = normalized JSON: employment spans with ISO dates, employers, titles, education, explicit skill list, location, certifications. THIS LAYER IS REQUISITION-INDEPENDENT.

layers.name: enrich_facts
layers.consumes: llm_normalize_resume (2 ops per candidate: employer->size/industry lookup against an internal company graph; school->ranking + title->IC/M level taxonomy lookup)
layers.reads_artifacts: 3 shared reference tables (company DB snapshot, school ranking table, title taxonomy) — these version quarterly, and when they do they invalidate this layer for the whole tenant

layers.name: llm_score_group_a
layers.consumes: llm_normalize_resume (1:1) + enrich_facts (2:1)
layers.reads_artifacts: the 6800-token shared requisition prefix (instructions+schema+few-shots+JD+rubric), then per-candidate: normalized JSON (700) + enrichment facts (250). Scores the ~9 hard-requirement and skills-match criteria, returning JSON [{criterion_id, score 1-5, evidence_span verbatim, confidence}].

layers.name: llm_score_group_b
layers.consumes: llm_score_group_a (1:1) — issued as turn 2 of the SAME conversation so turn 1's full input and output serve as cached prefix
layers.reads_artifacts: none new; adds a ~150-token instruction switching to the 7 experience-depth / level-fit / trajectory / tenure-stability criteria

layers.name: aggregate_score
layers.consumes: llm_score_group_a + llm_score_group_b (2:1); deterministic integer weighted sum plus knockout mask
layers.reads_artifacts: rubric weights (already fetched)

layers.name: gate_shortlist
layers.consumes: aggregate_score (200:1); vectorized threshold + knockout filter, emits shortlist set (~20% = 40) and borderline band (~12% = 24)
layers.reads_artifacts: threshold config

layers.name: llm_summarize_card
layers.consumes: aggregate_score + gate_shortlist (survivors only — cost control, you do not write prose for the 160 rejects)
layers.reads_artifacts: 400-token role summary + candidate normalized JSON and scores (1400). Emits the 2-4 sentence recruiter-facing rationale with quoted evidence.

layers.name: llm_adjudicate_borderline
layers.consumes: aggregate_score + gate_shortlist (borderline band only)
layers.reads_artifacts: full 6800 requisition prefix + RAW resume text (1000, not the normalized JSON — the point is to re-read the source) + prior scores (1050). Stronger/more expensive model. Emits revised scores with reasoning.

layers.name: llm_rank_shortlist
layers.consumes: llm_summarize_card (40:1) + llm_adjudicate_borderline (24:1) — the single high-fan-in op in the graph
layers.reads_artifacts: 6800 requisition prefix + 40 compressed candidate cards at ~350 tokens each (14000). Emits the ranked list with cross-candidate comparative notes.

layers.name: adverse_impact_stats
layers.consumes: aggregate_score (200:1); deterministic four-fifths-rule selection-rate computation by protected category, required for LL144
layers.reads_artifacts: EEO self-ID data (separate store)

layers.name: writeback_ats
layers.consumes: llm_rank_shortlist + adverse_impact_stats; batched writes of 40 scorecards/page plus the audit record
layers.reads_artifacts: none

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 3-25% new artifacts; 0% mutated artifacts (structural, not statistical)
change_rate.basis:
Derived, with the dominant term sourced. Sourced inputs: Employ 2025 Recruiter Nation / hiring benchmarks report gives 257.6 applications per job in 2025 (up from 207.2 in 2024) and 63.5 median days to fill (SMB 83.5, enterprise 51.7); SmartRecruiters' 2025 benchmark over 89M applications gives a lower 73 applicants/role because it includes low-volume reqs; industry posting-lifecycle data puts ~50% of a posting's total applications in week 1. Arithmetic: 257.6 apps, half in week 1, the rest spread over the following ~8 weeks gives ~16 arrivals/week in weeks 2-9. A req in week 3-4 has a cumulative pool of ~160-180, so week-over-week new arrivals are 16/177 = 9.0%. Range endpoints: 3% for a late-stage req in week 8+ where arrivals have tailed off, 25% for a week-2 req where the pool is still compounding off a small base.

Structural (not statistical, and I want to be explicit that this is a fact about ATS design rather than a measurement): a submitted resume file is IMMUTABLE. No ATS lets an applicant mutate a submitted document in place; a corrected resume is a new attachment with a new id and a new content hash. So the mutation rate on previously-seen resume artifacts is exactly 0%, and pool change is purely additive. This is dramatically more favorable to content-hash reuse than the code domain, where the same file is edited in place run after run.

ESTIMATED, NOT SOURCED — and these are the two numbers that swing the conclusion most, so treat them as the weak link: (a) rubric-edit frequency. I could find no published telemetry on how often a hiring manager revises a structured screening rubric mid-search. My estimate of 2-4 edits per 63-day search comes from the structure of the calibration loop (an edit follows the first shortlist review and typically the first onsite loop), which puts a rubric change on roughly 40% of full-pool re-runs. (b) Repeat-applicant rate — the fraction of applicants who apply to 2+ reqs at the same employer. Search returned only qualitative confirmation that every ATS merges multi-application candidates into one profile, no percentage. My estimate is 8-15% at a professional-hiring enterprise and 25-40% at high-volume/hourly employers or anywhere the careers site prompts 'apply to similar roles'.
change_rate.where_changes_land:
This is the single most important thing about this domain, and it is unusually clean: real changes land at exactly TWO places, and they are structurally separated by the layer-5/6 split.

LEAVES (200 resume artifacts): 0% mutate, ~9%/week are net-new additions. Adding a leaf invalidates that leaf's own chain of ~9 ops and nothing else — per-candidate scores are independent, so a new applicant does not perturb any existing candidate's score. The only op it touches downstream is llm_rank_shortlist, and only if the newcomer clears the gate (~20% chance). So leaf churn is close to the best case a content-addressed reuse system can be handed: ~91% of the per-candidate work is untouched.

ROOT (1 rubric artifact out of 206 = 0.5% of artifact count): changes on ~40% of full-pool re-runs, and when it does it invalidates 100% of the scoring layer, the cards, the adjudication and the ranking — everything above llm_normalize_resume, which is 63% of the run's output tokens. One artifact at 0.5% of the count controls the majority of the cost. Any headline 'only 9% of inputs changed' number is therefore actively misleading here unless you say where.

The saving grace, and it is a real one: a rubric edit almost never touches all 16 criteria. It touches 1-3. If the scoring prompt is sharded so that group A and group B each carry only their own criteria in the reuse key, an edit confined to group B leaves 100% of group A's 200 ops reusable. If the rubric is passed as one blob in a shared prefix, one changed word invalidates all 400 scoring ops. Same workload, same edit, 50% reuse versus 0% reuse, decided entirely by prompt-partitioning granularity.

THIRD CASE, and it is the honest downside: a model/prompt version bump changes the model id, which is in every reuse key by construction. 100% invalidation of all 665 model ops. The reuse layer is worth exactly zero on those runs, and they are roughly 2/month per tenant.

Also worth flagging: the 3 shared reference tables (company graph, school rankings, title taxonomy) version quarterly. When one rolls, it invalidates all 400 enrich_facts ops and everything downstream for every requisition in the tenant simultaneously — a rare but total wipe.

session_structure:
A competent engineer gets this workload to 86% prefix-cached without any reuse layer at all. Measured from the layer spec: 3.35M of the 3.91M input tokens sit in a cacheable prefix. This is the bar, and it is a high one.

Seven things they do, all of which I am crediting to the baseline:

1. NESTED BREAKPOINTS, ordered most-shared-first. The prompt is assembled as [screening instructions + anti-injection preamble + output JSON schema + 4 few-shot calibration anchors] (3,800 tokens, IDENTICAL across every requisition in the tenant) -> breakpoint -> [job description + anchored rubric] (3,000 tokens, identical across every candidate in this req) -> breakpoint -> [per-candidate normalized JSON + enrichment facts] (950 tokens, varies). With ~60 full-pool runs a night on one tenant, the first 3,800 tokens are hot across ALL of them, not just within one req. Engineers routinely miss this and put the JD first; putting the tenant-constant block ahead of the req-constant block is worth another few points for free.

2. ONE WARMING CALL, THEN FAN OUT. This is the failure mode our own field measurement caught (112 real sessions, $1.08 live probe): with a cold prefix and N concurrent callers, every one of the N pays the 1.25x cache-write price because none has finished writing the entry when the others start. Fanning 200 candidates out at concurrency 20 against a cold prefix costs 20 writes instead of 1. So: issue a single throwaway call to populate the 6,800-token prefix, await it, then fan out. One write at 1.25x, then 199 x 2 reads at 0.1x.

3. TIGHT TIME WINDOW, so the TTL never matters. 400 scoring calls at concurrency 20 and ~3s/call is ~60 seconds of wall clock for the whole requisition. That is inside the 5-minute default TTL with 4x headroom, so the engineer does NOT pay for the 1-hour extended tier. Our own measurement found the TTL cliff sits at 1h rather than 5m for long-running agent sessions, but this workload never approaches it — batch screening is bursty and short, which is the ideal shape for provider caching. Requisitions are processed one at a time, not interleaved, precisely to keep one prefix hot at a time.

4. THE TWO SCORING CALLS ARE TURNS IN ONE CONVERSATION. group_b is issued as turn 2, so turn 1's entire 7,750-token input AND its 550-token output are cached prefix for turn 2. Splitting them into two independent calls would re-send the candidate block uncached and lose ~8% of the total. (Note the tension with the sharding point above: making group_b a continuation of group_a maximizes provider caching but couples their reuse keys, so a rubric edit in group A now also invalidates group B. The provider-optimal structure and the reuse-optimal structure are in direct conflict here — that is a genuine, unavoidable tradeoff, not an implementation oversight.)

5. EXTRACTION PREFIX PADDED OVER THE MINIMUM. llm_normalize_resume's natural invariant prefix is only ~800 tokens, below Anthropic's 1,024-token minimum cacheable prefix for Sonnet-class models, so it would silently cache nothing. The engineer pads it to ~1,400 by folding in two anchor extraction examples (which improve schema adherence anyway). Now 58% of that layer's input is cached.

6. BATCH API for the nightly path. 50% off, composes with prefix caching, and the workload is inherently latency-insensitive (results are read by a human the next morning). Orthogonal to the reuse question but it halves the number the reuse layer is measured against, so it belongs in the baseline.

7. NORMALIZED JSON, NOT RAW RESUME TEXT, in the scoring calls. Passing the 700-token structured extraction instead of the 1,000-token raw text shrinks the uncached suffix by 30% and makes it stable under cosmetic resume reformatting.

BASELINE ECONOMICS, computed: untuned = 3.91M x $3 + 381k x $15 = $17.43/run. Tuned = 3.35M x $0.30 + 0.55M x $3 + 381k x $15 = $8.38/run. Provider caching alone removes 52% of total cost. Halve again with the Batch API.

And here is the fact that defines the whole opportunity: after that tuning, OUTPUT TOKENS ARE 68% OF THE REMAINING BILL ($5.72 of $8.38). Provider prefix caching is structurally incapable of touching a single output token. The tuned baseline has already harvested essentially all of the input side and none of the output side.
grader:
Fully deterministic, no LLM anywhere in the loop, ground truth computed for free from the generator's own seed.

CORPUS GENERATION. A seeded generator (numpy PRNG, fixed seed per benchmark instance) emits N=200 candidates. Each candidate starts as a TRUTH RECORD: a JSON object with employment spans [{employer_id, title_id, start YYYY-MM, end YYYY-MM|null}], degree {level, field, institution_id, grad_year}, an explicit skill_id set, location, certification ids. The generator then RENDERS that record into natural-language resume prose through templates with deliberate lexical variation — 4-6 alternative phrasings per bullet, a synonym table over skill surface forms (Kubernetes/K8s/k8s, "led"/"spearheaded"/"owned"), reordered sections, 3 date formats ("Jan 2019 - Mar 2022", "01/2019-03/2022", "2019-2022"), and 3 page layouts — then typesets it to PDF. Rendering to PDF matters: it exercises download_resume -> extract_text -> llm_normalize_resume for real rather than short-circuiting the layers where a third of the reuse surface lives. The generator records the exact character span in the rendered text where each atomic fact appears; that span table is the ground truth for evidence grounding.

RUBRIC. 16 criteria, every one a pure computable predicate over the truth record, so the gold score is a computed value and costs nothing:
- C1 (knockout, boolean): union-merged total months of in-field professional experience >= 60. Union-merge is essential — overlapping spans are the case where naive implementations and LLMs both fail.
- C2 (knockout, boolean): degree.level in {BS,MS,PhD} AND degree.field in a fixed accepted-field list.
- C3, C4 (knockout, boolean): required skill_id present in the truth skill set.
- C5-C10 (graded 1-5): bucketed counts — distinct years at employers with size >= 1000; number of distinct skill_ids intersecting the preferred set, bucketed at fixed thresholds; certifications held; etc.
- C11 (graded 1-5): longest employment gap in months, bucketed (0-2 -> 5, 3-6 -> 4, 7-12 -> 3, 13-24 -> 2, >24 -> 1).
- C12 (graded 1-5): level of the most recent title under a fixed title->IC1..IC6/M1..M3 taxonomy table.
- C13-C16 (graded 1-5): tenure stability (mean span length, bucketed), trajectory (monotonicity of the level sequence), institution tier from a fixed table, recency of the required skill.
Gold weighted total = sum(w_i * s_i) over integer weights, exact integer arithmetic, no floats, no ties ambiguity.

METRICS, all pure computation:
1. Per-criterion exact-match rate: fraction of the 200 x 16 = 3,200 (candidate, criterion) pairs where the emitted integer equals gold.
2. Knockout confusion matrix: exact FP and FN counts on C1-C4 separately. These are the legally consequential decisions and a false negative here is a qualified candidate silently rejected.
3. Shortlist set equality: gold top-25 by weighted total, ties broken by candidate_id ascending (deterministic), against the pipeline's top-25. Report Jaccard and an exact-set-equal boolean.
4. Rank correlation: Spearman rho between the pipeline's 200 weighted totals and gold, computed in scipy.
5. Evidence grounding: every emitted evidence_span must (a) be a verbatim byte-substring of the rendered resume text, and (b) overlap the generator's recorded character range for the fact the criterion cites. Pure string containment plus interval intersection. Catches the failure that matters most in an audit — a plausible-sounding citation to text that is not in the document.
6. REUSE-CORRECTNESS INVARIANT (this is the metric that actually tests the system under evaluation, not the workload). Execute the run twice, once with the reuse store enabled and once with it bypassed, over byte-identical inputs. For every operation served from the store, assert the stored output is byte-identical to the freshly-executed output under the same key. Any mismatch is a key collision, i.e. under-keying — the classic instance being a rubric_version or model_id omitted from the canonical encoding. This is a hard fail regardless of savings, because in this domain an under-keyed hit means a candidate scored against a rubric that was never applied to them, which is a discrimination claim.
7. Cost/latency ledger: input, cache-read-input, cache-write-input and output tokens plus wall time, read from provider response usage fields — measured, never modeled.

PASS RULE for a run: per-criterion exact-match >= 0.92 AND knockout FN == 0 AND evidence-grounding == 1.00 AND reuse-correctness == 1.00 AND top-25 Jaccard >= 0.90. Savings figures are reported only over runs that pass; a run that fails reports no savings at all.

CHANGE INJECTION between runs, seeded to match the production rates established above: append 9% new candidates (fresh truth records, rendered to fresh PDFs); mutate ZERO existing resume bytes (matching the structural immutability fact); on 40% of runs edit the rubric by changing 2 of the 16 criteria (a weight change or a bucket-threshold change, drawn so that on half of those edits both changed criteria fall inside one scoring group and on the other half they straddle both groups — this is precisely the sharding-granularity question); on 8% of runs bump the model id; on 2% of runs roll one reference table. Gold scores are recomputed for free from the truth records under the new rubric, so the grader never drifts.

WHY THIS IS GRADABLE AT ALL: because I redesigned the task away from "does the model agree with a human recruiter" (which needs an LLM judge or expensive human labels and has an irreducible inter-rater disagreement floor) toward "does the model correctly evaluate a set of computable predicates over facts that are genuinely present in a document it must parse". That is still a faithful model of the production task — real anchored rubrics are mostly countable predicates over resume facts, which is exactly why they survive legal review — and it makes ground truth exact and free.
reuse_story:
Three mechanisms, in descending order of how much I believe them.

1. OUTPUT TOKENS ARE THE RESIDUAL, AND ONLY OPERATION-LEVEL REUSE TOUCHES THEM. After the tuned baseline, 68% of the remaining bill ($5.72 of $8.38 per run) is output tokens, which the provider's prefix cache cannot address by construction — it caches what you send, never what the model generates. Reuse serves the stored output without generating it. This is the one argument in this domain that is not a rounding error, and it survives contact with a strong baseline rather than depending on the baseline being weak.

2. THE REQUISITION-INDEPENDENT EXTRACTION LAYER, WHICH THE APP-LEVEL CACHE STRUCTURALLY CANNOT SEE. llm_normalize_resume depends only on (resume bytes, model id). Every ATS-integrated screener already caches at candidate x requisition granularity, so when a candidate applies to a second req, the app cache misses on everything and re-extracts a resume it has already parsed. Content-addressed keying hits. At an estimated 8-15% repeat-applicant rate this is worth 8-15% of a layer carrying 140k output tokens per 200 candidates — modest, but it is pure incremental gain over what the customer has already built, and it compounds with silver-medalist pools and sourced-candidate rescreens where the repeat rate is far higher.

3. IMMUTABLE LEAVES MAKE FULL-POOL RE-RUNS UNUSUALLY CHEAP. Resume files never mutate; pool change is purely additive at ~9%/week. On a full-pool re-run triggered by a rubric edit confined to one scoring group, the reuse profile is: extraction 91% hit, enrichment 91% hit, unedited scoring group 91% hit, edited scoring group 0%, cards/adjudication/ranking mostly invalidated. Working that through the cost model lands near $4 saved on an $8.38 tuned run, ~47%, and nearly all of it is output tokens. Compare code, where the same file is edited in place run after run and reuse keys break at the root constantly — this domain hands the reuse system a genuinely easier problem.

4. THE COMPLIANCE REPLAY IS a near-100% hit by construction. A quarterly adverse-impact re-score over an unchanged historical cohort with an unchanged rubric and model is the ideal case: every key hits, the run costs approximately zero, and the customer gets the byte-identical scores that the audit actually requires. Byte-identical reproduction is not a nice-to-have there — under LL144 the auditor is checking that the stated scores are what the system produces, and a re-sampled model output that differs slightly is a finding.
reuse_threats:
Six, and the first one is close to decisive.

1. THE CUSTOMER HAS ALREADY BUILT A COARSE VERSION OF THIS. Every production ATS screener stores a `candidate_requisition_score` row keyed on (candidate_id, requisition_id, rubric_version, model_version) and skips re-scoring on a match. That is the Bazel model at whole-candidate granularity, hand-rolled, already shipped, already free. It fully covers the nightly incremental path — the highest-frequency repeat trigger. So the reuse layer's incremental value is NOT "9% changed therefore 91% reuse"; it is only the delta the app cache misses: finer-than-candidate granularity (per-criterion-group invalidation on a partial rubric edit) plus cross-requisition sharing of the extraction layer. Both are real. Neither is 91%. Any evaluation that measures against a screener with no score table is measuring a straw man.

2. THE PROVIDER-OPTIMAL AND REUSE-OPTIMAL STRUCTURES ACTIVELY CONFLICT. Maximum prefix caching wants one long shared prefix (all 16 criteria in one block) and group_b as a continuation turn of group_a. Maximum reuse wants the rubric sharded per criterion group with independent keys and the two scoring calls decoupled. You cannot have both. Decoupling them to gain partial-invalidation costs ~8% of the tuned baseline's prefix savings on every run, including the ~60% of re-runs where the rubric did not change at all. On this workload that trade is plausibly net-negative, and it is exactly the shape of the finding we already measured elsewhere: shaping the workload for the reuse layer degrades the provider-native path that was already working.

3. MODEL BUMPS ZERO IT OUT, AND THEY ARE FREQUENT. The model id is in every key by construction, so a version bump invalidates all 665 model ops. At ~2 bumps/month against a ~weekly full-pool cadence, roughly a third of full-pool re-runs get nothing from the reuse layer. Worse, model bumps and rubric edits are the two triggers that CAUSE full-pool re-runs, so the reuse layer's hit rate is anti-correlated with the very events that generate its traffic.

4. PII AND CROSS-TENANT PROHIBITION. Resumes are PII under GDPR/CCPA and employment AI is high-risk under the EU AI Act. A reuse store holding candidate extractions cannot be shared across tenants — not because it is technically unsound (content hashes are content hashes) but because no enterprise DPA permits it and no auditor would accept it. So "across days and users" collapses to "across days, within one tenant". The cross-customer pooling that would make the extraction layer genuinely valuable is off the table, and it is off the table for reasons no engineering can fix. Retention rules cut further: several jurisdictions require applicant data deletion at 1-2 years, forcing eviction of exactly the long-lived entries that pay best.

5. NONDETERMINISM MAKES A HIT AND A MISS DIFFERENT EVEN WHEN BOTH ARE CORRECT. Provider serving is not bit-reproducible even at temperature 0, so a stored output is one sample from a distribution. For a rubric criterion near a judgment boundary, reuse-on and reuse-off produce different shortlists that are both defensible. This is fine for cost accounting and actively GOOD for compliance (reuse gives you the reproducibility the auditor wants and the provider does not), but it means any quality comparison must be structural — which is why the grader above is built on computable predicates and byte-identity rather than semantic agreement.

6. THE UNSOURCED NUMBERS ARE THE LOAD-BEARING ONES. Rubric-edit frequency (my 40%-of-runs estimate) sets how often the root invalidates, and repeat-applicant rate (my 8-15%) sets the size of mechanism 2. I found no published data for either. If rubric edits are actually near-universal on re-runs and touch criteria in both groups, mechanism 3 collapses to roughly nothing and only the extraction layer survives.
confidence:
Medium.

HIGH confidence in: the graph shape and layer decomposition (this architecture — extract, normalize, enrich, score-against-rubric, gate, summarize survivors, rank — is what both the published multi-agent screening work and shipped vendor products converge on, and the convergence is forced by cost: you cannot afford a call per criterion or prose for every reject); the token sizes, which are bottom-up from resume length, anchored-rubric structure and few-shot calibration rather than guessed; the 0% mutation rate on resume artifacts, which is a structural property of every ATS rather than a statistic; the tuned-baseline construction and its arithmetic (86% cacheable, $8.38/run, output = 68% of residual), which is computed not asserted; and the observation that the app-level score table already exists and caps the claim.

MEDIUM confidence in: the 9% weekly change rate. The volume inputs are sourced (257.6 apps/job, 63.5 days to fill, ~50% of applications in week 1) but the arithmetic combining them into a per-run figure is mine, and it is sensitive to which requisition week you sample — 3% to 25% across the search lifecycle is a wide band around a 9% central estimate.

LOW confidence in: rubric-edit frequency (40% of re-runs) and repeat-applicant rate (8-15%). Both unsourced, both load-bearing.

WHAT WOULD RAISE IT, in priority order: (1) One ATS vendor's telemetry on rubric_version increments per requisition — a single `SELECT count(distinct rubric_version) FROM requisitions GROUP BY req` against any production screening database settles the most important unknown in this spec. (2) The same database's distinct-candidate-to-application ratio, which settles the repeat-applicant rate exactly. (3) A tenant's actual run log split by trigger (incremental / rubric edit / model bump / compliance), which would replace my estimated cadence with a measured one and would immediately show whether full-pool re-runs are frequent enough for any of this to matter. (4) Running the specified grader once end-to-end against a real provider, which would confirm or refute the 86%-cached baseline figure — that number is computed from the layer spec, not yet measured, and our own field work has repeatedly found measured cache behavior diverging from the modeled kind, always in the direction of the baseline being stronger than assumed.

customer: A mid-size fintech/e-commerce data platform team (4-6 analytics + data engineers) running Airflow/dbt Cloud over Snowflake or BigQuery. Warehouse ingests ~40 source tables (avg ~35 columns) from ~6 upstream systems (app Postgres via Fivetran, Stripe, Salesforce, a Kafka event stream, two internal services) into ~350 dbt models with ~1,400 dbt tests. Data contracts live as versioned YAML in the dbt repo (`contract: enforced` column/type blocks plus accepted_values, not_null, uniqueness, freshness and row-count bounds). Today they pay for: dbt Cloud + a data-observability vendor (Monte Carlo / Anomalo / Metaplane, $30-100K/yr), and increasingly for an LLM triage layer bolted onto the nightly DAG. What they are actually buying with the LLM is not detection — the deterministic tests already detect — it is (a) semantic judgement about whether a detected change is a real contract breach or expected drift, (b) blast-radius reasoning across the dbt lineage, (c) a drafted remediation PR, and (d) a decision to halt or release the load before downstream marts and reverse-ETL fire. The economic object being protected is "don't publish bad data to the CRM/finance close"; the LLM bill itself is small (~$1.75/nightly run/pipeline, ~$640/yr for one pipeline; this customer runs ~12 such pipelines plus hourly validation on 8 hot tables, so ~$15-25K/yr of model spend).
why_repeated: The work is repeated because the data is new, not because anyone asked for it again. Every scheduled load produces a fresh partition, and the contract must be re-enforced against that partition before downstream models run — this is a gate in the DAG, not an analysis someone requests. The *questions* asked are byte-for-byte the same every night ("does table X still conform to contract X, and are today's value distributions consistent with the documented semantics of each column?"); only the data under the question moves. That is the defining property of this domain and the source of both its reuse promise and its reuse trap: the query is perfectly stable and the evidence is 100% fresh. Secondary repetition drivers: the same upstream teams break the same contracts repeatedly (a Salesforce admin adding a picklist value, a mobile release adding an event field), so a meaningful minority of triage decisions are literal repeats of ones made weeks earlier.
run_cadence: Primary: nightly full-contract validation at ~02:00 local, once per pipeline per day (365 runs/yr/pipeline, ~4,400 runs/yr across 12 pipelines). Secondary: hourly validation on 8 hot tables (~24 runs/day, a ~1/5-scale subset of the same graph). Ad-hoc: re-run on every dbt PR in CI against a sampled dev partition (~10-15/week), and a manual re-run after each remediation. Wall clock of a nightly run is 6-15 minutes, dominated by warehouse profiling SQL, not by model latency; the model calls themselves land in a ~90-180 second burst. Critically for baseline analysis: consecutive nightly runs are 24 hours apart, which is far outside any provider prefix-cache TTL, and the hourly runs sit at exactly 3,600s — on the measured 1h-tier cliff edge.

graph.description: A wide, shallow base that narrows to a single convergent tail. 200 of the 299 ops are a 40-wide independent fan-out over source tables (5 tool ops per table), feeding a 40-wide model layer (semantic_check), which then funnels through a sharply narrowing incident tail (6 breach classifications -> 2 impact analyses -> 2 remediations) into exactly one run_report with fan-in 51. The critical path is only 10 deep and 8 of those 10 levels are single-threaded tail work on ~2 issues; 96% of the compute is in the 40-way base. Two structural facts dominate everything: (1) the 40 data-partition artifacts change 100% of the time and sit upstream of every one of the 51 model ops, so naive key-only reuse on model calls is ~0%; (2) the terminal run_report has fan-in 51, so it recomputes on essentially every run no matter what is reused beneath it. The graph is NOT a chain and it is NOT 500 independent ops — it is a 40-wide independent layer with a deterministic tool substrate under it and a short serial incident tail on top.
