The engineered decision that decides this workload's entire reuse profile is whether layer L7 (profile_delta) emits raw numeric statistics or tolerance-banded verdicts; see change_rate and reuse_threats.

layers.name: L1_contract_load
layers.consumes: nothing (root)
layers.reads_artifacts: one data-contract YAML block per source table from the dbt repo at the pinned commit SHA: column names, types, nullability, accepted_values enums, min/max ranges, PK declaration, max_null_pct, min_row_count, max_staleness, owner, semantic description per column

layers.name: L2_schema_snapshot
layers.consumes: nothing (root); MUST be marked volatile — this is the live observation the validation exists to make
layers.reads_artifacts: live INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS + table DDL for one source table in the warehouse (~35 rows: name, data_type, is_nullable, ordinal_position, comment)

layers.name: L3_manifest_load
layers.consumes: nothing (root)
layers.reads_artifacts: dbt manifest.json for the project (~350 nodes) parsed to a node->parents lineage index; 4-9 MB raw, ~40K tokens if serialized whole, but the op emits only the compacted index

layers.name: L4_history_query
layers.consumes: nothing (root)
layers.reads_artifacts: the run-history table: last 30 runs of per-table row counts, null rates, distinct counts, check outcomes and prior triage verdicts (40 tables x 30 days of banded stats)

layers.name: L5_schema_diff
layers.consumes: L1_contract_load (1:1) and L2_schema_snapshot (1:1)
layers.reads_artifacts: none (pure function of upstream outputs)

layers.name: L6_profile
layers.consumes: L2_schema_snapshot (1:1, to know which columns exist to profile)
layers.reads_artifacts: today's partition of one source table in the warehouse (10^5 to 10^8 rows). Emits raw per-column stats: count, null_count, distinct_count, min, max, mean, stddev, p50/p95, top-10 value histogram for low-cardinality columns

layers.name: L7_profile_delta
layers.consumes: L6_profile (1:1) and L4_history_query (40:1)
layers.reads_artifacts: none (pure function). THIS IS THE PIVOTAL LAYER. It converts raw stats into tolerance-banded verdicts against the 30-day baseline: row_count -> {within_seasonal_band | low | high} with the band from the contract's min_row_count and a 30-day MAD; null_rate -> {0 | <0.1% | 0.1-1% | 1-5% | >5%} bucket plus a breached/ok flag vs contract max_null_pct; distinct_count -> ratio band; new enum values listed explicitly (set difference vs contract accepted_values, exact); numeric range -> in/out of contract bounds. Output is a stable-hashing document on a healthy table-night and changes only when a band boundary is crossed.

layers.name: L8_check_run
layers.consumes: L1_contract_load (1:1, which tests to run)
layers.reads_artifacts: today's partition of one source table (dbt test / Great Expectations suite: ~35 tests per table — not_null, unique, accepted_values, relationships, freshness, row-count bounds). Emits {test_id, status, failure_row_count} per test; on an all-pass table the output is a fixed-order list of PASS/0 rows and hashes identically run to run

layers.name: L9_semantic_check
layers.consumes: L1_contract_load (1:1), L5_schema_diff (1:1), L7_profile_delta (1:1), L8_check_run (1:1) — fan-in 4
layers.reads_artifacts: none directly; all evidence arrives via upstream outputs. Prompt = shared system+rubric+few-shot+output JSON schema (~2,800 tok, identical across all 40 calls) ++ contract block (1,200) ++ schema snapshot (900) ++ schema diff (60, usually 'no diff') ++ banded profile delta (2,200) ++ check results (700). Task: per-column conformance verdict, and specifically the judgement the deterministic tests cannot make — is a new enum value a legitimate business event or a corrupt write, is a distribution shift seasonal or a broken upstream join, does the column's data still match its documented semantic meaning. Output: JSON array of {column, verdict in {conforms, drift_benign, drift_suspect, breach}, defect_class, evidence}.

layers.name: L10_breach_classify
layers.consumes: L9_semantic_check (1:1 for the ~6 tables emitting drift_suspect or breach) and L4_history_query (6:1) — fan-in 2
layers.reads_artifacts: none. Prompt = severity policy + escalation rubric (~3,000) ++ the finding (800) ++ 30-day recurrence history for that check (1,500) ++ full contract text for the table (1,200) ++ SLA/owner routing table (1,500). Output: {severity in {block, warn, accept}, contract_clause_id, is_recurrence, rationale}.

layers.name: L11_lineage_extract
layers.consumes: L3_manifest_load (2:1) and L10_breach_classify (1:1 for block-severity only) — fan-in 2
layers.reads_artifacts: the dbt manifest index plus the compiled SQL of ~12 downstream models transitively depending on the breached column, plus exposure/reverse-ETL definitions

layers.name: L12_impact_analysis
layers.consumes: L11_lineage_extract (1:1) and L10_breach_classify (1:1) — fan-in 2
layers.reads_artifacts: ~12 downstream dbt model .sql files surfaced by L11 (~8,000 tok) . Prompt = system (1,500) ++ lineage subgraph (4,000) ++ downstream model SQL (8,000) ++ the breach (900). Output: which downstream marts/exposures corrupt, whether the corruption is silent or loud, recommended halt scope.

layers.name: L13_git_blame
layers.consumes: L10_breach_classify (1:1)
layers.reads_artifacts: git log/blame on the contract YAML file and the owning upstream repo for the affected column

layers.name: L14_remediation
layers.consumes: L12_impact_analysis (1:1), L10_breach_classify (1:1), L13_git_blame (1:1) — fan-in 3
layers.reads_artifacts: the full contract YAML file to be patched (~2,500 tok) and the repo's dbt YAML conventions doc (~4,000 tok). Output: a unified-diff YAML patch amending the contract or tightening a test, a backfill plan if data is already published, and a PR title/body.

layers.name: L15_run_report
layers.consumes: all 40 L9_semantic_check + all 6 L10_breach_classify + 2 L12_impact_analysis + 2 L14_remediation + L4_history_query — fan-in 51
layers.reads_artifacts: none. Prompt = system (1,200) ++ 40 condensed per-table verdicts (10,000) ++ 6 breach classifications (2,700) ++ 2 impact analyses (1,800) ++ 2 remediations (2,600) ++ run metadata (500). Output: the machine-readable finding set the grader scores, plus decision in {proceed, proceed_with_warning, halt} and a human Slack summary.

layers.name: L16_publish
layers.consumes: L15_run_report (1:1) and L14_remediation (1:1)
layers.reads_artifacts: none; writes to Slack/PagerDuty and opens a GitHub PR

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 27% (hard floor, every run) to ~37% on a heavy release day; 27-28% on weekends
change_rate.basis:
Decomposed by artifact class over the 148 artifacts, because they have wildly different churn and averaging them hides the whole story.

CLASS A - DATA (40 daily partitions, 27.0% of all artifacts): changes 100% of the time, every run, by construction. This is not an estimate, it is the definition of a scheduled load. This alone sets a hard floor of 27.0% on the change rate and nothing can lower it.

CLASS B - LIVE SOURCE SCHEMAS (40, 27.0%): SOURCED. Qiu, Li & Su (FSE 2013, 10 OSS database applications, >160K revisions) measure ~90 atomic schema changes per year per application schema, with 60-90% of changes concentrated in 20% of tables and ~40% of tables never changing at all. Skoulis/Vassiliadis (via EDBT 2023 paper-160, 2.8M GitHub projects -> 327 schema histories) find 132 of 327 (40%) never changed the schema after the initial commit. The EDBT 2023 case study (mapbox/osm-comments-parser) records 9 schema-active commits out of 119 total commits over 22 months = 7.6% of commits touch the schema, ~0.4 schema-changing commits/month per schema file. Scaling: 6 upstream systems x ~90 changes/yr, but only the ~40 replicated tables are in scope and ~40% of tables are rigid, so I estimate ~0.4 changed source-table schemas per nightly run = ~1% of class B, ~0.3% of all artifacts. Equivalently: roughly 1 night in 3 sees at least one source-schema change somewhere, and when it does it touches 1-2 tables.

CLASS C - CODE/CONFIG (40 contract YAMLs + 1 manifest + 25 dbt model SQL + 1 checks config = 67 artifacts, 45.3%): ESTIMATED, anchored on commit-size literature I am recalling rather than fetched (Alali/Kagdi/Maletic ICPC 2008 and successors: commit size is heavily right-skewed, median ~2-3 files touched). A 4-6 person analytics team merging 5-15 dbt PRs/week at ~2-3 files each gives ~2-4 changed artifacts on a weekday and 0 on a weekend. Note the manifest.json is a derived artifact that changes whenever ANY of the 350 models changes, so it flips on most weekdays even though it is 1 artifact. Weekday ~2.5/67 = 3.7% of class C; blended over a 7-day week ~1.7% of all artifacts.

TOTAL typical = 40 (data) + ~2.5 (code) + ~0.4 (schema) = 42.9/148 = 29.0%. Weekend = 40.4/148 = 27.3%. Heavy release day (a 12-file dbt refactor + 2 schema changes) = 54/148 = 36.5%.

CONFIDENCE SPLIT: the 27.0% data floor is certain. The class-B schema rate is sourced to peer-reviewed measurement but transferred from OSS application schemas to a warehouse's replicated source tables, which is a real extrapolation. The class-C rate is an estimate from team size and general commit-size priors, not from this domain's data.
change_rate.where_changes_land:
This is the decisive fact and it is unfavourable. The 27% that changes unconditionally every single run (the data partitions) sits at the ROOT of the widest part of the graph: each partition feeds L6_profile and L8_check_run, which feed all 40 L9_semantic_check model calls, which feed the entire tail including the fan-in-51 L15_run_report. So the artifact class with a 100% change rate is an ancestor of 100% of the model operations. Under strict input-hash keying, cross-run reuse of model ops is ZERO for this workload, always, regardless of how stable the contracts are. The rare changes (schemas, contracts) also land at roots, but at roots of narrow slices — a contract change invalidates 1 of 40 base columns of the fan-out, and a dbt model SQL change invalidates only the manifest and the ~2 tail ops that read lineage.

What rescues the workload is NOT input-hash reuse but Bazel-style EARLY CUTOFF / change pruning: L6_profile must always re-execute (its input changed) but L7_profile_delta's banded OUTPUT is unchanged on a healthy table-night, and L8_check_run's all-PASS output hashes identically run to run. Once an op re-executes and produces a byte-identical output, its descendants' keys are unchanged and stay cached. I estimate the banded delta plus check verdicts plus schema diff are all unchanged on ~85-92% of table-nights, so ~34-37 of 40 L9_semantic_check calls are reusable, i.e. ~70% of model ops and ~65% of input tokens. The tail is not reusable: L10-L14 fire precisely on things that just changed (only recurring known-benign breaches reuse, ~15-20%), and L15_run_report with fan-in 51 recomputes on essentially every run.

So: changes land at roots, the always-changing root dominates, and the entire value of the reuse layer in this domain rests on early cutoff at exactly one op (L7_profile_delta) — and on the width of the bands it quantizes with, which is a detection-sensitivity dial, not a free parameter.

session_structure:
A competent engineer would extract most of the available prefix-cache value here, and the reuse layer has to beat this, not a naive per-call baseline.

1. CACHE-FIRST PROMPT ORDER for L9. Of the 7,800 input tokens per semantic_check, exactly 2,800 (system prompt, conformance rubric, few-shot examples, tool definitions, output JSON schema) are byte-identical across all 40 calls. Put that block first, one cache_control breakpoint after it. It is comfortably above the 1,024-token minimum. The remaining ~5,000 tokens (contract, schema, banded delta, check results) are genuinely unique per table and are not cacheable across tables at any ordering.

2. PRIME BEFORE FANNING OUT — this is the single largest and most commonly missed win. This repo's own live billing probe (docs/FIELD_CACHE_MEASUREMENT.md, $1.08 of measured spend) shows that under genuinely simultaneous fan-out every caller is billed cache_creation: at 0 ms inter-arrival skew all 5 of 5 callers wrote and none read, so the cached arm paid 5 x 1.25x with zero reads and was strictly worse than not caching. One writer emerges only once skew exceeds ~1 s. A 40-way parallel table validation fired from an Airflow task group is exactly the 0 ms regime. So: issue ONE priming call (or table 1's call) against the shared 2,800-token block, await its response, then fan out the remaining 39 concurrently. That converts 40 writes into 1 write + 39 reads: 39 x 2,800 x 0.9 = 98,280 tokens off the input bill = 22.9% of the run's 429,800 input tokens, ~$0.29 of the $1.75 run, for free.

3. SECOND BREAKPOINT AFTER THE STABLE PER-TABLE BLOCK. Order each L9 prompt as [shared rubric | breakpoint | contract + schema snapshot (2,100 tok, stable across runs) | breakpoint | banded delta + check results (2,900 tok, volatile)]. Within a nightly run this buys nothing (each table is seen once), but it is what makes the HOURLY hot-table runs work, and it is required for the segmented-invalidation property: this repo's X3/X4 probe found that with a SINGLE breakpoint any byte change anywhere — even a trailing space or a token appended at the tail — gives 0% recovery of the whole block, so putting volatile evidence past the last breakpoint is the only thing that protects the stable head.

4. ONE GROWING CONVERSATION FOR THE TAIL. L10 -> L12 -> L14 -> L15 for a given issue should be a single conversation with a breakpoint per turn, not 4 independent calls. This is the within-session growing-prefix mechanism that this repo measured at a 97.63% hit rate carrying 99.86% of all realized cache value across 112 real sessions and 9,224 billed requests. It recovers most of the ~57K tokens of tail input.

5. TTL CHOICE. The model burst is ~90-180 s wide, so the default 5m ephemeral tier suffices for the fan-out and avoids the 2x write premium of the 1h tier. Buy 1h only if warehouse profiling SQL can stall a model call past 5 minutes. For the HOURLY runs the gap is exactly 3,600 s, which the field measurement puts precisely on the cliff (median recovery 100% in the 1800-3600 s bucket, 0.0% in the 3600-7200 s bucket) — so a competent engineer schedules the hot-table validation every 55 minutes rather than every 60, buys the 1h tier, and keeps the stable per-table blocks alive across runs. That is slightly absurd and it works.

6. BATCHING AS THE ALTERNATIVE. Putting 5 tables per call (8 calls instead of 40) eliminates 32 x 2,800 = 89,600 repeated prefix tokens outright with no 1.25x write premium at all — comparable to the caching win and cheaper. Real teams mostly do not, because per-table calls give clean retries and per-table output parsing; a strong baseline should be measured both ways.

7. CROSS-RUN: ZERO, AND THIS IS THE HONEST OPENING FOR THE REUSE LAYER. Nightly runs are 24 h apart, an order of magnitude beyond the maximum 1 h TTL. No prompt ordering, no breakpoint placement and no tier purchase recovers a single token across two consecutive nightly runs. The tuned provider baseline therefore saves ~17-23% of input cost WITHIN a run and exactly 0% ACROSS runs. Any cross-run claim by a reuse layer is claiming territory the provider genuinely does not occupy — but it must be measured as an increment on top of the ~20% the baseline already takes, not on top of an uncached run.
grader:
Fully deterministic, no LLM anywhere in the grading path, ground truth exact and free because a seeded generator MANUFACTURES the truth before the agent sees anything.

GENERATOR (seeded, reproducible from an integer): emits a 30-run series representing 30 consecutive nightly loads. For run N it produces (a) 40 table DDLs + 40 contract YAMLs, (b) 40 daily partitions of synthetic rows drawn from the per-column distributions DECLARED in the contract, so conformance is definitionally checkable, (c) a dbt project of 350 models with a real lineage graph, (d) a 30-day run-history table. Churn is dialled to the measured rates: data regenerates every run (100%); contract/dbt files mutate on a seeded weekday schedule at ~2.5 files/weekday, 0 on weekends; source schemas mutate at ~0.4 tables/run.

DEFECT INJECTOR: with seeded probability applies labelled mutations from a fixed catalogue, each with a predetermined severity. BLOCK class: DROP_COLUMN referenced downstream, TYPE_NARROW (string->int), RENAME (drop+add at equal cardinality — the one every tool lies about), NULL_RATE_SPIKE past contract max_null_pct, ENUM_NEW_VALUE outside accepted_values, VOLUME_DROP below min_row_count, FRESHNESS_LAG past max_staleness, UNIQUE_VIOLATION on the declared PK, RANGE_VIOLATION outside declared bounds. WARN class: ADD_COLUMN (additive, compliant), TYPE_WIDEN (int->bigint). PASS/DECOY class: BENIGN_DISTRIBUTION_SHIFT inside declared tolerance, SEASONAL_VOLUME_SWING inside the seasonal band, ENUM_VALUE_ALREADY_IN_CONTRACT. The decoys are load-bearing — they are what separate a competent agent from one that halts the pipeline every night.

AGENT OUTPUT CONTRACT: L15_run_report must emit JSON {decision: proceed|proceed_with_warning|halt, findings: [{table, column, defect_class, severity}]}.

SCORING (all exact, all free):
1. HALT CORRECTNESS (primary, binary per run): decision == halt iff the injector planted >=1 BLOCK defect. This is the business outcome and it is a single exact comparison.
2. FINDING F1: set-match on the exact tuple (table, column, defect_class) against the injector's label set. Recall punishes missed breaches; precision punishes firing on decoys.
3. SEVERITY EXACT-MATCH RATE over correctly identified findings.
4. REUSE-INTEGRITY GATE (the one that actually grades the reuse system, not the agent): run the identical seeded 30-run series twice — once with the reuse store cold, once warm — and require the two series' finding sets and decisions to be byte-identical after canonicalization. ANY divergence is a lossy-reuse violation and fails the benchmark outright regardless of tokens saved. This is what stops a reuse layer from buying its hit rate by widening the L7 bands.
5. COST: per run, record provider-reported input / output / cache_read / cache_creation tokens (and the 5m vs 1h split) plus warehouse bytes scanned. Headline metric is cost(warm run N) / cost(tuned-baseline run N) for N in 2..30, reported only for series that passed gate 4 at equal F1.

Why this is gradeable at all: the deterministic layers (L5, L7, L8) already produce machine-checkable verdicts, and the only genuinely subjective judgement — benign drift vs real breach — is made objective by having the generator decide it in advance and construct the data to match. No human and no judge model is ever consulted.
reuse_story:
Provider prefix caching is structurally incapable of crossing a 24-hour scheduling gap, so 100% of the cross-run surface is unclaimed. The question the same identical query is asked of new data every night, and 73% of the run's input tokens sit in 40 semantic_check calls whose prompts are 36% shared boilerplate and 64% evidence that, on a healthy table-night, says exactly what it said last night.

The mechanism that would pay is NOT input-hash action caching — that returns ~0% here, because the 40 data partitions change unconditionally and are ancestors of every model op. It is Bazel-style EARLY CUTOFF at one specific op, L7_profile_delta. That op must always re-execute (its raw input changed), but it emits tolerance-BANDED verdicts, and on a healthy table-night the banded document is byte-identical to yesterday's. Same for L8_check_run (all-PASS with fixed test ordering and zero failure rows) and L5_schema_diff (empty on ~99% of table-nights). When all three upstream outputs hash unchanged, the downstream L9_semantic_check key is unchanged and the model call is served from the store without being issued. I estimate 34-37 of 40 L9 calls hit on a typical night: ~70% of model ops, ~65% of input tokens, and since the tuned provider baseline already takes ~20% within-run and the reused calls are the same ones that would have read the shared prefix, the honest incremental over the tuned baseline is roughly 50-58% of input cost.

The second, smaller mechanism is genuine cross-run and cross-CUSTOMER repeat triage: the same upstream teams break the same contracts repeatedly, and the same defect_class on the same column with the same banded evidence is a literal key hit weeks later. That covers maybe 15-20% of the tail ops. It is small in tokens but it is the part with no provider-side analogue at all.

The cadence multiplies whatever the rate is: 4,400 nightly runs/year plus ~105,000 hourly hot-table runs/year across 12 pipelines, all asking a question that never changes.
reuse_threats:
Six, roughly in descending order of how likely each is to kill the thesis in this domain.

1. REUSING AN OBSERVATION OF LIVE STATE IS A VALIDATION BYPASS. L2_schema_snapshot is the most cacheable op in the graph (~99% stable) and it is the one that must NEVER be served from a store: if the reuse layer returns yesterday's INFORMATION_SCHEMA, the pipeline reports "contract holds" without having looked at the schema, and the product silently becomes a no-op. Same for L6_profile and L8_check_run. The ops with the highest naive hit rate are exactly the ops whose whole purpose is to be re-executed. Any system here needs a volatility annotation, and applying it removes ~120 of the 299 ops (all the high-stability tool reads) from the eligible set before any value is counted. A reuse layer that reports a high hit rate on this workload without that annotation is reporting a bug.

2. THE EARLY-CUTOFF WIN IS PURCHASED WITH DETECTION SENSITIVITY. Every token of reuse in the L9 layer comes from L7's banding. Widen the null-rate buckets or the seasonal row-count band and the hit rate goes up and the false-negative rate goes up with it — in a VALIDATION product, where a missed breach is the worst possible failure and a saved dollar is worth almost nothing next to a corrupted finance close. The band width is a dial that trades money against the thing the customer is actually buying. It is not a free lossless optimization and must not be sold as one; the grader's reuse-integrity gate exists specifically to catch a system that quietly turns this dial.

3. COMPUTING THE REUSE KEY CAN COST MORE THAN THE OPERATION. L6_profile's key needs the content hash of today's partition. Getting a true content hash of a 10^8-row table means a full scan — $1-5 of BigQuery slot/bytes cost against a $1.75 total model bill for the entire run. The reuse layer would be net-negative on arithmetic alone. The escape is real but narrows the addressable market sharply: Delta Lake and Iceberg hand you a snapshot ID that IS an exact free content version, and Snowflake/BigQuery expose LAST_ALTERED / last_modified_time (cheap, but a coarser proxy that flips on no-op rewrites and misses nothing only by luck). Lakehouse customers get free reuse keys; classic-warehouse customers may not, and for them this workload is unservable.

4. MODEL NONDETERMINISM POISONS THE TRANSITIVE KEY. L9's output hash is an ancestor key for the whole tail. At temperature > 0 it varies run to run even on identical inputs, so 40 reusable calls still produce 40 different hashes and the tail never hits. Even at temperature 0, provider-side batching nondeterminism makes raw text unstable. Mitigation is to canonicalize the key on the PARSED JSON verdict rather than the raw completion — which works, but means the store is keyed on a lossy projection of the output, and two semantically different rationales collapse to the same key.

5. PROMPT AND MODEL VERSION CHURN COLD-STARTS EVERYTHING. The rubric in L9's shared 2,800-token prefix is exactly the artifact the data team iterates on — every false positive that wakes someone at 3am produces a rubric tweak. Each tweak invalidates 100% of the store. If the rubric changes weekly, the store is cold ~1 day in 7 and the effective saving drops by ~14% before anything else. A model upgrade nukes it entirely.

6. THE FAN-IN-51 TERMINAL OP NEVER REUSES, AND THE ABSOLUTE STAKES ARE SMALL. L15_run_report depends on all 51 model outputs, so it recomputes on essentially every run — that is correct behaviour, and it is only 18,800 tokens, but it caps the achievable saving. More importantly the whole run costs $1.75. Saving 55% of it saves $0.96/run, ~$4,200/yr across the customer's 12 pipelines and hourly runs. That is a real number but it is small next to their $30-100K observability spend, and it means the reuse infrastructure has to be nearly free to operate and effectively invisible to install. This domain is a good TECHNICAL demonstration of cross-run reuse — the cleanest one I can construct, because the query is perfectly stable and the provider genuinely cannot cross the 24h gap — and a mediocre commercial one.
confidence:
Medium. SOURCED and reasonably firm: the source-schema churn rate (Qiu/Li/Su FSE 2013 via the EDBT 2023 study I extracted directly from the PDF — ~90 atomic changes/yr/schema, ~40% of tables never change, 60-90% of changes in 20% of tables, 9/119 commits schema-active in the case study; Skoulis/Vassiliadis 132/327 histories with zero post-initial change); the 27.0% unconditional data-churn floor (definitional); and the provider-caching baseline behaviour, which rests on this repo's own live-measured probes rather than on vendor docs — the 0 ms-skew fan-out inversion (5/5 callers write, 0 read), the 3,600 s TTL cliff (100% -> 0% median recovery at the tier boundary), single-breakpoint all-or-nothing invalidation, and the 97.63%/99.86% within-session continuation dominance across 112 sessions and 9,224 billed requests.

ESTIMATED, not sourced: the 40-table/350-model/1,400-test shape (a plausible mid-market composite, not a surveyed median); all per-op token sizes; the ~6 triage-worthy findings and ~2 blocking issues per night; the class-C code-churn rate of ~2.5 files/weekday (anchored on recalled commit-size literature, which I did not fetch and should not be treated as cited); and the 85-92% table-night stability of the banded profile delta, which is the number the entire reuse estimate hangs on and which I have not measured at all.

WHAT WOULD RAISE IT, in priority order: (1) instrument one real customer's nightly DAG for 30 days and log, per table-night, whether the banded profile delta and check verdicts are byte-identical to the prior night — this single measurement converts the 65% input-token reuse estimate from a guess into a fact, and it is cheap because it needs no model calls; (2) determine empirically whether real implementations pass raw numeric profiles or banded ones to the model, since raw profiles make cross-run reuse structurally zero and I picked banded because it is what I believe competent teams do; (3) pull the actual git history of a production dbt repo to replace the recalled commit-size prior with a measured per-day changed-file count; (4) price the reuse-key computation on a real warehouse to confirm whether Iceberg/Delta snapshot IDs are available, because threat #3 is potentially disqualifying and is answerable in an afternoon.

customer: A 30-50 engineer product org running a Python monorepo service (~1,200 source files / ~180k LOC, ~480 existing test files, 71% line coverage) with a coverage floor enforced in CI. They pay for an agentic test-generation product -- Qodo Cover (open-source agent, CLI + GitHub Action), Diffblue Cover, or most commonly an in-house Claude-based agent wired into CI -- plus the provider API bill underneath it. What they pay for is a nightly job that finds functions below the coverage floor, writes tests for them, verifies the tests compile / pass / raise measured coverage, and opens one PR per package with the survivors. The buyer's line item is "coverage debt burn-down"; the costs they feel are the per-run API bill (~$54/run uncached) and 35-45 min of CI runner time.
why_repeated: Three independent reasons, all real. (1) The coverage floor is a ratchet: new code lands daily and drags coverage down, so the sweep must run again to claw it back. (2) Acceptance is human-gated and lossy -- Meta's TestGen-LLM reported 75% of generated test classes built, 57% passed reliably, only 25% raised coverage, and 73% of surviving recommendations were accepted; so roughly 4 of every 5 targets attempted last night are still uncovered tonight and get attempted again. (3) Model/prompt changes: teams re-run the whole sweep after a model upgrade or prompt-template edit to see whether previously-failed targets now succeed. Crucially, most deployments run this as a FULL repo sweep, not an incremental one, because the tool's selection step is coverage-driven ("everything below 80%"), not diff-driven. The repeat is therefore ~95% identical work by construction -- which is as much an indictment of the pipeline as an opportunity.
run_cadence: Nightly, scheduled (typically 02:00 repo-local, on a CI runner). Some orgs run it weekly on a Sunday. The same product also has a per-PR mode that fires on every pull request (25-40x/day) but that mode reads only the diff and is a different, far less reuse-friendly workload -- see reuse_threats. This benchmark specifies the nightly sweep.

graph.description: A wide layered DAG with a narrow, poisonous neck. The top is a 3-op chain (inventory -> full-suite coverage run -> coverage parse) whose inputs are literally every file in the repo. Below the neck it fans out to 340 near-independent per-target subgraphs, each ~6 ops wide, that never talk to each other. Everything re-converges at one PR-assembly op. So: not a chain, and not 500 independent ops either -- 340 independent subtrees sitting under a whole-repo root and over a whole-repo sink. Token economics per run: ~12.6M model input tokens, ~1.10M output tokens; at Sonnet-class rates ($3/$15 per M) that is ~$38 + ~$17 = ~$54/run uncached. Wall clock 35-45 min at 16-way parallelism, of which ~15 min is the 570 pytest invocations and ~12 min is model latency. Two structural facts decide whether reuse works: (1) generate_tests has fan-in 8 and one of those 8 (coverage_parse) is a whole-repo artifact -- keep that edge as-is and a one-line change anywhere invalidates all 340 generate ops, reuse rate exactly zero; (2) run_candidate_tests depends on the environment, not just the repo, so the 570 wall-clock-dominant tool ops are keyed on the lockfile.

layers.name: repo_inventory
layers.consumes: nothing (root)
layers.reads_artifacts: git tree: paths + blob hashes of all 1,686 tracked files (hashes only, not contents)

layers.name: coverage_baseline_run
layers.consumes: repo_inventory (1 op)
layers.reads_artifacts: all 1,200 source + 480 test files + conftest.py + pyproject.toml + uv.lock + CI config. Runs pytest --cov --cov-branch --cov-report=xml. 4-25 min wall clock.

layers.name: coverage_parse
layers.consumes: coverage_baseline_run (1 op)
layers.reads_artifacts: coverage.xml (~4MB); emits per-file uncovered line ranges and unhit branches. NOTE: real implementations do this as ONE op, so its key contains every source file hash and it invalidates every single night, poisoning every descendant. Splitting it into 1,200 per-file keyed slices is a precondition for any reuse here, and it is a code change the customer must make.

layers.name: import_graph
layers.consumes: repo_inventory (1 op)
layers.reads_artifacts: AST-parses all 1,200 source files; emits module->imports and symbol->definition-site maps used to select context

layers.name: exemplar_read
layers.consumes: repo_inventory (1 op)
layers.reads_artifacts: one high-coverage hand-written test file each, chosen as house-style exemplars

layers.name: conventions_synthesis
layers.consumes: exemplar_read (10 ops)
layers.reads_artifacts: the 10 exemplar test files + conftest.py + pyproject.toml; emits fixture inventory, parametrize idioms, mocking policy, naming rules

layers.name: target_read
layers.consumes: coverage_parse (1 op) -- the ranked list of 340 files below the 80% floor
layers.reads_artifacts: one source file under test (~600 LOC)

layers.name: existing_test_read
layers.consumes: target_read (1 op). 40 of the 340 targets have no test file, hence 300 not 340.
layers.reads_artifacts: the target's existing test file (~350 LOC)

layers.name: context_gather
layers.consumes: target_read (1) + import_graph (1); 4 ops per target
layers.reads_artifacts: 2-4 neighbour files each, in four kinds: (a) definition sites of imported types/dataclasses, (b) two call-sites of the target function elsewhere (ripgrep), (c) nearest package conftest.py and shared factories, (d) one sibling test file in the same package as a local style sample

layers.name: generate_tests
layers.consumes: conventions_synthesis (1) + coverage_parse (1) + target_read (1) + existing_test_read (1) + context_gather (4) = fan-in 8
layers.reads_artifacts: transitively: 1 target source, 1 existing test, ~3 neighbour sources, conftest.py, the target's uncovered-line list

layers.name: run_candidate_tests
layers.consumes: generate_tests or repair_tests (1 op each): 340 first attempts + 230 retries
layers.reads_artifacts: candidate test file, target module, AND the whole installed environment (lockfile-pinned dep versions, DB fixture image, PYTHONHASHSEED). pytest <candidate> -x, 15-60s. NOT a pure function of the repo.

layers.name: repair_tests
layers.consumes: generate_tests or prior repair_tests (1) + run_candidate_tests (1) = fan-in 2
layers.reads_artifacts: nothing new; re-sends the generate prompt plus the failing candidate and its traceback. ~45% of first attempts fail to build or pass (consistent with Meta's 75% build / 57% pass), and ~50% of those fail again: 153 + 77 = 230 repairs at max_iterations 3.

layers.name: coverage_delta_check
layers.consumes: run_candidate_tests (1 passing) + coverage_baseline_run (1) = fan-in 2
layers.reads_artifacts: target module + accepted candidate; re-runs coverage scoped to that module and diffs against the baseline slice. Candidates not strictly raising branch coverage are dropped here.

layers.name: lint_dedupe
layers.consumes: coverage_delta_check (1 op)
layers.reads_artifacts: candidate test + ruff.toml + existing test file (AST-level duplicate-assertion check); runs ruff format + ruff check --fix

layers.name: pr_assembly
layers.consumes: lint_dedupe (290 surviving ops)
layers.reads_artifacts: nothing new; summarises accepted diffs and coverage deltas into PR bodies grouped by package

layers.name: commit_push
layers.consumes: pr_assembly (1 op)
layers.reads_artifacts: git index; writes ~290 test files across ~25 branch/PR pairs

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 1-12% of source files between two consecutive nightly runs; 15-35% between two weekly runs; ~100% for the per-PR mode of the same product
change_rate.basis: ESTIMATE, assembled from sourced components plus one direct measurement. SOURCED: (a) commit shape -- a study of 1M commits across the 24 most active Java projects on GitHub finds most commits touch 1-10 files and most touch 1-4 SOURCE files, heavy-tailed (Characterizing Commits in Open-Source Software, SBQS 2022, dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3571473.3571508); (b) PR size -- median GitHub PR ~20 lines changed, Google median 24, Linux 32, Chrome 78, and Code Climate Velocity's 2024 data puts the median org at 197 LOC/PR (insights.adadot.com/2023/11/23/does-size-matter-in-pull-requests-insights-from-30k-developers/, docs.velocity.codeclimate.com/en/articles/2913568-pull-request-size); (c) rework -- GitClear's analysis of 211M changed lines from Google/Microsoft/Meta/enterprise repos finds code revised within two weeks of commit rose 3.3% pre-AI -> 5.7% (2024) -> 7.1% (2025), i.e. churn is rising (gitclear.com/ai_assistant_code_quality_2025_research). MEASURED: I ran the churn calculation directly on this repo (348 tracked .py files, 313 commits/90d): median 3 .py files per commit, mean 6.4, p90 14, max 81; distinct still-existing .py files touched in 1 day = 6 (1.7%), 7 days = 21 (6.0%), 14 days = 47 (13.5%). ASSUMED: the scale-up to a 1,200-file repo with 30-50 engineers merging 25-40 PRs/day -- 30 PRs x ~4 source files, minus overlap on hot files, gives ~70-100 distinct files/day = 6-8%; a 5,000-file enterprise monorepo with the same team gives 1.5-2%. I take 4% as typical. There is no published figure of the form 'X% of a repo's files change per day'; that composite is my derivation, not a citation, which is why sourced=false.
change_rate.where_changes_land: Real changes land at the LEAVES of the artifact graph -- individual source files, each read by exactly one target_read and a few context_gather ops. But the naive OPERATION graph puts them at the ROOT, and that mismatch is the whole story. Three amplification paths turn 4% file churn into much more op invalidation: (1) WHOLE-REPO ROOTS -- coverage_baseline_run and coverage_parse read every file, so their keys change every night without exception; if generate_tests keeps its edge to a monolithic coverage_parse, invalidation is 100% at 4% churn, and that is what the shipped tools actually do. (2) TRANSITIVE CONTEXT EDGES -- each generate op reads ~3 neighbour files it does not own, and churn concentrates in hub modules (models, config, base classes, the store layer); a hub is imported by 3-6% of files in this repo (measured: 14/348 for the store module, 12/348 for the engine module) and 10-20% in enterprise monorepos with a shared models layer, so one hub edit invalidates 40-80 of the 340 targets. (3) ENVIRONMENT EDGES -- a Dependabot/Renovate lockfile bump, 2-5x/week, is a single artifact change that invalidates all 570 run_candidate_tests and all 290 coverage_delta_check ops at once. Net: 4% raw file churn maps to roughly 10-15% generate-op invalidation on a normal night, and to 100% of the execution layer on the 2-5 nights/week a lockfile moves. Churn is also Pareto-distributed -- the same ~15% of files absorb most of it week after week -- which is good for the cold tail (the other 85% stays reusable indefinitely) and bad for the value story, because the churny files are exactly the ones the customer wants tested.

session_structure:
A competent engineer gets a great deal here for free, and the reuse layer must beat this, not the naive $54 run.

Prompt layout for generate_tests, longest-lived prefix first:
[1] system prompt + test-writing instructions + output schema -- 1.2k tokens, byte-identical across all 340 calls and across every run for months.
[2] conventions_synthesis output + 3 verbatim exemplar test files -- 8.0k, identical across all 340 calls in a run, stable for weeks.
[3] shared fixture inventory: root conftest.py, factory/mock helpers, pytest+ruff config -- 6.0k, changes ~weekly.
---- cache breakpoint (15.2k cacheable) ----
[4] per-target tail: target source 7.0k + existing test 4.2k + context bundle 5.6k + uncovered-line list 0.6k.

That is 15.2k of 20.4k input tokens cacheable (75%). Further tuning a good engineer does:
- SORT TARGETS BY PACKAGE and insert a second breakpoint after package-level context (package conftest, package-shared types). Within a package of ~14 targets that lifts the cacheable prefix to ~18k of 24k. Free, and the highest-leverage line of code in the job.
- KEEP REPAIRS IN THE SAME CONVERSATION as their generate call, so the repair's 22k of prior context is a cache read at 0.1x and only the ~2.2k traceback+candidate is fresh. Repairs are 40% of model calls, so this alone is worth ~$14/run -- and it means the reuse layer gets almost nothing extra from repairs, which are already ~90% discounted.
- WARM-ONE-THEN-FAN-OUT: fire a single call and wait for it to return before releasing the other 339 concurrently, otherwise all N pay the 1.25x cache write and the shared prefix is written N times. This is the biggest single mistake in naive parallel agent code.
- Use the 1h TTL tier for segments [1]-[3] so they survive the whole 35-45 min sweep instead of expiring at 5 min mid-run.
- Do NOT put the coverage-gap list high in the prompt; it is per-target and hoisting it destroys the shared prefix.

Resulting tuned cost: generate input drops 6.94M -> ~2.30M billable (one write at 1.25x + 339 reads at 0.1x + 340 x 5.2k fresh); repair input drops 5.57M -> ~1.01M. Input ~$10 vs ~$38; output unchanged at ~$17. TUNED BASELINE ~= $26.5/run vs $54 naive. Provider prefix caching, used correctly, already removes half the bill.

Its hard ceiling: TTLs top out at ~1h and the cadence is 24h, so every nightly run starts with a completely cold provider cache and nothing in segments [1]-[3] survives from last night. Free within a run, zero across runs -- that gap is the only ground the reuse layer has to stand on.
grader:
Fully deterministic, no LLM, ground truth free and exact by construction, because the repo under test is GENERATED rather than found.

GENERATOR: `gen_repo.py --seed S --files 1200 --run T` emits a synthetic Python repo from ~30 module templates (validators, state machines, parsers, date/arithmetic helpers, small class hierarchies, retry wrappers), 3-8 functions per module. Because the generator built the control flow, it writes a sidecar truth.json containing exactly: every (file, function, branch_id, branch_condition) tuple; which branches the pre-seeded partial test suite already covers; and per function M=5 seeded MUTANTS (comparison flip, off-by-one boundary, dropped null guard, swapped operands, inverted early return), each stored as a pre-generated mutant source file with a known id. No LLM produces ground truth and it costs nothing.

RUN T+1: `gen_repo.py --seed S --run T+1 --churn 4 --hotspot-pareto 80/20` applies a seeded change script to p% of modules so 80% of edits land in 20% of files. Edit kinds are mixed deliberately: (a) SEMANTIC -- add a branch, move a boundary constant; (b) COSMETIC -- reformat whitespace, rewrite a docstring, rename a private helper; (c) HUB -- edit a module imported by 15% of files. (b) changes the file hash without changing anything a test should care about; (c) exercises transitive invalidation. The split is recorded so reuse rate can be reported separately for semantic vs cosmetic vs hub churn -- precisely where a content-hash key and a semantic key diverge.

EXECUTION: pinned container, network disabled, PYTHONHASHSEED=0, frozen clock, pytest -p no:randomly.

SCORING, all computed from files on disk:
- Gate 1 BUILD: `pytest --collect-only` exit 0 for every emitted test file; failures score 0 for that target.
- Gate 2 PASS: `pytest` exit 0 on the emitted suite.
- Gate 3 DETERMINISM: run the suite twice; pass/fail sets must be byte-identical (catches flaky, time- and random-dependent tests).
- Gate 4 NON-TAMPERING: sha256 every source file before and after; any change fails the whole run (catches "make the test pass by editing the code").
- Score A COVERAGE: from `coverage json --show-contexts` with --branch, (branches newly covered by emitted tests) / (branches truth.json marks coverable-and-uncovered-at-baseline). Exact rational.
- Score B MUTATION KILL: for each of the 5N seeded mutants, swap in the mutant file and run the emitted suite; killed = suite fails. Score = killed/total. This is the anti-`assert True` defence and the thing that stops a reuse layer from "saving money" by serving vacuous tests. Fully deterministic -- mutants are files with ids, not generated on the fly.
- Score C COST: provider-reported input / cache-write / cache-read / output tokens, ops executed vs ops served from the store, wall-clock seconds. Recorded, not scored.

PRIMARY METRIC: dollars and wall-clock at matched quality. A reuse-enabled run PASSES only if Score A and Score B are each within 2 percentage points of the no-reuse control on the same seed; it is then ranked by Score C dollars and wall-clock. A reuse layer that serves a stale test for a function whose signature changed does not quietly win on cost -- it fails Gate 1 and is disqualified. One that serves a stale test which still compiles but no longer exercises the new branch loses on Score A. Both failure modes are caught with no human and no judge model.
reuse_story:
Two distinct mechanisms, one strong and one weak; conflating them is how this gets oversold.

STRONG (wall-clock, tool layer): 570 run_candidate_tests + 290 coverage_delta_check ops -- ~15 of the 35-45 min -- are pure re-execution of pytest over inputs that did not move. If 88% of targets are untouched, ~750 of those 860 executions are keyed-identical and skippable. Provider prefix caching cannot touch this at all; it is not a model call. This is the cleanest win in the workload and it is denominated in CI-runner minutes, which the customer also pays for.

WEAK-BUT-REAL (dollars, model layer): the 24h cadence exceeds every provider TTL, so the tuned baseline's 15.2k shared prefix is written cold every single night. A cross-run key store serves the ~88% of generate_tests ops whose 8 inputs are all unchanged straight from disk: no input tokens, no output tokens, no latency. Ceiling is roughly $26.5 x ~12% invalidated = ~$3.2/run of unavoidable model spend, so ~$23/run or ~$700/month on one repo, plus ~13 min/night of runner time.

The part that genuinely composes: conventions_synthesis is a fan-in root consumed by all 340 generate ops and changes only when the exemplar test files change (weeks). Under a correct key it is served from the store for months and, because its output hash then stays constant, it contributes nothing to any descendant's invalidation. That is the transitive property doing real work -- a stable root keeps 340 subtrees stable.

Cross-user / cross-branch reuse is the second-order story: six engineers with feature branches off the same main each run this sweep, and the ~96% of files identical across their branches produce identical keys. Provider caching shares nothing between them; a key store does.
reuse_threats:
Strongest first, and the first is close to fatal.

1. THE INCUMBENT IS FREE AND TRIVIAL. `git diff --name-only HEAD@{1}` piped into a per-file skip is ~30 lines of bash and captures most of the same savings, because this graph's per-target subtrees are independent and file-scoped. A general reuse-key store has to beat THAT, not the naive full sweep. Its honest marginal value over file-level skipping: (a) partial invalidation -- skipping is all-or-nothing per file, whereas a keyed store still reuses the 4 context_gather ops and the coverage slice of a file whose docstring changed; (b) cross-branch/cross-user sharing, which file-skip cannot do because each branch has its own HEAD@{1}; (c) reuse of run_candidate_tests. I estimate that at 20-35% on top of file-level skipping, not 90%.

2. THE WHOLE-REPO ROOT. As shipped, generate_tests transitively depends on one coverage_parse over one coverage.xml over the entire repo. That key changes every night, always, driving reuse to exactly 0%. Making this workload reusable requires the customer to restructure coverage_parse into 1,200 per-file keyed slices -- a real change in their pipeline, not something a drop-in layer can do. And if the slicing leaks (file X's coverage legitimately changes because unrelated file Y's new test imports X), the invalidation comes straight back.

3. run_candidate_tests IS NOT A PURE FUNCTION. It depends on installed dependency versions, the DB fixture image, the clock, the RNG. Key it on the lockfile and a Dependabot bump (2-5x/week) invalidates all 860 execution-layer ops at once, erasing the strong win on those nights. Key it on less than the lockfile and you will eventually serve a cached PASS for a test the current dependency set fails -- a correctness bug in a system whose entire pitch is "this test provably raises coverage".

4. FLAKINESS POISONS THE STORE. A flaky test that happened to pass gets its PASS cached permanently, and the coverage-delta claim built on it is then wrong forever, and wrong silently.

5. CACHING KILLS RETRY SEMANTICS. max_iterations exists because resampling at temperature>0 IS the repair mechanism. If a target failed all 3 attempts last night and its keys are unchanged, a reuse layer serves the same 3 failures tonight and the target can never recover. You need an explicit policy -- do not cache negative outcomes, or put an attempt index in the key -- and that policy carves out the ~45% of model calls that are repairs.

6. MODEL PINS. Any model id or sampling-parameter change invalidates 100% of model ops by construction. Snapshots rotate and teams upgrade at least quarterly: expect 3-6 total-invalidation events per year.

7. THE VALUE IS WHERE THE REUSE ISN'T. The 4% churned files are exactly the ones with fresh uncovered code -- the ones the customer wants tested tonight. The 96% served from the store is work whose output was already reviewed and merged last night. The honest framing is not "we cut the bill 90%" but "the bill should always have been 4% of that, and the full sweep was the bug." Any customer already running the per-PR/incremental mode has near-zero reuse surface here: for them every run's input diff is 100% new, and this benchmark measures nothing they would pay for.
confidence:
MEDIUM overall, and unevenly distributed.

HIGH confidence: the graph SHAPE (whole-repo neck -> 340 independent subtrees -> single sink) and the fact that the provider prefix cache is worth ~50% here but zero across a 24h gap. Both follow from the published architecture of Qodo Cover (source file + existing test + coverage report + failed-test logs per prompt, --max-iterations, --desired-coverage) and from arithmetic on TTLs, not from guesswork.

MEDIUM: the failure/repair rates (45% first-attempt failure, 230 repair calls). These are extrapolated from Meta's TestGen-LLM figures (75% built, 57% passed reliably, 25% raised coverage) on Kotlin at Meta, applied to Python at a much smaller org. Could be off by +/-15 points, which moves the model-token total by ~20%.

LOW: the 4% nightly change rate as a point estimate. The component distributions are sourced and the local measurement is real, but the scale-up assumes a team size and PR cadence. The range 1-12% is what I would actually defend; the 4% is a midpoint.

WHAT WOULD RAISE IT, in order of value per hour spent: (1) instrument ONE real nightly test-gen run at a customer -- op counts, token histograms per layer, first-attempt failure rate, wall-clock split -- which settles the medium and most of the low band in a single night; (2) compute day-over-day distinct-source-file churn on 3-5 customer repos of different sizes and team ratios, replacing the derivation with a measurement; (3) measure how often lockfiles actually move in those repos, since that single number decides whether the strong (tool-layer) win survives contact with reality; (4) run the control experiment that matters most -- tuned-prefix-cache baseline vs `git diff` file-skip vs full reuse-key store on the same seeded repo -- because threat #1 says the second of those three may already capture most of the value.

customer: A platform/API-governance team at a company that ships a public or partner-facing HTTP API (~200 operations, ~450 component schemas) to a dozen named consumers — the buyer for oasdiff Pro, Bump.sh, Optic, Buf Schema Registry, Postman API Governance. Today they pay for three things, in this order of willingness: (1) a merge-gating CI check that fails a PR when the spec introduces a breaking change (this part is already 100% deterministic — oasdiff/openapi-changes/buf breaking, no LLM anywhere); (2) a published, human-readable changelog and migration guide per release; (3) per-consumer notification — "Acme's integration calls POST /v1/transfers and reads `.source_balance`, which you just removed." Pricing is per-API or per-seat, low thousands/yr; the LLM budget inside it is small, which matters for any reuse economics. The second and third items are where model calls actually live. Secondary buyer, same graph inverted: a fintech that CONSUMES 6-10 vendor APIs (Stripe, Plaid, Adyen, Shopify) and pays to be told, before the vendor's version pin rolls, which of its own call sites break.
why_repeated: The API keeps shipping. Every release boundary produces a new (base, head) spec pair and the whole review runs again against a spec that is 92-99% identical to last time. It is not run once because the artifact under review is a living contract with a monotonically advancing version, and because the output (changelog, migration guide, consumer notifications) is a per-release deliverable with a publication deadline. There is also within-release repetition that nobody talks about: the same spec pair gets reviewed on the feature PR, again on the release branch, and again at tag time, plus CI reruns after flakes — 3-5 near-identical executions per genuine release.
run_cadence: Two cadences, and conflating them is the main way people get this workload wrong. (a) The mechanical merge gate fires on every PR that touches the spec — measured on twilio/twilio-oai, spec-touching commits arrive in bursts around releases; for a mid-size API in active development this is 10-25/week. That gate contains ZERO model calls in production today. (b) The full LLM review — the graph specified here — fires at release boundaries. Measured cadence of the real artifact: stripe/openapi's stable `openapi/spec3.json` changed 12 times in the ~10 months to 2026-08 (roughly monthly, tracking Stripe's dated API versions); twilio/twilio-oai's spec bundle is regenerated every 2-4 weeks. So: weekly for a fast-moving internal API, monthly for a large stable one. Benchmark run = one release boundary. Critical consequence: the inter-run gap (7-30 days) is 200-700x the provider prefix cache TTL, so provider caching contributes exactly nothing across runs.

graph.description: A wide-fan-out layered DAG with a narrow synthesis tail, and one structural feature that dominates every reuse question: the fan-out width is set by a deterministic differ that runs BEFORE any model call. Layers 1-2 are pure tool work (fetch, normalize, oasdiff). Layer 3 fans out one model call per CHANGED operation — 24 of the API's 200, because the differ already scoped the work. Layer 4 fans out 117 cheap ripgrep/manifest tool ops over 9 flagged endpoints x 12 consumer repos. Layer 5 fans out one model call per (flagged endpoint, consumer that actually calls it) = 27. Layer 6 is a parallel model sweep over description-only changes that oasdiff structurally cannot see (20 ops) — this is the layer that justifies an LLM being here at all. Layer 7 rolls up per consumer (7). Layer 8 is a single wide-fan-in synthesis reading all 78 upstream verdicts (52k input). Layer 9 emits. Total ~522k input tokens and ~52k output tokens per run. Measured grounding for the widths: on stripe/openapi spec3.json the last release pair (d5d11f66 -> af5309ca) had 589 operations, 1,440 schemas, 66 raw-changed operations of which 44 were structural and 22 docs-only, and 55 changed schemas of which 43 structural and 12 docs-only — a 2:1 structural:docs-only ratio that the 16+8 split in layer 3 and the 20 ops in layer 6 reproduce at 200-operation scale. oasdiff on that same pair emitted 54,396 raw findings that deduplicate to 737 (rule, endpoint) pairs across 587 endpoints, which is why layer 2 must include a normalizer/bucketer before any model sees the diff. The hub problem: EVERY Stripe operation directly $refs `error`, and the transitive closure of a median operation covers 865 of 1,440 schemas — so any operation-level key that resolves refs transitively is dirty on 100% of releases. Correct depth-bounded closure: depth-1 median 2 schemas / 18.8% of ops affected; depth-2 median 7 / 45.7%; depth-3 100%.

layers.name: fetch_normalize
layers.consumes: nothing — these are the graph roots
layers.reads_artifacts: op1: base spec at previous release tag (git show); op2: head spec at candidate tag; op3: API-gateway usage export, rolling 90 days, per (consumer, endpoint, response-field) access counts; op4: policy bundle (deprecation policy, versioning policy, notification SLA, previous release's published changelog). Each op canonicalizes JSON/YAML: sorts keys, strips x- vendor extensions on an allowlist, resolves internal $refs to a depth-bounded form, and emits a per-operation and per-schema content hash table.

layers.name: mechanical_diff
layers.consumes: fetch_normalize — 2 upstream ops each (base + head normalized specs)
layers.reads_artifacts: normalized base and head. op1: `oasdiff changelog -f json` (full change set); op2: `oasdiff breaking -o ERR -f json`; op3: a normalizer that (i) collapses the $ref-path explosion — on Stripe one enum addition produced 53,020 raw entries because paths like `error/payment_intent/latest_charge/anyOf[#2:Charge]/balance_transaction/...` are enumerated combinatorially — (ii) buckets surviving findings by (path, method), and (iii) emits per-endpoint finding slices of ~600 tokens. For a 200-operation API expect 2,000-8,000 raw findings deduplicating to 150-400 (rule, endpoint) pairs.

layers.name: op_triage
layers.consumes: mechanical_diff (1 op: the normalizer's slice for this endpoint) + fetch_normalize (the two spec hash tables). 16 structurally-changed operations + 8 docs-only ones, matching the measured 2:1 ratio.
layers.reads_artifacts: This operation's before/after subtree (measured Stripe median 522 tokens each, p90 1,891) + its depth-1 referenced schemas before and after (measured median 1,182 tokens each, p90 3,492) + the endpoint's mechanical finding slice (~600) + the endpoint's row from the usage manifest, which consumer ids touch it and which response fields they read (~300) + the relevant deprecation-policy excerpt (~800) + a shared 2,500-token system rubric enumerating the breaking-change taxonomy. Output: strict JSON {severity: none|cosmetic|additive|minor-breaking|breaking, rule_ids[], affected_json_pointers[], rationale}.

layers.name: callsite_search
layers.consumes: op_triage — 1 upstream op each (only the 9 endpoints whose triage returned minor-breaking or breaking fan out here)
layers.reads_artifacts: 9 flagged endpoints x 12 consumer client repositories = 108 ripgrep/AST-index queries for the endpoint path, its operationId, and each affected json_pointer's field name; plus 9 usage-manifest queries returning per-consumer 90-day call counts and field-read counts. Deterministic, cheap, and the single most reusable layer in the graph.

layers.name: consumer_impact
layers.consumes: op_triage (1 verdict) + callsite_search (~4 grep results). 9 flagged endpoints x a measured-typical 3 of 12 consumers that actually touch a given endpoint.
layers.reads_artifacts: The op_triage verdict (700) + the endpoint before/after (~1,000) + this consumer's matched call sites with +/-20 lines of surrounding source (~4 sites x 350 = 1,400) + this consumer's contract tier, notification SLA and prior migration history (~400) + a 2,000-token shared rubric. Output: {consumer_id, breaks: bool, blast_radius, concrete_migration_steps[], deadline}.

layers.name: prose_semantics
layers.consumes: mechanical_diff (1 op: the normalizer's docs-only change list). 8 operation-level + 12 schema-level description-only changes, scaled from the measured Stripe counts (22 docs-only ops and 12 docs-only schemas at 589 ops / 1,440 schemas).
layers.reads_artifacts: Before/after `description`, `summary`, `example` and `default` text plus the enclosing schema for context (~1,800) + a 2,000-token rubric of prose-break patterns (unit changes, documented-default changes, pagination-cap reductions, silently dropped idempotency or ordering guarantees, 'now required in practice' language) + a 1,200-token glossary of this API's prior prose-break precedents. This layer exists because oasdiff scores exactly 0 on this class by construction — it is the only reason a model is in the pipeline. Output: {is_semantic_break: bool, evidence_span, severity}.

layers.name: consumer_rollup
layers.consumes: consumer_impact — ~4 upstream ops each (7 of the 12 consumers accumulate at least one finding)
layers.reads_artifacts: All consumer_impact verdicts for this consumer (~4 x 600 = 2,400) + the previous release's notification to this consumer, for tone and continuity (~1,500) + the notification template and SLA policy (~1,200). Output: a drafted per-consumer migration notice, ~1,200 tokens.

layers.name: release_synthesis
layers.consumes: op_triage (24) + consumer_impact (27) + prose_semantics (20) + consumer_rollup (7) = 78 upstream ops. The single widest fan-in in the graph.
layers.reads_artifacts: All 78 upstream verdicts (24x700 + 27x600 + 20x400 + 7x1200 = 49k) + the versioning/deprecation policy (~3k). Output: the public changelog, a risk summary, and a go/no-go recommendation, ~3,000 tokens.

layers.name: emit
layers.consumes: release_synthesis (1) and consumer_rollup (7) — 1 upstream op each
layers.reads_artifacts: Writes CHANGELOG.md, posts the PR/release comment, and opens 7 per-consumer tickets or draft emails. No artifacts read.

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 26-100% at file granularity; 0.6-8% at operation granularity (measured median), with a p90 of ~11% and an observed tail to 34%
change_rate.basis: MEASURED, not estimated, for the spec artifacts — I cloned the two real spec repositories and computed operation-level and schema-level content-hash churn across consecutive real release pairs. Scripts and downloaded specs are at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-jamesyang-Documents-GitHub-Brevitas-Systems/30a08619-bfdd-4d15-a8c6-1c8b59d5d979/scratchpad/ (churn.py, churn2.py, twchurn.py, cosmetic.py, specs/, plus an oasdiff 1.29.1 binary). (1) stripe/openapi openapi/spec3.json, 11 consecutive release pairs from 2025-11-05 to 2026-07-29, 585-589 operations and 1,271-1,440 schemas: percentage of operations added/modified/removed per release median 5.8%, mean 8.2%, min 0.0%, max 34.4%; percentage of component schemas changed median 4.5%, mean 5.7%, max 19.8%. One pair (f4ac6d9->d5d11f6) was byte-identical, 0.0%. (2) twilio/twilio-oai, 11 consecutive release commits over 2026-01 to 2026-08, 60 spec files and ~1,550 operations: percentage of SPEC FILES whose content hash changed median 20.0% / mean 27.6%, but percentage of OPERATIONS changed median only 0.6% / mean 2.2% / max 10.3%. (3) The gap between those two Twilio numbers is the most useful measurement here: across 7 pairs, a median of ~50% of content-changed spec files contained ZERO operation change (one release touched all 54 files and only 4 had any operation change — 93% cosmetic). (4) Same effect at element level on Stripe: of 66 raw-changed operations in the last pair, only 44 differed after stripping description/summary/example/title — 33% were docs-only; of 55 changed schemas, 43 structural and 12 docs-only. (5) The 58% headline is at the granularity of the 19 declared artifacts, and it is arithmetic rather than measured: base spec (always differs, it is last run's head), head spec (always), gateway usage manifest (always — it is a rolling 90-day counter), 12 consumer client repos (~8 differ at weekly cadence, ~12 at monthly; per-commit file churn is small — published data has a median of 1 file changed per commit and 2 per merged commit), 4 policy docs (~0.2). Weekly: (2+1+8+0.2)/19 = 59%. Monthly: (2+1+12+0.3)/19 = 80%. Floor: (2+1+2)/19 = 26%. ESTIMATED, not sourced: the consumer-side numbers — 12 consumers, 3-of-12 endpoint attach rate, 4 call sites per consumer per endpoint. Gateway usage exports are not public and I could not find published distributions; these come from the shape of typical partner-API programs and should be treated as the weakest part of this spec.
change_rate.where_changes_land: Changes land at the ROOT and they land there on 100% of runs — which is the worst possible place for a naive content-addressed store. The three roots that gate everything (base spec, head spec, usage manifest) all differ every single run by construction. A whole-file content hash on the spec therefore yields a 0% hit rate, always. The reuse surface, if any exists, only appears BELOW the file: the spec must be shredded into per-operation and per-schema sub-artifacts, at which point 92-99.4% of those sub-artifacts are byte-identical across a release (median 5.8% of Stripe operations change, 0.6% of Twilio's). Two further hazards decide whether that surface survives. First, the transitive-$ref hazard: every Stripe operation directly references the `error` schema, whose closure pulls in a median of 865 of 1,440 schemas, so a sound transitive key marks 100% of operations dirty on every release; depth-1 gives 18.8% dirty and depth-2 gives 45.7%, but bounding the depth is unsound because a genuine break can hide inside a hub schema. Second, the usage manifest is a monotonic counter feeding 51 of the 79 model ops; unquantized it single-handedly forces a full recompute, and it must be bucketed (log-scale call counts, boolean field-touched flags) before it is admitted to any key. Leaf changes — policy docs, notification templates — are rare (~5% of runs) and only affect the 7 rollup ops and the single synthesis op, so they are cheap. And the decisive structural fact: the model fan-out in layer 3 is not over all 200 operations, it is over the 24 the deterministic differ already identified as changed. The workload arrives at the model pre-scoped to exactly the changed inputs, so by construction nearly every model-op key is new.

session_structure: A competent engineer gets a large amount out of provider prefix caching here, and the baseline must be specified at that level. (1) Layer 3's 24 calls are independent single-turn calls sharing a 5,200-token invariant head: the 2,500-token breaking-change rubric, the 1,200-token deprecation/versioning policy excerpt, and 1,500 tokens of few-shot examples. Put one cache_control breakpoint at the end of that head; the per-call tail is ~2,300 tokens of endpoint-specific material. Cost goes from 24 x 7,500 = 180k input tokens to 1 x (5,200 x 1.25) + 23 x (5,200 x 0.1) + 24 x 2,300 = ~74k effective — a 59% cut on the biggest layer, for free. (2) Do NOT fire the 24 calls concurrently from cold. Concurrent fan-out makes every caller miss and pay the 1.25x write, which erases the benefit; issue one warm-up call, await it, then fan out. (3) Go further by sorting the fan-out by resource family. For each of ~6 families, open one conversation whose cached prefix is rubric + policy + that family's base AND head schema block (~6-12k tokens), then take 3-5 turns, one per changed operation in the family. The family schema block is written once and read 2-4 times, and it removes the per-call schema tail entirely — the depth-1 schema material is a measured median 1,182 tokens per side, p90 3,492, so this is the single largest remaining win. (4) Reuse the SAME cached prefix across layers where the rubric overlaps: layer 6's prose-semantics rubric should be authored as an extension of layer 3's prefix rather than a separate one, so the 2,500-token head is written once for 44 calls instead of twice. (5) Layer 5's 27 calls share a 2,000-token rubric plus, per consumer, that consumer's contract tier and history — so group by consumer, not by endpoint, and the per-consumer block (~400 tokens) also caches across that consumer's 3 calls. (6) Order layer 8 so the 49k of upstream verdicts are appended in a stable canonical order; if the release-synthesis call is retried or re-run with a tweaked instruction, the whole 49k is a cache hit. (7) Keep the entire run inside one TTL window: the run is 79 model calls and completes in 5-20 minutes wall clock, comfortably inside the 1-hour tier (field measurement says the real cliff is 1h, not 5m), so a well-ordered run gets essentially full within-run prefix reuse without any custom infrastructure. Net effect of a properly tuned baseline: roughly 55-65% off the ~522k input tokens, achieved with cache_control breakpoints and call ordering alone. What this baseline provably CANNOT do is span runs — the release cadence is 7-30 days, which is 200-700x the maximum TTL. That single gap is the entire opportunity for a persistent store, and it should be measured as such rather than against an untuned straw man.
grader: A seeded mutation harness with generator-authored ground truth. No LLM, exact, free. CORPUS: 12 vendored (base, head) real spec pairs pinned by commit sha — 5 from stripe/openapi openapi/spec3.json (e.g. c36976f8->8820133a, 8820133a->03af4046, ... d5d11f66->af5309ca), 5 from twilio/twilio-oai, 2 from a mid-size third API; content is public and free to vendor. GENERATOR: `contractbench gen --pair P --seed N` produces head' from head by applying a deterministic mutation plan of exactly 100 edits: (a) 40 mechanical breaks sampled from oasdiff's ERR-level rule set — request-parameter-removed, response-required-property-removed, api-path-removed-without-deprecation, request-property-became-required, response-property-type-changed, request-parameter-enum-value-removed, api-operation-id-removed, request-body-media-type-removed, response-success-status-removed; (b) 25 additive non-breaking decoys — new optional request property, new response property, new endpoint, new response enum value; (c) 15 PROSE-ONLY breaks where the schema is untouched and only `description`/`default`/`example` text changes semantics: amount unit cents->major units, documented pagination cap 100->25, a documented idempotency or ordering guarantee deleted, "optional" -> "required unless X"; oasdiff scores exactly 0 on this class by construction, so a pure-tool baseline cannot saturate the grader; (d) 20 pure-cosmetic edits — whitespace, x- metadata, semantically-identical rewordings — which must NOT be reported. Alongside, a fixed `consumers.json` (12 consumers x per-endpoint, per-field 90-day access counts) and 12 deterministically generated client repositories containing exactly the call sites the manifest implies, so the set of consumers broken by any mutation is computed exactly by the generator, never inferred. GROUND TRUTH: the generator emits `truth.json`, an array of {path, method, json_pointer, rule_id, breaking: bool, consumer_ids: []}. AGENT CONTRACT: write `findings.json`, same shape minus rule_id (optional). SCORING (pure set arithmetic): a finding matches iff (path, method, RFC-6901-normalized json_pointer) is exactly equal and `breaking` agrees; consumer attribution scored as Jaccard of the two id sets; score = 0.45*recall(breaking) + 0.25*precision(breaking) + 0.20*mean Jaccard + 0.10*(1 - false-positive rate over the 20 cosmetic edits). HARD GATE, evaluated first: recall over the 40 mechanical breaks must equal 1.00 and zero cosmetic edits may be reported; failing either scores 0 outright, which mirrors the real product where a missed break ships a customer outage and a noisy report gets the check disabled. REUSE EVALUATION: run seed N to populate, then run `--carry --seed N --delta 0.06`, which re-mutates only 6% of operations, matching the measured median release churn. Report (score, billed input tokens, billed output tokens, cache-read tokens, wall clock) for three arms: cold, provider-prefix-cache-tuned (the session structure above), and reuse store. The reuse arm must reproduce the tuned arm's score to the digit — any score delta is a correctness regression, not a saving, and should be reported as a failure rather than netted against tokens. Reference points for calibration, both computable offline and free: oasdiff 1.29.1 alone achieves recall 1.00 on class (a), 0.00 on class (c), 0.00 on consumer attribution, and floods — on the real d5d11f66->af5309ca pair it emitted 54,396 findings that dedupe to 737 (rule, endpoint) pairs, so its uncontrolled precision term is near zero.
reuse_story: Four mechanisms, in descending order of how much I believe them. (1) CROSS-RUN SUB-ARTIFACT REUSE, but only for pipelines whose differ is line-based. Many real teams do not run oasdiff — they `git diff` the YAML and hand the hunks to a model. For those, a semantic reuse key over the normalized operation subtree kills the measured 50% of content-changed spec files that contain zero operation change, and the measured 33% of raw-changed operations that are docs-only. That is a real, large, measurable win — but note what it actually is: it is the deterministic differ, delivered as a cache key. (2) WITHIN-RELEASE REPETITION. The same spec pair is reviewed on the feature PR, on the release branch, and at tag time, plus CI reruns after flakes: 3-5 executions per genuine release over identical or near-identical inputs. Every one after the first is a near-total cache hit, and the gaps between them (hours to days) exceed the 1h provider TTL, so provider caching cannot serve them. This is the cleanest win in the domain and it is unglamorous. (3) LAYER 4 IS ALMOST FREE TO REUSE. 117 of the 211 operations are ripgrep queries against 12 consumer repos whose HEAD trees move slowly at the call-site level; keyed on (repo tree hash, query), most hit across runs. They cost no tokens, so this saves wall clock and CI minutes, not money. (4) CROSS-CUSTOMER, for the consumer-side buyer only. Every fintech consuming Stripe runs prose_semantics over the identical public (base, head) spec pair. Those 20 of 79 model ops are consumer-independent, so a store shared across users computes them once for everyone — a 25% cut on model ops, with an amplification factor equal to the number of customers tracking that vendor. This is the only mechanism in the domain with a genuine network effect. It requires a cross-user store and a byte-identical rubric, and it does not extend to layers 3, 5, or 7, all of which are contaminated by customer-private manifests and policies.
reuse_threats: (1) THE DIFFER ALREADY DID IT, and it is free. Layer 3 fans out over the 24 operations the deterministic diff identified as changed, not over all 200. The workload arrives at the model pre-scoped to exactly the dirty inputs, so by construction ~100% of layer 3, 5, and 6 keys are new every run. A Bazel-style store is largely redundant with a tool that is already in the pipeline, ships in CI, and costs nothing — the incremental-computation win has been claimed by oasdiff before any model call happens. This is the single strongest argument against the reuse layer in this domain and it should not be softened. (2) HUB-SCHEMA CLOSURE EXPLOSION, measured and severe. Every Stripe operation directly references `error`; the transitive closure of a median operation covers 865 of 1,440 schemas. Any key that resolves $refs transitively — which soundness requires — marks 100% of operations dirty on every release. Depth-1 pruning gives 18.8% dirty and depth-2 gives 45.7%, but both are unsound: a genuine response-property-type-changed can sit three hops down a shared envelope. The reuse layer must choose between correct and useful, and in a workload whose hard grader gate is zero missed breaks, it has to choose correct. (3) THE USAGE MANIFEST IS A COUNTER. A rolling 90-day gateway export feeds 51 of the 79 model ops and changes on every run without exception. Unquantized it forces a full recompute on its own. Quantizing it (log-bucket call counts, boolean field-touched flags) fixes the key but silently changes the semantics of "who is affected", which is exactly the dimension the grader scores by Jaccard. (4) THE TUNED BASELINE ALREADY TAKES 55-65%. Most of the token mass is shared rubric and policy across 79 calls, and cache_control breakpoints plus family-grouped ordering capture that for free. The store only gets the residual. (5) DETERMINISM OF UPSTREAM MODEL OUTPUTS. Layers 5, 7, and 8 key on layer 3's verdicts. At temperature > 0 the verdict text differs run to run and every descendant key busts; even at temperature 0, a model-id change invalidates the entire store, and model ids turn over faster (weeks to a few months) than the release cadence this store is meant to span. The store's useful lifetime may be shorter than its reuse horizon. (6) THE BUDGET IS SMALL. The whole run is ~522k input and ~52k output tokens, weekly-to-monthly. Even a 100% hit rate saves single-digit dollars per run per customer. The defensible pitch here is latency and CI determinism, not spend — and it should be priced that way rather than as savings.
confidence: Medium-high overall, unevenly distributed. HIGH on the change-rate numbers and the token sizes for spec material: I measured them directly on two real production spec repositories (11 Stripe release pairs, 11 Twilio release pairs), and computed the operation/schema token distributions from the actual JSON rather than estimating them. HIGH on the hub-closure finding (865 of 1,440 schemas in a median operation's closure; 100% of operations dirty at depth >= 3) — that is a measured property of the real artifact and it is the most consequential fact in this specification. HIGH on the claim that the merge gate contains no model calls today. MEDIUM on the graph widths in layers 3, 5, and 6 — the ratios are anchored in measurement (2:1 structural:docs-only, 8% mean operation churn), but I scaled them from a 589-operation Stripe spec to a 200-operation benchmark API, and I chose the release size at the measured MEAN rather than the median, which makes the graph roughly 3-10x wider than a typical release. A median release would give ~2-12 operations in layer 3 and a much less interesting benchmark; that choice is defensible but it is a choice. LOW on the entire consumer dimension — 12 consumers, 3-of-12 endpoint attach rate, 4 call sites per consumer-endpoint, 7-of-12 rollup attach rate. Gateway usage exports are not public and I found no published distributions; these numbers set the width of layer 5 (27 ops) and layer 7 (7 ops), i.e. 34 of 79 model ops, so they are load-bearing and unsourced. WHAT WOULD RAISE IT: (a) one real API-gateway usage export from a partner-API program, which would replace the whole estimated consumer dimension with measurement and is the highest-value single input; (b) instrumenting an actual production deployment of a tool like oasdiff Pro or Optic to count real LLM calls per release, which would confirm or refute my claim that layer 3 is 24 calls rather than one long-context call over the whole diff; (c) running the mutation harness described above against both baselines to get a measured rather than modelled figure for what the tuned provider cache captures — I computed 55-65% analytically from published cache pricing, not from receipts; (d) a churn measurement over 20+ pairs from 6+ APIs rather than 2, since Stripe's monolith and Twilio's 60-file modular bundle bracket the design space but do not sample it.

customer: Mid-size B2B SaaS product team (Grafana / Element / Signal shape) shipping web + mobile localized into ~30 locales from a ~10,000-key English source catalog. They pay for two things today: (1) a TMS seat plus per-word MT/post-edit spend (Lokalise, Crowdin, Smartling, Phrase; ~$0.02-0.12/word human post-edit, near-zero raw MT), and (2) engineering time on the CI job that extracts strings, calls the model, lints output, and opens the PR. The billing unit is the NET NEW WORD — words translation memory could not fill. That is the crucial commercial fact: this customer already buys a reuse layer, and it is priced explicitly as the thing that stops them paying.
