Measured catalog properties (grafana/grafana public/locales/en-US/grafana.json @ origin/main, 11,110 keys): mean 27.7 chars/string, median 16, p90 62, ~77k tokens total; 6.6% of values carry a placeholder, 1.8% inline markup, 2.5% of keys are plural variants; 42.1% of values are exact duplicates of another value in the same file. signalapp/Signal-Desktop (2,914 keys) is the same shape: 12.3% placeholders, 3.6% ICU plural, 26.7% duplicate values, developer descriptions on 98.7% of keys (mean 71 chars).
why_repeated: Strings change continuously because product changes continuously. Every merge to main can add, edit, or delete UI copy, and each change must propagate to 30 locales before the next release ships or the feature launches English-only in 29 markets. The run is not "translate the catalog" once — it is a standing CI job reconciling 30 target catalogs against a moving English source, forever. Separately, four events force a FULL re-pass over all 10,000 keys: adding a locale, a termbase/style-guide revision (marketing renames a feature; legal changes how a term must render in de-DE), a model or prompt-template upgrade, and a periodic consistency re-baseline. Those full passes are 50-100x the incremental run and are the only shape with real money on the table.
run_cadence: Two cadences, both real. (1) Incremental: fires per merge to main, executed as a nightly batch in most shops — measured daily churn median 0.08% of keys (~9 keys); per-release/weekly reconciliation at median 0.2-1.0% (~20-110 keys). (2) Full-catalog pass over all 30 locales: on new-locale onboarding, glossary revision, or model upgrade — roughly 4-12 times a year. The graph below specifies the FULL pass, because it is the only shape with enough operations to measure reuse against, and the incremental run is a strict subgraph of it (~293 ops, ~170 of them model calls). A harness should seed with one full pass, then measure N consecutive incremental runs against it.

graph.description: Wide, shallow, locale-major layered DAG. Config: 10,000-key English source catalog, 30 target locales, batch size 25 segments per model call, 400 batches per locale. Structurally it is 30 near-independent per-locale pipelines with ZERO cross-locale edges, each being 400 independent translate->lint->repair chains, converging only at a per-locale assemble step and then one PR op. Depth-9 path: extract -> diff -> tm_lookup -> glossary_match -> translate -> lint -> repair -> assemble -> PR. Fan-out is enormous (12,000 mutually independent translate calls); fan-in is trivial except at assemble (613-1,013 upstream ops per locale). The only edges into a translate op are its two per-locale prep ops: translate batch k does NOT consume batch k-1, and locale A never consumes locale B. That independence is what makes this a good reuse candidate in principle. Total edges 76,801. Lint is modelled per-batch rather than per-locale deliberately: a per-locale lint has fan-in 400 and is invalidated by any single batch change, so per-batch is both more faithful to how these pipelines run and more reusable. Incremental subgraph (weekly, 110 touched keys, ~30% absorbed by exact TM match): 123 tool ops + ~170 model ops.

layers.name: extract_source_catalog
layers.consumes: nothing - graph root
layers.reads_artifacts: the application source tree (~4,000 files); runs i18next-parser / formatjs extract / xgettext and emits en.json

layers.name: diff_and_segment
layers.consumes: extract_source_catalog (1 op)
layers.reads_artifacts: previous run's en.json (1 artifact)

layers.name: tm_lookup
layers.consumes: diff_and_segment (1 op) - 1 upstream op per tm_lookup op
layers.reads_artifacts: that locale's existing translation file + the shared TM database (30 artifacts). Splits changed segments into exact-100%-match (auto-filled, no model call), fuzzy 75-99% (model call with the fuzzy hit as a hint), and new.

layers.name: glossary_term_match
layers.consumes: tm_lookup (1 op, same locale)
layers.reads_artifacts: that locale's termbase (~300 terms) plus the CLDR cardinal plural-rule table (31 artifacts). Aho-Corasick over the termbase producing a per-key matched-term map, so only relevant terms get injected into each prompt.

layers.name: translate_batch
layers.consumes: tm_lookup (1) + glossary_term_match (1) = 2 upstream ops each. 400 batches x 30 locales; batch k is independent of batch k-1.
layers.reads_artifacts: none directly - all artifact content arrives via layers 3-4. Input = 1,800-token frozen global prefix + 3,200-token frozen per-locale prefix (termbase + style guide + required CLDR plural categories) + 1,750 tokens of varying batch payload (25 segments x ~64 tok: key path 12, source text 10, developer description 20, constraints 10, fuzzy-TM hint 12).

layers.name: qa_lint
layers.consumes: translate_batch (1 op each)
layers.reads_artifacts: CLDR plural-rules table (1 artifact). Deterministic: ICU parse, placeholder multiset, plural-category completeness, markup tag multiset, do-not-translate verbatim, length cap, key-set identity.

layers.name: repair_batch
layers.consumes: qa_lint (1) + translate_batch (1) = 2 upstream ops each. Fires only for batches containing >=1 lint failure: at a 3% per-segment failure rate and 25 segments/batch, P(batch has a failure) = 1-0.97^25 = 53%, so 12,000 x 0.53 = 6,360 ops.
layers.reads_artifacts: none - reuses the same frozen prefix as translate_batch plus the failing segment, its lint error, and the rejected output

layers.name: llm_review
layers.consumes: repair_batch or translate_batch (1) + glossary_term_match (1) = 2 upstream ops each. Applied only to the 8 tier-1 revenue locales x 400 batches; the other 22 locales ship raw MT.
layers.reads_artifacts: that locale's style guide (8 artifacts). Input = 1,200-token review system block + 3,200-token locale block + ~2,600 tokens of source/translation pairs.

layers.name: assemble_locale_file
layers.consumes: tm_lookup (1) + all 400 qa_lint of that locale + its ~212 repair_batch + 400 llm_review for the 8 tier-1 locales. Fan-in 613 (non-review locales) to 1,013 (review locales).
layers.reads_artifacts: the previous locale JSON (30 artifacts). Merges TM auto-fills with model output, sorted-key serialize.

layers.name: open_pull_request
layers.consumes: assemble_locale_file (30 ops)
layers.reads_artifacts: none - writes 30 locale JSONs and opens the PR

change_rate.pct_inputs_changed_range: 0.0-4.6% of source-catalog keys per release; median 0.18-0.28% and p90 0.84-1.65% on mature catalogs; median 1.02% (p90 2.84%) per 7 days on an actively-expanding catalog; median 3.59% (p90 6.70%) per 30 days; daily median 0.00-0.08%.
change_rate.basis: SOURCED - measured directly, not estimated. I cloned three open-source products with long-lived single-file English source catalogs and diffed key sets AND values across consecutive release tags and time-windowed snapshots of the main branch. (a) signalapp/Signal-Desktop _locales/en/messages.json, 2,919 keys, 44 consecutive tag pairs v7.76.0..v8.23.0: touched (added+value-changed) median 0.28%, mean 0.59%, p90 1.65%, max 4.61%; 7-day windows N=29 median 0.33%, p90 1.43%; 1-day windows N=39 median 0.00%, mean 0.04%. (b) element-hq/element-web apps/web/src/i18n/strings/en_EN.json, 3,476 keys, 44 tag pairs v1.11.94..v1.12.25: median 0.18%, mean 0.33%, p90 0.84%, max 2.01%; 7-day windows N=23 median 0.06%, p90 0.54%. (c) grafana/grafana public/locales/en-US/grafana.json, 10,990 keys, main branch Jan-Aug 2026: 7-day windows N=29 median 1.02%, mean 1.18%, p90 2.84%, max 3.68%; 30-day windows N=13 median 3.59%, p90 6.70%; 1-day windows N=39 median 0.08%, p90 0.95%. Grafana is the high end because it is still actively i18n-izing existing screens (net +2,500 keys/year); Signal and Element are the mature steady state, and they agree closely with each other. Corroborating industry figure (weaker, vendor-published): TM leverage reaches 60-70% by the third release cycle, implying 30-40% net-new WORDS per release - a per-word measure over a much coarser cadence, consistent with rather than contradicting the per-key numbers. NOTE the artifact-count metric is different and misleading here: of the 93 input artifacts, en.json always differs (1) and all 30 prior-locale files always differ (they are last run's output), so naive artifact-level churn reads ~35% every single run. Ignore it. The load-bearing number is content churn inside the one artifact that fans out to 12,000 operations.
change_rate.where_changes_land: Overwhelmingly at LEAVES - that is the good news - and then batching destroys it, which is the bad news. Each string is an independent leaf feeding exactly one translate op; adds and value-edits touch individual keys scattered through the sorted catalog. But a translate op consumes 25 leaves, so one leaf change invalidates a 25-leaf operation. Arithmetic: 110 touched keys of 10,000 scattered over 400 batches of 25 invalidate 400*(1-(1-1/400)^110) = 96 batches = 24.1% of the translate layer, from 1.10% key churn. A 22x amplification. At batch=50 it is 42.4%; batch=10, 10.4%; batch=1, 1.1%. Batch size is the single dial deciding whether this workload has a reuse surface, and it points the opposite way from the provider-cache dial. Worse: a pipeline batching by POSITION in the sorted catalog rather than by content-addressed bucket sees one insertion near the top shift every downstream boundary - 100% invalidation from one added key. Common, easy bug. Separately there are three genuine ROOTS whose change invalidates everything below: the per-locale termbase (one added term -> all 400 batches for that locale, ~3,300 ops), the per-locale style guide (same blast radius), and model id / prompt template / decode params (all 21,560 model ops). Termbase edits are human-driven, unpredictable, and land monthly-to-quarterly per locale; when they land they are a total loss for that locale. Removals (measured 0-64 keys/release) are free - they invalidate nothing, they just drop leaves.

session_structure: Single-turn, stateless, locale-major, two-breakpoint. Strong baseline, specified as such. (1) NOT a conversation — each of the 12,000 translate calls is an independent messages.create. A design that keeps one conversation per locale and appends batches makes input cost quadratic in batch count; the correct design shares only a cached prefix. (2) Prefix block A, byte-identical across every call in the whole run and across all locales: task instructions, ICU/placeholder preservation rules, JSON output contract, few-shot examples. ~1,800 tokens, cache_control {type: ephemeral, ttl: "1h"}. (3) Prefix block B, frozen per locale for the run: that locale's full termbase (~300 terms) + style guide + formality/tone spec + the CLDR plural categories that locale requires. ~3,200 tokens, second breakpoint, also ttl "1h" — a full pass runs far longer than 5 minutes per locale so the 5m default would thrash. Cacheable prefix = 5,000 tokens, comfortably over every model minimum (512 on Opus 5, 1024 on Opus 4.8 / Sonnet 5); only 2 of the 4 allowed breakpoints used. (4) Only the 25 segments vary per call (~1,750 tokens). (5) Order calls locale-major — all 400 de batches, then all 400 fr — so block B is read 399 times per write. (6) Fan-out discipline: a cache entry only becomes readable once the first response BEGINS STREAMING, so N parallel identical-prefix requests all pay full price. Fire one call per locale, await first token, then fan out the remaining 399 concurrently. Optionally pre-warm block A once with max_tokens: 0. (7) Route the bulk translate layer through the Batch API for another 50% off — localization is not latency-sensitive and this is what real pipelines do. (8) Hygiene: sorted-key JSON everywhere, no run ID / timestamp / UUID in the prefix, tool list byte-stable, model pinned for the run. ECONOMICS: prefix effective multiplier = (2.0 + 0.1*399)/400 = 0.105x, i.e. 89.5% off the prefix, which is 74% of input tokens — so provider caching alone removes 66% of input cost. Per translate call at Opus 5 list: $0.0114 input + $0.0200 output = $0.0314; full pass 12,000 calls = $376 (plus ~$104 review, ~$32 repair), halved again by Batch API. THE STRUCTURAL GAP: output tokens are 64% of cost and provider prefix caching cannot touch them by construction. That is the only opening a reuse layer has — and it is a real one.
grader: Fully deterministic, no LLM, ground truth computed from a seeded generator plus CLDR — exact and free. SETUP: generate the source catalog from seeded templates so every constraint is known by construction — placeholder slots ({count}, {{name}}, %(user)s, %1$s), ICU plural blocks, inline markup (<b>, <a href=…>), injected do-not-translate brand tokens, and maxLength attributes on a seeded subset. Reproduce the measured distributions: 6.6-12.3% of keys carry a placeholder, 2.5-3.6% are plurals, 1.8-5.6% carry markup, 26-42% of values are exact duplicates of another key's value. GRADER INPUTS: (source catalog, locale id, produced locale JSON, previous run's locale JSON). CHECKS — a segment passes iff all hold. G1 key-set identity: output key set == input key set exactly. G2 placeholder multiset: multiset of placeholder tokens in the translation equals the source's exactly (order free). G3 ICU validity + plural completeness: translation parses under icu-messageformat-parser for the target locale, and for every plural argument the categories present equal EXACTLY the CLDR pluralRules-type-cardinal set for that locale (ru={one,few,many,other}, ar={zero,one,two,few,many,other}, pl={one,few,many,other}, ja/zh/ko/vi={other}); missing or spurious categories fail. This is the #1 real LLM localization defect and is exactly checkable from a data file. G4 markup: tags parse, tag-name multiset matches source. G5 DNT verbatim: every seeded brand token in the source appears byte-identically in the translation. G6 length: len(translation) <= maxLength where seeded. G7 duplicate consistency: any two keys whose stripped source strings are byte-identical must have byte-identical translations within a locale. G9 anti-passthrough: for non-Latin-script locales every segment whose source contains a letter must contain >=1 char in the target script's Unicode block; for Latin-script locales the translation must differ from source on the seeded-translatable subset — this defeats the degenerate "echo the English" strategy that would otherwise ace G1-G7. SCORE: quality = fraction of (locale, segment) pairs passing all of G1-G7 and G9, reported per locale and overall. SEPARATE METRIC G8 (drift): for every key whose source string, glossary slice, and style guide are unchanged between run k and run k+1, the translation must be byte-identical to run k's; drift = fraction of unchanged segments whose translation changed. G8 is the reuse-correctness metric — a reuse layer scores drift=0 trivially, a freshly sampled call scores drift near 1, and the experiment is whether serving from the store leaves quality flat while driving drift to zero. HONEST LIMITATION, stated not hidden: this does NOT measure semantic translation accuracy — that needs a reference corpus or an LLM judge, and I redesigned the task away from it deliberately. What it does measure is constraint satisfaction and consistency, which is exactly what breaks in production LLM localization and exactly what a reuse layer could plausibly change.
reuse_story: The translate op is one of the cleanest pure functions in any agent workload. Its result is fully determined by (source segment text, key path, developer description, length/plural constraints, locale, matched glossary slice, style guide, model id, decode params) — no hidden state, no clock, no filesystem, no ordering dependency. The reuse key is therefore exactly right and composes transitively with no fudging. Three concrete payoffs. (1) It serves OUTPUT tokens, 64% of per-call cost, which provider prefix caching structurally cannot reach — the one place the reuse layer is not competing with a free mechanism. (2) The domain has extraordinary string overlap: 42.1% of Grafana's 11,110 values and 26.7% of Signal's 2,914 are exact duplicates of another value in the same catalog, so even a single cold pass has a ~30-40% internal hit rate before any cross-run history exists; and UI microcopy ("Cancel", "Settings", "Loading…", "Are you sure?") is near-universal across products, so cross-tenant hit rates on the short-string head would be very high. (3) It caches the whole graph, not just the leaf — lint, repair, and per-locale assemble results all key cleanly, whereas translation memory caches only the translation. And the pure-function property drives the drift metric (G8) to zero for free, which is a genuine quality improvement customers already pay TMS vendors to approximate.
reuse_threats: Seven, and the first is close to disqualifying. (1) TRANSLATION MEMORY IS ALREADY THIS SYSTEM, AND IT IS FREE. Every TMS the customer already pays for stores (source-string-hash, locale) -> translation and auto-fills 100% matches with zero model calls. It is content-addressed, cross-run, cross-day, cross-project, and thirty years old. A reuse layer here is not competing against zero; it is competing against a mature incumbent that already captures the leaf-level win. Its genuine incremental value is narrow but real: TM keys on the source segment ALONE, so it happily serves a stale hit when the glossary, key path, or length constraint changed — the composed reuse key would not. Quantifying that delta is the actual experiment, and it is a far smaller number than "97% of segments repeat". (2) BATCHING AMPLIFIES CHURN ~22x. 1.10% key churn -> 24.1% of translate ops invalidated at batch=25, 42.4% at batch=50. Shrinking to batch=1 recovers 98.9% operation-level reuse but forces a 5,000-token prefix per 64-token segment and 10,000 calls per locale instead of 400, destroying exactly the prefix-cache amortization the tuned baseline depends on. The two mechanisms are in direct mechanical tension; a benchmark that does not sweep batch size is measuring an arbitrary point. (3) ROOT CHANGES ARE TOTAL LOSSES. One added termbase entry for de-DE invalidates all ~3,300 de-DE ops; a model version bump invalidates all 21,560. (4) THE REPAIR LAYER BARELY REUSES. 6,360 of 21,560 model ops are repairs keyed on a specific bad output; those keys almost never recur. (5) CROSS-TENANT REUSE IS A CONFIDENTIALITY PROBLEM. Source strings are unreleased product copy — sharing a translation across customers leaks that customer A has a string containing an unannounced feature name. Most enterprise contracts will forbid it, killing the highest-value sharing (the near-universal microcopy head) and leaving only within-tenant reuse, which is what TM already does. (6) STEADY-STATE VOLUME IS TINY. The real production incremental run is ~170 model calls costing single-digit dollars. There is almost nothing to save. The money is entirely in the full pass — which by definition has no prior run to reuse from, except across tenants, see (5). (7) NONDETERMINISM CUTS BOTH WAYS. At any sampling temperature the translate op is not reproducible, so the incumbent baseline already tolerates drift; serving from the store removes it. Defensible as a quality win, but it means the reuse layer changes behavior, not just cost, and any A/B must hold G1-G7 and G9 flat to claim it.
confidence: Medium-high overall, with components at very different levels. HIGH on the change rate: directly measured, not estimated — 88 consecutive release-pair diffs plus 133 time-windowed snapshots across three real production catalogs (Signal-Desktop, element-web, Grafana), and the two mature catalogs agree closely with each other (median 0.28% vs 0.18% per release) while Grafana's higher figure is explained by an ongoing i18n-coverage push. HIGH on catalog properties: placeholder rates, plural rates, duplicate-value rates and length distributions computed directly from the shipped files. HIGH on the batch-amplification arithmetic and cache economics — both closed-form given the stated parameters. MEDIUM on pipeline layer structure and on batch size = 25: from common practice and vendor documentation, not from instrumenting a real pipeline — and batch size is the parameter the entire reuse conclusion hinges on. MEDIUM on locale count (30 is a defensible midpoint: Grafana ships ~12, Element ~70, Signal 100+), on the 3% first-pass lint failure rate, on the presence and scope of the LLM review layer, and on termbase edit frequency. LOW-MEDIUM on cross-tenant string overlap, where I have within-catalog duplicate rates (measured) but only intuition across catalogs. WHAT WOULD RAISE IT: (a) pull job logs from a real Lokalise/Crowdin/Phrase account — their APIs expose per-job segment counts, batch sizes and TM leverage percentages, which would replace three medium-confidence guesses with measurements and would directly quantify how much of the reuse surface TM already owns; (b) instrument one real in-house pipeline for a quarter for actual glossary-edit frequency and lint failure rate; (c) compute cross-catalog string overlap by intersecting the three catalogs already on disk plus a dozen more — a couple of hours of work, and it would settle the cross-tenant question, the largest single swing factor in the reuse case.
